events.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ reaches $3.79 billion in sales in one day
events.summary: People walk past a large banner promoting "Grand Theft Auto VI." LaMaxitie/Nexpher Images via Getty Images Take-Two said "Grand Theft Auto 6" generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales. It took "Grand Theft Auto 5" three days to reach $1 billion in sales when it came out in 2013. Hype around the new game's debut was exceptional, and many workers said they were taking PTO to play it. For "Grand Theft Auto 6" to become the fastest-selling entertainment property — video game or movie — of all time, publisher Take-Two Interactive Software only had to beat itself. Mission accomplished, and by a landslide. Take-Two said on Friday that the latest installment in the crime-drama series generated $3.79 billion in worldwide sales in its first day. The last game in the series, "GTA 5," rang up $1 billion in worldwide sales within three days of its 2013 release, making it the fastest-selling entertainment property at the time, per Guinness World Records. It beat Activision Blizzard's "Call of Duty: Black Ops II," which reached the milestone in 15 days in 2012, and Hollywood's then-fastest-grossing film, "The Avengers," which did so at the worldwide box office in 10 days. Now, "GTA 6," made by Take-Two's Rockstar Games studio, owns the top spot. Its predecessor had held onto the video game record all this time, while the previous movie benchmark, the 2019 Marvel release "Avengers: Endgame," reached $1 billion at the worldwide box office in five days, according to Guinness World Records. "It's a cultural event," said former longtime game-industry analyst Michael Pachter of the launch of "GTA 6" on November 19. "People are going to remember this day." The higher price tag for "GTA 6" versus its predecessor likely helped. The new standard edition costs $80, while a $100 Ultimate Edition includes premium vehicles, weapons, apparel, and other in-game content tied to the story. When "GTA 5" debuted, the standard edition retailed for $60, and a special version for $80. 'GTA 6' frenzy Early forecasts had pointed to a blockbuster launch for the new game, so the milestone isn't all that surprising. Analytics firm Newzoo estimated in July that "GTA 6" was on pace for $3.3 billion to $5.2 billion in worldwide sales by the end of its launch week, while Benchmark analyst Mike Hickey noted in August that Take-Two's fiscal 2027 guidance embedded roughly 30 million unit sales. Take-Two's fiscal year ends March 31, 2027. Hype surrounding the game's debut was exceptional. Workforce management tech company UKG said time-off requests for the day "GTA 6" debuted were about 20% higher than it has seen in comparable pre-Thanksgiving weeks. Some employers leaned into the frenzy. The CEO of UK-based Raptor PR gave the agency's nine employees an extra day of annual leave for the release and bought each a copy of the game. Logitech, meanwhile, offered its more than 7,000 employees an extra paid day off to play any game they choose through a new "Logi Game Day" benefit. In addition to "GTA 6," two other nostalgia-filled games debuted this month: Activision Blizzard's "World of Warcraft: Forever" and Nintendo's "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" remake. Beyond the initial rush, "GTA 6" has more sales drivers ahead. A PC version expected next year could bring another wave of buyers, while price cuts and downloadable add-on content could also keep money flowing to Take-Two. "I think people are still pricing the stock like it's a one-hit wonder," said Pachter, now managing director of strategic planning at financial-services firm Wedbush Securities. "It's not." events.title: Nepali cricket fans in Qatar want to see their team competing with the best
events.summary: As thousands from Qatar’s Nepali community watch their team play, they hope for the team to rise in global rankings. Nepal cricket fans celebrate their team’s global rise Doha, Qatar – On a warm Friday afternoon in Qatar, the country’s only international cricket stadium was a sea of Nepal’s uniquely triangular crimson and deep blue flags. Nepal’s supporters arrived with flags draped across their shoulders, held them aloft to flutter in the breeze, cheering every delivery and waving them wildly in celebration of every wicket. The events on the field seemed nearly inconsequential against the loud cheers of the thousands of fans who had filled the West End International Cricket Stadium on the outskirts of the Qatari capital, as the nation with the world’s highest mountain faced the most powerful force in cricket. Nepal were bowling first against India A – India’s second XI – in their first group match of the Asian Cricket Council’s (ACC) Rising Star Asia Cup 2026 in Qatar. Indian captain Tilak Varma and his batting partner Kumar Kushagra kept finding boundaries. Nepal’s bowlers faced the wrath and their fielders could barely keep up. But the noise in the stands barely subsided. The supporters followed every ball closely, their attention firmly focused on the team they rarely get to watch up close, especially living thousands of kilometres from home. Qatar is home to at least 367,000 Nepalis, according to the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Qatar, making them the Gulf country’s third-biggest diaspora community. Pradeep Kumar Yadav was one of the few thousand Nepali fans who were on a mission to provide vociferous support to their cricket team this weekend. Yadav arrived at the stadium with seven Nepali friends, who had been planning to come as soon as the tournament’s fixtures were announced. “This is our first time watching Nepal play outside our country,” Yadav told Al Jazeera. For Nepal’s sizeable diaspora in Qatar, the cricket team provides a reason to gather around a national passion and often draws large crowds. The supporters are happy to travel to stadiums to back a team that has risen through the international ranks over the past decade. Nepal’s modern cricketing journey can be traced back to 1996, when the country became a member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) and the men’s team first competed in an international tournament. The turning point came when the South Asian nation qualified for its first ICC event at the T20 World Cup 2014. Soon, Nepal’s players were being noticed on the international stage and leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane’s selection in major T20 leagues around the world raised the country’s cricketing profile. Back home, cricket has spread far beyond the capital Kathmandu into towns and villages, backed by efforts to build the sport’s structure at grassroots level. For Qatar-based fan Himmat Joshi, the Nepali cricket team’s success has resulted in a sharp rise in the popularity of the sport. “I feel a lot of happiness,” Joshi said while watching the team play against India. “In the past, fewer people followed it but it has grown over the years,” he said. Mohammad Zahoor, who was among the thousands in the stands, sees the national team’s progress as a source of pride. He describes the Nepalis as a hardworking nation and says the country is building a domestic cricket system capable of competing with higher-ranked international teams. “There is a lot of pride in seeing Nepali cricketers represent the country. We are a passionate people,” Zahoor said. The ambitions extend beyond the T20 format. Nepal’s supporters want to see the country compete against established cricketing nations and eventually earn a place among the teams playing Test cricket. For Zahoor, defeating a Test-playing country would be an important step towards that ambition. He also hopes cricket will become part of Nepal’s international identity, alongside its reputation for mountaineering, the Himalayas and being home to Mount Everest. “Nepalis play the game like a festival,” Zahoor explained. “Our expectations and hopes are that one day Nepali people are known for their cricket as they are known for their culture of mountaineering and Mount Everest.” At the stadium in Qatar, the flags, chants and sheer number of supporters reflected that ambition. In the end, India broke their hearts with a crushing 306-run win. But it mattered little to the thousands cheering on their team, despite the loss. For some, including Yadav and his friends, it offered a unique opportunity to watch Nepal play abroad. Others were simply happy to get a chance to follow a team that has given the country, and its passionate supporters, a growing presence in international cricket.

events.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
events.summary: Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold? Published 20 November 2026, 14:36 GMT Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens. The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets through Friday, with the S&P 500 down about 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% by mid-afternoon. Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 4% by afternoon trading as shares in major tech companies continued to fall. The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when. Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50. The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading. The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17. Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers. Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading. Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time. But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world. Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market. While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth. "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said. "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability." Nvidia shares had plunged by more than 11% by the afternoon, while Musk's firms SpaceX and Tesla had both fallen by more than 6%. Meta was down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 3.5%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls. Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit. Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower. Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses. Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990. events.title: Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off
events.summary: Prediction market traders see a weakening outlook for the stock market, as the artificial intelligence sell-off continues to send major indexes lower Friday. Traders on the platform Kalshi now think there's just a 6% chance that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. Odds were once as high as 70% that it would happen this year. As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year. On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%. Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too. The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%. The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year. "The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said. The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting. In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week." Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: Palestinian anti-Hamas groups accused of role in Israel Gaza operation
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Israeli-backed Palestinian militias accused of expanding operations, raising concerns over their role in Gaza’s future security arrangements. Nuseirat refugee camp, Gaza Strip – It was late on Tuesday evening when a group of armed men stopped outside a house sheltering displaced Palestinian women on ad-Dawa Street, on the northern edge of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza. The streets were gradually emptying, and drones could be heard overhead. The men wore no military uniforms or insignia. They were Palestinians in civilian clothes carrying light weapons, believed to be members of Israeli-backed local militias, locals said. list 1 of 3 Families flee Gaza’s Bureij camp as Israel launches new offensive list 2 of 3 Gaza Civil Defence struggles to rescue lives as vehicles break down list 3 of 3 Save the Children: Gaza’s children face ‘unmatched dangers’ The gunmen surrounded the house and forced the women into the street and questioned them by torchlight about a man they were looking for. They threatened those who refused to answer and fired into the air before withdrawing minutes later without detaining anyone. Hours later, on Wednesday, the Israeli military launched a ground operation near the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps, west of the so-called “Yellow Line” that demarcates areas under Israeli military control following the October 2025 ceasefire. The military closed Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare. About 6,000 Palestinians fled, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that posed a threat to its troops. On Thursday, the military said that the operation had been completed. At least one Palestinian was killed in Israeli attacks near where the incursion took place. The sequence of events raises questions about the extent of coordination between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups, whose activities have expanded across Gaza in recent weeks. A Palestinian security source in Gaza told Al Jazeera that security authorities had documented the local armed groups’ participation in this week’s Israeli military operation in central Gaza. Their activities included “terrorising civilians and pressuring families to evacuate homes and shelters”, the source said. Speaking on condition of anonymity, the source said the groups benefitted from Israeli military fire cover and the closure of Salah al-Din Street, which also impeded humanitarian operations. The source described them as “gangs”, financed and armed by Israel to undermine Palestinian internal cohesion by “engineering chaos”. Israel has publicly acknowledged supporting armed groups opposed to Hamas in Gaza, as it fought its genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave, killing more than 74,000 people. “What’s wrong with that?” asked Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last year, claiming that the policy had saved the lives of Israeli soldiers. Expanding military and intelligence roles Palestinian political analyst Iyad al-Qarra told Al Jazeera that Israel had expanded the armed groups’ reach from Rafah and Khan Younis in the south to central Gaza and Gaza City. He accused the groups of carrying out kidnappings and attempted assassinations targeting Palestinians, including members of Palestinian factions, in which they benefitted from Israeli aerial protection and fire cover. Al-Qarra linked their expanding activities to Israel’s demolition of buildings and forced displacement of Palestinians, which have enabled the groups to operate in areas that Israeli forces would otherwise struggle to access. He said the Israeli military uses the fighters in front-line operations before committing its own troops. The groups also gather intelligence through local social and family networks while receiving information from the Israeli military, al-Qarra said. Who are the Israeli-backed anti-Hamas groups? The groups emerged during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, with some accused of looting aid supplies before taking on broader roles through Israeli funding, weapons and coordination with the military and intelligence services. Published estimates point to about five main groups with several hundred members in total. In April, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) monitor reported that Israel had increased its support for them, including deploying attack drones during their clashes with Hamas. The groups include the Popular Forces in Rafah, led by Ghassan al-Duhaini, since founder Yasser Abu Shabab was killed in December 2025; Hussam al-Astal’s group east of Khan Younis; and Shawqi Abu Nuseira’s group in central Gaza. Two others, led by Rami Helles and Ashraf al-Mansi, operate in eastern Gaza City and northern Gaza, respectively. Palestinian political analyst Wesam Afifa told Al Jazeera that Israel seeks to establish local security influence that it could retain even after a partial military withdrawal.

events.title: Nvidia stock plunges 12%, rides longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
events.summary: Nvidia shares fell 12% on Friday and headed for their seventh straight weekly drop. The stock is down 44% over the period, shedding $2.5 trillion in market cap. Once the most valuable company, Nvidia is now fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Google. The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis. Nvidia shares fell 12% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock is poised to close lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008. On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further. Once the most valuable company, now, at a market cap of $3.1 trillion, Nvidia is fourth behind Apple and Microsoft and Alphabet . Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD. Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere. On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December. For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT. Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression. WATCH: Walter Isaacson on Nvidia export control scrutiny

events.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
events.summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The UK-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion. Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California. Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations. Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy. Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviating concerns about AI’s energy consumption. Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI. “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
events.summary: Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members. While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy. But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf. According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED. After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.” “It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said. In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified. Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia. For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis. Already the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel Tim Teter has also been called to Washington, DC to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls. Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board. In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18 , board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.” Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk , have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “ honored ” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US President Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.” The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return. Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him.

events.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
events.summary: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so. "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time. Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction. Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear. "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said. Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI. Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT. As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre. Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November. "You ought to take advantage of the the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said. "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets." Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far. Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out. In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres. Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen". Google has been contacted for comment. events.title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
events.summary: Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. An Indian national has been sentenced to more ⁠⁠than 19-and-a-half years in prison in the United States in a murder-for-hire plot targeting a prominent Sikh separatist leader living in New York City. Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to three conspiracy charges for plotting to hire a hitman to assassinate Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen, lawyer and vocal advocate for a sovereign Sikh state. list 1 of 3 Sikh assassinations: Are the US and Canada raising the heat on India? list 2 of 3 Canada accuses India’s Amit Shah over campaign targeting Sikh separatists list 3 of 3 Canada moves to rebuild trade ties with India after years of tension US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a federal court in Manhattan on Friday. Gupta faces deportation to India after completing his prison term. Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader ‌‌Mahatma Gandhi. “I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” he said. Prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with an Indian government official to kill Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer for the US-based separatist group Sikhs for Justice, in New York. Pannun is also a proponent of independence for Punjab, the northern Indian state where Sikhism was founded. Court documents showed that Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in ⁠⁠cash delivered to someone who could kill Pannun. But the person turned out to be an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman. Gupta was arrested in Prague and has been held without bail since his extradition to the US in June 2023. A plea agreement called for him to serve at least two decades in prison. Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defence lawyer. India’s government has denied any involvement in the plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy. However, multiple alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists have been uncovered in the US and Canada, testing relations with India. New Delhi denies involvement in the plots. Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years ⁠⁠in prison for Gupta. “This case cuts to the very core of ⁠⁠American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.” Pannun was in court on Friday to see the sentence handed down. He described Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement. Pannun said the Modi government wanted him dead “because I lead the campaign openly, defy threats and intimidation”. Pannun also told the court he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty. “Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

events.title: Anthropic mathematician says he used AI to solve the Riemann hypothesis
events.summary: Math's "white whale" may have just been cracked with the help of Anthropic's Claude. J Studios/Getty Images A mathematician said on Friday that he cracked one of the biggest problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said he used Claude to solve it. Mathematicians told Business Insider the result hasn't been fully verified yet. One of the biggest open problems in all of mathematics may have just been cracked by a mathematician using AI. Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said on Friday that he solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which involves prime numbers, using Claude. "I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe," Alpöge said in a post on his website. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Though Alpöge's solution has yet to be formally verified, leading scholars in the field told Business Insider on Friday that should it stand, this would be the biggest breakthrough in math yet. "If it holds up, it's an extremely big deal," said Steven Strogatz , a math professor at Cornell. "This is the Moby Dick of Mathematics, the great white whale." Sergei Gukov , a math professor at Caltech, called the claim a "HUGE deal." "This is not a small potato," he said. "RH was the biggest problem in math." Strogatz said Alpöge's solution has been verified by a computer-based system, but added that it sometimes makes mistakes . "So it's fair to say that the claimed proof has not yet been independently verified," he said. The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed 167 years ago by a German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers. The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician a $1 million prize. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category. Alpöge's solution is, by his own admission, incredibly long and complicated. The solution's written proof comprises more than 250,000 pages, Alpöge said. Terence Tao, a leading scholar based at UCLA, said in a post on his website Friday that "digesting" the proposed solution "will take some time." Alpöge, who joined Anthropic in 2024, said he actually solved the problem on Sunday, but decided to hold off on announcing it after speaking with CEO Dario Amodei and consulting with other mathematicians. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, went public on the stock market on Thursday. As of Friday afternoon, the price of Anthropic shares has steadily declined. Alpöge said he didn't want to release "slop" to the public, adding that he still doesn't fully understand the math involved. Still, he said that as other mathematicians attempt to grapple with the results, Alpöge said he plans to be there every step of the way to help them. "I intend to do my best to understand and impart understanding of this argument," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Melania Trump says public displays of affection with Donald Trump are 'not my style' in new Amazon docuseries
events.summary: First lady Melania Trump spoke about her relationship with President Donald Trump in her new Amazon docuseries. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images "Melania: The Series," a companion to her documentary, premiered on Amazon Prime Video on Friday. Melania Trump spoke about her relationship with President Donald Trump. She said public displays of affection are "not my style," and she's not always a fan of his dancing. Toward the end of the second episode of "Melania: The Series," director Brett Ratner told first lady Melania Trump that one of his takeaways from filming her is the "beautiful relationship" that she shares with President Donald Trump. "Well, people, they don't see that because we are not so public outside," Melania Trump said in the two-part docuseries, which premiered on Amazon Prime Video on Friday. "We are not that way. It's not my style. You know, that's private." In "Melania: The Series" — for which Amazon paid $40 million for the licensing rights, alongside the " Melania" documentary released in January — the notoriously private first lady opens up about her nearly 22-year marriage to Donald Trump, including their public disagreements. Donald Trump and Melania Trump married in January 2005 at Bethesda-by-the-Sea Episcopal Church in Palm Beach, Florida. Their reception was held at Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate. Marc Beckman, senior advisor to Melania Trump and an executive producer of both the film and docuseries, told Business Insider that the series "goes deeper into her relationships with her husband, her son, and her father, so at a certain level, it's more personal." The Office of the First Lady declined to comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. PDA and public scrutiny The president and first lady's public displays of affection — or apparent lack thereof — have made headlines in the past. In her 2024 memoir, also titled "Melania," the first lady recalled a widely reported incident where she appeared to swat her husband's hand away on a 2017 trip to Israel, characterizing it as "a mere misunderstanding" caused by protocol when greeting foreign leaders. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport in 2017. JACK GUEZ/AFP via Getty Images In the docuseries, the first lady said that she doesn't dwell on the public scrutiny. "I don't need to answer to anybody," she said. "I don't need to explain anything to anybody. Whatever anybody thinks about me, let them think. I know who I am and that's all that matters." 'I let him be who he is' When asked about being married to Donald Trump for over 20 years, Melania Trump cited their support for each other despite their differences of opinion. "I think you need to let them be who they are, and you cannot change the person," she said in the docuseries aboard a presidential jet . "Sometimes, of course, you disagree with them, and that's normal. That's healthy for the relationship. That's nothing wrong. I let him be who he is, and he supports me and lets me be who I am." First lady Melania Trump is not always a fan of President Donald Trump's dance moves. Alex Brandon - Pool/Getty Images Melania Trump has occasionally publicly broken with her husband and the Republican Party on political issues. In her 2024 "Melania" memoir, she expressed support for abortion rights, writing that "A woman's fundamental right of individual liberty, to her own life, grants her the authority to terminate her pregnancy if she wishes." In the docuseries, Donald Trump said that he and his wife "don't have very many arguments," but that when she spoke about her stance on abortion, "people respected her views." Another issue the couple will continue to disagree on: Donald Trump's dance moves . "She feels very strongly that everything should be very presidential," Donald Trump said. "And when we were doing rallies, if, on occasion, I'd break into a dance, I'm not sure she loved it so much. But the people loved it." "Well, sometimes the situations were like, 'I don't think it's a good day to dance,'" Melania Trump said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A massive bearish trade just happened in the chip stocks
events.summary: The biggest options trade of the day was a bearish bet on the SMH. Traders are targeting an additional 8% decline. So much for buying the dip. As the S&P 500 entered correction territory and the Nasdaq-100 flirted with bear-market territory, down 19% from highs as of midday Friday, the single biggest options trade of the day was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) has a long way more to fall. Around 12:30 E.T., someone spent $93 million buying 20,000 380-strike puts expiring Sep. 17, 2027, according to trading data reviewed by SpotGamma and Volland, options-analytics platforms that both show the trade as a likely opening position, with volume exceeding existing open interest in the contract. The trade bets that the index will fall below $380, a nearly 8% decline from its current level. The SMH is off 40% from its recent all-time highs. "That trade stands out big-time," wrote Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner of Volland. "It is either a hedge or speculative, but either way it isn't a vote of confidence." The puts were bought for $46.50 a piece, an arguably expensive choice for a downside bet with volatility in the ETF trading at 70. "You're paying a metric ton of Vega for that thing," added SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, referring to the contract's sensitivity to changes in volatility of the underlying chip ETF. "Maybe they were a forced buyer, or maybe they're actually selling this, which can still be the case even though the price shows it happening closer to the ask." The semiconductor index headed for a 9% drop this week alone.

events.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis — and a human did, too
events.summary: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The Hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more. For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means. But that comment was followed by twenty readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source language that essentially helps verify mathematical proofs. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann Hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” In a brief introduction his proof, which he said is the result of twelve years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Trump floats major tax on U.S. companies constructing data centers overseas
events.summary: President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do. Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint , as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose. What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials. "They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he said of the data centers being built across the country. Trump also claimed data center expansion would help lower Americans' costs and taxes. He also encouraged Americans to negotiate deals with companies proposing data centers in their communities. "They have plenty of money," he said. "Take it." Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes. Trump did not specify whether he would seek congressional approval or use existing executive powers to penalize companies that attempt to build data centers globally. Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried : Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country. Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S. "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said Friday. Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence." events.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi, apparently contradicting Bessent
events.summary: President Donald Trump said Chinese leader Xi Jinping called Jensen Huang a "brilliant man" when they discussed the former Nvidia CEO. Earlier Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that Huang was not mentioned in the Trump administration's latest talks with China. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged. President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang this week, appearing to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent who earlier in the day said the ousted leader was not mentioned in the Trump administration's latest talks with China in Shenzhen. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference. Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in those talks, Bessent said "no," without elaborating. The Treasury Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the apparent discrepancy between Trump and Bessent. Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO. "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies." Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week. The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries. Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week. "We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said. "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China. The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors. Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO. Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race. Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI. They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI. In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed. Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview. On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.

events.title: Belgrade mayor charged with assaulting opposition politician in Serbia
events.summary: Prosecutors say Aleksandar Sapic caused serious facial injuries to a female councillor and seek a three-year sentence. The mayor of Serbia’s capital city, Belgrade, has been charged with injuring a female opposition politician during an argument they had in September. Serbian prosecutors charged Aleksandar Sapic, a senior figure in the right-wing nationalist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), on Friday. He is accused of grabbing Belgrade city councillor Tatjana Micic by the arm and punching her in the face. list 1 of 2 Germany thrash Netherlands to book Nations League quarterfinal spot list 2 of 2 Joy, anticipation as student movement enters Serbia’s new parliament Prosecutors said Micic suffered fractures to her nose and part of her upper jaw, and injuries to her right arm and neck, which the prosecutors said constituted grievous bodily harm. “Within less than two months of the incident, the Prosecutor’s Office examined witnesses, reviewed video surveillance footage, obtained medical records as well as the findings and opinion of a forensic expert, and filed an indictment proposal,” prosecutors said in a statement. “In protecting the physical integrity and safety of citizens, the Prosecutor’s Office applies the same criteria to every defendant, regardless of the position they hold,” it added. They are seeking a three-year sentence for Belgrade mayor Sapic, and are seeking to block him from approaching and communicating with councillor Micic. Sapic denied attacking Micic, but acknowledged an argument and a scuffle with her husband. Opposition parties have demanded Sapic resign from his role, but he has resisted their calls. Sapic’s SNS party, which had headed up the government since 2012, lost an election to a student-led opposition movement in October. The party, however, retains control of the capital, Belgrade.

But I'm telling them now they're here," Trump said. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures. CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one. If Trump follows through on his threat to clamp down on overseas data center construction, he will have to contend with the fact that numerous U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta and Oracle — have already built them in other countries. International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said. The remarks came a day after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit that appeared to produce few concrete deliverables on an array of pressing global issues. Xi "congratulated me on how well we're doing" in artificial intelligence, Trump said, using his preferred term "super intelligence," which he said the Chinese president also likes better. events.title: The ending of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' didn't quite match the book's epilogue. Here's what changed.
events.summary: Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is finally in theaters. The final scenes include appearances by Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence, and Josh Hutcherson. The scene is adapted from the novel's epilogue, but it left out some important details. There were many reasons to be excited for the premiere of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," and the star-studded cast was one of the biggest. The film, released on Friday, is an adaptation of Suzanne Collins' prequel to "The Hunger Games" trilogy about Haymitch Abernathy's experience in the 50th Hunger Games. It featured newcomers to the "The Hunger Games" universe, such as Joseph Zada as a younger Haymitch and Elle Fanning as young Effie Trinket. It also brought back three of the franchise's original stars for the end of the movie. Woody Harrelson reprised his performance as Haymitch in the film's final scene, alongside Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark. Fans were thrilled to see the trio reunite on screen, but their appearance differed slightly from the epilogue of the  "Sunrise on the Reaping" book . In particular, the scenes omitted some important details about Haymitch and Katniss' relationship . Spoilers ahead for "Sunrise on the Reaping." Haymitch and Katniss The brief epilogue in "Sunrise on the Reaping" ties together Haymitch's experience after the 50th Hunger Games and the life readers know he has in the postwar world of "Mockingjay," where he has returned to District 12 with Katniss and Peeta. "Haymitch drinks until the liquor runs out, and then raises geese until the next train arrives," Katniss says of her mentor in "Mockingjay." "Fortunately, the geese can take pretty good care of themselves." The "Sunrise on the Reaping" epilogue opens with Haymitch saying he still has visions of his love, Lenore Dove, over 25 years after her death. He then details how he came to know Katniss after pushing her father, Burdock Everdeen, away before she was born for his safety. (Burdock and Katniss are also revealed to be relatives of Lenore Dove and the Covey family earlier in the novel.) Woody Harrelson as Haymitch Abernathy and Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate Haymitch says he saw Burdock carrying Katniss around when she was a baby, and he later noticed her at the Hob when she came to trade "the odd squirrel or rabbit" after her father died. "Tough and smart, her hair in two braids then, reminding me for all the world of Louella McCoy, my sweetheart of old," Haymitch says of Katniss in the book. Louella was reaped into the Hunger Games with Haymitch, and he jokingly called her sweetheart because she had a crush on him briefly when she was young. Louella dies before the Games begin and is replaced by a body double, Lou Lou. Her loss profoundly impacts Haymitch, kickstarting his acts of rebellion against President Snow and the Capitol. In the "Sunrise on the Reaping" epilogue, Haymitch reveals he began calling Katniss sweetheart after they met because of her resemblance to Louella. "And after she volunteered for the Games, that nickname couldn't help but slip out," Haymitch says of Katniss. Haymitch does see a young Katniss in the final scenes of the movie, but only as a baby. Zada as Haymitch spots Burdock and her mother Asterid walking with an infant Katniss in the woods, before cutting to Woody Harrelson as Haymitch after the war. Because Haymitch doesn't see Katniss with two braids on screen, the tether between her and Louella in Haymitch's mind isn't clear. Die-hard "Hunger Games" fans probably still caught the connection, but more casual viewers may have missed it. The geese The movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping" also left out an important interaction between Haymitch and Katniss involving geese. In the epilogue, Haymitch tells Katniss and Peeta the truth about his experience in the Quarter Quell and the loss of his loved ones as they work on a memorial book about the war. After he shares his past with them, Katniss brings Haymitch goose eggs for him to raise. The gift harkens back to Lenore Dove, as a gaggle followed her around when she was alive, particularly when she sang. Lenore Dove raised geese in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate Katniss' offering highlights her deep understanding of Haymitch, a theme Collins played up in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Plutarch Heavensbee tells Haymitch the revolution needs "someone exactly like" him, only "luckier, or with better timing," to bring the Capitol down. Katniss is that person, the flame finally lit from the spark of rebellion Haymitch stoked. The goose eggs underscore their connection in the book, while the movie relies on Haymitch and Plutarch's conversation to show that Katniss was the luckier, better-timed version of Haymitch. At the end of the film, Lawrence as Katniss and Hutcherson as Peeta embrace Haymitch, again played by Harrelson, on his birthday, which always fell on Reaping Day. He overlooks a memorial listing the number of children who died in the Hunger Games, which seems to be a stand-in for the memorial book that Peeta and Katniss worked on in the novel. Haymitch then decides to visit the geese in the meadow on his own, sitting on the same log he and Lenore Dove did years ago. Haymitch doesn't make it clear that the geese belong to him or indicate that Katniss gave them to him, but Katniss and Peeta do thank Haymitch before he heads off to sit with the geese. The interaction is sweet — if a bit cheesy — but it didn't include the full scope of Katniss' care for Haymitch after the war. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Second judge blocks Trump's contested D.C. arch
events.summary: A second federal judge will block construction on President Trump 's embattled arch set to be erected near Arlington National Cemetery , multiple outlets reported Friday. Why it matters: It represents yet another barrier to the multi-year project to build a 250-foot arch that challengers said would obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema's preliminary injunction will indefinitely block the project, which she reportedly called a "rushed job" from the bench Friday. Zoom out: Brinkema's rebuke comes after D.C.-based District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday extended her separate order blocking construction on the arch for two weeks. Chutkan, who is overseeing consolidated challenges from military veterans and from the District of Columbia and Virginia, issued her initial temporary restraining order earlier this month. That order prohibited construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch, Axios D.C.'s Mimi Montgomery reported. What they're saying: "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The National Park Service did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. State of play: The legal hurdles came after the National Capital Planning Commission , which is stacked with Trump loyalists, gave its final approval for the project. Challengers, however, have argued the project requires congressional approval — and as Chutkan noted , "Congress has not enacted any statute authorizing construction of the Arch." Between the lines: The arch is one prime example of the president's quest to remake the nation's capital as he sees fit, from a sprawling White House ballroom to a community golf course . The NPS has backed Trump's arch, despite noting it "would alter several historic views." The FAA deemed the arch, which would sit near Ronald Reagan National Airport, safe for air travel, but said it should have "a non-standard eternal flame on top" and "floodlight projectors pointed" toward it. What we're watching: A Justice Department spokesperson said they would appeal the decision "immediately." Go deeper: The next two months are pivotal for Trump's D.C. projects

events.title: GTA VI made an estimated $2.36 billion on day one. Now 1,600 Rockstar workers are voting on a union
events.summary: Vice City has opened its doors. Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday, and by the end of its first day the game had sold an estimated 24.6 million copies worth about $2.36 billion, including preorders, according to tracking firm Sensor Tower . Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has not confirmed sales figures. If the estimate holds, that is nearly triple the roughly $800 million GTA V took on its first day in 2013, and it would make GTA VI the biggest entertainment launch on record . But beyond the sales figures, cultural conversation, and think pieces, the people who built the game are asking for eyes on what lies beyond the pixels. More than 1,600 Rockstar employees in the U.K. are voting through Nov. 26 on whether the company should formally recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB). The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and staff, and a yes vote would make it the largest recognized union in the U.K. games industry, according to the IWGB. The outcome will test whether the studio behind the biggest launch in entertainment history will give the workers who made it a formal say, at a moment when the rest of the industry is cutting jobs and betting on AI. A developer makes the case before launch day In an op-ed for The Guardian published Wednesday, the day before the game’s release, Rockstar North animation programmer and union representative Nestor Uriarte laid out the stakes. “Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that,” he wrote. Games like this take years and hundreds of people to make. GTA VI arrives 13 years after its predecessor. Those long development cycles bring constant reshuffling of teams, which can leave workers exposed to layoffs. Firings, a tribunal, and a history of crunch That anxiety is not abstract at Rockstar. In late October 2025, the studio dismissed 31 employees in the U.K. and three in Canada, and the IWGB accused the company of union-busting . Rockstar said it fired the staffers for leaking confidential information and that the dismissals were “in no way related to people’s right to join a union or engage in union activities.” The dispute is before an employment tribunal in Glasgow, where closing submissions were scheduled for this week. There has also been a long-running debate about working conditions at the studio. In a 2018 Kotaku investigation into the making of Red Dead Redemption 2 , employees described a culture of “crunch,” the long hours and intense pushes that come before a deadline. One former employee recalled the development of the original Red Dead Redemption : “If you left early on a weekday or weekend, you’d get dirty looks. You’d feel the stare down, and sometimes you’d see it as you were leaving. There was this culture of, if you don’t put in the hours, you’re not worth working here.” In a Fortune profile of Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick , Zelnick said delays are sometimes part of game development and that the company’s focus is first and foremost on making a quality game. A precedent for an industry under pressure The vote reaches beyond Rockstar. Uriarte argues a union would also give workers a voice on AI, warning that “the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.” Former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder made a related argument in Fortune this month, calling GTA VI the last pre-AI blockbuster video game of its kind . The cuts are already visible elsewhere. In July, Microsoft said its Xbox division would eliminate 3,200 jobs , about 20% of its staff, over the following year and divest five studios , even as the company trims costs to fund its AI buildout . With GTA VI marking a generational feat, Rockstar’s union hopes to lock in job security and fair treatment for the teams behind one of the most successful game developers of the modern era. In Uriarte’s words: “It’s something we can, and must, embrace for ourselves. The future of the industry shouldn’t be a game played over our heads.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.summary: Work New grads say employers set the bar too high for entry-level roles Work September surge or October offload? Jobs experts on this fall’s hiring trends Work Students are reconsidering majors, career paths due to AI: CNBC survey Work AI resumes, cover letters are out: The new rules of finding a job right now Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Frustrated workers could trigger a wave of turnover, creating a shift in the sluggish job market, according to experts at the job boards Indeed and Glassdoor. That sluggishness, or what labor economists call a low-hire, low-fire economy , means that fewer people are getting hired, and fewer workers are leaving their jobs — even as a growing share of job holders report frustration with their career opportunities. In 2026, 21% of workers report feeling dissatisfied with their career prospects, according to Glassdoor reviewer data. Dissatisfied workers rated their jobs at a one or two out of five stars. A stagnant job market can discourage even the unhappiest of workers from quitting, but hiring could soon ramp up. Indeed's Job Posting Index, or JPI, which tracks the level of job postings on Indeed relative to a pre-pandemic baseline, saw year-over-year growth for the first time in September 2026 since 2022. The upward trend suggests that the job market is "heating up," Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao tells CNBC Make It. As more opportunities open up, job holders might regain the confidence to exit, turning into "a wave of quits and turnover," Zhao says. Turnover could also help those who are out of a job secure employment as roles that were once filled become vacant. "The labor market is a bit like a coiled spring right now," Zhao said at a press event Tuesday in New York City. "There's a lot of pent-up potential energy, and it's unclear exactly which way that that spring is going to release that energy." In a healthy job market, employee dissatisfaction can forecast turnover rates. When employee dissatisfaction reached 17% in April 2022, per Glassdoor reviews, quit rates also reached their highest levels at 3%, seasonally adjusted, according to data from Bureau of Labor Statistics Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey data published by the St. Louis Federal Reserve. However, when workers feel anxious about their future job prospects, turnover can stall. Though workers feel dissatisfied with their jobs at higher rates in September 2026 than they did in April 2022, only 2.1% of workers quit their job in the month, according to the BLS JOLTS . "There aren't those opportunities to climb the career ranks internally or externally," Zhao says of the job market. "There's no outlet for the frustration or dissatisfaction that [workers] might be feeling." Employee turnover was one focus of Indeed and Glassdoor's 2027 Hiring and Worklife Trends Report , published Wednesday. Their research, which assumed a consistent relationship between worker dissatisfaction and resignations based on historical data, found that the quit rate is 0.22% lower than what employee sentiment would typically suggest. While the figure seems small, it is equivalent to an additional 349,000 quits per month. "Workers are very hesitant to quit, especially without something lined up, because hiring is very sluggish, and long-term unemployment is looming over them," Zhao tells CNBC Make It. While unemployment levels are stable, people are remaining jobless for longer, according to data from the BLS. Those who face long-term unemployment, job seekers who have been out of work for 27 weeks or more, accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people in October 2026. Even if more jobs open, turnover across sectors could vary. Industries that are highly exposed to artificial intelligence like software development, engineering and banking previously dragged Indeed's JPI down, meaning employers in these sectors posted fewer jobs. Indeed's data shows that postings in these sectors have since seen growth, and could result in what experts call "pent-up quits," which occur when dissatisfied workers leave their jobs once market conditions improve. Job posts on Indeed for employers in industries with less AI exposure like healthcare have softened, according to experts. However, business and professional services, which includes banking, shed 27,000 jobs in October 2026, according to data from ADP Research. "As we look ahead to 2027, that increase in demand might not necessarily translate into more hires, and it also might not be enough hires to give workers the confidence that they can actually quit their jobs and move on to something better," Zhao says. Even as the job market appears to be trending in a positive direction, further economic pressure could continue to place a strain on employers and their hiring plans.
