events.title: Here's what our readers are saying about Amazon's threat to raise NYC delivery costs
events.summary: A worker carries an Amazon package. Bloomberg/Getty Images Amazon said it would increase delivery fees if the New York City Council passes a delivery bill. The threat sparked debate, including in Business Insider's comment section. Here's what our readers make of the Delivery Protection Act — and Amazon's response. Amazon's in-app call to action in New York City is provoking debate — including in Business Insider's comment section. On Thursday, we wrote about Amazon adding a notice in its app and on its website pushing back against the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, the proposal, which is before the New York City Council and has the support of Mayor Zohran Mamdani , would require companies like Amazon to directly employ their delivery drivers rather than use contractors. The notice, marked with a bright red "Attention" tag, indicated that Amazon would increase its fees by up to $5 per order if the measure becomes law. The strategy drew reactions from Amazon customers to the speaker of the New York City Council. Our readers also had thoughts, as evidenced by roughly three dozen comments on the story. Screenshot of the message Amazon began showing to customers in New York City on Thursday. Andy Kiersz/BI Some came out in support of the Delivery Protection Act, saying the proposal could benefit the workers who deliver Amazon orders in the city as well as other businesses. "It is time these trillion dollar companies to pay their workers their fair share," one commenter wrote. Another commenter compared Amazon to "the robber barons of old trying to dictate laws that it may not like." "I'm hoping we restore mom and pop stores," the commenter said. Even if Amazon goes through with charging more for delivery, some commenters wrote, New Yorkers will either absorb the cost or find other places to shop. "You can just take the hit to your pockets like the rest of us normal people do every day," one commenter wrote. "Or just leave the city then. I'm sure another company will be happy to take your place." Other commenters said the proposal could hurt businesses like those that Amazon contracts with under its current delivery service provider model. One reader wrote that last-mile delivery is "inherently unpredictable and messy" and lends itself to using contractors instead of full-time employees. "Anyoneeee who thinks this is a good idea doesn't know what they are talking about," the commenter wrote of the Delivery Protection Act. "People will just lose their jobs." "People who don't work in the industry don't understand what a nightmare for logistics this legislation will be," another wrote. "The only losers will be the customers and the 100's of people who do the deliveries," still another commenter wrote. Do you have a story idea about Amazon ' s delivery efforts? events.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
events.summary: Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge. Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route into Crimea off the map. “The short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed,” declared Ukraine’s General Staff. list 1 of 4 Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defence list 2 of 4 ‘Groundbreaking’ Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Five key takeaways list 3 of 4 Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it? list 4 of 4 Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations “Once again, the myth of Russia’s greatness has been shaken,” said Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), which took part in the operation. It was part of a wider set of strikes against oil facilities and supply routes in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions abutting Ukraine – an apparent strategy to asphyxiate Russian forces in southern Ukraine. “The alternative route is overland, along the front line, where our drones are waiting for the cargo,” said the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence. For a month, Ukraine’s military said it “systematically destroyed enemy air defence systems, radars, and electronic warfare equipment along the way to the target.” On November 16, Ukrainian drones damaged the bridge’s road surface and compromised its steel arched span that allows shipping between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. On November 17, the SBU said it used “Palyanytsia kamikaze drones to target the roadway section of the Crimean Bridge, causing it to collapse.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Neptune and Flamingo missiles and Ruta drones struck the separate railway span. During this 48-hour period, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones compared with a daily average of 882 during the previous week. On November 18-19, Ukraine again used Neptune missiles to strike the railway span, saying rail service had been suspended. It was unclear whether those strikes had permanently disabled the rail bridge. Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the operation as a strike against “a purely civilian facility … We haven’t even transported oil or petroleum products across the bridge.” Ukraine’s General Staff disagreed, saying it had targeted the Kerch Bridge because it “was a vital artery, supplying fuel, ammunition, equipment, and personnel”. The Ukrainian Defence Ministry called the bridge “a war machine”. On the same day as the main strike on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine also struck Russia’s main overland route to its southern forces, the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway. In addition, Kyiv also struck a series of refineries and oil depots in southwestern Russia that are nearest to the front, including in Azov, Ilsky and Afipsky. “Fuel from such depots has a short route to the front,” it said. Ukraine has already put Russia’s Black Sea and Azov Sea fleet of oil and fuel carriers out of action, striking at least 300 ships between July and September, leaving fuel supply dependent on road and rail transport. Southern Ukraine is where Russian offensive efforts are now most active. Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has said Russian casualties are heaviest near Dobropillya and Huliaipole in Zaporizhia. Ukraine’s General Staff has also confirmed this is where the highest number of assaults takes place. Ukraine made a point of saying its Kerch operation was entirely autonomous. “The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – our technology, our solutions,” said Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara. This also meant that Ukraine did not rely on the US-controlled Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, on which it depends for short-range drone navigation. On November 6, those services began to cut out when drones exceed 160km/h (100mph). They were later restored, but Zelenskyy said they were again compromised beginning on November 13. For the Kerch Bridge operation, Ukraine instead designed a system of drones that acted as signal repeaters. Video released by Ukraine showed an FP-5 missile relaying video up to the moment of impact, indicating that operators had control of it. During the past week, Ukraine also targeted Russian refineries as far-flung as Volgograd and Samara, Salavat and Tatarstan, in an ongoing strategy to deprive Russia’s war machine of export revenue and diesel. Almost half of the output of the Volgograd refinery is diesel, Ukraine said – a blow not only to Russia’s military, which consumes the fuel, but also to its promise to export 1.7 million tonnes of diesel this year as part of a deal struck with US President Donald Trump to lower fuel prices.

events.title: Nearly 15% of Americans expect prices to rise 15% or more next year, a pace the U.S. hasn’t seen in 79 years
events.summary: Even in 1979, the year of the Iranian revolution, gas lines and Paul Volcker, American inflation never got above 15%. It peaked just below that level in early 1980 before Volcker’s rate hikes broke it, according to the Federal Reserve’s own history . Prices haven’t risen faster than 15% a year since 1947. A meaningful slice of Americans expects prices to rise faster than that over the next year anyway. “Almost 15% of consumers expect (or claim they expect) inflation of over 15%,” UBS chief economist Paul Donovan wrote in a Nov. 20 note titled “The benign inflation scenario.” In the University of Michigan’s October survey, 16% of consumers said prices would rise 15% or more over the next year, about the same share as a year earlier, according to the survey’s own tables . About 1 in 6 consumers in the University of Michigan survey said in October 2026 that they expect prices to rise 15% or more over the next year, the same share as a year earlier. Fortune chart; data: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers The typical household is far calmer, and getting calmer. Median year-ahead inflation expectations “plunged from 4.7% last month to 3.7% this month,” University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers director Joanne Hsu said in the final November reading released Friday. That gap between the most frightened consumers and the data is what anyone setting prices or pay should watch. In the late 1970s, expectations that came loose from the numbers ended up feeding the inflation. A once-in-79-years bet Since the government’s consumer price records begin in 1913, 12-month inflation has cleared it in only two stretches: on and off from 1917 to 1920, peaking at 23.7% in June 1920, and from November 1946 to June 1947, after World War II price controls came off, according to BLS data compiled by the St. Louis Fed and the BLS’s own history of the index . To hit 15% next year, prices would have to rise about four times as fast as the 3.7% they rose in the 12 months through September. Consumers “tend to expect future inflation that is higher than official estimates of current inflation,” Fed economists wrote in a 2016 note , in part because they remember price increases more readily than cuts and weight the things they buy most often. They also feel price levels, not rates: grocery prices were up more than 27% from five years earlier as of early 2025, the Minneapolis Fed noted , even as the inflation rate itself had cooled. Partisanship matters, too, Michigan’s survey team has found. Independents’ inflation expectations “have consistently been closer to the political party not in the White House,” Michigan’s survey team found in 2024 , and survey director Joanne Hsu said “the overwhelming size and persistence of the partisan gap has generated substantial economic uncertainty.” Voters have already said what they think of prices. About 9 in 10 midterm voters called the cost of living a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress, and about 6 in 10 of them backed Democratic House candidates, according to the AP Voter Poll of roughly 100,000 voters. Republicans took a blistering set of losses in House , Senate and governor’s races, AP reported. About two-thirds of voters said President Trump’s policies had fueled inflation; in 2022, only about half said the same of President Biden’s, AP reported. Everyday costs weighed hardest. About 6 in 10 voters said they were “very concerned” about food and grocery costs, according to AP’s analysis of the poll , and about 1 in 5 said inflation had caused their family severe hardship, according to CBS News exit polls . Among voters earning less than $50,000, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off than two years earlier. Freakouts past Americans have braced for price spikes before. In May 2008, with gas at records, Michigan’s year-ahead expectations jumped to 5.2%, the highest since February 1982, CNBC reported . Inflation did climb, to 5.6% in July 2008. Then the financial crisis hit, and by July 2009 prices were 2.1% lower than a year earlier, per BLS data. The bigger miss came last year. Tariff announcements pushed Michigan’s year-ahead expectations to 6.5% in April 2025, the highest since 1981, with 60% of respondents volunteering comments about tariffs, the Boston Globe reported ; the preliminary May reading hit 7.3%, before the final came in at 6.6%, per the University of Michigan. Actual inflation that April was 2.3%. This time the median isn’t the outlier. Michigan’s typical household now expects 3.7%, the same rate as September’s actual inflation. Why it feels like 1979 to more than one in 10 people In 1979, the Iranian revolution cut output by 4.8 million barrels a day, about 7% of world production, and oil prices more than doubled between April 1979 and April 1980, per the Fed . This year it’s the Iran war. Brent crude is up more than 60% from before the fighting and briefly topped $117 a barrel in late October, Al Jazeera reported . U.S. diesel hit records in September. Gasoline was up 37.4% in the 12 months through October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . Those are the prices people see every week, and they drive what households expect. Donovan’s argument is that U.S. median inflation “has been falling to near pre-pandemic norms,” while the visible costs, airfares and diesel-driven shipping, come from the Iran war. Airline fares rose again in October, per BLS. Fed researchers have tracked this pattern for decades. A 2016 Fed note found households hear more news about prices when gas prices swing hard; in 1979, a year when gas rose around 20% or more, more than 10% of households reported hearing bad news about rising prices. Why it isn’t 1979, yet Back then the inflation was everywhere. Consumer prices rose 13.3% in 1979 and 12.5% in 1980. This October, BLS said prices rose 0.4% for the month, with core prices up 0.3%. It couldn’t publish an annual rate, because it collected no prices in October 2025, when the government shut down. Bank of America estimates the rate at about 3.8% headline and 2.7% core. The 12-month change in the consumer price index last topped 15% in 1947; it peaked at 14.8% in March 1980 and was 3.7% in September 2026. Fortune chart; data: Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED Michigan’s median household expected 9.7% inflation in both 1979 and 1980, according to the 2016 Fed note. Boston Fed researchers Philippe Andrade and Michael Wicklein found in 2025 that the 1978–80 surge in expectations was “much larger than the increase that rising prices usually would imply.” More than 5 percentage points of it couldn’t be explained by actual prices at all; gasoline accounted for about one point. They call it the de-anchoring of expectations, and it’s what Volcker spent the early 1980s grinding out. The central bank is the other difference. events.title: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes
events.summary: Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all. The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal. Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers. An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential. The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more. Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep. Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo. Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists. XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches. Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures. Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool. The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO 2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO 2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused. In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive. Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates. As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO 2 -cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch. That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up. events.title: ‘It might be too tough’: Trump second-guessed his immigration crackdown after the midterms. Then his Labor Department doubled down
events.summary: After a blue wave in the November midterms, President Donald Trump told CBS News ’ 60 Minutes on Nov. 8 that his immigration crackdown “might be too tough.” His administration just doubled down anyway. On Nov. 17, the Labor Department proposed an overhaul of the Permanent Labor Certification Program , or PERM, the step most employers have to clear before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card. Companies would face longer recruitment campaigns and a two-year bar on filing after laying off U.S. workers in similar jobs, and occupations in short supply, including nurses, would lose their exemption from the standard labor market test. For companies that sponsor foreign hires, that means more time, more paperwork and more ways to get turned down. The Labor Department received 117,849 PERM applications in fiscal 2025, down 22.4% from the year before. “I think I got an A plus for closing up the border. I got very high marks for getting the bad ones out,” Trump said. “But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation of breaking the law—and that was that they came into the country illegally.”  “I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump continued, regarding his immigration policy. “And a lotta people would say that it’s great. But a lotta people think it’s too tough.” And Trump has made the case for foreign workers before. In an interview with Fox News in November 2025, Trump conceded that the U.S. needs foreign labor due to domestic workers lacking “certain talents.” “You also do have to bring in talent,” Trump said. “We don’t have talented people here. You don’t have certain talents, and you have to. People have to learn.” The White House and Donald Trump did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune . A longer and harder process Under the existing system, employers generally have to obtain Labor Department certification demonstrating that there are not enough qualified and available U.S. workers for a particular position—meaning hiring a foreign worker won’t negatively affect wages and working conditions for domestic workers. The employers typically use the process to sponsor foreign laborers for employment-based green cards. But the proposed changes would require employers to conduct more extensive recruitment campaigns, eliminate administrative exemptions and prohibit employers from filing PERM applications for positions in the same or similar occupations for two years after laying off domestic workers in those same roles. The department is also proposing to extend recruitment advertising periods to at least 90 days and impose additional documentation and reporting requirements on employers. The consequential part of the proposal lands on the bypass standards—which have allowed certain occupations to be exempt from the standard labor market test if the roles were in need of workers. The standard requirement would be extended to occupations that are in short supply —including professional nurses and scientists of “exceptional ability.” But Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said these changes would ensure American workers will receive priority for high-skilled, high-paying positions. “American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a press release . “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor.” A continuation of immigration policy And in May, USCIS issued a policy memorandum introducing guidance that would also make it harder for foreign workers already living in the U.S. to obtain green cards without leaving the country. The memorandum emphasizes that adjustment of status is a “discretionary decision” over an automatic entitlement. Essentially, eligible immigrants already in the U.S. that can apply for lawful permanent residency through USCIS are not guaranteed. “Given the significant privileges granted to lawful permanent residents, USCIS reminds its officers that they must consider and weigh all the relevant evidence in the record,” the memo read, “taking into account the totality of the circumstances to determine whether the alien is suitable for permanent residence and if approval of the alien’s adjustment of status application is in the best interest of the United States.” The Trump administration also tightened employment-based green card sponsorship in September 2025, with an imposed $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa applications.  “The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a press release . Comments on the proposal are due Jan. 19, 2027. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trading soars on Jensen Huang-related prediction market bets
events.summary: The Jensen Huang scandal is turning into a prediction-market bonanza for some traders. There are more than 90 separate bets on Polymarket and Kalshi relating to the outcome of various elements of the Huang story and investigations. “ Will Jensen Huang be arrested ” currently has $153,000 of trading volume on Polymarket. More than 13,000 people have bet on Kalshi on whether President Donald Trump will pardon Huang. And nearly a million people have bet on if, or when, Huang will testify in front of Congress. Some people have cashed in by making big trades right before new developments. A user named paule334 made their first Polymarket trade ever on Nov. 10, betting that Jensen Huang would resign, and continued trading until the morning of Nov. 11, the day The New York Times broke the story of Huang’s second affair . The user made about $38,000. Others made windfalls by betting quickly after news breaks. Bertapotamous, another user, made nearly $100,000 on the same trade in the late afternoon of Nov. 11, minutes after The Wall Street Journal reported Huang was set to resign . — Reed Albergotti

events.title: OpenAI tightens grip on model resellers
events.summary: OpenAI put a new rule in place that gives the company more control over how much of the world — including China — can access its AI models. Gateways and routers that provide third-party access to OpenAI’s tech now need the company’s review and approval . Such gateways, the most prominent of which is OpenRouter, have become increasingly popular with developers and companies seeking access to a wide range of AI models: Instead of individual contracts with each lab, one account with a router can let you access hundreds of models from the US, Europe, and China. Beyond the technical details, the move has implications in the global AI race. US security agencies and companies, including Anthropic, have accused Chinese AI labs of distilling, or copying, American frontier models by routing requests through intermediaries that resell access to their models, which obscures the identity of the end user. Those cases largely involved gray-market resellers, known in China as “transfer stations,” but OpenAI’s new rule extends its oversight to any service standing between it and the people using its models. — J.D. events.title: Johnson urges Republicans to show up to work
events.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is warning House Republicans that their jobs aren't over yet after so many skipped town this week that GOP leaders had to call it quits. Why it matters: Republicans still have a month-plus left in the majority, but Johnson is struggling to get enough members to show up to make last-minute headway on the GOP's legislative agenda. GOP leaders were forced to cut the week short after 14 Republicans missed votes, leaving Johnson without the headcount needed to advance party-line legislation. Eleven of those 14 won't be returning next Congress. Driving the news: "To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote in a Friday letter to his colleagues . "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," he added. Zoom in: The outgoing speaker pointed to government funding, the annual defense authorization bill and permitting reform as priorities for the final weeks of the Republican majority. He also said he wants to pass "every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes" and force Democrats to take politically difficult votes. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson wrote.

events.title: Silicon Valley should ditch the 'handover' talking point
events.summary: The tech industry has enough of a public image problem with its warnings about AI leading to human extinction, and it risks further alienating people outside of Silicon Valley if it starts popularizing “the handover.” The handover is the period in which AI becomes so intelligent that it no longer makes sense for humans to make any decisions. Sam Altman brought the idea up on stage with me this week at Silicon Valley & The World, and he believes AI companies should do everything possible to avoid it. In a “positive” scenario, the handover turns humans into pets of AI overlords (Altman referenced Labradors): Humans have everything they need, from food to entertainment, and don’t need to work much. The dystopian idea is mostly a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where those inside AI companies see advanced models in their raw forms, doing both scary things like breaking into the internet and amazing things like solving the world’s most difficult math theorems. There’s no evidence we’re on the verge of a handover or anything remotely like it, so tech leaders would be wise to find a more optimistic talking point.

events.title: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
events.summary: The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10 After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed? The two sides have struck three deals long expected from this summit: food and drink, emissions trading and a youth exchange programme. The food and drink deal will ease Brexit controls on the vast majority of animal and plant products being traded between Britain and the EU, a boon for producers of meat, dairy, wine and flowers among many other products. If all goes well – and there is still an if – the deal will apply from 1 March 2028. The energy deal relinks the British and EU emissions trading schemes, shielding industrial producers on both sides from levies on polluting products, such as steel and fertilisers, as well as electricity. This should enter into force in 2028. Under the youth experience scheme, up to 100,000 British people each year would be able to live, work, travel and study in the EU for up to three years. The same number of young Europeans would be able to come to the UK. Young people should be able to take advantage of the scheme by 2030 at the latest. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, who studied at the London School of Economics when she was young, said it was a “very emotional moment” to strike the youth mobility agreement, while Andy Burnham addressed young people – saying: “This deal really is about lifting your life chances.” The two sides agreed to kick the can down the road for six months. The EU wants to ensure that young Europeans pay the domestic rate of tuition to study at British universities, capped at £9,790 in the current academic year, rather than the international rate, which can be four or five times higher. Under pressure from cash-strapped universities, the government has resisted this claim. The EU agreed a statement on Friday – not part of the joint text – that said it would not sign off the three deals (food and drink, emissions trading youth mobility), without a deal on equal treatment on tuition fees. The prime minister rejected this link, saying the deal was done. EU leaders have also expressed confidence in resolving the issue within six months. As a condition of getting the food and drink and emissions trading deals, the UK will be required to align with EU law in these areas, including new rules that it never had a say in writing. The UK will be allowed to attend relevant EU meetings as an observer without voting rights. After lobbying from Britain’s EU allies in northern Europe, Britain got a small upgrade to be in the room to observe discussions on future laws when they relate to “emergencies of specific relevance” to the UK, such as animal disease outbreaks. But it still cannot vote. The details are outlined in a separate text not in the main agreement. The next major agreement is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. The two sides aimed to wrap up this deal in 2027. This is a priority for five EU member states : Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions. But there are no details on the size of the UK contribution. The UK agreed to work closely with the EU’s “Channel action plan”, which aims to crack down on smugglers who organise small boat crossings. The agreement will see law enforcement intelligence sharing between the UK and the EU, working closer with agencies such as Europol and the European border agency Frontex, and improved maritime surveillance from French authorities. The agreement promises “a new structured dialogue” on migration, with both sides pledging to disrupt smuggling networks, strengthening border management in the Channel to stop small boat crossings, and work more closely with countries along migration routes. Both sides will require “shared financial commitments” given the “shared nature” of the challenges, according to the agreement. Von der Leyen said Britain and the bloc would work together along the entire migration route and to prevent dangerous Channel crossings, which she argued would also save lives. Burnham also expressed interest in the plans of five EU member states to negotiate an offshore “returns hub” with Rwanda for people with no right to stay in the EU. In a significant win for the UK, the EU has agreed to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” on touring artists. This does not sound like much.

events.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
events.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.  The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down. Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task. In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. events.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains A ndy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits? Mr Burnham is on to something: polls consistently show that many voters think that Brexit has not worked out well and rejoining the bloc has gained popularity. The rise of the European radical right also probably changes the EU’s calculation about Britain. Building closer ties with a broadly pro-European British government could mean the terms of future agreements allow for Britain’s preferential access to the bloc. However, Brussels won’t offer something for nothing. As the Swiss ambassador to the UK told a Lords committee earlier this year: “If you want to have access to the common market, you will need to pay some cohesion money.” Horse-trading is a feature of geopolitical life for Brexit Britain. The EU is using public borrowing and procurement rules to encourage defence production within Europe, create economies of scale and strengthen European supply chains. Britain balked at the financial contrib ution Brussels wanted in order to join up. With British defence manufacturers in danger of losing access to an expanding European market, both sides have made noises about getting around the table – but so far a deal remains elusive. Brussels’ “ Made in Europe ” industrial strategy poses another challenge. Britain imports cheap Chinese electric vehicles while the EU seeks to protect its producers. British carmakers, however, depend on European demand. Under proposals advanced before this meeting they risked being shut out of the market. The summit recognised this danger, promising closer cooperation on electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require Britain to align its policies with Brussels – without having a vote over them. This week Labour’s Stella Creasy, and Bernd Lange, a senior German MEP, proposed a Swiss-style deal to restore Britain’s economic and diplomatic influence without rejoining the EU. But greater market access without membership means accepting rules that Britain cannot influence. Mr Burnham’s reset pursued selective agreements – allowing Brussels to press for concessions. Switzerland offers a warning: frustrated by more than 120 bilateral deals , the EU insisted on a new framework. Down the line, Britain could face the same dilemma. Mr Burnham must calculate how long the country can negotiate the benefits of membership without confronting the costs of staying outside. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Bitcoin's regulation bull case is played out. What could drive crypto gains moving forward
events.summary: The Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act on Sept. 15, leaving the industry without the broad market-structure law it had sought. Crypto executives interviewed by CNBC point to tokenization and Wall Street's use of blockchain infrastructure as a potential next catalyst. Investors are also watching inflation, geopolitical risk, cybersecurity and the maturation of the artificial intelligence trade. Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said.

events.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
events.summary: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged. An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable. News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries. Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran . The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August. Experts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious. “This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM). He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.” After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM. Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.” Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence. That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said. He added that Pen Test Partners had also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said. “The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.” A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it had “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”. RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved as it “included dismantling our hardware”. Evans saidd: “In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps.”

events.title: Gen X’s $2.3 trillion caregiving curse: I’m the sister from John Mulaney’s SNL skit and I did the math
events.summary: On Saturday Night Live this weekend, John Mulaney sold America its oldest elder-care product. “Sister,” his pitchman explains, is a live-in, 24/7 caregiver who is “completely free, and also your sister.” Mikey Day’s Dr. Grant, author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works: years of internalized sexism have convinced her that caring for Mom and Dad is her job and somehow not yours. The best part, another brother adds, is that the parents drew up the will before she moved in, so you still get half the house she’s deep cleaning. Within a day, the sketch had 2 million views on YouTube, and women all over the country were sending it to their brothers. The joke lands because it isn’t one, particularly the part about finances. It’s impossible to create or maintain wealth while caregiving. I have no brothers, but I’m the sister. For the last 14 years (and several years in the past) I have been my parents’ full-time caregiver, without pay. My father passed away in 2022 and somehow the work increased taking care of one parent. I clean up after her at every meal, several times a day. I manage her medications, take her to specialists, deal with her insurers, rub lotion on her feet, run her errands, log in for her on some device several times a day. I’m a columnist, and my work has shrunk to fit around her care: missed meetings, moved deadlines, the same explanation of her health given again to every editor and board I work with. Each year I earn less than I would have, and each of those years goes into my Social Security record as a smaller number, almost a zero in 2024. Whatever I do earn goes to medical supplies and surprise expenses. I don’t invoice for any of this so, technically, nobody owes me anything. But he cost is borne by me. Earlier this month, AARP released a report , built on the Urban Institute’s long-range income model, estimating that the typical working caregiver will lose $120,500 over her lifetime in wages, workplace retirement income and Social Security. Across a single generation of caregivers, those born in the early 1980s, the losses come to $2.3 trillion. And that study counts only caregivers who kept their jobs. The sister in the sketch, the one who moved in, isn’t in that number. Her losses are larger because the damage doesn’t end when the caregiving does. Social Security calculates benefits from a worker’s 35 highest-earning years, and every year without a paycheck goes into that average as a zero. A woman who leaves work for five years to care for a parent doesn’t just lose five years of income. She locks in a smaller check for the rest of her life, long after the person she cared for has died. In 2024, America’s 59 million family caregivers provided 49.5 billion hours of care, work the AARP Public Policy Institute values at $1.01 trillion , more than total Medicaid spending that year. Three in five of those caregivers are women. But the trillion-dollar figure measures only what the care is worth. It says nothing about what the care costs the person giving it, or where that money ends up. The will joke does. It is the most precise line of economic analysis anyone has delivered on caregiving this year: she does the work, and the family’s wealth is split as if she hadn’t. Meanwhile, she is spending down whatever she had. AARP’s 2026 out-of-pocket study , released in October, found that caregivers now spend an average of $11,508 a year on caregiving, nearly 60 percent more than in 2021 and about 31 percent of household income. Caregivers who retired earlier than planned spend more, $18,940 a year. Most of it goes to housing, food and medical bills: the mortgage on the parents’ house, the groceries, the copays. Research cited by the TIAA Institute found that nearly a quarter of caregivers have less than $1,000 saved for retirement. Caregiving doesn’t just stop a woman from building wealth. It eats the wealth she already had. Her lost wages are a leave policy her employer never had to fund. Her unpaid hours are home-health services the state never had to buy. Her savings pay down the expenses of a household that isn’t legally hers. And her labor keeps her parents out of a nursing home, which keeps their house and savings from being spent on one. That intact estate is then divided, often equally, among children who did not do the work. The brothers in the sketch aren’t only getting their weekends back. They’re getting their raises, their 401(k) matches, their full Social Security records, and half the house. This is why caregiving is so rarely described as a financial arrangement, and so often described as love. Calling it love settles the accounts in advance. No one owes her anything, because what she gave was a gift. Employers that face no leave costs, governments that avoid paying for home care, and siblings who get back to “my life and the stuff I like to do” all benefit from keeping it that way. The rhetoric of priceless care conveniently treats it as worthless. Some of the fixes are already written. The Social Security Caregiver Credit Act , reintroduced in April by Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy and New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, would credit caregivers who provide at least 80 hours of care a month with up to five years of deemed earnings, so that those years stop counting as zeros. Congress should pass it, and extend it. Caregiving should earn retirement contributions, not just retirement credits. States can pay family caregivers through Medicaid at real wages, not token stipends. And families can do what the law doesn’t require: put the caregiving into the will. A sibling who gave years of labor to keep the estate intact has contributed to it, and an even split that ignores that contribution isn’t fair. It’s a transfer from her to everyone else who retires on full pensions and she retires on a three-digit Social Security check, in an apartment, while the house she cleaned for years is sold and split down the middle. events.title: The case for an AI downturn
events.summary: Reed’s view Anthropic’s IPO went on as well as anyone could have reasonably hoped. It was up 17% over its initial price with a valuation of about $1.3 trillion, making it the biggest debut in history. But Anthropic shares are down 11% so far today, and the rest of the market is down, too, as skepticism of the AI trade builds. The funny thing is, there are a lot of people in the tech industry who say they would actually like to see things slow down. That’s because all of the resources are being funneled into a small group of companies building essentially the same product, leaving little room for other ideas. The “tokenmaxxing” craze earlier this year has accelerated revenue growth at the frontier labs and hyperscalers. But if every unit of computer memory and every accelerator is concentrated among only a handful of players, innovation — and AI adoption — starts to slow down. I’ve heard this from tech companies that work with industry players but it’s also backed up by a report by Wasabi and the Centre for Economics and Business Research. Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia is also bad news for the pro-innovation crowd. Huang was a major proponent of open-weight AI models and a healthy startup ecosystem. The open-weight models, many of them coming out of China, were helping seed wider AI adoption, and it’s likely that will slow down if Chinese entrepreneurs and tech companies can’t get their hands on enough Nvidia chips. Another thing that could slow AI development: the number of cybersecurity worries building up at businesses around the world (more on that below). AI is helping everyone become more productive, including threat actors and nefarious nation states. The next period could be one of massive growth for the biggest players in tech, but it’s increasingly looking like one in which the real-life impacts of AI take longer to materialize than we initially expected. Notable Despite CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to slow down model development , Anthropic is accelerating its AI advancement , AP reported.

events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today issued a proposal to address the inefficiencies in the current governance and funding model of the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT). The Commission is proposing to rescind Rule 613 of Regulation NMS, which obligates the national securities exchanges and national securities associations (SROs) to establish, implement, and maintain the CAT. In its place, the Commission proposes to require SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to the Commission or its designee substantially the same information currently required to be recorded and reported pursuant to current CAT requirements. This proposal would bring the CAT under the SEC’s direct control, while ensuring its continued operation with minimal disruption. The proposal came as a result of the comprehensive review of the CAT directed by SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins and follows exemptive relief and approved amendments that have, among other benefits, helped reduce the CAT’s projected annual operating costs by over $100 million and permanently eliminated the reporting of personally identifiable information to the CAT. In April, the Commission issued a concept release soliciting public comment on the CAT. In public comment, both investors and market participants voiced support for the Commission exercising more control over the management and funding of the CAT. “Today’s proposal addresses persistent concerns with cost overruns, funding, and governance of the Consolidated Audit Trail. The proposed rule would encompass the changes that we have already made towards rightsizing the CAT, including increasing its cost-effectiveness and eliminating the collection of personally identifiable information. The proposal is intended to put the CAT on a sustainable footing: accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs, to the benefit of our markets and those who participate in them,” said Chairman Atkins. The CAT supports regulatory efforts to administer and enforce the federal securities laws, but the decentralized governance structure established by the CAT NMS Plan has presented certain challenges to administering the CAT and warrants revisiting. The proposal would rescind Rule 613 of Regulation NMS and add new Rule 17a-26 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, requiring SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to the Commission or its designee substantially the same information that is currently required pursuant to current CAT requirements, such as Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, related SRO compliance rules, and related exemptive relief previously issued by the Commission. Proposed Rule 17a-26 would require that data to be reported to the Commission or its designee instead of to a CAT system independently administered by the participants under a national market system plan. The Commission intends to use funds appropriated by Congress to pay the Commission’s costs relating to use, operation, and maintenance of the CAT system. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. events.title: Grand Theft Auto made crime a game. AI is doing the same for hacking
events.summary: Fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI. The wait for GTA V’s sequel dragged on through so many delays that it became a meme. When a game takes that long, you’d expect it to feel dated on arrival. But when GTA VI finally arrived this week, the opposite thing happened. The real world has started to look a lot like the game. Six days before the launch, the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an open-source tool that lets AI agents carry out an intrusion “at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” Some attacks reached privileged access in under three hours. The GitHub repository has since been taken down, but copies are still out there, and it has already been used against banks, government agencies, and tech companies. Skill, time, and money used to separate a bored teenager from a professional crew. Now a bored teenager with AI can operate like one. Rockstar knows what a bored teenager can do. In 2022, a 17-year-old broke into the company and leaked early GTA VI footage from a hotel room, using an Amazon Fire Stick and a phone. That took some serious skills and marked the last time anyone would need them. Rockstar spent 13 years building a game that feels like real life. In the same stretch, real life took on the rules of the game. AI turned the hacking craft into a criminal loop. You pick a target, try, fail, try again, at almost no cost, with the push of a button, from your couch. While developing the latest GTA took more than a decade, reality caught up in a fraction of that. That shift left defenses behind, because they were built for a slower pace. Attackers now run on three-hour clocks, while most security programs run on fiscal years. The best attacks don’t look like attacks at all. They arrive as job offers, invoices, calendar invites, and logins that look almost normal. Meanwhile, defenders are being asked to move faster and to tell real from fake at the same time. When the first GTA VI trailer came out, half of the internet asked the same question. Is this gameplay or real footage? Corporate security teams ask that every day now. In September, a Binance engineer went through two rounds of interviews for what looked like a great job and downloaded the take-home assignment. It was malware. The FBI blamed North Korea, and Binance puts the theft that followed at about $6.3 billion . A day after Microsoft 365 went down this month, attackers were already exploiting the confusion, sending fake outage notices that cited the real incident number. Now look at how slowly most companies change their defenses. Adopting a new approach means a six-month evaluation, a few more months to roll it out, and a pilot that waits for next year’s plan. I understand the caution, because security leaders have been burned by tools that promised a lot and broke things in production. But an attack that moves at machine speed doesn’t wait for procurement. Attackers are playing on easy mode, and the defense is stuck on a loading screen. The obvious answer is to make defense faster, and speed does matter. But fast and wrong is still wrong. A team that misreads that signal will shut down its own business over a broken router, while the real attack walks in looking like a job offer. Making the right call takes context that even the best AI model doesn’t have on its own, like who owns the server, whether that user really logged in from Lisbon, and what breaks if a system goes offline. That context lives inside your company, and defense only works when your AI agents know it too. The leaders I see handling this well have changed three things. Know the business first. Before buying more detection, they make sure their defenses understand which systems matter, who relies on them, and what normal looks like. AI can’t tell an attack from a failure without that context. Save the caution for what can’t be undone. Ending one session can be reversed in minutes, so it can happen right away, within rules the team sets. Decisions that can’t be taken back get a closer look and a person’s sign-off. Change in weeks, not quarters. They try agentic defense early, measure how often it gets real cases right, and give it more room as it earns trust. In GTA, players can reload their last save. Security teams don’t have that luxury. Companies that make the right call at machine speed will still be around for the next GTA installment, however long it takes. events.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
events.summary: Staffers at the Internet Archive , the nonprofit “ digital library ” that runs the Wayback Machine , are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996 . Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals. “Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED. Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company. “We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.” The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation , the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet. Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit. Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI . The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.) Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better. “We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.” Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.
