events.title: Slowing economy and rising AI create new generation of unemployed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tom Kearney lost his job in advertising and was forced to sell his home. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) More Australians are losing their jobs as the economy slows and the use of AI increases. One former advertising worker has been laid off four times since 2019 and now has to sell his house. Unemployment could hit 5 per cent amid questions about what will happen to middle-aged workers whose jobs no longer exist. For Tom Kearney, the past two years have meant agonising uncertainty. He lost his job in advertising in February last year and hasn't been able to get full-time work since. He has been through four redundancies since 2019. After falling months behind on mortgage repayments, he put his home up for sale at the end of September, and signed the sale contract this week. "I've really held on as long as I can." Mr Kearney said his bank had allowed him to pause mortgage repayments for about five months, but he had not been able to make repayments since about June. "It has been an absolute roller-coaster," he explained. "I've been through the seven stages of grief and I've hit acceptance. "But I have had rage. I have had sadness. I have had disbelief. I just can't believe what's happening." Mr Kearney had built up 17 years of experience in advertising, but like many other white-collar workers, he has been hit by a slowing economy and the rise of AI. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com Since the latest job loss in February, he said he had put in more than 100 job applications but only had three interviews. Mr Kearney fears things are going to get far worse as AI takes more jobs away. 'Collateral damage' the RBA expected The number of Australians losing their jobs is rapidly accelerating. Unemployment rate surges to 4.9pc in October The number of people in employment fell by 43,500 last month and the number of officially unemployed increased by 17,800, in seasonally adjusted terms. The unemployment rate jumped to 4.9 per cent in October as the number of unemployed Australians grew by 17,800. Some also dropped out of the workforce, pushing the participation rate down. It is the highest unemployment rate in the post-COVID era, but the figure is tipped to rise further. The rise is also happening much faster than the Reserve Bank had been anticipating. Economists expect the central bank will keep interest rates on hold next month. Leonora Risse says Australians already feel like they are in a recession. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) "It shows that the Reserve Bank's efforts to slow down the economy are working," Queensland University of Technology associate professor in economics Leonora Risse said. National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Dr Risse said while Australia was not technically in a recession, for many Australians facing higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressures, it felt like they already were in one. "The Reserve Bank is trying to tap the brakes on the economy to avoid the economy falling into a recession," she said. "The problem is it can still very much feel like a recession when we see unemployment increase so quickly." Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said the latest jobs numbers showed the Australian economy "already has one foot in a recession" and that "could well mean we've seen the last interest rate hike" for a while. On Wednesday, retailer General Pants went into administration, placing 500 jobs in doubt . It follows the loss of about 1,500 roles at David Jones . From big retailers to banks to airlines and even tech companies, mass lay-offs are emerging. Corporate Australia is undergoing a restructure and investing in AI while some companies are sending jobs offshore. Experts speculate companies might be looking to ultimately replace those offshore jobs with AI. "That could be a financial strategy for some companies," Dr Risse said. What becomes of workers replaced by AI? Dr Risse said the country was now at a place where the unemployment rate could soon tip over the 5 per cent mark. Regulator warns of 'interruptions' as AI evolves The regulator that oversees Australia's banks, super funds and insurers will run "stress tests" to examine hypothetical doomsday scenarios linked to AI. "There's still a lot more shifting in the economy to come in terms of that structural change where people are moving out of jobs that are being affected by AI," she said. Mr Kearney is still looking for a job.

events.title: SNL’s viral ‘Sister’ sketch asks why pay for elder care when a daughter does it free — a home health aide runs about $6,688 a month
events.summary: A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free? The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families. According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women. As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts. While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide. Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities. Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements . This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately $6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025. For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends. Medicaid can help, but access is limited Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer. Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023 . The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew. However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance. Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services . Who provides care in the meantime? There’s a shortage of paid caregivers Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle. The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born . The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned. Caregiving often has financial consequences When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care. Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out. Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks. Families often have to shoulder responsibility Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs . In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers . Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage . In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance , an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place. When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter. events.title: Trump, Putin and Xi signed onto a 1985 Reagan-Gorbachev nuclear line in 90 minutes of talks — Ukraine didn’t even come up by name
events.summary: It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit , for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders. Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine , Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them. But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver? As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School , I saw a lot of style, but less substance. What were the key takeaways from the meeting? The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order. And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi . Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president. And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades. It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom ,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen. In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds. So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body. And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls . In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985 : “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.” All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago , and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter. What wasn’t discussed? The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations. For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged. But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting. At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi. Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings. This was touted as Yalta II – was it? There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table. Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years. Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed. Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary. What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that. events.title: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032
events.summary: The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, setting out how his administration hopes to shut down a facility long criticised for violence, overcrowding and poor sanitation. The plan, released on Friday, proposes closing the jail five years after a deadline of August 2027 that was set under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio. list 1 of 3 Mamdani: ‘it’s morning again in America’ after blue wave list 2 of 3 Zohran Mamdani’s influence grows as Democrats eye 2028 strategies list 3 of 3 New York Democratic Socialists urge Ocasio-Cortez to run for US president With less than a year to go, the four smaller jails in four New York boroughs that are meant to replace Rikers are still under construction. The jail complex mostly holds people awaiting trial rather than serving sentences after conviction. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” said Mamdani in a statement. “We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” he said. How does Mamdani plan to close Rikers Island? The mayor’s strategy involves reducing the number of people held at Rikers from 6,700 to no more than 4,100 by expanding alternatives to detention, restoring online bail payments, investing in programmes that aim to reduce repeat offending, and shortening court delays. Court delays can leave people “detained for years in what is essentially legal purgatory”, said Mamdani at a news conference on Friday. The city plans to set up a task force to deal with bottlenecks and improve how agencies share evidence. Under the new timeline, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, with the rest completed by 2032. The city plans to also make hospital beds available for people in custody who have serious mental health or medical needs. “Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is, how it can take hours to visit a loved one,” Mamdani said, adding that the new jails would be closer to courts and public transport, and would help integrate imprisoned New Yorkers back into the city. Rikers Island, near LaGuardia airport in New York’s East River, opened in 1932 and has long faced criticism over violence, abuse, and unsanitary conditions, with campaigners pushing for its closure for over a decade. The facility has been tied to cases like that of Kalief Browder, who spent three years there awaiting trial before the charges against him were dismissed. He died by suicide in 2015 aged 22, two years after his release. City lawmakers voted to close Rikers in 2019, and Mamdani has blamed the city’s inability to meet the 2027 deadline to build the replacement jails on the previous administration. Once the jail closes, Mamdani said he wants the island to be used for renewable energy and projects to help the city withstand the effects of climate change. “Our hope is that the new Rikers Island will be unrecognisable,” he said.

events.title: Is having debt actually bad?
events.summary: Ask most people whether debt is bad , and the answer will come quickly. Ask a financial adviser the same question, however, and the response is more considered. “ Debt isn’t inherently bad,” says finance coach and chartered accountant Carol Glynn. “Having debt doesn’t mean you have failed financially. What matters is the purpose behind the debt and why you’re using it.” Steve Cronin, financial adviser and founder of Dead Simple Saving, frames his response in straightforward economic terms. “There is cheap debt like mortgages and car loans , then there is expensive debt like personal loans and credit card debt. Expensive debt is bad and can ruin your life. Cheap debt is fine and can help you get ahead in life, as long as you can afford the monthly payments.” A mortgage sits at the better end of the spectrum for both advisers. The interest rate is typically low, and the borrowing is attached to an asset that builds equity or generates income. For UAE residents, however, the mortgage question depends on how long you’ll stay . “Buying is worth it when you plan to spend at least seven to 10 years in the country, and you value stability,” says Mr Cronin. “If you prefer flexibility of location or country, then renting is much better.” The gap between good and damaging debt The gap between good debt and damaging debt often comes down to basic knowledge. Ms Glynn identifies a cluster of common failures among borrowers, including not understanding interest rates or the effect debt has on their monthly income. “They don’t check their debt ratio, which is how much of their income the debt absorbs. They don’t do scenario planning to check whether they could still afford the debt if their income dropped,” she adds. Mr Cronin says many borrowers do not even know what interest rate they are paying. Knowing your limits matters as much as knowing your rate. The UAE has a regulatory safeguard – a debt burden ratio that caps total loan repayments at 50 per cent of monthly income – but both advisers recommend more conservative personal thresholds. Mr Cronin becomes concerned once repayments exceed 40 per cent of income. “You could easily lose your job, face a pay cut or see your variable loan payments increase when interest rates go up,” he says. Ms Glynn’s rule for mortgage debt is 30 per cent, and she recommends holding a larger emergency fund for anyone carrying debt beyond that level. The UAE’s particular pressures Living in the UAE brings its own pressures. The country’s visible wealth can make certain kinds of spending feel expected. “Lots of people appear wealthy and successful in the UAE,” says Mr Cronin. “People are attracted to the glamorous lifestyle they see around them, and they go into debt to fund it. But it’s a trap, and it makes you vulnerable if anything happens to your income.” He also points to the supply side of the problem. “The banks are quite willing to give you loan top-ups, card limit increases and new cards, so the temptation is coming from both sides: extra spending and extra debt.” Ms Glynn, who works with clients across several markets, says the UAE has a lifestyle expectation she doesn’t often see elsewhere. Credit is significantly easier to obtain here than in other countries, with attractive perks – points, gym memberships, travel benefits – that draw people in before they fully understand the terms, she adds. “The issue is that not everyone understands how credit cards work, so they get into credit card debt without meaning to.” Navigating the products Credit cards, used correctly, draw measured praise from both advisers. Ms Glynn puts all her spending on hers to accumulate points, then clears the balance in full each month. “I never pay interest, because the rates are so high they would cancel out any benefit I get from points systems.” Mr Cronin agrees that credit cards are useful, offering purchase protection as well as points or cashback. But, he warns, “you must pay off your card in full each month, otherwise you’ll end up in a debt spiral”. Buy now, pay later services – prominent in the UAE through Tabby and Tamara – draw far more caution. “You are just kicking the can down the road,” says Mr Cronin. For Ms Glynn, they’re useful for covering a high, unexpected cost you cannot meet using cash. “Spreading that cost over a few months can help. They shouldn’t be used for everyday payments, because you lose clarity over your finances very quickly.” Personal loans, meanwhile, draw the harshest verdicts. “I don’t recommend personal loans at all,” says Mr Cronin. Ms Glynn has one exception: consolidation – moving multiple high-rate credit card balances into a single, lower-interest structured repayment. If you’re already worried For anyone concerned about existing debt, both advisers begin with the same instruction: clarity first. “Write down every debt,” advises Ms Glynn. “For each credit card or loan, note how much is owed, the interest rate and the minimum monthly payment. Then rank them from most to least expensive by interest, and from lowest to highest balance.” It is also important to be honest with yourself about why you ended up in debt, she adds. “Look at your financial habits and your money mindset. If you clear the debt without changing the behaviour behind it, you’re at high risk of building it up again and repeating the cycle.” Mr Cronin warns that debt problems build slowly, then all at once. “Don’t allow yourself to get anywhere close to the edge: make sure you are able to save some money each month and have an emergency fund so you can be resilient against whatever life throws at you.” The right size of emergency fund, which Ms Glynn calls a “cash cushion”, is personal, “but I would start with at least three months of living expenses”, she says. “Then decide if that would be enough to cover loss of income until you can find a new role. If not, then consider saving six months of living expenses. Keep it in a high-interest account so it is also growing in value while serving its purpose to protect you in the case of financial emergencies.”

events.title: 'Sunrise on the Reaping' answers lingering questions about 'The Hunger Games.' Here's what you might've missed.
events.summary: Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Courtesy of Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is finally out in theaters. It's based on the novel by Suzanne Collins about Haymitch Abernathy. "Sunrise on the Reaping" sheds new light on the entire "Hunger Games" series. It's a good time to be a "Hunger Games" fan . On Friday, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" premiered worldwide, bringing Haymitch Abernathy's Hunger Games to the big screen. The film is an adaptation of Suzanne Collins' novel " Sunrise on the Reaping ," released in March 2025. Joseph Zada stars as a young Haymitch in the adaptation, and he's joined on screen by a slew of A-list actors , including Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson in a much-anticipated return to their roles as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark. Fans have been curious about Haymitch's Hunger Games since Katniss and Peeta got a peek at them in "Catching Fire," where they learned Haymitch outsmarted the gamemakers to survive the arena. "Sunrise on the Reaping" breaks down how Haymitch took aim at the arena itself and offers new details about the entire "Hunger Games" series , from lore about Katniss' family to backstory on how the revolution came to be. Here are some of the details from the novel (and some snippets left out of the movie) you might have missed. Warning: Heavy spoilers for the entire "Hunger Games" series ahead. The book is full of information about Katniss Everdeen's family Katniss is the protagonist of the original "Hunger Games" trilogy , but the books don't include much information about her family beyond her and her sister Primrose. Her parents' names aren't even mentioned in books one through three. Her parents do appear by name in "Sunrise on the Reaping," though. Collins reveals that Katniss' father, Burdock, was one of Haymitch's best friends and that he was already courting Asterid, Katniss' mother, when Haymitch was sent to the Hunger Games. Haymitch's interactions with Burdock highlight the similarities between Katniss and her father, as they are full of nods to Katniss . For instance, in the book, Burdock takes Haymitch into the woods, where he sings and shows Haymitch how to get apples and set hunting snares. Katniss uses those same hunting skills she learned in the woods to survive her first Hunger Games, and her beautiful singing voice comes up multiple times in the original series. Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate Katniss' parents' long-awaited names also reflect those they gave their children; both Asterid and Burdock are plants, as are Primrose and Katniss. Haymitch also mentions that Burdock is a distant cousin of his girlfriend, Lenore Dove Baird, a member of the Covey family. The Covey first appears in Collins' "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." They are the musically inclined family of Lucy Gray Baird, who wins the Hunger Games and has a doomed relationship with Coriolanus Snow . Based on Haymitch's comment, Katniss' paternal grandmother is likely Lucy Gray's cousin, Barb Azure Baird. Haymitch sees graves for Lucy Gray and her other cousin, Maude Ivory Baird, when visiting Lenore Dove's resting place. Lenore Dove's mother is dead in "Sunrise on the Reaping," while Burdock's seems to be alive, indicating Barb Azure is his mom. Katniss' and Peeta's fathers share an important interaction During the reaping for the Hunger Games, one of the boys reaped from District 12, Woodbine Chance, flees, and Peacekeepers immediately shoot him. They order everyone to the ground, and most people in the area obey, though Otho Mellark, Peeta's father, freezes. Burdock gets Otho to lie down on the ground by punching him in the knee, saving him from becoming the Peacekeepers' next target. If Otho had died in the shooting, Peeta would never have been born, so he wouldn't have been there to fight alongside Katniss. In fact, Katniss likely wouldn't have made it to the Hunger Games without Peeta, as he saved her from starvation by giving her bread after her father died. The small interaction between their fathers — at a pivotal moment in Haymitch's life — eventually leads to Peeta, Katniss, and Haymitch uniting decades later. Haymitch's nickname for Katniss holds special meaning In the original "Hunger Games" trilogy, Haymitch often refers to Katniss as "sweetheart." She initially takes the nickname as condescending but later comes to see it as a term of endearment. "Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the pet name was always a term of affection for Haymitch. Woody Harrelson as Haymitch Abernathy and Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate One of the three people Haymitch competes in the Hunger Games with from District 12 is Louella McCoy. Louella is three years younger than Haymitch, and he shares in "Sunrise on the Reaping" that he has long called her "sweetheart" as an inside joke, referencing a crush she had on him when she was 5. The pair were close and planned to be allies in the Hunger Games, but Louella died before even reaching the arena. As Haymitch mourns her, he calls her "my one and only sweetheart." In the book's epilogue, Haymitch says that Katniss reminded him of Louella when he saw her at the Hob after her father died, as she wore her hair in braids like his old friend. He said the resemblance was so strong in his mind that "the nickname couldn't help but slip out" when he became Katniss' mentor for the Hunger Games . Haymitch also sits in some katniss during his games, foreshadowing her eventual presence in the arena. Haymitch's Hunger Games offer more insight into the plot of 'Catching Fire' "Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals that Haymitch has a long history with several characters from "Catching Fire," including Plutarch Heavensbee, Beetee Latier, Mags Flanagan, and Wiress, as he tried to break the arena with their help during his time in the games. When Mags and Wiress compete alongside Katniss in "Catching Fire," Mags is said to be weakened from a stroke, while Wiress' mind seems damaged. Katniss assumes they are both in poor health because they fought in the Hunger Games. But in "Sunrise on the Reaping," Mags and Wiress are mentors to Haymitch and the other District 12 tributes, and both are physically and mentally sound when he meets them. Lili Taylor as Mags Flanagan and Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate/Murray Close/Lionsgate After he wins his games, Haymitch discovers that they were both tortured because they attempted to help him break the arena. He spots Mags in a wheelchair and sees Wiress mumbling to herself. It was Capitol torture that caused lasting damage to them, not the games themselves. events.title: US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
events.summary: Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing but that was not the case on Friday. Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT). list 1 of 4 Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX list 2 of 4 Can Anthropic afford to put AI safety first? list 3 of 4 Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO list 4 of 4 Asia’s stock markets dive as Anthropic debut fails to allay AI bubble fears Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. But the slump in price within a day of listing – though still higher than its offer price of $83.30 – while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff. “Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds. Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia was down nearly 7 percent, Meta Platforms fell almost 4 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2.1 percent and 1.7 percent, respectively. Chip stocks also slid, with AMD down 11.2 percent, Sandisk down nearly 15 percent and Intel losing 4.3 percent. More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the Republican Party, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep. Anthropic’s stock could find support later in the year; London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of Anthropic’s shares by year-end. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 percent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. On Friday, the stock was down about 7.4 percent.

events.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
events.summary: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips? The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue. Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024. But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision. That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers. However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue. Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space. Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts. That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale. events.title: Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
events.summary: Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating. Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people. Inspired by demonstrations that have shaken France in recent months, thousands took to the streets in countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Spain, Italy, Sweden and Croatia on Friday. list 1 of 4 A tale of two protesters: Young Germans resist military expansion list 2 of 4 ‘What’s wrong with citizens taking to the streets with a Palestinian flag?’ list 4 of 4 More than 100,000 take part in France pay protests Tens of thousands of workers and students protested in more than 100 Italian cities to demand higher wages ⁠⁠and greater investment in public services. The rallies coincided with a general strike by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, that involved workers in ‌‌both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare. “Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change is growing,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said at a rally in Rome. Demonstrators in Rome threw objects at the Ministry of Education, while in Bologna some protesters clashed with police, news agency ANSA reported. In Milan, demonstrators set fire to a cardboard tanker as well as cardboard figures depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and United States President Donald Trump. The Italian rallies ⁠⁠followed a nationwide mobilisation on October 17 that descended into rioting and looting and prompted the right-wing government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to approve sweeping security measures and deploy the army alongside police in subsequent demonstrations. Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry. Opposition leaders joining demonstrations on Friday criticised Meloni’s government and its budget policies amid rising living costs. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said the 2027 Budget Law “does not have a vision for the future of the country” as it does not help industries but slashes funding for public healthcare and education. Meanwhile, in Germany, campaign group “Gen Z regelt” (German for “Gen Z sorts it”) said it ⁠⁠was organising protests in 73 cities and towns. In Berlin, roughly 4,000 people attended a protest in the city’s ⁠⁠Alexanderplatz square. The Cologne protest drew fewer than the 5,000 people expected, though ⁠⁠demonstrators still numbered in the thousands, police said. Protesters gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service. In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests. In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending. Demonstrations across Europe were inspired by much larger protests in France that began in September and descended into violent confrontations with the police and looting. On Tuesday, France’s Interior Ministry said a total of 146,000 people took part in protests across the country , with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators. The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency. Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 percent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 percent in Spain, 11 percent in France and 20 percent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

events.title: ADGM aims to rank among top five global financial centres
events.summary: ADGM is aiming to join New York as one of the world's top financial centres, the head of its regulatory authority has said. ADGM ranked 13th on the Global Financial Centres Index, released in September. Financial centres are ranked by data from third parties including the World Bank, the OECD and the UN, as well as a questionnaire that attracts thousands of respondents. New York, London, Hong Kong, Singapore and Shanghai made up the top five, while Dubai International Financial Centre ranked ninth. “We want to be among the top five,” Rashed Al Blooshi, chief executive of the Regulatory Authority at ADGM, told The National on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in New York. “That means our services, our rules, our regulations, all of these things could be developed." ADGM currently holds roughly 14,000 total active licences after about 1,800 were added in the first half this year. Its assets under management grew 54 per cent year-over-year, while the workforce has climbed above 49,000. Mr Al Blooshi pointed to ADGM providing digital services and using artificial intelligence to speed up the licensing process, while also noting the need to attract high-net-worth people and asset management. “But we don't want them to come and just do the operation. We need them to get jobs, training, innovations, and in Abu Dhabi, and from Abu Dhabi to do investment even abroad,” Mr Al Blooshi said. Along with Dubai, ADGM operates under English Common Law, with independent courts and a regulatory framework supporting it. Mr Al Blooshi said operating under this framework makes it easier for multinational companies to understand the language and settle disputes. Mr Al Blooshi was part of a delegation this week that participated in the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum, which aims to advance partnerships with US companies and explore commercial opportunities. The first forum to take place in New York was held last year and resulted in agreements across digital infrastructure, financial services and other sectors. In his remarks on Thursday, Abu Dhabi Investment Office director Badr Al Olama said 26 financial institutions have announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM . More than half of those are US firms, he said. Cepa strategy Abu Dhabi's emergence as a major financial centre comes as the UAE continues to press forward with its Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa) initiative. The Emirates launched its Cepa strategy in 2001 as part of its diversification strategy to expand global market access and strengthen the country's position as a trade and logistics hub. The UAE has signed 38 Cepa agreements with trading partners, and aims to increase its non-oil foreign trade to $1.1 trillion by 2031. These agreements typically aim to reduce tariffs and other barriers to entry, facilitate investment and simplify customs procedures. The UAE signed its first Cepa with India in 2022, and most recently with Canada in October, although the latter has not yet gone into force. Mr Al Blooshi said the UAE has seen rising demand from other countries to enter into agreements that would boost bilateral trade. “It's becoming so effective to the economies," he said.

events.title: Bitcoin sell-off: Crypto is failing the 'digital gold' test again as it sinks with stocks
events.summary: Bitcoin’s recent sell-off has moved with risk assets again, weakening the case that it behaves as an independent market hedge. Experts point to rates, broad risk-off trading, ETF outflows and crypto-specific shocks as pressures on bitcoin. Institutional and corporate adoption has deepened, but it also gives investors more liquid ways to add or cut bitcoin exposure. Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency. Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors. The heavy midterm elections losses for the Republicans, the Binance hack, and a world on edge about the security of all things technology — FAA ground stop, the outage of the National Security Agency's highly classified internal communications system, several online banking outages — have not helped the mood when it comes to putting trust in the digital world. But the market itself may be the biggest factor. Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data. Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic. Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety. In the past month alone, bitcoin had dropped roughly $20,000, as of Friday morning, according to CNBC data. Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago." What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say. There have been many theories about how bitcoin would react based on different market and economic conditions. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida. When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said. Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield. Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show. How bitcoin is like gold, but also like the S&P 500 Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies. But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said. Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said. Did Democrats' midterms blue wave matter? Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective.

events.title: Stock market sell-off deepens as Anthropic slides
events.summary: The US tech sell-off deepened on Friday as shares of the newly public AI giant Anthropic dropped more than 12.8 per cent, a day after the company made its debut on the Nasdaq. The Nasdaq was down 3.45 per cent, adding to the tech-heavy index's recent declines. It has lost more than 12 per cent in value over the past month as a storm of bad news and fears swirls. Anthropic opened on Thursday at about $105 per share. It was trading at around $84.74 as of noon on Friday. Another of the companies fuelling the sell-off is Nvidia, which was down another 7.25 per cent on Friday. The past month has seen it lose more than a third of its value, after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. The gloom is dragging other indexes down too, with the S&P 500 losing more than 2 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down about 0.55 per cent. “We are in the midst of a garden-variety correction, with the market’s leadership moving around,” said Gaurav Mallik at Modera Wealth Management. “While we expect technology to recover and perform well, it may cede its leadership to other sectors like industrials and financials and more value-orientated areas of the market.” The sell-off has affected other assets too. Gold dropped more than 4 per cent to $3,535, while Bitcoin was down about 4 per cent to roughly $59,250. The resurgence in volatility spurred demand for defensive shares and haven assets including Treasuries. The US dollar headed for a fourth straight weekly gain. Emerging markets were on the cusp of a bear market. Anthropic’s debut consumed the attention of investors, with stocks along the supply chain moving on even minor developments around the deal’s size or pricing. Now that the IPO is wrapped up, that exuberance is giving way to mounting doubts over the durability of the AI trade. Questions remain over whether the vast spending on the AI buildout can be sustained as regulation looks set to tighten and interest rates are likely to rise further. “In some investors’ eyes, the IPO was supposed to serve as a clearing event for stocks,” said Chris Senyek at Wolfe Research. “Instead, we see markets struggling for upside and continuing their downward trend.”

events.title: Gap stock soars as retailer says Old Navy turnaround shows signs of improvement
events.summary: Gap on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the new CEO of Athleta effective next month. Athleta's previous CEO, Maggie Gauger, left the company for Lululemon last month. Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC that he's "disappointed" with Athleta's performance but confident in its turnaround strategy and potential. The retailer also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings, with overall comparable sales coming in flat. Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14. The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 12% in trading Friday. Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that. "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement. The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month. "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode." Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success. While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential. Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount. Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%. Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year. The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share. Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season. "We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 82 cents adjusted vs. 78 cents expected Revenue: $4.01 billion vs. $4.02 billion expected For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior. At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. ` The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales. "Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said. The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2. Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount. Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country. "We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said.

events.title: Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records
events.summary: What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from the meeting? Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? In a new letter, Congressman Jamie Raskin says officials in the US government are ignoring federal recordkeeping laws. A top Democrat, who will wield significant investigative powers in the United States Congress starting in January, has warned US law enforcement agencies to preserve records, including encrypted communications on digital messaging apps. In letters sent on Thursday to the US Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Congressman Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the next likely chairman of the US House Judiciary Committee, wrote to the cabinet-level agencies to remind their employees of a legal obligation to “safeguard” records against destruction. list 1 of 3 What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia? list 2 of 3 How the US House of Representatives chooses its leaders: A visual guide list 3 of 3 Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration Letters were also sent to the heads of three subagencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Prisons (BOP). Raskin disclosed he has obtained evidence that government officials in the Trump administration have been using non-government apps, like Signal, to send disappearing messages. The Maryland Democrat, who is currently the Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, appended a screenshot of a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of President Donald Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, showing a conversation where messages were set to automatically delete after one week. “The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records”, Raskin wrote to US Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications.” The incident, Raskin wrote, is “just one of many” that have been reported to the Judiciary Committee, raising concern among Democrats that the Trump administration could be ignoring federal recordkeeping laws by destroying documents before likely congressional investigations. “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records”, Raskin wrote. “This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials”. Raskin instructed the federal officials to take “immediate action to recover these records” from data backups or “associated metadata,” asking them to comply by December 3. The Trump administration has signalled it intends to fight any probes by US Democrats, who won control of both chambers of the US Congress earlier this month in the country’s midterm elections . According to a letter viewed by Al Jazeera, the White House’s top lawyer, Will Scharf, wrote to US House Democrats on Wednesday, pushing back against demands from the incoming Democratic majorities, such as Raskin’s, because the new Congress has not yet been sworn in. “Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated,” Scharf wrote. “As a result, Ranking Member requests in the 119th Congress do not trigger any obligation to ‘accommodate[e] … the needs of the conflicting branches'”. In response to Raskin’s letter, a White House official told Al Jazeera the administration complies “with all federal record retention laws and regulations”. The DOJ echoed the White House’s response, saying it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” “The men and women of the DOJ who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated by a congressman who once called 2020 riots ‘magnificent’ and ‘nonviolent'”, the agency said about Raskin. Al Jazeera also reached out to DHS, FBI, ICE and BOP for comment but has not yet heard back.

events.title: UK far-right activist ‘Danny Tommo’ jailed for slashing migrant boat
events.summary: Daniel Thomas livestreamed himself slashing a dinghy used to bring migrants from France to the UK. A British far-right anti-immigration activist has been jailed for 15 months for criminal damage for slashing a small boat which had brought migrants from France to the United Kingdom. Daniel Thomas, also known as “Danny Tommo”, is the founder of the British anti-migrant Patriot Platform group, which mobilised hundreds of protesters earlier this year. He pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month, after slashing the inflatable vessel while a French emergency responder was on board. list 1 of 3 Far-right UK activist Daniel Thomas arrested after slashing dinghy list 2 of 3 ‘They told me to go back to my country’: Inside the UK’s wave of racism list 3 of 3 Child among three killed off French coast in Channel crossing attempt Sentencing Thomas on Friday, judge James Newton-Price said the offence “amounted to flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption” of French and British authorities’ important activities in the English Channel. “They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover,” he added. Thomas livestreamed himself on September 22 as he followed a small boat ⁠⁠carrying migrants across the Channel, who were transferred ⁠⁠onto another vessel and taken ashore. The 37-year-old later approached the dinghy and slashed it with a knife, soon after a French rescue worker had stepped on board. British police arrested him shortly after the incident. Prosecutor Joel Smith told Portsmouth Crown Court that Thomas had shouted “get off the boat, you’ve got time to get off the ⁠⁠boat … take them back, no more ⁠⁠of these”. Thomas appeared in court via videolink from prison, with his head bowed and rarely looked up as footage of ‌‌the incident was played. Judge Newton-Price accepted that “there was no immediate danger to the rescue worker”, but said Thomas’s actions were a deliberate ‌‌attempt ‌‌to disrupt rescue efforts. The far-right activist had built a large online following and organised gatherings of protesters on the UK’s southern coast in response to the arrivals of small boats. A government minister described the demonstrations as “thuggish”. The court heard that Thomas had five previous convictions, including in 2016 for kidnapping. Separately, he is set to stand trial in London next June accused of multiple offences, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover in March. UK government data shows the number of people arriving in small boats to British shores has fallen, though the crossings remain a prominent political issue which has dogged successive governments. Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration activists have called for more action.

events.title: 'Life is hell on board': Dozens of crew members remain on Villa Vie's Odyssey 3 weeks after residents disembarked
events.summary: Villa Vie Residences' cruise ship, Odyssey, is at anchorage near Singapore. TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images The residents got off, but more than 60 crew members are still stuck aboard Villa Vie's Odyssey. Crew members say cabins lost AC, WiFi cuts out, and no one knows when they'll leave. "I just want to go home," one staffer told Business Insider. The residents of Villa Vie's Odyssey left more than three weeks ago, but dozens of crew members are still marooned on the cruise ship while it's anchored near Singapore . Two crew members told Business Insider they are struggling with difficult conditions aboard and a growing desperation to get home. "For us, it's becoming a real torture because all we want is to go home," one of them said. If you have worked on the Villa Vie Odyssey and have a story to share, get in touch with this reporter: jzitser@businessinsider.com . More than 60 crew members remain aboard On October 27, Villa Vie residents were given a few hours' notice to disembark in Cambodia after the company suspended operations of the never-ending cruise — which offered passengers the chance to live out the rest of their days at sea by buying cabins for between $119,999 and $439,999. The shutdown followed months of cash-flow difficulties that Villa Vie attributed to rising fuel prices, resulting in deteriorating services, shifting itineraries, and requests for residents to provide additional funds . While residents are now ashore trying to salvage their retirement plans , Villa Vie cofounder Mikael Petterson confirmed to Business Insider on Thursday that between 63 and 67 crew members remain aboard the Odyssey, which was placed under arrest pursuant to a court order. In a November 8 statement, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said that "the crew onboard are reported to be well, and arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors." This week, two crew members said life aboard had taken its toll. "While we have been at anchorage, the atmosphere has been quite difficult," said the first crew member. The second said, "Life is hell on board." 'The conditions aren't ideal' During the past 24 days, the crew members said some cabins lacked air conditioning as temperatures climbed above 90 degrees. Both complained of frequent internet outages, making it difficult to call their families at home. The second crew member said laundry services had been suspended and the crew bar had been closed. The crew members also said the uncertainty over when they will be able to disembark has been particularly challenging, "We feel like everybody forgot about us," the second crew member said. "The conditions aren't ideal," Petterson said Thursday, "but they're not torturous." A view of Singapore from the Odyssey, which is at anchorage. Business Insider Petterson said the Singapore sheriff must approve the Odyssey's move from anchorage to a berth before crew members can disembark because the vessel is under arrest. Singaporean authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. He said Columbia Cruise Services, the vessel's manager, is responsible for operating the ship. "It's Columbia's responsibility completely to operate the vessel and improve welfare and all that stuff," Petterson said. Petterson said NRP Maritime Asset Management, which now controls the ship as the administrator of Oceanus Capital's loan, is responsible for putting money toward improving conditions. Oceanus Capital's mortgage claims against Villa Vie led to the ship's arrest. Julia Siebert, Columbia Cruise Services' chief operating officer, declined to comment. Nicolai Heidenreich, managing partner of NRP Maritime Asset Management, told Business Insider he does not "dispute" the crew members' claims of internet and air conditioning outages and reduced services, but pushed back against their framing of the overall experience. "What you're telling me, what you're describing, is not correct," he said. Heidenreich added that crew members have now been paid for September and October, acknowledging that Villa Vie had previously fallen behind on paying out salaries, prompting some residents to organize fundraisers for the crew. The crew members said they hope to disembark by the end of the week, though they said their expected departure dates have repeatedly shifted. "I just want to go home," the second crew member said. "I want to forget about Columbia, Villa Vie, and everything." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026
events.summary: The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. The demand was driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence. Costs rose 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. It also pushed timelines and risk for contractors. All that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. The gain this year was about three times the last ten-year average. The report looked at over 500 live or recently completed projects in 62 global markets. It also included a survey of 400 experts in the global data center industry. While there was some stabilization in cost inflation this year, it was not enough to offset the huge growth in not just demand but speed of construction and delivery. "More aggressive schedules tie to contractors in particular and subcontractors baking in more risk allowances in their pricing," said Paul Barry, North America data center lead for Turner & Townsend. "So whether that's acceleration allowances, whether that's more overtime and labor attraction allowances, even just higher fees for taking on the risk of delivering at a faster pace than what they would traditionally take on." All of those things, combined with the spike in demand and the strain on the supply chain, translate into higher costs, he added. Capital expenditure on global data centers is projected to rise from about $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion per year in 2050, according to a recent report from PwC. The U.S. is expected to capture almost half of all global investment in AI infrastructure, which includes both data centers and chips. Power is, of course, key to all data centers, and 56% of those surveyed by Turner & Townsend globally said it was a major obstacle to delivery. Just over half said utility connections typically take between one and two years, and almost a third reported timeframes of over two years. Costs for power vary regionally — from $15.01 per watt in Silicon Valley to $10.51 per watt in Dallas, based on a typical 60-megawatt design. As with every type of construction in the U.S., labor continues to be a significant headwind. Just over one quarter of respondents said their contractor capacity, that is, the ability to manage construction backlogs, was sufficient. Going forward, Barry said he expects costs to moderate somewhat, with cost increases in the 6% to 10% range in the next year. A lot of the major projects have already started or are starting now, so cost risk has been baked into those contracts. "If this demand continues, then there'll be more continued flow of project starts and so on, but I think we've hit a big surge in 2026, especially of new big major projects that have been procured," said Barry. events.title: The Pentagon has been reacting to weapons shortages instead of getting ahead of the problem, watchdog finds
events.summary: Without a broader plan that links production, requirements, and funding, the US risks ongoing shortages. US Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Emilio Murphy The Department of Defense is risking running low on munitions without better planning, a watchdog report said. Officials told the GAO that DoD is reacting to global events rather than focusing on total requirements. Major concerns surround US stockpiles and munitions management. The Pentagon's lack of an overarching plan for munitions production and requirements risks leaving it poorly positioned to adequately address munitions shortages, according to a new government watchdog report. The US war in Iran has raised major concerns about the state of weapons stockpiles, especially for critical munitions. While the Department of Defense can track munitions across the department, it lacks a broader plan and a centralized office for its long-term munitions goals and strategies. On Thursday, the Government Accountability Office , a Congressional watchdog agency, released a report on the need for planning and leadership to address persistent munitions shortages. The GAO said that the US war in Iran has spotlighted the importance of addressing munitions stockpiles and industrial base production issues. Conflicts in the Middle East, as well as US support for Ukraine, have taken a heavy toll on US munitions stocks. The problem, the GAO said, is that "DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements. According to DoD officials, in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements." The office cited the US Army's ramp-up in production of  155mm artillery shells as an example. The increase addressed shortages from US support for partner nations, Ukraine in particular, rather than the deeper need for better overall munitions management. "Without developing an overarching munitions plan that identifies long-term goals, strategies for achieving such goals, and metrics to gauge progress, DOD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement," the report said. Further, the Pentagon doesn't have a single office that's in charge of improving munitions stockpiles or planning. The services told the GAO that without dedicated leadership to address these issues, it could be challenging to pursue progress. And while DoD can track munitions data across the services, the report said that there is limited oversight and regularity for reviewing this information. The department-wide data is fueled by individual tools from each service. The GAO recommended developing an overarching plan to improve production-linked inventory levels, funding, and long-term goals; establishing a single point of authority for that plan; setting regular timelines; and developing a data management plan to track munitions. When asked about the GAO report, a DoD official told Business Insider the US is "fully equipped to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing, and has already conducted successful operations across multiple combatant commands while preserving a deep, ready stockpile to defend our people and interests." It declined to comment on external studies or reports. The Pentagon has been working with US defense firms to significantly increase Patriot interceptor and Tomahawk missile production, among other weapons. The US has burned through critical munitions like these combating Iran and its proxies in the Middle East. Replenishing key stockpiles, however, could be a substantial undertaking. In the meantime, some officials and analysts have raised concerns that US stockpiles of certain weapons may be dangerously low, threatening readiness for other conflicts, including a potential war with China .
