events.title: We took our 4- and 6-year-olds to Europe and hardly visited kid-focused attractions. It made the trip better for us all.
events.summary: Our family spent almost three weeks in Europe learning about local culture and history through a range of activities — most not kid-focused. Blythe Chadim On a family trip to Europe , my husband & I chose activities that appealed to us, not just our kids. We kept our kids engaged in more adult activities by finding ways to relate them to their interests. We set expectations ahead of each activity and left room for spontaneity and flexibility. In July, my husband and I took our then 4- and 6-year-olds to Europe for almost three weeks. We began in Poland visiting Warsaw and Krakow, then spent almost a week in Prague before ending our trip at a resort in the Austrian Alps . At each destination, we prioritized things we, as adults, would enjoy — and it made the trip better for everyone. Everything we did was kid-friendly, but our activities weren't necessarily kid-centric. Of course, we made time for park play, and we even visited a children's museum in Prague, but by choosing activities my husband and I wanted to experience, we gave our children a more culturally rich vacation, which is exactly what we wanted. We avoided sightseeing fatigue by keeping the activities varied We let our kids guide us through the Royal Castle to keep them engaged. Blythe Chadim I love learning about history, especially in places I've never visited, but even I don't want to spend every waking moment in a museum. Luckily, there are many ways to experience history and culture, and we kept that in mind as we chose activities for our family. In Warsaw, we visited the Royal Castle, which was severely damaged in World War II. My husband and I wanted to see this incredible story of resilience and reconstruction firsthand, and we knew our kids would enjoy the opulence and grandeur of a real-life castle. We chose a self-guided tour, and our kids enjoyed having their own earbuds and listening devices. We let our boys guide us through the castle, which kept them more engaged, and we left when they'd had enough. In Krakow, we tried one of Poland's most iconic foods in a family-friendly pierogi-making class. Our cooking-class guide shared her family's pierogi recipe, passed down through generations. My husband and I loved connecting to Polish culture in such a special way, and our kids loved the hands-on experience of kneading the dough and shaping their own dumplings. The best part was how excited they were to try the pierogi because they had helped make them. It's an experience we still talk about, and can even recreate at home once in a while. We made a few special stops at the Czartoryski Museum in Krakow. Blythe Chadim Though museums weren't our main focus, we toured two in Prague and one in Krakow. In each place, we chose a few exhibits we wanted to see and left the rest of our time open. At the Czartoryski Museum, we saw Leonardo da Vinci's "Lady with an Ermine," and it was a highlight of our trip. The museum was also small enough to walk through without our kids getting antsy. At the National Museum in Prague, we saw gems and minerals. Blythe Chadim At the National Museum in Prague, we focused on the gems exhibit and Czech history. The museum is quite large, so we broke it up into multiple days, including a stop at the children's museum. We also took ice-cream breaks when the kids needed to rest. We found fun ways to relate our cultural activities to our kids' interests Our kids were intrigued by the Wieliczka Salt Mine. Blythe Chadim Tell your kids you're taking them to visit a salt mine and you might get some eye rolls. But tell them you're going on a real-life Minecraft adventure, and their reaction becomes wonder and excitement. And for our tour of the Wieliczka Salt Mine near Krakow, we did just that. The 135-meter descent was a lot of stairs for young kids, but the excitement of bringing their favorite video game to life kept them motivated. The Wieliczka Salt Mine made the boys feel like they were in a video game. Blythe Chadim We explored excavated caves and intricate carvings, and the kids may have licked the walls a time or two, but with something different around every corner, our boys stayed engaged. Our children also love music, and now that our oldest takes guitar lessons, he's become more interested in how other instruments work. We used that interest to introduce our boys to classical music by taking them to a nighttime concert at Saints Peter & Paul Church in Krakow. We enjoyed live music together at Saints Peter & Paul Church. Blythe Chadim After a long day of exploring, we knew our kids would be tired, so we sat in the back so we could sneak out when we needed to. They especially enjoyed watching the violinists, and our youngest pretended to play along. When we took the kids to Europe, we did the things we wanted to do as adults, but we also kept our expectations in check and got creative. We found that by keeping our expectations grounded in reality and finding fun ways to include our kids in more adult activities, we enjoyed a more well-rounded experience. events.title: Anthropic slid to just 5 cents above its IPO price, a stunning reversal of its first day pop
events.summary: Anthropic’s stock has come within a hair of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made one day earlier during the AI company’s blockbuster Wall Street debut . Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.05 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading, before recovering some ground and climbing to roughly $87 in midday trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded. At its lowest point on Friday, Anthropic’s stock traded just a nickel above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion. The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks. Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day. Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless of how the stock trades in the coming days and weeks. events.title: Silicon Valley needs to listen to the AI backlash
events.summary: Ashley’s view Earlier this week at Semafor’s inaugural Silicon Valley & the World conference in Palo Alto, I interviewed Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat with some 2028 presidential buzz. At one point during our conversation, as he beamed in virtually from Washington, he described one particular data center project in New Mexico as being the size of “a thousand football fields.” A participant in the front row rolled their eyes and shook their head, clearly exasperated at the comment. As the interview continued, the audience laughed when Kelly joked about President Donald Trump threatening to jail him, stared blankly when he spoke about regulating AI, and perked up when he talked about how Washington is thinking about investigating the controversy surrounding ousted Nvidia leader Jensen Huang. Toward the end of the interview, Kelly made the 1,000 football field comment again, in the context of data center projects needing to be built thoughtfully — with guardrails and input from the local community. The same audience member that rolled their eyes raised their hands in disbelief. After the interview, I fact checked the claim that a data center project could be quite so large. According to a report in the investigative outlet Searchlight New Mexico, the project’s acreage is indeed equivalent to about 1,000 football fields. The exchange was a perfect encapsulation of the dynamic between Silicon Valley and the rest of the United States right now: Those building the AI-powered future are well aware that not everyone is bought in on their vision. That was abundantly clear after the midterm elections, in which more than 40 ballot measures seeking limits on data center growth passed across the country, and candidates who embraced pro-AI regulation messaging handily won in competitive districts. But the post-midterms soul-searching only goes so far, at least at the Rosewood Sand Hill, nestled among top venture capital firms dotting Menlo Park. From my permanent perch in Washington, I know that Silicon Valley knows they have a problem. But they’re squinting at it, red-teaming it and trying to invent their way out of it. It’s reminiscent of how Big Tech companies viewed the lawsuits, Capitol Hill investigations, and Justice Department antitrust cases that piled up as anti-tech sentiment grew in the last decade: Expensive, and a hindrance to all-out growth; but ultimately, the cost of doing business. Tech executives are looking to keep building and growing, even as the financing gets more precarious and the infrastructure as well as the regulations that control it get harder to navigate. For many in Silicon Valley, AI anxiety and disdain can be explained away as a marketing problem, an education problem, or a location problem. For these innovators, it is not, however, a sign to stop. This attitude from AI and tech companies is not new. But the raging anti-AI public sentiment, considerably more intense than the tech anxiety of past years, is. And governors and state lawmakers across the country are ready to pounce (some are already pouncing ). So while newly empowered Democrats on Capitol Hill may not ever manage to pass significant AI regulation in the new Congress, and companies will surely find ways to appease Washington, tech leaders should perhaps take complaints about the scale of AI growth, including data center projects matching the size of 1,000 football fields — more seriously. Room for Disagreement Tech executives may face a hostile environment in Congress and in most of the states, but they’ve still got a powerful ally in the White House. Trump this week warned that “robust” regulation of AI could “stifle” development. “We won’t allow that to happen, frankly,” he said at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

events.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
events.summary: The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times. In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports. And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move. The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers". Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow". Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK? This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout. Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East. It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers. This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry. However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced. No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports. Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape. In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market. But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports. The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040. Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation. The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes. The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale. Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people". Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year. A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal. This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments. The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations. Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions. The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off. There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents. The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere. Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals. The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market. The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

events.title: 10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
events.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start. A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse. For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive. list 1 of 4 UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail list 2 of 4 Andy Burnham says Brexit is what the UK’s ‘enemies’ wanted list 3 of 4 Britain’s Brexit woes: ‘I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did’ list 4 of 4 EU and UK agree a reset deal to end ‘decade of drift’ Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world. As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician , a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British. Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice. The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner. On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”. The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit. Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc. According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded. “Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera. According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto. However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular. “The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda. “I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.” Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain. Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership. While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held. “Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option. Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.

events.title: Anthropic shares slump on second day of trading as markets reel from AI sell-off
events.summary: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains and Asian markets record worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? Anthropic’s shares fell at the start of its second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies. As they dropped, the wider stock market fell with them, with the Nasdaq Composite erasing all its gains for 2026. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly entered correction territory. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began. US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2.9% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1.66% in morning trading in New York. Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.” Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies. In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI. European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO . Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said. Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending. “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.” Nvidia shares fell by 7% after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China. Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war. Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March. Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

events.title: Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’
events.summary: Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds. Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm. "We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's " Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business. Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday. "We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here." The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic. In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF , Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX , representing more than 21% of the fund together. Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses. The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year. Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble. "Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

events.title: I've been to all 50 states. There's one unexpectedly cozy city that should be on everyone's winter bucket list.
events.summary: In my opinion, Charleston, South Carolina, is the best US city to visit in the winter. Emily Hart I've traveled to all 50 states and have found that some cities are even better in the winter months. In my opinion, Charleston, South Carolina, is the perfect winter-travel destination. From lower rates at some hotels to quieter beaches, I love visiting Charleston in the offseason. When thinking about a winter getaway , many travelers likely imagine either a snow-covered mountain town or a warm, tropical destination. After visiting all 50 states, though, I've found that my favorite destinations generally fall somewhere in between. For instance, Charleston, South Carolina , might not be the first place you think of when booking a winter getaway, but in my opinion, it's well worth the trip. The winter weather in Charleston is pretty mild. Emily Hart Unlike more traditional winter destinations like Aspen or Stowe, Charleston doesn't revolve around snow or skiing. It also doesn't have the heat of a tropical beach destination . However, the mild winter means I can enjoy plenty of time outside. With average highs in the 60s and lows around 40 degrees Fahrenheit from December through February, I feel like I get the best of both worlds — and it's part of the reason why I keep going back. I love being able to grab a coffee and stroll through the historic downtown and French Quarter in the morning, enjoy a patio lunch or happy hour in the afternoon, and even walk along a nearby beach in just a light jacket. The offseason means I can enjoy the city without the usual tourist crowds. Emily Hart Hospitality is a major part of Charleston's economy, with tourists visiting in large numbers year-round. But if, like me, you enjoy a more peaceful winter getaway, the offseason is where you'll find the fewest crowds. Especially after the holidays, I've found the city is quieter for a month or two before spring festivals and higher tourism begin again. Luckily, though, there's still plenty to do in the cooler months. The holiday season brings many street fairs and special events, and the popular Southeastern Wildlife Exposition and Lowcountry Oyster Festival — which are both on my Charleston bucket list — take place in February. Visiting in the winter can be more affordable, too. Emily Hart For me, one of the best parts of traveling in the winter offseason has been the chance to stay at some of the area's high-end, luxury hotels for a fraction of what they might cost during peak season. Some hotels even offer discounted rates and complimentary upgrades during the cooler months. During my last visit in December, I was able to combine lower rates with my American Express Platinum Card hotel credit to stay at The Dewberry — a luxury property right downtown — for less than half of what I'd pay during other seasons. The holiday season is especially cozy in historic downtown Charleston. DenisTangneyJr/Getty Images There's something magical about the holiday season in Charleston. My last visit was about a week before Christmas, and I loved spending my days walking around the extravagantly decorated homes on the Battery, wandering through the American Gardens Holiday Market, and strolling King Street to browse shops for holiday gifts. I especially love that I don't need an itinerary to enjoy Charleston — during any season. Some of my favorite moments have been simply wandering the historic streets, taking in the decorations, and stopping into shops wherever something caught my eye. The nearby beaches are typically quiet in the offseason. Emily Hart One of the things I love most about visiting Charleston in the winter is that the coast feels completely different from the busy summer months. Several beautiful beaches are within driving distance of downtown, and in the winter, I can often walk for long stretches without seeing many other people. Edisto Beach, Isle of Palms, Folly Beach, and Kiawah Island are a few of my favorites, each with its own personality. Although it might not be swimming weather, I love taking a long walk along the shoreline, watching the waves, and enjoying the kind of peace and quiet you rarely find at these beaches during peak season. The shorter days also make it easier to catch a sunrise or sunset along the coast before heading into town for dinner at one of Charleston's seafood restaurants. events.title: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
events.summary: Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit. Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell. Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares. Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock. Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources. “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July . events.title: Qatar and Germany deepen strategic ties during emir’s Berlin visit
events.summary: German chancellor says Qatar pledged $16.5bn in new investments as the two countries deepen defence and technology ties. Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has held talks with German leaders in Berlin on expanding defence and diplomatic cooperation, broadening a relationship long focused on trade and investment. At a joint news conference with the emir on Friday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Qatar had pledged an additional 15 billion euros ($16.5bn) in investment, while the two governments planned closer cooperation on security and technology. list 1 of 3 What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza? list 2 of 3 US official says Hormuz insurance hits $64m: Is the strait really open? list 3 of 3 Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island Merz said the investment would strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), computer chips and aviation. He also expressed Germany’s interest in developing defence industry partnerships with Qatar, while the two countries agreed to work together to improve protection against cyberattacks. The discussions come as Qatar continues pushing for a diplomatic solution to end the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and gas supplies. Sheikh Tamim also held talks with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who proposed a regional security conference for the Middle East. Their meeting on Friday covered efforts to end the Iran war and restore maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a joint statement by both countries. Steinmeier suggested bringing regional governments together to build trust and address security disputes. The emir invited him to the Doha Forum, an international policy conference in Qatar on December 5–6, to discuss the proposal further with other countries. At the emir’s news conference with Merz, the German leader acknowledged Qatar’s role in mediating between the US and Iran and called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen permanently. He also urged Tehran to halt its military nuclear programme. Sheikh Tamim stressed that “peace and sustainable peace and security can only be reached through a political agreement”, adding that dialogue is the only way forward. He also described Germany as an important partner. Sheikha Alanoud bint Hamad Al Thani, a fellow at the Middle East Council for Global Affairs, a regional research institute, told Al Jazeera in Berlin that the relationship had previously been driven mainly by commerce. “But now we’re seeing a strategic dialogue,” she said, pointing to increasingly similar security concerns, including drone attacks on Qatar and hybrid warfare threats facing European countries. That shift builds on a 2023 agreement to establish formal strategic talks between the two countries. Sheikh Tamim told Steinmeier on Friday that Qatar wanted the first round to take place, according to Qatar’s state news agency, QNA.

events.title: US Senate passes bill to speed up energy project approvals
events.summary: The legislation aims to lower energy bills by making energy project approvals faster and limiting court challenges. The United States Senate has passed a bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects as lawmakers face pressure to bring down electricity bills and meet growing demand fuelled by the growth of artificial intelligence. The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday as 15 Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, backed the bill and two Republicans voted against it. list 1 of 4 As AI data centres guzzle energy, can we harness their wasted heat? list 2 of 4 US Senate advances major bill boosting energy infrastructure list 3 of 4 Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO list 4 of 4 Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up President Donald Trump had urged senators to pass the measure and said he would sign the bill if it passes the House of Representatives. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten timelines for federal reviews for energy projects and limit how approvals may be challenged in court. It would change several environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to weigh a project’s environmental effects and gives the public a chance to weigh in before a project is approved. The four senators who coauthored the bill, two from each party, argued that Americans are tired of paying high utility bills while projects that could lower them are stuck in the planning phase. “We are going to make it easier to build in America again and make life more affordable for American families,” Republican Senator Mike Lee of Utah said. Lee negotiated the deal with fellow Republican Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The bill would also require large AI data centres to pay for more of the cost of upgrading power grids to serve their needs. The vote came after rising electricity bills and opposition to data centres became major issues in the midterm elections this month. Democrats campaigned on promises to rein in the industry and swept to victory. They won control of both chambers of the new US Congress, which will convene on January 3. Until then, Republicans hold slim majorities in both chambers. Industry groups representing both renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies backed the bill, saying current delays can stretch timelines by a decade or more. Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the National Wildlife Federation, warned that the bill would weaken protections for water and wildlife and make it harder for communities to challenge project approvals. Other groups said it would lead to more fossil fuel development. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centres, oil and gas pipelines and [liquefied natural gas] terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the US,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. She called it a “gift to some of the biggest polluters in America”, arguing that any gains in renewable energy would be outweighed by emissions and pollution from the fossil fuel industry. Critics also took issue with how quickly the bill was moving, arguing that it was being rushed through Congress. Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell from Washington state said after meeting with tribal leaders that it would undermine tribal nations’ sovereignty and weaken protections for their water, land and wildlife. She called for more time to consider those concerns and amend the bill. Some Democrats who opposed the bill also argued the party should wait until January to push through stronger legislation that limits fossil fuel development while doing more to expand wind and solar power. The Senate passed the measure without adopting amendments pushed by Oregon’s two senators, including one that would ban data centres on public land and another that would prevent the Trump administration from cancelling energy grants and other Democratic initiatives for “purely political purposes”.

events.title: A judge confirms student-loan borrowers can be forced off a key affordable repayment plan
events.summary: A judge ruled that the Department of Education can involuntarily transfer student-loan borrowers off the SAVE repayment plan. J. David Ake/Getty Images A judge will allow the Education Department's forced transfer of student-loan borrowers off the SAVE plan. Borrowers said that, despite reaching their deadline to leave the repayment plan, no action has been taken. The department originally gave borrowers 90 days to transition off SAVE after eliminating the plan. The Education Department is allowed to move student-loan borrowers off an affordable repayment plan, a new legal filing said. A federal judge this week denied a motion filed by the law firm Public Goods Practice to stop the forced transfer of borrowers off the SAVE repayment plan. The Trump administration eliminated SAVE — a Biden-era plan that allowed for cheaper payments and a shorter timeline to debt relief — and started sending notices to enrolled borrowers in July with a 90-day timeframe to transition off the plan. If they did not move within their timeframe, the Education Department said, they would be automatically placed on a standard plan with the most expensive payments. Judge Loren Alikhan wrote in her ruling that the plaintiffs did not sufficiently establish harm, thus permitting the department to involuntarily move borrowers off SAVE. The case, however, is still ongoing — the ruling did not decide on the merits of the lawsuit, including whether borrowers should receive the relief they might have qualified for under SAVE before it was eliminated. While the department emphasized a 90-day timeframe to leave the plan, the deadlines have shifted. After 90 days, borrowers received a "final notice" extending their timeframe by an additional 30 days. The notice told borrowers this was their last opportunity to switch plans before being placed in a standard plan. However, some borrowers who remained on SAVE past their final 30 days told Business Insider they have remained in forbearance, and no action has been taken on their accounts. Public Goods Practice filed a request earlier this month to provide details on the timeline for the transfer. The law firm said in its filing that, when it asked the Education Department's counsel about timing for the transfer, it said it didn't "'know when borrowers whose 30-day period has expired will be moved to new plans.'" The department has not commented on its plans to involuntarily move borrowers off SAVE. Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com . events.title: All the connections between Haymitch and Katniss in 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping'
events.summary: Haymitch Abernathy and Katniss Everdeen are connected. Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is out in theaters now. The story sheds new light on the relationship between Haymitch Abernathy and Katniss Everdeen. This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games" series. After months of anticipation, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is finally in theaters. Fans have been clamoring for its release since Suzanne Collins published the "Sunrise on the Reaping" novel, which follows Haymitch Abernathy's experience in the 50th Hunger Games, in March 2025. Haymitch — portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in "Sunrise on the Reaping" — has long been one of the most fascinating characters in the "Hunger Games" universe, as the reclusive drunk Katniss meets in book one transforms over the course of the trilogy into one of her fiercest allies and protectors. The pair understand each other so well they can almost read each other's minds throughout the books, and in "Sunrise on the Reaping," Collins revealed Katniss and Haymitch are even more connected than readers thought. This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games" series . Katniss' father tied her and Haymitch together before she was born. In the original series, Katniss is from District 12. Murray Close/Lionsgate Katniss' father dies in a mining explosion before the events of the original "Hunger Games" trilogy . However, in "Sunrise on the Reaping," Collins reveals that Katniss' father, Burdock Everdeen, was Haymitch's best friend throughout their childhoods, and their close relationship helped Haymitch be better prepared for the Hunger Games. Specifically, Burdock taught Haymitch to set snares, which helped him find food in the arena. Burdock taught Katniss to make snares as well, and he also showed her how to hunt with a bow and arrow, which became her weapon of choice in the arena. The knowledge he gave her about plants also helped her survive. Burdock gave both Katniss and Haymitch skills that ensured they survived the Hunger Games. The Covey family shaped both Haymitch and Katniss. Rachel Zegler as Lucy Gray Baird in a still for "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." Murray Close/Lionsgate In her first "Hunger Games" prequel , "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," Suzanne Collins introduced readers to the Covey , a group of traveling musicians forced to remain in District 12 after the first rebellion. In the novel , the found family consists of three cousins, Lucy Gray Baird, Maude Ivory Baird, and Barb Azure Baird; a set of brothers, Clerk Carmine and Billy Taupe; and a wandering soul named Tam Amber. Lucy Gray won the 10th Hunger Games, becoming the first tribute from District 12 to survive the arena. A young Coriolanus Snow mentored her during her Hunger Games, and they had an ill-fated love affair that led to her mysterious disappearance at the novel's end. Collins leaves "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" open-ended, as it's unclear if Snow killed her or if Lucy Gray fled to the woods. In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch says that Burdock has Covey cousins on his mother's side, making Katniss a descendant of the Covey. Likewise, Haymitch's girlfriend, Lenore Dove, is a member of the next generation of the Covey, tying both Katniss and Haymitch to the family. In fact, Haymitch wouldn't have even been in the Hunger Games if not for his love for Lenore Dove. Katniss and Haymitch had parallel reaping experiences. Lionsgate Fims In "The Hunger Games," Katniss volunteers as a tribute after her younger sister, Primrose Everdeen, is reaped. Katniss is widely known as the first volunteer for District 12 — making it all the more surprising that Haymitch was not actually reaped for his Hunger Games either. During the reaping for the 50th Hunger Games, Woodbine, one of the male tributes from District 12, fled after his name was called. Peacekeepers responded by shooting him, and when Lenore Dove tried to help Woodbine's mother protect his body, Haymitch threw himself in front of her to stop Peacekeepers from hitting her. His interference led the Peacekeepers to select Haymitch as Woodbine's replacement. Later, in "Catching Fire," Haymitch and Katniss became the last two people ever reaped for the Hunger Games. The tributes were reaped from the existing victors in the 75th annual Hunger Games, making Katniss the only option for female tributes and Haymitch and Peeta Mellark the options for male tributes in District 12. Haymitch's name is selected, but Peeta volunteers as tribute in his place. Haymitch tried to protect Katniss the same way he did Lenore Dove. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate For longtime "Hunger Games" fans , Haymitch's decision to jump in front of Lenore Dove on Reaping Day likely felt familiar. He makes a similar decision in "Catching Fire" when Katniss attempts to stop a Peacekeeper from whipping her friend Gale Hawthorne. Haymitch jumps in front of Katniss and scolds the officer for cutting Katniss' face ahead of her wedding to Peeta Mellark. The scene is eerily similar, but unlike his teen experience, Haymitch helps de-escalate the situation with the Peacekeeper during the interaction instead of making things more tense, protecting Katniss in a way he ultimately couldn't protect Lenore Dove. The mockingjay pin is significant to them both. A Mockingjay pin from "The Hunger Games." MediaNews Group/Bay Area News via Getty Images In the "Hunger Games" universe, mockingjays symbolize rebellion against the Capitol. They came to exist after jabberjays, mutts the Capitol designed to spy on rebels, mated with mockingbirds, creating a new species. Their existence highlights that the Capitol cannot control everything. Mockingjays are also meaningful to Katniss and Haymitch specifically. Katniss wears a gold mockingjay pin that originally belonged to Haymitch's competitor, Maysilee Donner, as her token from her district during the games. In "Sunrise on the Reaping," we learn that Tam Amber made the pin for Maysilee, who didn't like mockingjays until Haymitch taught her their symbolism. She says she will wear it if she survives the games, but she isn't given the opportunity. Years later, Katniss dons it, bringing down the Capitol with the pin on her chest. Katniss reminds Haymitch of his district partner from his Hunger Games. Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate One of Haymitch's fellow tributes from District 12 is Louella McCoy, a 13-year-old girl who wears her hair in two braids. Haymitch grew up close to Louella, who had a crush on Haymitch when she was 5 and told him he was her sweetheart. She got over her feelings quickly, but Haymitch called her "sweetheart" for the rest of their friendship, which was cut short when she died before the Hunger Games started. events.title: ‘Expel invaders’: The dangerous promises of Spain’s far-right Vox party
events.summary: Spain heads to a snap election on November 29 with Vox campaigning on mass deportations, ‘remigration’ and ‘national priority’. Santiago Abascal, wearing a blue suit and tie, looks straight into the camera. His campaign poster makes three promises: giving Spanish nationals priority in access to benefits, cutting regulation and “remigration”. “It’s common sense,” the poster of his far-right Vox party reads. list 1 of 4 Catalonia’s new far right: How anti-Muslim sentiment is reshaping politics list 2 of 4 ‘I pay $500 for 5 square metres’: Spain’s protesters, in their own words list 3 of 4 Spanish court suspends far-right group over alleged hate crimes list 4 of 4 How will Spain’s housing crisis affect elections? With little more than a week to go until Spain’s November 29 snap election, opinion polls put Vox in third place behind the conservative Popular Party (PP), which is leading the race, and the governing Socialist Party. But with the Socialists’ potential allies fragmented and the PP projected to fall short of an outright majority, Vox could emerge as a kingmaker. The party, which once struggled to win a single seat in parliament, could join a PP-led coalition or back a minority PP government from outside the cabinet. Abascal was a regional lawmaker for the PP in the Basque Country. He left the party in 2013, accusing then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy of being too soft on the issue of Catalan separatism. He went on to cofound Vox. The new party positioned itself to the PP’s right, making Spanish unity its central cause. It called for an end to the country’s system of regional autonomy and championed the idea of the “true Spaniard”, who was Catholic, Castilian-speaking and loyal to the monarchy. Over time, the party started to adopt themes and tactics from other European far-right parties. “At the beginning, they were the ultra-conservatives of the right, but then they started to study the handbook of the populist radical right across Europe, and they became the Spanish version of it,” said Carles Ferreira, lecturer in politics at the University of Girona. In January 2017, Abascal made his international debut at a gathering of Europe’s far right in the German city of Koblenz alongside France’s Marine Le Pen and Frauke Petry, then-leader of the Alternative for Germany. But Vox was still a minor force at home, having won 0.2 percent of the vote and no seats in the previous year’s general election. That October nine years ago, Catalonia held an independence referendum in defiance of Spain’s Constitutional Court. A few weeks later, the Parliament of Catalonia unilaterally declared independence, plunging the country into a constitutional crisis. Vox, which had filed a legal complaint over the preparation for the vote, used the crisis to raise its national profile over its opposition to Catalan independence. It worked. Just over a year later, the party made its electoral breakthrough, winning 12 seats in the regional parliament of Andalusia in southern Spain. Four months later, it entered the national parliament for the first time by winning 24 seats. Vox had transformed from a fringe party with zero representation into a relevant political force. The first bullet point in its manifesto calls for the “immediate expulsion of all invaders”. Abascal has accused the Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people”. “It may well be that the upcoming elections will be the last ones to be decided by the Spanish people,” Abascal said on Thursday on X. He wants to ban the mass regularisation of undocumented immigrants and deport them. His manifesto calls for “remigration”, a plan to facilitate the expulsion of people who the party says do not contribute or who rely on public benefits. Throughout the eight-year tenure of the current government, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, according to the National Statistics Institute. Vox is also campaigning for “national priority”, a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits. Its exclusionary discourse often focuses on Muslim migrants. “With Catalan independence no longer dominating the political debate, Vox has shifted its focus to what it calls the ‘Islamisation of Spain’ and the threat of a ‘Spanish caliphate’,” said Steven Forti, professor of contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. “By hammering away at the issue, the party has turned it into a rallying point for voters.” Vox draws on the idea of Hispanidad, a shared Hispanic identity, to portray Latin American migrants as culturally closer to Spaniards. Spain has long welcomed Spanish-speaking people from Latin America. They represent the largest group of undocumented and documented foreigners in Spain, according to the Spanish think tank Funcas.

events.title: Don’t Bring Jensen Back
events.summary: Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar , the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd. Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . Under his leadership, billions of dollars ’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two ?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers. Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered. It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette? The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return. At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge. Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance.

events.title: White House replaces cyber director Sean Cairncross amid widespread tech outages
events.summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, and Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies is set to serve as acting director. The change follows a week of major U.S. technology outages affecting aviation, Microsoft services and government systems. The White House says it has no indication the recent outages were coordinated, state-sponsored or caused by a malign actor. White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies set to serve as acting director after a week of high-profile U.S. technology outages. The role, which advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates U.S. cyber policy across federal agencies, has been handed to Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, on an interim basis. A permanent national cyber director must first be nominated by the president and then confirmed by the Senate. Axios first reported Cairncross' exit, citing two White House officials who said President Donald Trump's chief of staff, Stephen Miller, pushed for his departure. The White House declined to comment. However, a source familiar with the White House's thinking told CNBC that the President fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position because he lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job. Davies has the credentials to excel in the position and has been Senate-confirmed, the person added. The Office of the National Cyber Director did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. It comes after a series of technology outages, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a worldwide Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency 's classified communications network. The White House has insisted that there are no indications of a coordinated cyberattack , state-sponsored activity or malign actor behind recent tech outages. Davies addressed her responsibilities in the new position and thanked Miller and Trump for their confidence late Thursday. "Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on," she wrote on X. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both congratulated Davies on her appointment. events.title: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
events.summary: Former GM CEO Dan Akerson says whoever replaces Mary Barra will have a difficult task because the next CEO will inherit rapid change in technology and the auto industry. Barra is the first female CEO of any major automaker, and the industry is facing ongoing challenges including artificial intelligence. Akerson's comments to CNBC come after The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside CEO candidates in addition to internal prospects. Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough." He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014. Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles. "It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change." Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson , CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable." His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession. Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise. "Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said. The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession. Stellantis , BMW , Toyota Motor , Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years. Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board. A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director. GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing. That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates." When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said. Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job. Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann , an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021. "Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job." Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946. Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker. "This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

events.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
events.summary: Published 20 November 2026, 00:12 GMT New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force. Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason. Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all". But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers. The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed. Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities. Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said. Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it. If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks". Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients. But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests. Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party. There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers. Airbnb host Lisa Clewes said her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests Edinburgh-based holiday home owner Fiona Venter told the BBC that Airbnb's new rules were "nonsense" and would not accept bookings if guests refuse to take their rubbish away. Talking about a time when she was worried she might get a mice infestation after six bags of rubbish were left in her cottage, she said: "I would rather have my house still standing." But Fiona said increased cleaning costs due to the rule change would be unfair to those who do clean up after themselves: "Why should they pay extra for the guests that choose to abuse a cottage?" Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules Published 21 October No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests Published 1 November The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said. The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees. Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably. events.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
events.summary: A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web. The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices. According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed. The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk. Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution. Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.” From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts. Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish. Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket. “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.” “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg. The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter. It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email. Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online. The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes. Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors. “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted. Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web. Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes. “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
