events.title: Home Depot's AI bot helps shoppers avoid the dreaded second trip
events.summary: Home Depot says its Magic Apron AI assistant now fields millions of questions per month. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Home Depot was one of the first major retailers to deliver a customer-facing AI bot. The Magic Apron assistant now fields millions of questions per month, often about DIY projects. The retailer says the tech is leading to more complete carts and higher customer satisfaction. If there's one frustration many DIYers experience, it's the sudden realization that you brought home the wrong supplies for the job. It's a problem Home Depot is hoping to solve with AI . The home improvement giant originally built its early reputation in part on knowledgeable store associates, including plumbers, electricians, and other tradespeople who could help do-it-yourself customers. Now, with AI, the company is trying to put that project-based know-how right into consumers' hands. The company was one of the first major retailers to deliver a customer-facing AI bot, called Magic Apron. The platform was specifically trained on products and projects that Home Depot has loaded into the tool over the past two years, so it can serve as an advisor to shoppers. "What's important for our customers is the project and not the product," Rebecca Godecke, president of Home Depot's online division, said in an interview. "I think it's really easy to do single-item selling, but that's actually not what we think AI is best suited for." Godecke said she was recently with a shopper who had loaded her cart with a replacement toilet and other items for the project. They used Magic Apron to snap a photo of the cart's contents to make sure they had everything, and it delivered a helpful warning. "Magic Apron was able to identify that and say, 'You have an incompatible wax ring. You need to go back to this aisle and try again,'" Godecke said. A Home Depot store in Colma, California David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images "The last thing you want is you've taken off the old toilet, and you're about to put the new one on and you figure out that, 'Oh, I've got the wrong wax ring!'" she added. "That's a terrible conundrum to be in." Home Depot's journey with its AI assistant was an evolution to add more and more capabilities. When it first launched, Home Depot began by putting its know-how into a chatbot on its website. In March 2025, the assistant made a public introduction in the company's app and on millions of product pages. The app could answer product questions, summarize reviews, and give some how-to guidance. At a December 2025 investor meeting, a Home Depot executive said the app was beginning to move away from just answering questions and that the company was using the AI tool to build shopping carts for customers. The next month, the company expanded its partnership with Google to extend the app's AI capabilities. After testing in stores, the company rolled out in-store capability in August tailored to each of Home Depot's 2,000-plus locations, so that the assistant could guide shoppers to the inventory and layout of a particular store. It can also detect and communicate in multiple languages. As consumers have been using AI more in their own lives, shopping assistants are fast becoming a must-have for major retailers , including Walmart's Sparky, Amazon's Alexa, and Target's Ask Target. Walmart and Target both said this week that customer adoption of their AI agents is growing fast. A Home Depot store in San Jose, California David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Home improvement rival Lowe's has Mylow , which was developed in collaboration with OpenAI and serves functions similar to Magic Apron. Lowe's CEO Marvin Ellison said Wednesday that MyLow answers over a million questions per month and that users have a conversion rate three times that of non-users shopping online. Godecke said Magic Apron now fields millions of questions per month, and they're often about DIY projects that go well beyond simply finding a single item. Employees are also using Magic Apron to help shoppers complete projects that might extend beyond their specialties, she said. For example, a garden center associate may know a lot about plants, but feel less confident about exterior lighting. By solving for an entire project, she said the Magic Apron tool is leading to more complete shopping carts that get it right the first time. And that translates to fewer return trips to replace or return improper items. "What we're seeing is that as you use it once and you're familiar with it, you come back and use it more," Godecke said. events.title: Trump secretary's Christian messages to staff went "too far," judge rules
events.summary: A federal judge said Thursday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins' overtly Christian messages to department employees went "too far" and put enough pressure on staff to raise a First Amendment violation. The big picture: The Supreme Court has repeatedly weighed the boundaries of the Establishment Clause . While the judge said Rollins could express her religious beliefs with interested colleagues, she concluded the department-wide messages overstepped those boundaries by amounting to coercion. But a USDA spokesperson slammed the decision as "a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary" in a statement to Axios. Catch up quick: The complaint from a federal employees union and individual staffers alleged Rollins sent "increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including an Easter email where she celebrated "the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind." The USDA employees who sued, who came from varied religious — and nonreligious — backgrounds, reported that the messages made them feel pressured to share Rollins' beliefs. What's inside: District Judge Trina Thompson ordered Rollins to "recognize certain boundaries when disseminating messages which convey religious content." She determined the messages overstepped and suggested "acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure." "After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion," Thompson wrote. She said she was not trying to regulate Rollins' own religiosity; rather, she directed Rollins to follow her own department memorandum on religious expression rights, which states employees can't "use official authority to pressure subordinates." The other side: The administration argued that the employees lacked jurisdiction and that the secretary's messages fell "within this Nation's deeply rooted history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse, including on holidays." Members of the Trump administration frequently discuss their Christian faith, though the president himself has had a complicated relationship with Christians despite the evangelical MAGA base helping him reach the White House. The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What we're watching: A USDA spokesperson said the department "is evaluating all options including a prompt appeal." events.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
events.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how? Mercedes-Benz 's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it. In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high. Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure." The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant. German auto industry faces restructuring Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure. Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country. "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot." A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Berger agreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation." In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable. Unions dig in amid fight for survival Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek . The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached. Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic. Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation. "We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW. China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage. Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500. Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?' A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security." PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China. These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms. "The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany. With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit. Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi , which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year. "Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned. Production remains resilient despite decline Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well. Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA). IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability. In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result?

events.title: My ex-husband and I celebrated our divorce at Olive Garden. We had breadsticks, went shopping, and went viral.
events.summary: Holly Zeilenga and her former husband, James, lunched at Olive Garden on the day their divorce came through. Courtesy of Holly Zeilenga Holly Zeilinger, a single mother by choice, married her fiancé, James, in December 2021. Their relationship ended five-and-a-half years later, but the pair remained on amicable terms. They celebrated the finalization of the divorce with lunch at Olive Garden , then a shopping trip. This story is based on an interview with Holly Zeilinger , 37, a piano teacher-turned-content creator from Madison, Wisconsin. It has been edited for length and clarity. I met my future husband, James, 37, online during the pandemic in August 2020. As a single mom by choice, I'd recently had my second baby. I was playing the video game "Guns of Glory" to win gift cards to put toward diapers. James and I were in the same alliance. For some reason, I mentioned the COVID-19 restrictions at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, which is near my home. He said he lived about 45 minutes away. Friendship evolved into romance We chatted online for about a month before I gave him my phone number. Then, in October, he came over to visit my kids and me, now 8 and 6. They got on with him like a house on fire, and he soon became a father figure in their lives. What began as a friendship developed into romance. James, a legal assistant, proposed the following April, and we got married at a small elopement chapel in December 2021. Zeilinga with James on their wedding day in December 2021. Courtesy of Holly Zeilinga Things were great. The children called him Dad, and we enjoyed doing things together as a family. James and I wanted a baby together, but experienced infertility. I probably had about 14 procedures, including IVF . We had a miscarriage, and then the little boy we were expecting died in my second trimester. Surrogacy became our only option, and we worked all hours to save up for the $100,000 fee. I was also doing crowdfunding, which took up a lot of time and energy. The whole thing was amicable Things came to a head this spring, when James and I had a frank conversation. I'm very open about my feelings, and he is more reserved. However, he told me that he needed to lessen his responsibilities and take a step back. We no longer had the same goals and decided to call it a day, filing for divorce in June. The whole thing was amicable. It was mainly because it had started off as such a good friendship that we went back to being only friends so easily. The couple on vacation during their marriage. Courtesy of Holly Zeilenga He moved out in July and got his own place. Still, he was always coming around to hang with the kids. They knew he was the kind of person who was going to stick around. There was a four-month waiting period before the divorce was finalized on November 2. It was a pretty straightforward financial agreement. I picked him up on the way to the courthouse. They said we could sit on different sides if we wanted, but we sat together. We each held up our hands to say, "I agree," and then it was over. We hadn't been to Olive Garden in forever James had texted me a few days prior to ask if I wanted to go out to eat after. My mom was picking up the kids from school, so it made sense. I mentioned Olive Garden because we hadn't been there in forever. We'd eaten there every so often during our marriage. So we drove to the restaurant and ordered our favorite super salad and breadsticks . It was relaxing and fun. There was a sense of excitement as we moved on with our lives. The pair celebrated their divorce over Olive Garden's famous breadsticks. Courtesy of Holly Zeilenga After lunch, we went to JCPenney to look for a nightgown for me. They didn't have anything good, so we went to Hobby Lobby to buy a star for the top of my holiday tree. I filmed the entire outing and put it on my social media platforms. It struck a chord with people and got more than five million views. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holly (@hollyzeilenga) Meanwhile, I dropped James at home, and he came around later that night to hang out again. We're keeping it consistent with regular visits so the kids see their dad. I'd be happy if James met someone else I'm going ahead with the surrogacy — using my eggs and sperm from the children's original donor — and James has my back. We discussed how we'd feel if one of us met someone else. It wouldn't be a problem at all. We'd be happy that the other person was happy. I'd definitely recommend that people have some form of celebration of their divorce when circumstances allow. It helped close one chapter and open another. events.title: Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more
events.summary: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh wants central bankers to talk less about where they expect interest rates to go. Instead, they're talking more. Bank of America says there has been more so-called Fedspeak over the past two weeks than in any similar period going back to the beginning of 2025. The conflicting communications strategies come at a critical time for monetary policy and the economy. In his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void. Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake. Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem , entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time. Largely on the sidelines in the debate is Warsh, who has expressed disdain for that sort of forward guidance and argued that it handcuffs policymakers long before they actually have to make a decision. But that hasn't stopped most of the other 18 officials who sit in on Federal Open Market Committee meetings. In fact, according to a Bank of America analysis, there has been more so-called Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any similar period since the start of 2025. "Warsh's refusal to guide markets might be encouraging the rest of the FOMC to speak more, not less," Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave said in a note Thursday. "There is always a range of views across the 19 FOMC participants. Typically, the Chair would weigh in, indicating to markets whether the hawks or doves are in ascendence," he added. "Absent this leadership, however, both sides might feel incentivized to speak more often and more forcefully." The increasingly vocal debate comes at a critical time for the Fed and has myriad policy implications. Bhave noted "a deepening divide" on the FOMC. The Fed's decision not to increase its benchmark rate at its October meeting "increasingly looks like a mistake," and as a result "the hawks have been very vocal of late," he wrote. Leading the charge is Waller, who has raised the possibility of hiking by half a percentage point when the committee next meets in December. Minutes from the October meeting hint at the tension, particularly when it comes to Warsh's refusal to provide guidance. The summary related that some officials who were looking for a hike in October "could have supported no change in the federal funds rate provided that it was clearly understood by market participants that further tightening was likely" — a statement that points toward the forward guidance that Warsh has insisted the Fed avoid. The minutes "revealed that some officials favoring a hike would have accepted a hold if the Fed had clearly communicated further tightening," market veteran Ed Yardeni wrote Thursday. "Warsh's communication philosophy may thus be limiting the Fed's flexibility precisely when it needs it most." Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted against the October pause in favor of a quarter-point hike, tiptoed around the forward guidance issue during a recent public appearance. Prefacing some observations she made about where she sees policy headed, Hammack noted that, "Those are not promises. Those are not commitments. They're not forward guidance, which is a hot-button topic. But what they are are a conditional set of expectations of where I think the economy can go, based on what I'm seeing." Hammack's comments illustrate a needle that Fed officials have been trying to thread: continuing to be transparent about their thinking without appearing locked into a future policy that changing economic conditions could render obsolete. Speaking Thursday, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee framed the argument around credibility. "I am sympathetic to the view that [Warsh] has expressed that let's not be so, in in our language, forward guidance-oriented, saying here is what I think rates are going to be at the next meeting," Goolsbee said, calling such pronouncements "falsely precise." However, he quickly separated forward guidance from transparency. "I think central banks should be careful about doing anything that undermines credibility," Goolsbee said. "That said, I also think that it's pretty important [that] each person who sits around that table explain how they see the world. What do you see in business conditions? You don't want to surprise everybody.

events.title: AI can help find holiday deals — but it's not great at spotting scams, experts say
events.summary: CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board About 16% of respondents in a Norton-commissioned survey said they had been scammed while shopping online during the holidays. AI can help scammers create convincing fake stores, while shopping assistants may recommend unfamiliar sellers, Norton's Leyla Bilge said. Verify unfamiliar sellers independently, compare reviews across sources and use a credit card when possible, consumer experts say. Artificial intelligence shopping tools can help consumers compare prices and find gift ideas, but experts say shoppers still need to verify unfamiliar retailers and sellers before buying. Scammers can use AI to make fake stores, product photos and reviews look convincing. It can also make creating and deploying websites easier, said Leyla Bilge, global head of scam research at cybersecurity company Norton. "The biggest impact right now we're seeing in AI is on coding," Bilge said. Scammers can register "thousands and thousands of fake e-shops online," she said, which increases the chances shoppers will encounter one. A Norton survey of 1,000 U.S. adults found that 16% of respondents had been scammed while shopping online during the holidays. Of those victims, 88% lost money, with an average loss of $394. The survey was conducted from an opt-in online panel between Sept. 10 and 21 by Dynata on behalf of Norton's parent company, Gen. Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead. Living abroad doesn't end U.S. tax obligations. What young expats need to know Inheriting a home can leave siblings with financial headaches — how to avoid mistakes Is the K-shaped economy ending? Finance pros weigh in SEC proposes investor exam to expand private-market access — how it could work Scams can have impacts beyond financial losses. In a survey of 3,110 U.S. adults released in June, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance found that 82% of respondents had encountered a scam in the past year. More than half, 59%, said the scam affected their mental well-being. More than half of GASA survey respondents said they had experienced repeat scams. If you put your address or phone number in an AI tool that turns out to be fraudulent, "you might get reached out to again with a much more sophisticated, much more targeted and personalized attack and scam," Bilge said. AI recommendations need a second look Among respondents who had used an AI shopping assistant or agent, 56% said it had recommended or completed a purchase from a retailer they didn't recognize, the Norton survey found. An agent focused on finding the lowest price may steer a shopper toward an unfamiliar seller, so experts say shoppers shouldn't treat its recommendation as vetted. "You absolutely need to check with the retailer directly," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More." Bilge said many shoppers make purchases on their phones through social media, sometimes with a single click, leaving them little time or incentive to assess where the link goes. Then, some still buy even if they're unsure of the site's legitimacy. The Norton survey also found that 35% of Americans had bought from a website or seller they thought might be a scam because the deal seemed too good to pass up. How to check a seller before buying Before buying from a seller or retailer, consumer experts recommend these steps : Go directly to a retailer's official website or app. Don't rely solely on a link from an AI tool or social media ad. Look for reputation red flags. Search the seller's name with terms such as "complaint" or "scam." Compare reviews across multiple sites. The Federal Trade Commission cautions that reviews and ratings can be fake or misleading. Verify the seller, even if the site uses "https." The FTC notes that "https" means a site is encrypted, not that the seller is legitimate. Pause before buying. Schulz recommends trying the "24-hour rule." Put the item in your cart, step away, and decide the next day whether you still want it. The pause can help prevent buyer's remorse and give you time to check for scam warning signs before you pay. While AI can narrow gift options and find the lowest prices, experts say shoppers should verify the store before handing over payment details — and, when possible, pay by credit card. Keep order details and receipts, too. The FTC says cardholders can dispute charges in certain cases, such as when merchandise never arrives. — CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

events.title: Anthropic's founders have a safeguard Jensen Huang never had
events.summary: Anthropic cofounders at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on the day of the company's IPO. CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . I bet Jensen Huang wishes he'd thought of this. Anthropic's founders have devised an ingenious way to make sure they don't suffer the same fate as Nvidia's ousted CEO : Give themselves control of the company. I've seen this movie before. In 2004, I covered Google's IPO for MarketWatch . Cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin insisted their search engine was so important to the world that they needed special voting stock to protect their mission. It worked. They retained control, and other tech founders, including Mark Zuckerberg , followed their lead. Now Anthropic is taking this idea even further. Its seven cofounders, including CEO Dario Amodei , collectively control 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special Class F share. No matter how many ordinary shares Anthropic sells, that voting power remains intact. A separate, independent trust , established to protect Anthropic's AI safety mission , holds Class T stock that generally lets it appoint and remove a majority of the board. Anthropic says these protections are necessary because AI is so powerful that its development must be shielded from short-term investor pressure. There's a more practical benefit: It's extremely difficult to oust leaders who control their company's voting power. Which brings me back to Jensen. He cofounded Nvidia 33 years ago , when it made video game chips . Back then, special voting stock was rare in tech. And claiming video games were too important to humanity to leave to ordinary shareholders would have been a tough sell. Today, Nvidia powers the AI revolution . But Huang owns only about 3.5% of its shares, without special voting rights. His board pushed him out. His supporters want him back . I suspect Jensen would do things differently if he could start again. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
events.summary: Anthropic underwriters exercised the “greenshoe” overallotment of shares, bringing the total amount raised to $93.5 billion. The AI company sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares at $83 per share in the record IPO. ANT stock closed 17% higher on the debut trading day. Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering , bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday. The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX , which held a record IPO in June. Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe." Anthropic defies the odds, holding record IPO despite ‘massively disruptive’ market Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices , Google , Microsoft , Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses. Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multitrillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout . CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI , now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise. The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone" in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic. "For us, it's like one stop on the journey," Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'" events.title: ‘Gloucestershire nouveau’: UK vineyard uncorks its 2026 answer to beaujolais
events.summary: Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years F orget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest. Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine. The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November . Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest. Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s. Customers can buy the wine directly from the vineyard’s shop or try it in its restaurant. In the 1980s, the harvest used to begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year, according to Three Choir’s winemaking director, Martin Fowke. This year’s prolonged summer of warm temperatures – and rain at the right time – meant the first grapes were picked on 20 August, a week earlier than the previous record set in 2025. The harvest ended on 9 October, by which time 200 tonnes of grapes had been collected across the vineyard’s 30 hectares (74 acres). The 2026 First Release is a run of 5,000 bottles of a dry, white wine containing solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes. “We now have an extra month to make the wine. We had riper raw material and longer in the winery,” said Fowke, calling 2026 a “record-breaking year”. He added that higher sugar levels and lower acidity allowed winemakers to make a product that was not possible in Britain 30 years ago. The early timing of the harvest surprised even the Three Choirs winemaker Jack Abbotts, who was on his summer break when picking started. “It’s usually a safe week for me, but this year it all snowballed,” he said. The changing climate has made it possible to grow grapes on a commercial scale in Britain, but it also brings challenges. “We found it hard this year,” said Fowke. “People kept saying: ‘This hot weather must be good for you’, but it was difficult because we knew the heat and lack of rain was challenging for farmers. We don’t need it to get any warmer, that’s for sure.” Vines have been planted as far north as Yorkshire and Scotland , as Britain’s wine industry expands. More than 1,100 vineyards are now registered in Britain. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning While Britain remains far down the list of global wine producers in terms of volume – behind countries including Uzbekistan and Tunisia – it is the fastest-growing wine region in the world , according to the property group Knight Frank. The area of planted vineyards in the country has quadrupled since the turn of the century, it reports. Some of the newer, smaller vineyards do not have their own winemaking facilities, relying on contract winemakers such as Three Choirs. The Gloucestershire vineyard also produces wine for about 40 others, including Llanerch, located west of Cardiff. English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, when the equivalent of 16.5m bottles, or 124,377 hectolitres, was produced, according to the industry body WineGB. The data for the 2026 harvest will not be available until early next year, although WineGB said in August it was “optimistic” about the size and quality after the hot growing season. If the UK climate continues to change and summers such as 2026’s become the norm, Three Choirs may consider growing new varieties. “We can evolve and change, but we would be planting cabernet sauvignon like they did in Bordeaux 50 years ago,” said Fowke, noting the shift from white to red grapes. “But that is not what we set out to do.” In the fog and damp of November in Gloucestershire, pruning of the vines ready for the 2027 growing season has already begun. “To have two good years in a row is not uncommon, to have three is unusual,” said Fowke.

Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all. I didn’t say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell. — Cassandra Unchained (@michaeljburry) November 19, 2026 Nvidia shares opened about 4% lower on Friday, while CoreWeave and Nebius fell around 7%. The trio are down about 42%, 55%, and 65% respectively from their intraday highs on October 6, the day before the current AI drawdown began. The NYSE Semiconductor Index has slumped by about 30% over the same period. On November 11, the day before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO, Burry urged shareholders in a Substack post to " get out " of the AI chipmaker's stock. He predicted it would grow more slowly and its profit margins would shrink without the prolific dealmaker in charge. Burry cautioned that Nvidia partners such as Nebius and CoreWeave — so-called "neoclouds" that build data centers and rent access to Nvidia chips and other AI infrastructure — could be caught in the fallout in a November 12 post. He said they've "benefited greatly from Nvidia's market power and largesse, which seems to have entered a new paradigm now." Burry declared on August 12 that "Nebius is what the top of a boom looks like." The stock closed at $259 that day, 62% higher than its November 19 close. A week earlier, on August 6, Burry said he couldn't resist shorting Nebius and Oracle, saying it was a "bit like shooting fish in a barrel." He's also shorted Nvidia, CoreWeave, and chip indexes this year. Burry has been loudly skeptical of the stratospheric rise in AI stocks since he pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing a Substack about his personal investments a year ago. The contrarian investor, one of the few people to predict and profit from the collapse of the mid-2000s housing bubble, has warned AI companies are overinvesting in fast-depreciating assets such as microchips and data centers. He's also called out their aggressive accounting, circular-financing deals, and dangerous levels of debt and off-balance-sheet liabilities. Burry emphasized in a late Thursday post on X that he has far deeper concerns about Nvidia and its partners and peers than Huang's alleged extramarital affairs, and a potentially less AI-friendly environment with Democrats in charge of the House and Senate. "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough," he wrote. events.title: The man behind the Millennium machine
events.summary: Photo Courtesy of Millennium; BI One of the most important people in the hedge fund industry has never traded, doesn't oversee investing calls, and rarely meets with backers. That Ajay Nagpal, the president and chief operating officer of $95 billion Millennium Management, is considered so vital is a testament to how much he has transformed an industry centered on star traders and billionaire founders into institutions designed to outlast them all. The infrastructure Nagpal has built over his 13-year stint has allowed the New York-based manager to grow from less than $20 billion when he joined in mid-2013 to five times that today and trade countless asset classes across more than 140 outposts globally. Now, the machine Nagpal helped build will be under a microscope. Millennium has raised $22 billion in fresh capital (more than the firm managed when he joined) as choppy markets and fierce competition for investing talent complicate the task of putting that money to work. The fact that Nagpal's platform can handle new money at all — to say nothing of tens of billions of fresh cash — shows how much of an outlier Millennium is. Many of the manager's peers are closed to new capital, including, most recently, Balyasny Asset Management. He "might have the hardest job in hedge funds," according to one former Millennium executive who worked with him. "He has to manage the organization and Izzy," who isn't "known for his patience," this individual said, referring to Israel Englander, the firm's billionaire founder who launched the fund 36 years ago. Business Insider spoke to dozens of people who know the press-shy executive, who cut his teeth across different banking giants before moving to the buy side, to understand how he got to his seat, what makes him an effective leader, and how he's changed the industry for good. Millennium declined to comment. The firm did not make Nagpal available for an interview. The unlikely hedge fund executive Despite the 2008 financial crisis upending the banking industry he'd spent 16 years working in, Nagpal adapted quickly. At Barclays, which had acquired his former employer, Lehman Brothers, out of bankruptcy, he focused on clients with big ambitions and an appetite for taking risks that banks no longer could: multistrategy hedge funds like Millennium. Two people who worked with him at Barclays at the time remember him identifying the opportunity these now-omnipresent funds presented and focusing the bank's prime brokerage on servicing them. Millennium was the unit's biggest client during Nagpal's time as global head of prime services, these people said, but it was still a surprise when he left to join them. While hedge funds have poached banks' traders for decades, executives like Nagpal weren't high on many funds' wish lists. The industry was known for being founder-driven and light on management layers and bureaucracy, two things sprawling investment banks have in spades. But Englander's vision for his firm doesn't end with him. The ambitions of the billionaire required someone with Nagpal's expertise to transform it into an institution that, like Ken Griffin's rival firm Citadel, many in the industry compare to pre-IPO Goldman Sachs. "The machine is going to keep going. It's not dependent on one person. But 10 years ago, that wasn't the case," a former Millennium executive said. Izzy Englander founded his firm in New York in 1989. Millennium Since then, Millennium has become, in many ways, the gold standard for a multistrategy hedge fund platform, also known as a "pod shop." These firms manage money through independent teams focused on different asset classes and geographies, rather than a single portfolio with one decision-maker calling the shots. It's the largest employer in the space with more than 7,200 employees across the globe and 370-plus investing teams. Underpinning the entire operation is what one former Millennium leader called the organization's "core" — the non-investing operations, like technology, investor relations, trade settlement, recruiting, and more, typically seen as the less glamorous part of the industry. It allows them to constantly review the risks of the hundreds of portfolios run by its investing talent, whom the firm is quick to cut if they lose money. Nagpal, this person said, "industrialized" these operations so that part of Millennium felt more like an old-school investment bank. "It balanced the non-investment side and the investment side — they're equally powerful," this person said. Nagpal described his approach as finding the balance between using its scale while still giving its trading personnel a personalized feel in a Q&A posted on Millennium's website. "The best of big and the best of small," he said. Scale and the never-ending need for talent The dozens-strong internal recruiting force known as business development is one of the firm's most important units. The team is responsible for replenishing and expanding its portfolio manager stock to keep the Millennium machine humming. Since Nagpal added president to his title in 2022, the group has reported to him and evolved into a quasi-allocator, flexible enough to offer compelling investment talent a PM seat within Millennium or a chunk of money to run as an independent fund manager. In 2024, the firm hired roughly 160 PMs , about three a week, Business Insider previously reported. It's put billions to work with dozens of externally run managers, including the firm of Millennium's former chief investment officer, Jain Global. Nagpal's fingerprints are all over the deal to bring Bobby Jain back into the firm's orbit. Jain, Millennium's former CIO, shocked the industry when he decided to return $6 billion in assets to his external investors to exclusively manage money for Millennium. The deal moved fast thanks to the long-standing relationship and "reservoir of trust" between Nagpal and Jain, a person involved said. "We didn't have to wait for lawyers to wordsmith it," the person said. Bobby Jain, second from the left, and Ajay Nagpal, far right, worked side-by-side at Millennium. Jared Siskin/Getty Images for Madison Square Park Conservancy One allocator who invested in the firm's most recent fundraise argues that the machine is more important than its investing talent at any one point in time. None of this is cheap, of course, and multistrategy funds have increasingly relied on pass-through fees, which allow them to charge investors for the costs of running the business, to fuel their growth. Millennium has also been the most aggressive among its peers in extending the time it takes for an investor to withdraw their money. A decade ago, roughly 25% of the firm's capital could be redeemed in a quarter. Now, only 5% can, a person familiar with the firm's capital base said. events.title: I traveled in business class on Amtrak's fastest train. It wasn't worth the $180 price tag.
events.summary: The author rode in business class on the Amtrak NextGen Acela train. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I could have saved $140. My seat wouldn't have been as comfortable or spacious, and I would have spent 30 more minutes in it. Still, business-class on Amtrak's fastest train wasn't worth the price to me. Business class means different things to different trains. Take it from me. I've spent 26 hours riding the rails in business class around the world. The best business-class experience I've ever had in the US was an Amtrak ride I took in September 2025. I booked a trip from New York City to Washington, DC, on the Amtrak NextGen Acela train for $180. The three-hour ride felt extremely comfortable and a tad luxurious. In the end, though, I couldn't see myself splurging for it again. I took Amtrak's NextGen Acela train from New York City to Washington, DC. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The Amtrak Acela is an express service between Boston and Washington, DC. The train line introduced a new fleet on the route in August 2025, known as NextGen Acela. In addition to being the fastest Amtrak train with a top speed of 160 miles per hour, the NextGen Acela has modern interiors and high-tech amenities. I spent $180 on a business-class ticket. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The Amtrak Acela trains only have two classes — business and first. I booked my business-class ticket for $180. Out of curiosity, I looked at the pricing for coach seating on the regional Amtrak train, which is 30 minutes slower than the Acela. It was $40. When I arrived at Penn Station in NYC, I sat on the floor to wait for my train. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My train was scheduled to leave at 10 a.m., but it was 90 minutes late. I briefly considered passing the time in the Metropolitan Lounge, an elevated space overlooking the train hall with cozy seating and complimentary snacks and refreshments. First-class passengers and those traveling in sleeper accommodations can enter the lounge for free, but other Amtrak riders must pay $50 for a single-visit pass. Since I'd already splurged on the business-class ticket, I headed to the standard waiting room instead, but there wasn't a single empty seat. So I plopped on the floor against the wall until it was time to board. Since I wasn't in first class, I didn't get priority boarding. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When I got in line to board, I was reminded that business class is just a standard ticket on the Amtrak Acela. Unlike business-class rides I've taken that also had coach seating, this trip didn't include the perk of priority boarding. The business-class car had a sleek, modern look. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Retractable window shades, exposed overhead bin space , informative screens, and ergonomic seats made the car feel like a step up compared to business-class Amtrak trains I've booked in the past. The seat was much more comfortable than most I've booked on Amtrak trains. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Soft, cushy, spacious, supportive — these words popped into my head when I settled into my business-class seat. A reclining function and footrest made the ride even more comfortable. Power outlets, USB ports, and a reading light were all conveniently located on the side of the seat. In front of me was a tray table and a foldout cupholder. With 5G WiFi on board, I spent most of the ride streaming YouTube videos. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Most Amtrak trains I've been on have had WiFi, but in my experience, the connection is often too weak for much more than a Google search. I was stoked when the NextGen Acela's 5G WiFi was fast enough to stream YouTube videos without any issues. I passed the time by watching live sessions of my favorite bands. The bathroom was spacious, clean, and modern. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I've learned to set the bar low for train bathrooms. Stocked toilet paper, soap, and paper towels are not a given. Cleanliness and extra space aren't either. In my experience, some business-class bathrooms are no different from those in coach. So I was ecstatic when I stepped inside the lavatory on the NextGen Acela. The automatic door opened into a spotless space that felt big enough for two people to do jumping jacks simultaneously. I also appreciated the touchless water, soap, and dryer functions on the sink. I found it aesthetically pleasing too, with bold red accents and trendy touches, from the shelf to the mirror. Although it was much more comfortable than sitting in coach, I didn't think a business-class ticket was worth the high price point. A coach car on another Amtrak train. Joey Hadden/Business Insider "Amtrak travelers always have their preference. If they want to experience these premium trains with enhanced amenities, they can," an Amtrak representative told Business Insider. "Or, if they prefer convenient and affordable downtown-to-downtown service up and down the Northeast Corridor, Northeast Regional trains offer a comfortable and enjoyable way to travel throughout the Northeast Corridor and points beyond." The next time I take an Amtrak train, I'll miss the cozy seat, elevated bathroom, high-speed WiFi, and shorter travel time. Still, these perks weren't enough for me to consider Acela's business class to be worth more than quadruple the price of a coach ticket. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: First lady Melania Trump with President Donald Trump in the White House Rose Garden. Ron Sachs/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesNIH Melania Trump is an enigmatic first lady who has, at times, been an infrequent White House presence. There was a 32-day stretch this summer where she did not make any public appearances. Recently, she announced a scholarship fund at an LSU football game and gave out candy on Halloween. Melania Trump has been known as an enigmatic first lady since President Donald Trump's first term, but her public appearances and outfit choices can provide a window into her approach to the role. Ahead of the 2025 inauguration, Melania Trump told Fox News that she planned to divide her time between the White House, Trump Tower in New York City, and Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida. This schedule has at times made her an infrequent presence at the White House. Over the summer, there was a 32-day stretch from mid-July to mid-August where she did not make any public appearances. However, she has attended numerous events during Donald Trump's second, non-consecutive term, such as the premieres of her "Melania" documentary and docuseries, King Charles and Queen Camilla's state visit, and appearances promoting her Fostering the Future and Presidential AI Challenge initiatives. Melania Trump's muted fashion choices could also indicate a more guarded approach to the role of first lady. At White House events, she has largely appeared wearing suits and neutral basics in black, beige, cream, and gray. It's a departure from the bold outfits she often chose during Donald Trump's first term. A spokesperson for the Office of the first lady declined to comment. Take a look at the first lady's White House activities and appearances thus far. January 20, 2025: Melania Trump attended the inauguration. US President Donald Trump (L) and First Lady Melania Trump arrive for the Liberty inaugural ball in Washington, DC, on January 20, 2025. JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images Melania Trump held the Bible as Donald Trump was sworn in for his second non-consecutive term, and the couple danced together at several inaugural balls later that evening. For the swearing-in ceremony, Melania Trump wore a navy coat and skirt by Adam Lippes, an American designer. She accessorized with a matching wide-brimmed hat by Eric Javits. Her black-and-white inaugural gown was designed by Hervé Pierre. January 21, 2025: The president and first lady joined Vice President JD Vance and Usha Vance at the National Prayer Service. U.S. President Donald Trump, first lady Melania and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance with second lady Usha attend the National Day of Prayer Service at the Washington National Cathedral in Washington, U.S., January 21, 2025. Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS The service, the last of Donald Trump's inaugural events, was held at the Washington National Cathedral in Washington, DC. January 24, 2025: Melania Trump and Donald Trump visited California and North Carolina to survey damage caused by natural disasters. U.S. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump attend a briefing on wildfire damage as they visit the Pacific Palisades neighborhood that was damaged by the Palisades Fire, in Los Angeles, California, U.S., January 24, 2025. Leah Millis/REUTERS Melania Trump joined Donald Trump to visit Los Angeles in the aftermath of multiple wildfires and neighborhoods in North Carolina damaged by Hurricane Helene . Together, they met with first responders and residents who had lost their homes and businesses. Melania Trump was photographed hugging and shaking hands with those affected by the natural disasters. February 22, 2025: Donald Trump and Melania Trump hosted the National Governors Association dinner at the White House. US President Donald Trump and US First Lady Melania Trump arrive for the National Governors Association Evening Dinner and Reception in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on February 22, 2025. ROBERTO SCHMIDT/AFP via Getty Images Melania Trump wore a black Dolce & Gabbana tuxedo, similar to the outfit she chose for her official White House portrait , while posing for photos with governors from across the US. Donald Trump thanked Melania Trump in his speech, saying that she "made the evening beautiful." March 3, 2025: She participated in a roundtable discussion on the "TAKE IT DOWN" Act targeting revenge porn. U.S. first lady Melania Trump, U.S. Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Elliston Berry attend a roundtable discussion on the "Take it Down Act," a legislation against revenge porn, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., March 3, 2025. Kent Nishimura/REUTERS "TAKE IT DOWN" is an acronym for "Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks." The act criminalizes the publication of non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated deepfakes, and requires websites to remove them. events.title: Meet the potential 2028 presidential frontrunners from both parties
events.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Vice President JD Vance, and former Vice President Kamala Harris are among the early frontrunners for the 2028 presidential election. Ariana Drehsler / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images / Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images / Megan Varner/Getty Images Now that the midterms are over, the race for 2028 has unofficially kicked off. Dozens of Democrats have reportedly been considering a presidential bid. Meanwhile, the Republican Party is deciding who will be Donald Trump's political heir. The race for the 2028 presidential election has (unofficially) begun. After the Democratic blue tsunami in early November's midterm elections , both parties are starting to look ahead to their next presidential nominees. A wide range of political figures — from heirs apparent to former candidates and rising party stars — are already making moves that could lay the groundwork for a White House bid. In the Democratic Party , there are numerous potential candidates , and some reports have said that dozens are now being considered after the dust has settled from the midterms. Republicans, meanwhile, are starting to reckon with their own succession fight . Vice President JD Vance is widely seen as Trump's successor, but the GOP's midterm losses have raised questions about whether his close connection to some of the administration's most unpopular decisions could hurt a potential campaign. If you're looking ahead to 2028, these might be some faces worth familiarizing yourself with. JD Vance Tom Brenner/Getty Images Party: Republican Home state: Ohio Current role: Vice President of the United States As the current first-in-line in the US presidential succession, JD Vance is widely considered Trump's heir apparent and the most obvious Republican contender for 2028 . But Republican midterm losses have raised questions about whether Vance's close alignment with Trump could become a liability. Vance has said he has not made up his mind about whether to run for president in 2028. He has said that he and his wife would discuss "what comes next for our family" as a factor in determining his political future. Vance's office did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Kamala Harris Scott Olson/Getty Images Party: Democratic Home state: California Current role: Former Vice President of the United States Former Vice President Kamala Harris might be on the national ballot once again in 2028. The 2024 Democratic nominee has built-in name recognition and a vast national donor network, as well as strong support within the party, although some Democrats fear her record might be too closely attached to the pitfalls of the Biden administration . Harris has said she is thinking about another presidential run, though she has not yet made a decision. Harris' office did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Marco Rubio Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images Party: Republican Home state: Florida Current role: Secretary of State The many-hats-wearer of the Trump administration, Marco Rubio, has also emerged as a name to consider for the 2028 succession, with Trump even saying in a recent interview that " Marco's great " when asked about potential successors other than Vance. The former 2016 presidential candidate has publicly declined to discuss a possible presidential run, telling The New York Times in November that he "literally will not talk about 2028 anymore" and saying he would support Vance if he decides to run. Gavin Newsom David Swanson / AFP via Getty Images Party: Democratic Home state: California Current role: Governor California's outgoing governor Gavin Newsom has become one of the Democratic Party's most visible national messengers, directly challenging conservative opponents and adopting an aggressive communication style. Newsom has said that he is considering a run , though he has also said that he will not run if Harris enters the race. Newsom's office did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Ron DeSantis Alex Wong/Getty Images Party: Republican Home state: Florida Current role: Governor The outgoing Florida governor and former 2024 Republican primary candidate Ron DeSantis has remained a recognizable face in the Republican Party . In the aftermath of the midterm elections, some Republicans have renewed talks about DeSantis as a potential post-Trump alternative. DeSantis has not announced a 2028 bid but has declined to rule one out. At a discussion at the University of Notre Dame after the midterms, he said that if "there's an opening, there is an opening — if I think I can be of service, I can be of service." He also responded to a November Washington Post report that he had contacted a potential campaign consultant: "I have not called a single person," he said. DeSantis' office did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Pete Buttigieg Katie McTiernan/Anadolu via Getty Images Party: Democratic Home state: Indiana Current role: Former transportation secretary Having built an unexpectedly strong national following after his 2020 primary campaign, former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg has remained one of the party's most polished national communicators and has continued to campaign for Democratic candidates nationally. He has said he is "more inclined than not" to run again, while stressing that he has not made a final decision . Buttigieg's primary political action committee, Win The Era, did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Josh Shapiro Josh Shapiro, governor of Pennsylvania, during an election night event at The Fuge in Warminster Township, Pennsylvania, US, on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. Incumbent Josh Shapiro is projected to win the Democratic governor primary in Pennsylvania, according to the Associated Press. Photographer: Joe Lamberti/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg/Getty Images Party: Democratic Home state: Pennsylvania Current role: Governor A swing-state governor, Pennsylvania's Josh Shapiro has strengthened his national case with a commanding reelection victory. Shapiro has not publicly said whether he is considering a presidential run. After the midterms, Shapiro told NBC News' Kristen Welker that his focus "right now" is on governing Pennsylvania and taking advantage of the new legislative trifecta in the state to advance policy, saying "that's the work I'm focused on doing." Jon Ossoff Erik S. Lesser / AFP via Getty Images Party: Democratic Home state: Georgia Current role: US Senator Senator Jon Ossoff's reelection victory in Georgia prompted renewed speculation about a potential 2028 presidential run. The young lawmaker has a compelling profile as a Democrat who has proven capable of winning in a closely divided state. Ossoff has repeatedly and explicitly said he is not running for president in 2028 , despite some voters' enthusiasm for a potential campaign. Ossoff's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment

events.title: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next?
events.summary: Bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Though investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto also has had other pressures. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery. The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX. "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market." "Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin."

events.title: SEC Charges Indianapolis-Based Backward Hat Capital and Its Co-Founders With $560 Million Dollar Offering Fraud and Obtains Emergency Relief
events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has obtained a temporary restraining order, asset freeze, expedited discovery, and other relief against Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital, its co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s company Indianapolis-based Traders Point Capital, and Joseph Anderson to halt an ongoing Ponzi scheme. The SEC complaint alleges that Backward Hat, Williams, and Johnson fraudulently raised approximately $560 million from more than 2,000 investors and transferred more than $220 million to themselves to fund their luxurious lifestyles. According to the SEC’s complaint unsealed today, between about July 2022 and the present, Williams and Johnson utilized a web of entities to raise money from investors for alleged algorithmic high-frequency foreign exchange (FX) trading. Instead, the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi-like payments to previous investors and misappropriated investor funds to purchase exotic cars and expensive homes, to fund other unrelated businesses they owned, and to fund Johnson’s gambling habits. “The promise of a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money,” said Anne McKinley, Acting Associate Director for the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office. “We encourage the public to use the resources on Investor.gov to educate themselves on the traps and gimmicks bad actors use to lure them into fraudulent schemes.” As the complaint alleges, Williams and Johnson lured investors, including some of Williams’s investment advisory clients at a former employer, and used a network of promoters to sell limited partnership interests in a series of private funds to investors. All the while, Williams and Johnson promised that investor funds would be converted to crypto assets and then used to engage in FX arbitrage using a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm which they claimed always returned at least 6% per month. The complaint also alleges that Johnson expanded the scheme by raising money for another series of private funds he created under the names AI Capital and Traders Point Capital, which allegedly offered a similar investment opportunity as Backward Hat Capital. Also charged in the scheme is Joseph Anderson, who allegedly created fake financial reports for distribution to investors, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report, from a so-called third-party independent audit firm. The reports falsely stated that the purported returns generated by the Backward Hat funds had been confirmed and verified through a review of bank and brokerage records. In reality, Anderson and his company allegedly did not perform financial audit work, were not independent, and had significant financial interests in the scheme, and the reports contradicted bank records. The SEC’s complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, charges Backward Hat Capital, Traders Point Capital, Williams, Johnson, and Anderson with violations of the antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 and of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Williams and Traders Point Capital are also charged with violations of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against the defendants. The complaint also names an individual and several entities associated with the defendants as relief defendants and seeks from them disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest. In parallel actions, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York filed charges against Williams and Johnson and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) filed charges against Williams, Johnson, and several Backward Hat Capital entities. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the CFTC, the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Southern District of New York and the Southern District of Indiana, the FBI, the Indiana Securities Division, and the Utah Division of Securities. events.summary: Durban’s DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is among a number of African artists featured on the soundtrack of the highly acclaimed video game Grand Theft Auto VI. Born and raised in South Africa, he is considered a pioneer of Gqom , a subgenre of electronic music that emerged in the early 2010s. He began making dance music for his cousin, starting with Kwaito before turning to Tribal House and later helping to found Gqom alongside Naked Boyz and Rudeboyz. Nigerian singers Burna Boy and Asake also feature on the video game’s soundtrack alongside Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor , and South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela. — Leah Quinn

events.title: Senegal's president enacts budget by decree after rejection
events.summary: Senegal’s president enacted this year’s revised budget by decree on Thursday after it was rejected by parliament. Bassirou Diomaye Faye took the step a day after lawmakers voted down the first part of next year’s spending plan, widening a rift with the president that threatens to delay a new IMF loan. The proposed $12.3 billion budget for 2027 trims spending as the government tries to meet the lender’s conditions. Ousmane Sonko, the parliament speaker and a former ally of the president, opposes the government’s plans to cut expenditure and restructure foreign debt. Faye could again use his powers to enact next year’s budget by decree once parliament’s deadline expires in December, though some analysts expect him to dissolve the chamber first and call a parliamentary election for early next year. Final approval of the $2.2 billion IMF deal, agreed in principle in September, would help Senegal regain access to international debt markets, where some of its bonds traded below half their face value on Thursday. The new program would replace one that was frozen after billions of dollars in unreported government debt surfaced in 2024. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Kenya selects US-led Frontier Minerals for mining project
events.summary: Kenya chose a US consortium to develop a key mining site, handing Washington an important asset in its strategic contest with China to secure access to critical minerals used in electronics and defense equipment. Kenya said preliminary studies suggest Mrima Hill, in the southeast of the country, contains rare earth mineral deposits worth billions of dollars, as well as niobium, a metal used in aerospace manufacturing. Frontier Minerals, a three-company grouping, said it would focus on developing processing and refining capacity in Kenya in line with the government’s push to add value to mineral exports. Kenya’s mining minister told Semafor in September that extractive industries currently make up around 1% of the country’s GDP, but the government was targeting a 10% contribution within the next decade. Beijing dominates global supply chains for the minerals needed for data center construction, defense equipment, and the energy transition. Washington has announced agreements with several African countries — including DR Congo, Nigeria , and Zambia — in its drive to reduce US manufacturers’ reliance on China. — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park
events.summary: Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset . Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory. Wendy Jones, 68, a grandmother from Hereford, was sitting in her mobility scooter for bingo with about 100 others when the ceiling collapsed. She was among six guests to be treated in hospital after the incident and died six months later. A postmortem examination revealed a clear link between the injuries she suffered and her subsequent death. Britannia Jinky Jersey, the parent company of Pontins, pleaded guilty at Bristol crown court to failing to discharge its duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. On Friday the company was fined £1m for the offence. Stephen Bennison, 60, an unqualified contractor who had been employed by Britannia Jinky Jersey to install soundproofing in the ceiling, was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months. An investigation by Avon and Somerset police, Somerset council and the Health and Safety Executive found that the ventilation ducting had originally been poorly installed decades earlier, before the site became a Pontins holiday park. But the immediate cause of the collapse was linked to soundproofing work carried out in 2015 when it was under Pontins’ control. During that work, Bennison stacked heavy sound-insulation slabs on top of the ventilation ducting, the investigation found. It concluded that the insulation in the ceiling appeared to have been leftover material which could not be returned to the supplier – and stacking it on the ducting served no practical purpose. The court heard that neither Britannia Jinky Jersey Ltd nor Bennison properly assessed whether the ducting could safely bear the significant additional weight. Rachael Taylor, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “A family holiday ended in tragedy because basic safety responsibilities were not met. “Wendy Jones had every right to expect she was entering a safe environment. Instead, failures by Britannia Jinky Jersey Limited and Stephen Bennison resulted in the collapse of ventilation ducting and the death of a grandmother who was there to play bingo.” Taylor said Jones’s death was avoidable. She added: “Those responsible for the safety of the public must ensure work is carried out competently and safely. Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Mrs Jones, and anyone else affected by this tragic incident.”
