events.title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
events.summary: Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams. Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack. But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked , spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries . Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing. The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether. Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”. Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees : “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.” And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks , with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration. Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered. Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany . AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days. And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC. Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say , was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.” “The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month. While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years , the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers. But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “ Black October ” and whatever other cyber horrors await us. In their quest to render us obsolete , Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months. The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too. When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up. These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .

events.title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
events.summary: María Jesús Contreras for ProPublica When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.  The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California. “I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?” Read More Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t. If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households. ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted. Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?  We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.   How does SNAP theft happen? Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby. Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.  In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case , a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits. What can I do to protect my benefits?  Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal. Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel , allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.  But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries. Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits. “I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said. Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there. An investigative analyst with the Secret Service removes an overlay from a skimming device they found on a card reader at a convenience store in California. Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica The inside of the card skimmer Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica What can I do after my benefits have been stolen? If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.  You can also report the crime to local law enforcement and to the agency within your state in charge of investigating SNAP fraud — for example, in Texas, SNAP theft victims are advised to report it to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. ( This map shows where to report SNAP fraud for each state).  A representative for Texas Health and Human Services said, “HHSC takes the security of our client’s benefits very seriously. SNAP card skimming has been a persistent problem across the country, including Texas.”  While there have been some large-scale investigations into SNAP theft, individual reports don’t often lead to an arrest. More than 40 of the victims we heard from said that they had reported their stolen benefits to a SNAP office, the EBT card customer service line, the police or all of the above. A handful also called the stores where they’d noticed unrecognized transactions on their card history, and two said they contacted the FBI. events.title: Outages trigger congressional scrutiny of AI-enabled attacks
events.summary: The Trump administration says the string of recent tech outages across the country can be attributed to companies rushing to patch their networks as AI exposes vulnerabilities in old software. Cybersecurity experts say the government is largely telling the truth about the crashes’ causes, but the situation reveals a bigger problem: Much more digital instability is coming, and it will be worse. At the same time, President Donald Trump’s hands-off approach to AI signals to the private sector and Congress that the government may not be there to help as outages multiply, or when AI-enabled attacks inevitably result in even more mayhem. A tech lobbyist and a Hill source told Semafor that a letter this week from Sens. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton urging the AI task force he leads to “launch a national effort to confront a new generation of AI-enabled cyber threats” is a bipartisan sign of things to come from Capitol Hill come January. Bolstering AI cybersecurity will emerge as a key legislative goal along with broader AI bills on catastrophic risk, the sources said. “It’s one thing that Hugging Face got attacked,” the lobbyist said. “Wait until it’s a mid-sized community bank. What’s the event that will get Congress and the White House to do something?” Meanwhile, the agency charged with protecting US infrastructure from cyber threats, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, may go even longer without a permanent director. Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said they would place holds on Trump’s nominee, Palantir Chief Information Security Officer Michael LoSapio, after he denied Thursday during his confirmation hearing that there was an attack on the US Capitol on Jan 6, 2021, and refused to say who won the 2020 presidential election.

events.title: Cairncross departs abruptly after widespread tech outages
events.summary: The News White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out and is being replaced by Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies, multiple officials told Semafor Thursday . The shakeup follows a series of disruptive tech outages that have raised fears about US cybersecurity — and has kicked off a heated dispute about whether Cairncross was fired or left voluntarily. One White House official and a person familiar with the White House told Semafor that Cairncross was fired on Thursday; the official said that finding a new cyber director was one of the first things Stephen Miller did in his new role as White House chief of staff, and both said Trump had supported Cairncross’ removal. But another senior White House official and a person familiar with the matter strongly disputed the idea that Cairncross had been fired, telling Semafor that he resigned — and not because he was asked to. A second source familiar with the matter, who said Cairncross had been fired, said the past week exposed the need for someone “more competent, with the expertise needed to execute this position.” Axios first reported the news of Cairncross’ departure and Davies’ new job. Ashley’s view Someone was bound to take the fall for a string of tech outages that have left the country terrified about what services might get disrupted next — even if the most basic (and likely true) explanation is that organizations are rushing to patch software bugs discovered by AI programs and are crashing their systems in the process. Cairncross told me as much this week after I interviewed him on stage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, in what would end up being his last public interview as a White House official. Director of National Intelligence Clayton echoed his words two days later, so I don’t think being off-message here was his issue. The alarming and disruptive outages over the last week, at least one of which appears to be ongoing , may have provided Cairncross’ detractors the perfect opportunity to bump him. But long before Miller took over for Susie Wiles, some in Washington said they’d seen Cairncross, whose previous experience includes being a lawyer for the Republican National Committee, as unqualified to be a cyber official. Rumors of his potential ouster go back as far as this spring, though he helped shape the administration’s June executive order on AI and cybersecurity, including its framework for voluntary pre-release testing of frontier models. He survived the “Mythos moment” — when Anthropic’s latest model made Washington freak out about AI’s cyber capabilities — but he couldn’t make it through FAA routers failing, Microsoft Outlook crashing, JP Morgan pausing services, and the NSA’s internal comms network going down. Davies does not have an easy job ahead; she will have to prove the public can trust her to help the country get through the precarious digital moment we’re in. I asked Cairncross this week if the administration would ever fully release that June executive order, much of which has not been public. “I expect that we will be making it much more clear how this is working in practice,” he said. He also told the room of CEOs that if they have questions about preparing for this cyber moment, they should reach out: “If you haven’t heard from my office, we are more than willing to engage,” he said. “We’re happy to be hyper-responsive.”

events.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
events.summary: Published 20 November 2026, 07:26 GMT Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures. Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said. The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks. Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying . The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes. Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended. Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser. The latest official sales figures , external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling. "Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said. "Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again." The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September. As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October. The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers. Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further". Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises. Published 23 October Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October. Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn. Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago. These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate. Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel. events.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
events.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned. Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets. The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members. Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs? This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million). The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful." " Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said. At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year. How else is Lufthansa planning to save money? The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets. Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter. The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing. In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization. In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook. events.title: The US national cyber director is stepping down
events.summary: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown. Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director. We’ve reached out to the White House for comment. events.title: Why is gold price going down?
events.summary: Gold is heading for its worst weekly decline in eight months as interest-rate fears, forced liquidation and bearish bets combine to intensify bullion’s sell-off, with investors increasingly betting on further declines. Analysts warn prices could fall further before finding a floor. Spot gold dropped 2.7 per cent to $3,525.25 an ounce on Friday, after touching a 14-month low, and was down about 9.2 per cent for the week. Gold prices hit a record $5,515 an ounce in January. A stronger US dollar and mounting expectations of another Federal Reserve interest-rate increase eroded demand for the metal. “Gold is facing a perfect storm of macro headwinds and forced liquidation,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone. A hawkish Federal Reserve has revived the dollar and pushed Treasury yields higher, creating a challenging environment for gold, which pays no interest and becomes less attractive when returns on other assets rise. However, the sell-off is being amplified as investors rush to raise cash, selling assets – including gold – to meet margin calls amid a broad decline in global equities, especially technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade . Buying into IPO boom? So, are investors liquidating gold assets to buy into the initial public offering IPO boom? The surge in demand for high-profile AI listings, including Anthropic , could offer another competing destination for investor capital as gold loses momentum, according to analysts. However, there is little evidence yet of a direct rotation from gold into IPOs. “The aggressive sell-off across global equities, notably the crowded AI trade, has forced investors to reduce leverage, meet margin calls and raise cash,” Mr Weston said. “Gold has become a source of liquidity rather than a destination for safety.” Gold’s Friday slide reflects bearish forces that are now reinforcing one another, said Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “A hawkish Federal Reserve has revived the dollar, pressuring gold,” he said. "At the same time, the sell-off in AI-linked equities has prompted investors to raise cash across asset classes instead of driving them into havens." The Fed’s message that inflation remains too high has prompted markets to price in an almost certain rate increase in December, with the possibility of further tightening in January and March, Mr Weston added. Investors bet on further declines The bigger concern is that selling pressure could have further to run. Trend-following funds have already increased their short positions in gold, while exchange-traded fund investors have yet to capitulate, leaving the possibility of more selling ahead, Mr Valecha said. Despite the aggressive decline since the onset of the Iran war , gold has struggled to find a durable bottom. Options markets are also signalling a shift in sentiment. Investors typically pay a premium for call options on gold as insurance against macroeconomic and geopolitical shocks. That premium is now shrinking relative to puts, which protect investors against price declines. But a sharp correction does not necessarily mean gold’s longer-term investment thesis has collapsed, but it marks a significant cyclical repricing after investors became heavily positioned for further gains. “The options market tells the story best,” Mr Valecha said. "Investors usually pay more for gold calls than for puts because they buy them as insurance against macro and geopolitical shocks. That premium is shrinking. Why isn’t gold acting as safe haven? Gold’s traditional role as a safe haven has not been lost, but it is being overshadowed by the need for investors to raise cash during a period of market stress. “Gold’s safe-haven characteristics haven’t disappeared, but they don’t operate in isolation,” Mr Weston said. "In periods of acute market stress, investors often sell what they can rather than what they want to." Gold is being sold alongside equities and other risk assets, while the dollar is attracting defensive demand and higher Treasury yields are making bullion less attractive relative to interest-bearing investments. “For buyers to return with conviction, I’d want to see three developments: a stabilisation in US real yields, a sustained pullback in the dollar and evidence that forced selling has largely run its course,” Mr Weston said. “Until then, geopolitical uncertainty alone may not be enough to restore gold's safe-haven appeal.” How low could gold prices go? With gold trading at about $3,525 an ounce, the immediate focus is whether buyers can defend the psychologically important $3,500 level. A sustained break below that could expose the $3,400 to $3,300 region, where longer-term investors and physical buyers may begin showing greater interest, Mr Weston said. Investors should wait for selling pressure to ease, volatility to moderate and, ideally, a reversal in the dollar and US real yields before concluding that gold has established a sustainable low, he added. The shift suggests traders are increasingly positioning for further downside rather than simply unwinding bullish bets, Mr Valecha said. Gold may, therefore, continue to fall more than it recovers, with any near-term rebound potentially proving temporary rather than marking a reversal in the trend. Mr Valecha also sees stronger support potentially emerging closer to $3,500 an ounce, despite the risk that prices could fall further in the near term. On the upside, bullion would need to reclaim $3,600 before moving towards $3,700. The former support zone of $3,800 to $3,850 could now act as resistance, Mr Weston said. Gold's price action suggests it could remain under pressure in the coming days, with next week's US economic data likely to prove important. For investors and jewellery buyers in the UAE, analysts advise adopting patience and a staggered approach to buying rather than committing all their money at a single price. Gold’s immediate downside focus is around $3,500 an ounce, following the break below the previous support level, said Frank Walbaum, market analyst at Naga.com. “A sustained move below this psychological level could expose the metal to further losses towards the $3,200 level,” he said.

events.title: Lufthansa to eliminate 1,000 jobs at struggling flagship airline
events.summary: Lufthansa will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees. Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its main airline in Munich and Frankfurt to help turn around the loss-making unit. It will also cut short- and medium-haul capacity and replace some Airbus A320 planes with smaller A220s. The airline faces high fuel costs, strikes and a €180 million operating loss, while talks with unions are still unresolved. Deutsche Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its namesake airline to turn around the unprofitable mainline unit, as high fuel costs put more pressure on Europe’s largest aviation group. The company will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees seen by Bloomberg. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its fleet of Airbus A320 aircraft, switching to the smaller A220 type, it said. The planned reductions are the second culling in little over a year and reveal the extent of the struggles to revive the fortunes of the airline’s flagship product. The airline group announced in September 2025 that it intended to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030. Lufthansa is undergoing its biggest efficiency drive in years as high jet-fuel prices and an underperforming mainline airline weigh on results. Lufthansa Airlines posted an operating loss of €180 million (S$254.8 million) in the first nine months. “After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future,” management wrote in the letter. “In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and our already very high cost base have made the situation more acute.” Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, said earlier in 2026 that “significantly greater efforts” may be needed to improve the airline’s flagging performance after losing ground to rivals in what he called self-inflicted damage. The measures revealed on Nov 20 come as Lufthansa tries to resolve a dispute with labour unions, though no agreement has been reached so far. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Oil prices on track to post third weekly decline despite Middle East tension
events.summary: Oil prices are on track to post a third weekly decline as investors weigh the risk of continued Middle East tension against a rise in crude supply. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil, was trading 1.34 per cent lower at $90.75 a barrel at 1.16pm UAE time on Friday. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading down 1.2 per cent at $81.36 a barrel. Brent is set to end the week more than 3 per cent lower, while WTI is on course to post a loss of more than 6 per cent. Tension in the region persists. Yemen’s Houthi rebels attacked a Public Investment Fund tower in Riyadh’s financial centre on Thursday and ships continue to face Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for one third of the world’s crude and liquefied natural gas supplies. This week, a vessel belonging to Adnoc Logistics and Services was attacked while passing through the strait. Eleven seafarers were injured and one is missing. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump appeared to push a decision whether to renew major strikes against Iran into next year. He gave three separate interviews as he returned to Washington from a historic trip to China, where he held talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin. “We’ll see what happens after January 1,” Mr Trump told Fox News in an interview broadcast on Thursday. In an interview with Axios and Israel’s News 12, he said he was "rushing to make any decisions on Iran". He made similar comments to Reuters. Rising supply from the Middle East is also affecting prices. The International Energy Agency said oil markets had returned to surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as Gulf exports recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly market report last week. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, rose to 18.4 million bpd in October but were still 26 per cent below prewar levels. The US Energy Information Administration said in a report that commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, rose by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week to November 13. That points to more supply in the market.

events.title: As attention spans move on from Iran and oil, the world is forever changed, and the conflict is escalating again
events.summary: The November news cycle has fixated on elections, Nvidia , and Anthropic, but the Iran war has quietly escalated this week, and there is no “credible pathway” for the world to return to its previous norm, the International Energy Agency warned in its annual World Energy Outlook released Thursday. Even as gasoline and diesel prices have fallen from record highs in recent weeks, the Middle East will never be the same, and the rest of the world is still racing to develop more of its own energy sources—both renewables and fossil fuels—as global supplies remain tight and food security is threatened in much of the world, especially Asia, the report stated. All this is transpiring as global energy demand spikes both from the AI boom and the rise of the middle class in developing countries. “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol. The nearly nine-month Iran war and the prolonged shuttering of the vital Strait of Hormuz represent the greatest energy supply shock in modern history—far more than the Iranian Revolution or the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s—and its reverberations will be felt in ways that remain unclear, the report said. After all, the war is ongoing, and Iran this week struck U.S. facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the U.S. countered by striking Iran’s Qeshm Island. “Attention is elsewhere now. I don’t know if it’s complacency or a lack of anxiety, but [the war] is still a pretty big deal,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm. “What I worry is if the Iranians feel they have to make people anxious again. Do they view it in their strategic interest to create more anxiety?” Pickering noted to Fortune . “I think we’ll have this uneasy conflict going on with Iran for a bunch of 2027.” Between alternative pipelines and routes, and U.S. escorts through Hormuz, Middle Eastern oil exports are approaching 90% of their prewar levels despite the ongoing military strikes, said Pavel Molchanov, Raymond James energy analyst. “This indicates that the oil market has become acclimated to periodic flare-ups, just as long as there is no return to all-out war,” he added. “That said, the lack of a U.S.-Iran deal still translates into a hefty risk premium.” Because of seasonal demand dips, rising Middle Eastern exports, and President Donald Trump’s emphasis on de-escalating the war since the midterm congressional elections, global oil prices have fallen below the $100 per barrel threshold, even though the global benchmark remains high at more than $90. After all, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is dangerously depleted at a 44-year low, and the world has cumulatively lost 2.8 billion barrels of oil over nearly nine months, the IEA report stated. A world forever changed The Iran war has triggered record-high fuel spikes in the U.S. But keep in mind that the U.S. leads the world in oil output, currently producing an all-time high of more than 14 million barrels daily. The rest of the world is left even more at the mercy of the war, and the price spikes and physical shortages are amplified, especially in Asia and Africa. More than 4 billion people—roughly half the global population—depended on the Middle East for over 30% of its oil supplies. And about 80% of Middle Eastern oil exports were destined for Asia before the war. Even as Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Iraq move to build pipelines to divert oil supplies through alternate routes, those projects will take years, and long-term Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would maintain uncertainty going forward. “That’s not a particularly comforting outlook to the consumers of Middle East crude,” Pickering said. “The finish matters, and I don’t think we have visibility on what the finish looks like.” The Americas are leading the increase in oil production—the U.S., Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Guyana, and now Venezuela—as well as a slate of African nations. And more countries are investing in renewable energy and electrification for electric vehicles. Birol and the IEA forecast that renewables—solar, wind, and batteries—are picking up momentum throughout the world even as the globe falls short of its climate change goals. Nuclear power also is gaining steam. EV sales are projected to rise in most of the world next year—less so in the U.S.—in part because of cheaper, subsidized Chinese EVs being exported worldwide. Global oil demand is now expected to peak by 2030 and slowly decline from there, the IEA said. Natural gas demand will grow through the mid-2030s and plateau. The IEA outlook noted that August was the hottest month ever on record worldwide and a strong El Niño could add to weather-related strains heading into 2027. “High energy prices and shortfalls in fertilizer supply are creating hazards for food security,” the report stated. “Emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) and air pollutants from fuel combustion remain dangerously high. Energy geopolitics are fracturing, and trade restrictions are on the rise. Trust is in short supply. Each vulnerability deepens the others.” That is why—more than ever—the world requires “credible road maps to phase out fossil fuels, backed by the public finance needed to ensure a fast and fair transition,” said David Tong, global industry lead at Oil Change International. “Fossil fuels are driving chaos and high energy bills, and the energy choices we make now will shape all our futures,” Tong added. “After yet another fossil fuel crisis, governments cannot afford to keep people and economies hooked on volatile oil and gas markets.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ‘Half philanthropy and half protest’: Noah Wyle and Figs pair up to erase $200 million in real patients’ medical debt
events.summary: After decades of playing a doctor on the long-running medical drama ER and today’s The Pitt, Noah Wyle has learned a thing or two about what it’s like to be a health care professional and the challenges patients face.  Now, he is taking that passion off-screen, partnering up with popular scrubs maker Figs with a goal to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt in the U.S. “In my countless interactions with health care professionals over the decades, one thing that stays with me is how they try to do everything right for a patient while the system makes it harder than it should be,” Wyle said in a statement. “Medical debt follows people home, creates long-term devastation, and changes the whole experience of care.” Americans owe at least $220 billion in medical debt, according to a 2024 KFF-Peterson analysis of federal survey data, and having insurance offers less protection than many assume. In a new Urban Institute study backed by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, more than one-quarter of U.S. adults said they or a family member owed medical debt at the end of 2025, including 26% of those with health coverage. Hospitals were the most common creditor.  Separately, a Commonwealth Fund survey released in September found that roughly one in three working-age adults with private insurance are paying off medical bills over time, with some pulling from savings or spending less on food and rent to keep up. The issue has also come up on-screen in Wyle’s shows. In one episode of The Pitt , a construction worker who already owes $100,000 in medical bills lands in the ER with serious diabetes complications after rationing his insulin because he can’t afford it. “Trust is the bedrock of the relationship between patients and clinicians like nurses, pharmacists, and doctors, and that trust is increasingly undermined by the burden, and even fear, of medical debt,” Allison Sesso, president and CEO of nonprofit Undue Medical Debt , said in a statement. During the next three years, Wyle and Figs will each donate $1 million to Undue Medical Debt, which wipes out, on average, $100 of qualifying medical debt for every $1 donated. The commitment is projected to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt for over 150,000 Americans. The first round of relief is set to take place in time for the upcoming holidays, according to the release. Actor Noah Wyle at health care apparel company Figs’ “Healthcare Is Human” rally in Washington, D.C., May 21, 2026. Drew ANGERER—AFP/Getty Images Wyle, Figs, and Undue Medical Debt over the same time frame will work to develop and share practical resources for health care professionals to help patients navigate affordability. This builds on Figs’ and Wyle’s broader “Healthcare Is Human” advocacy work, focused on addressing systemic pressures making it challenging for health care workers to care for their patients. “This is an act of half philanthropy and half protest, to underscore what the need is, and see if we can’t get our arms around some better solutions,” Wyle told CNN . Wyle also serves as Figs’ global brand ambassador and has joined the company on Capitol Hill to push for policies supporting health care workers . He wore the brand’s first black-tie scrubs to the Emmy Awards last year. Figs, a publicly traded company cofounded by CEO Trina Spear, reported third-quarter revenue of $190.7 million earlier this month, up nearly 26% from a year earlier. events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Deals and buys Intel Foundry signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P semiconductor manufacturing process, according to Intel executives. The customer has not been identified, and Intel has not disclosed a production timetable. Siemens plans to acquire Breker Verification Systems , a developer of AI-driven test suite synthesis and system-level verification technologies. The acquisition is expected to close in December. Microsoft selected Intel Foundry ‘s EMIB advanced packaging technology for custom silicon used in Azure’s infrastructure. The multiyear agreement also expands cooperation on Xeon processors, memory, and security technologies. Infineon and Megmeet are teaming up on 800V DC power architectures for AI data centers, using Infineon’s gen-2 CoolSiC MOSFETs in three-phase power shelves. GlobalFoundries and Boston Dynamics expanded their robotics collaboration to deploy autonomous Spot inspection robots across fabs in the U.S., Germany, and Singapore. GF also plans to begin evaluating Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots for semiconductor manufacturing tasks in early 2027. AMD completed acquisitions of AI inference chip developer Taalas and AI model research company World Labs . Funding The European Commission said more than 20 semiconductor projects have been approved under the EU Chips Act, representing over €33B in public and private investment . General Flash raised $128M to scale production of critical metals used in semiconductor and other industries. Atom Computing finalized an up to $100M CHIPS Act R&D award for neutral-atom quantum computers. Science Corporation raised $400M for its retinal implant chip that aims to restore form vision for certain types of macular degeneration. Chip trade and export controls The U.S. Department of Commerce introduced new restrictions addressing remote access to advanced U.S. AI computing through overseas data centers, along with new semiconductor licensing requirements affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The U.S. received license requests covering 3.4 million advanced Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China and approved more than 879,000 , according to U.S. government data. It is unclear how many were actually shipped. TSMC and Samsung reportedly suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following new U.S. export restrictions, pending licensing approvals, per the Financial Times. TSMC is also reportedly halting affected Chinese customer orders at 16nm and below without U.S. approval and generally limiting those customers to 28nm and 40nm processes, provided those chips do not use HBM or advanced packaging. The U.S. government released new details of an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed over suspected semiconductor export-control violations. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list in June 2025, but its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix , later received more than $800M in Nvidia AI technology , mostly through third-party manufacturers, per the NYT. Nvidia says it blocked new orders and obtained government authorization for certain repair parts shipments. An investigation is underway. The Trump administration is moving toward restrictions on Chinese optical transceiver imports , despite opposition from major U.S. cloud companies, reported Reuters. Manufacturing capacity Nvidia expanded its manufacturing agreements with Amkor , Samsung Electro-Mechanics , SPIL , TSMC , and others. The commitments cover additional substrate manufacturing, advanced packaging, and wafer capacity. As part of the expansion, ASE subsidiary SPIL signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Nvidia to triple its advanced semiconductor packaging capacity in Taiwan by mid-2029, including new production lines for wafer bumping, assembly, and testing. ASE Technology inaugurated the first phase and began construction of the second phase of its Lujhu advanced packaging facility in Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Lam Research broke ground on a technology center in Zhunan , Taiwan , as part of its five-year, $3B global R&D expansion. GlobalFoundries broke ground on a new 300mm semiconductor fab in Malta, New York , under a U.S.-Japan investment initiative providing up to $21B for two fabs. The first 300mm fab is expected to begin production in 2029. ADEKA and Entegris agreed to collaborate on advanced semiconductor materials production in Japan. Silicon Box advanced its proposed semiconductor packaging and test facility in Novara, Italy , into the basic design stage. events.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
events.summary: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 T he name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. “It was something quite different. Most people reacted really well to it,” said Steve Anderson, 57. “The only negative reaction I heard was to the ginger shot, which some found too strong … but that’s a preference thing. The pods themselves were very palatable.” Global packaging waste is on course to hit a projected 434.5m tonnes in 2025, rising to 525m tonnes by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 3.9%, according to research from Smithers . Plastic is at the heart of this: between 2000 and 2019, the volume of plastic waste doubled, with packaging responsible for about 40% of it. Yet plastic is among the least recycled materials, with a worldwide recycling rate of just 27.9% in 2024. The UK’s overall plastic packaging recycling reached 52.5% in 2023, up from 51.4% in 2022. Edible packaging could be part of the answer to this problem, with the market size valued at $1.04bn (£790m) in 2024 and poised to grow to $1.84bn by 2033, driven by consumers’ environmental concerns. But market research says challenges exist. One report said this was “due to the sensitivity of edible packaging to fluctuating environmental conditions, necessitating special handling during shipping and storage ”. It also said customers were reluctant to use edible utensils and the challenges hindered “widespread adoption”. However, beyond the science of packaging, a wider debate remains about our consumption habits. Environmental campaigners argue that the ultimate solution to the plastic waste crisis is not finding better ways to wrap single-use items, but moving away from a throwaway culture altogether. Even for those who do want to create better packaging, money remains a hurdle. Prof James Elliott at the University of Cambridge, who is working on plastic packaging alternatives, said manufacturers were not keen to pay more for biodegradable alternatives. “They are very cost driven,” he said, adding that the non-biodegradable plastic market was $265bn “so the $1bn proportion being edible is small”. Andrew Wallis, packaging lead at Innocent Drinks, said 78% of consumers would consider buying ginger shots encased in seaweed, according to a survey. He said it could also be used in Innocent’s kids’ range, which currently uses paper straws in plastic packaging. “Could that wrap be exchanged for a seaweed wrapper?” he said. Notpla created similar pods for the London Marathon. Other examples of innovation in this area include Xampla, which created a stock cube wrapped in edible film, and Cupffee, which made the world’s first edible cup. At Notpla’s headquarters, in east London, seaweed is used to encase small amounts of olive oil as well as for sandwich packaging and to replace plastic film in cardboard packaging. The team has also made spoons out of seaweed, which are used in ice-cream parlours including Ice Cream Union in London. Rodrigo García González, co-founder of Notpla, said seaweed was a good sustainable solution because it grew rapidly. “Some seaweed can grow up to 60cm a day,” he said. “It’s one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth, much faster than bamboo, and it doesn’t compete with anything on land.” He also said it biodegraded more quickly than a leaf. At Notpla, a machine pushes out ginger shots into seaweed casing, like sausages on a factory conveyor belt. The company is still working out how a product such as this could work in a supermarket: it lasts only three days, but in an unopened bottle could be kept for weeks. Elliott said one of the big problems with edible packaging was about scale: “About 30-40% of all plastics used worldwide are used in packaging … the scale is phenomenal. We use 2m tonnes of plastic in the UK per year.” He said it would be hard to “harvest that much seaweed without making huge changes”. But González said seaweed “already operates at a scale most people don’t realise”. He added: “Around 40m tonnes are harvested every year, almost all of it farmed, and it’s already in everyday products from toothpaste to ice-cream. It’s also one of the fastest-growing organisms on the planet.” Elliott has been working on developing a non-edible packaging made from cellulose. “It’s designed to be composted. Cellulose is abundant in every plant, so we take waste plant material and turn it into films.” The planet's most important stories.

events.title: A rare EU-UK summit as Andy Burnham seeks to mend Brexit damage
events.summary: A decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences and possibly pave a way to get back together BRUSSELS -- A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union , top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together . Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners. Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week. Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining. Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.” The two sides are expected to sign a trade deal for food and drink, an agreement on emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain’s economy. Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC Troops from 11 countries drill in Poland for potential postwar Ukraine mission American surfer Kurt Van Dyke's girlfriend among 2 arrested in his Costa Rica death The war in Ukraine , and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration. “Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.” Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions. events.title: Get rich quick, or lose it all: The shared fun and frustration of Monopoly's capitalist world
events.summary: Monopoly, with its colorful money and metal tokens, is a game night staple that has entertained and frustrated players for decades NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Buy Marvin Gardens. Draw a Get Out of Jail Free card. Put a hotel on Boardwalk or Baltic Avenue. And when you pass Go, collect $200. It’s easy to name the game being played . With its iconic colorful paper money and metal playing tokens , Monopoly has entertained and frustrated countless players as they vie to win it all or go “bankrupt” trying. Even with its reputation for long and cutthroat gameplay, the property-trading, rags-to-riches board game has become entrenched in the American experience and part of a global lexicon. It’s both a game-night staple and a cultural symbol that draws parallels to — and to some extent lampoons — the highs and lows of capitalism and the American dream. Parker Brothers launched its Monopoly in 1935 while America was still in the throes of the Great Depression. In “Monopoly: The World’s Most Famous Game and How It Got That Way,” Philip Orbanes, a former Parker Brothers executive, explains that the board game quickly became “a common language, a shared reservoir of enjoyment and experience that players from the four corners of the Earth could share with equanimity.” He gives Parker Brothers a lot of the credit for that. The American game maker didn’t invent Monopoly, though it bought the rights to Charles Darrow’s version and to its predecessor, Landlord’s Game by Elizabeth Magie . Monopoly evolved over time through various adaptations of Magie’s game. But according to Orbanes, Parker Brothers standardized Monopoly, including rewriting the rules. He explains that this “meant that consumers in every part of the country played Monopoly the same way,” personal house rules aside. A British game maker helped ensure that standardization carried over to international versions as well. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The game's standard rules continue to give players a shared starting point. But whether you know all the official rules or not, breaking them — or coming up with new ones — is also a Monopoly tradition. The instructions for several Monopoly editions advise against using personal house rules in order “to keep your game short and sweet.” But Hasbro, which owns Monopoly, recognizes that fan-created rules are part of gameplay for many. Some house rules have even inspired official Monopoly variations. In a news release about the game's 90th anniversary, Hasbro executive Brian Baker explained: “It’s a cultural phenomenon that has transcended generations and resonates deeply with players across the globe. ... We’re celebrating the elements our players have loved for nearly a century.” Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. events.title: Asia shares drop on AI worries, echoing Wall Street's decline despite the strong Anthropic debut
events.summary: Asian shares are dropping during a wide selloff in issues related to artificial intelligence and computer chips TOKYO -- Asian shares dropped in Friday trading as a wide selloff hits issues related to artificial intelligence and computer chips. Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 shed more than 3,000 points, or about 5.1%, to finish at 56,436.65. Australia's S & P/ASX 200 dropped 1.6% to 8,592.60. South Korea's Kospi shed 5.2% to 4,869.12. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 2.2% to 22,333.88, while the Shanghai Composite lost 1.3% to 3,532.10. The AI-related stocks dipping in the region included Advantest Corp. and SoftBank Group Corp. in Tokyo, as well as Samsung Electronics Co. in South Korea and Tencent in China. Worries that the AI boom may be over have been hanging over global markets for some time, despite the strong debut Thursday of Anthropic's stocks on Wall Street. On Wall Street, benchmarks declined, with the S & P 500 dropping 2% for a sixth straight loss . The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101 points, or 2.2%, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3%. The S & P 500 jumped as much as 1.3% after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold shares of its stock at $83 apiece in its initial public offering . Its price quickly surged above $115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. Anthropic later pared its gain and finished the day at $97.17, still up 17.1%. Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remained among investors in the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost following sharp recent drops for AI-related stocks on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology. Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 3.3%. The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO added to the damage. He was one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth. All told, the S & P 500 fell 147.80 points to 7,175.83. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 to 49,097.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 550.69 to 23,879.20. events.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
events.summary: Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud Published 20 November 2026, 07:32 GMT Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score. Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision. "When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says. It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud. "Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says. "Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says. Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story. "As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance. Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data. "A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa. "But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says. Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history. But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to? In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms. But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness. "Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement. Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk." If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion". But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns. "Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains. Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford. "We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past". While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation. She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past. "Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination." Upstart says it is tackling that issue. "We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement. Evangeline Atkinson (left) and Laura Mills co-founders of Noggin HQ Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score. "I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls. "When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies." That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

events.title: US chip equipment maker KLA opens expanded site in Singapore, with plans for further growth
events.summary: Semiconductor equipment maker KLA’s expanded site in Ang Mo Kio gives the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space. KLA opened its expanded Building 22B site in Ang Mo Kio, adding about 210,000 sq ft and making Singapore a major global production hub for the chip equipment maker. The firm plans a third expansion phase, pending land and approvals, and expects the site to support about 1,000 new jobs in R&D, supply chain and manufacturing engineering. Singapore leaders said KLA strengthens the country’s semiconductor ecosystem, supports local suppliers, and fits with $800 million in RIE 2030 research plans for the chip industry. SINGAPORE – US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened an expanded plant in Singapore and announced it has plans for a third phase of expansion, making the Republic one of its major production hubs globally. The expanded site, Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, was announced in October 2024 and is now fully operational – giving the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space. KLA, which makes machines and tools such as surface profilers, testers and semiconductor assembly solutions for chipmakers, established its presence in Singapore in 1996 and began manufacturing here in 2006. Theo Kneepkens, KLA Singapore country president and senior vice-president of global operations, said the company has also outlined plans for a further expansion phase here, subject to finalisation of land arrangements and relevant approvals. “I was actually hoping that this would already be a ground-breaking of our next phase. But we’re still defining a few details of our next phase of expansion before we can officially announce that,” he said. “But it’s clear that our next phase of growth will be bigger than the current expanded site .” Kneepkens said KLA’s plans for an additional phase reflect its conviction that Singapore – with its exceptional talent, supportive governance and strategic position – will remain indispensable in how the world manufactures critical semiconductor equipment powering AI and advanced computing. In the longer term, Building 22B and the planned phase are expected to support about 1,000 new jobs across research and development, supply chain and manufacturing engineering. KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins said: “We’ve added hundreds of new roles, with over 2,200 employees working across multiple shifts, and 90% of KLA Singapore employees are locals, including both Singaporean citizens and permanent residents.” He noted that KLA’s long-term investment in Singapore has been driven by the local talent, highly collaborative partners and access to suppliers and customers. “We are experiencing unprecedented growth across the industry, and our customers show no signs of slowing. If anything, the demand environment is only accelerating,” he said. KLA’s expansion comes on the heels of several investment commitments announced in the past few years by companies that fabricate semiconductors or are part of the manufacturing value chain, such as processors of silicon substrate materials and companies that test, assemble and package chips. Chip firms that have made fresh investments include GlobalFoundries, Micron, Siltronic, Soitec, UMC, Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP Semiconductors. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said at KLA’s opening ceremony that Singapore has built a strong ecosystem for semiconductor equipment manufacturing, and the Republic now accounts for around one-fifth of global production. “Singapore must keep building the specialised capabilities that companies need to compete. “By working with partners like KLA, we can support their growth while creating good opportunities for our people and enterprises,” he said. Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that as chips become more powerful and specialised, manufacturing them requires greater precision. Hence, equipment made by companies like KLA, which can measure process variations and detect defects early, is increasingly important. “KLA is a key part of Singapore’s strength in this field. Its process-control tools help chipmakers bring advanced technologies into reliable, high-volume production,” he added. He said Singapore is also investing in the research capabilities needed to seize new opportunities in the chip industry, committing $800 million under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to the RIE Flagship in Semiconductors. He lauded a three-year collaboration between KLA and A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics, saying such partnerships will help turn research into practical manufacturing solutions, so Singapore can continue to meet the semiconductor industry’s changing needs. Local suppliers are evolving alongside the multinational companies they support, Gan added.

events.title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
events.summary: UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent Treasury watchdog, said the latest figures were “broadly in line” with its October forecast for a £1.1bn fall in total borrowing for the 2026-27 financial year. However, it warned there were “several risks” amid the sharp rise in energy costs, and public spending on cost of living support measures. Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly. “However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.” The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October – £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997. Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs. Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s. Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran. “This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added. Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend. In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs. After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year. Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP. Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year. Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year. Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”
