events.title: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
events.summary: On his way back from China Thursday aboard Air Force One, President Trump called in to a meeting his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were holding in Berlin with a group of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. "Putin wants to end the war, he wants the deal done, he is getting tired of this," Trump said, according to people in the room. Why it matters: Instead of turning his historic trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin into a modern-day Yalta Conference, as some European and Ukrainian officials feared , Trump tried to use it to propel his push for peace in Europe. Driving the news: Trump met Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen. Their meeting wasn't originally on the schedule, but Trump wanted to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine directly with the Russian president, a U.S. official said. "Who is he? He's my friend," Trump said when he entered the meeting room where Putin was waiting. Later in the day, Witkoff and Kushner told European leaders in Berlin that Trump pressed Putin to move on the peace talks, telling the Russian leader that now is the time to get a deal, according to a European official. Trump also asked Xi for his help in ending the war during their bilateral meeting. "He sent a very strong message to both of them [Putin and Xi] on the desire for peace, and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said at a press conference on Thursday. Behind the scenes: As Trump wrapped up his meetings in China and headed back to Washington, his envoys started their talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Zelensky and other European leaders. Kushner and Witkoff tried to reassure the group that Trump doesn't intend to cut a deal with Putin over their heads. "President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He's not looking to impose anything unilaterally," Kushner said. Shortly after, when Trump called in to brief the European leaders, he urged them to engage directly with Putin. "Friedrich, you can make a call to Putin and this will make a deal," Trump said, referring to the German host. Trump added, "Xi respects Zelensky. Putin is ready to do the deal. Zelensky can do a great deal." What they're saying: A European official said the talks in Berlin were substantive, unlike the summit in Shenzhen, which was mostly symbolic. "We think we have good coordination between the U.S. and Europe," the European official said. State of play: One of the key U.S. objectives at the moment is to get Europe directly involved in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. At the same time, U.S. officials also want Europe to engage in talks with Russia on a new European-Russian security agreement . Putin said publicly for the first time Thursday that he is open to allowing the Europeans to participate in peace talks with Ukraine. "We understand that it is pointless to discuss security issues, including those in Europe, without them," he said at a press conference after meeting with Trump. Putin added that Russia needs to understand what the Europeans are prepared to bring to the negotiations. Putin also signaled willingness to present an updated proposal for a security agreement with Europe. "Life changes, so it makes no sense to return to geopolitical realities of the 1990s," he said. What to watch: After the leaders' meeting in Berlin, Kushner and Witkoff huddled for another few hours with Zelensky and national security advisers from Germany, the UK, France, Italy and Poland, as well as senior officials from the EU and NATO. The group coordinated ahead of the next round of talks with the Russians, possibly next week. The European official said the group was skeptical Russia will actually allow Europe to participate in peace talks. The bottom line: U.S. officials said their goal is to get the Europeans and Russians to start talking to each other. "We also will go back and relay to the Russians that we see strength and unity and commitment [in Europe], but we also see a real desire for peace," Kushner said. "And I think that we're doing a lot of work to organize on how to give it the best shot to get there."

events.title: Apple working on AI agent for device control, apps, browsing and coding
events.summary: Apple outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. Apple is developing an autonomous AI agent for device control, app use, web browsing and coding. Job listings say it will work privately and handle multistep tasks. The company is moving into a fast-growing market already led by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google. Apple’s App Store already shows strong demand for AI agents. Apple is also adding stricter warnings in macOS 27.3 for third-party computer-use tools. It wants stronger privacy and safety, while pushing Siri towards deeper app integration. Apple is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta Platforms and others. The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one listing, Apple said it is seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post. The move follows the breakout success of Meta’s Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel arrangements and prepare news briefings. There has also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software. Anthropic recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc’s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk’s Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user’s behalf – in addition to offering standard AI agent features. Apple’s App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No. 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Nov 19. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude were also in the top five. OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor. Bloomberg News reported earlier in November that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company’s plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as end- 2027 , but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the job listing reads. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” The listing says the company has a team building the “foundation for that future” and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to “make it real”. John Ternus, the tech giant’s new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI – with an agent being key to that effort. “People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same,” the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks” across apps, browsers, command lines, code and application programming interfaces, and they can “coordinate specialised subagents along the way”. The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of “general-purpose computer-use agents”, the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Nov 19. Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system’s design. “Agents that can run code, use credentials and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency.” Sandboxing is a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet. As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the upcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, it has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs. With the change in 27.3 , ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition.

events.title: Japan’s core inflation accelerates in October, cementing rate hike expectations
events.summary: Japan’s core consumer price index rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3% gain. It followed a 2.1% rise in September. Japan’s core inflation rose to 2.2% in October, above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for a second month, strengthening expectations of a near-term rate hike. The BOJ will review the data at its Dec 18 meeting, and many market players expect rates to rise to 1.5% from 1.25%. Capital Economics said firms are still passing on higher raw material costs, and it now expects the BOJ to lift rates to 2.5% by mid-next year. TOKYO – Japan’s annual core inflation accelerated in October and exceeded the central bank’s 2% target for the second straight month, a sign of broadening price pressures that cements the case for a near-term interest rate increase. The data will be among factors the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will scrutinise at its next two-day policy meeting ending on Dec 18, when many market players expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.5% from the current 1.25%. The core consumer price index (CPI), which strips away the effect of volatile fresh food, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, data showed on Nov 20, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3% gain. It followed a 2.1% rise in September. An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier after increasing 2.4% in September. Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, expects inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, to accelerate sharply over the coming months as firms continue to pass on rising raw material costs. “The upshot is that we now expect the Bank of Japan to lift rates to 2.5% by the middle of next year,” he wrote in a research note. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September after delivering a hike in June – a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept rates steady in October, declaring victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target. REUTERS

events.title: Future of $600m Maryvale mill waste incinerator in doubt
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Latrobe Valley waste to energy incinerator in doubt as grant quietly scrapped Opal Australia planned to generate energy from waste at its Maryvale paper mill. ( ABC News: Kerrin Thomas ) A $48m federal grant for an energy incinerator in the Latrobe Valley has been terminated, putting the project in doubt. The incinerator was to be fuelled in part by waste from a new transfer station in Melbourne, but that project has been rejected. A waste management expert doubts the incinerator project will go ahead. A federal government grant for a Victorian-first waste to energy (WTE) project in the Latrobe Valley has been quietly terminated, raising questions about its future. The $48 million grant was given to Opal Australia in 2022 to develop the $600 million incinerator at the Maryvale Paper Mill. It planned to burn residential and commercial waste, creating jobs and reducing the mill's use of gas. The Victorian Labor government later approved the project, the first WTE incinerator allowed under its circular economy laws. But the project hit a snare when a permit for the construction of a new transfer station in Melbourne's east was rejected by the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) in 2025. That station was proposed in part to receive waste from several councils to then be transferred to Maryvale for incineration. Many Hampton Park residents opposed the new waste transfer station that was needed for the Latrobe Valley incinerator. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) A Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) ruling from April upheld the EPA's rejection of the Hampton Park proposal and noted a "significant volume" of complaints from residents about potential odour. Deakin University senior lecturer in sustainability, Trevor Thornton, specialises in waste management and said getting a consistent supply of waste, or feed stock, for the Maryvale incinerator was crucial. "The refusal to grant a permit for the transfer station where their feed stock was going to come from was the main catalyst for this waste to energy facility not being viable," he said. The federal Department of Industry confirmed the grant had wound up just a few months later. "The department and Maryvale mutually agreed to terminate the agreement in July 2026," a spokesperson said. "All unspent funds have been fully repaid to the Commonwealth." The ABC asked how much of the money was returned and received this response: "The department will not comment further on the terms of the termination, including financial arrangements or other information that is confidential or commercially sensitive." Waste from Melbourne's east was to be used to generate energy for the Maryvale paper mill. ( ABC News: Rick Rifici ) The consortium behind the incinerator project includes Opal Australia, waste management multinational Veolia, and WTE incinerator specialist Masdar Tribe. Veolia was also behind the failed application for the Hampton Park transfer station. A spokesperson for the consortium declined to answer questions or comment on the future of the project. Dr Thornton suggested the grant termination may have been linked to missed milestones on securing consistent supply of waste. Trevor Thornton says without a transfer station, the incinerator project will not be viable. ( Supplied: Trevor Thornton ) "I would imagine the consortium putting it together would have done a lot of work to try to find solutions to the existing problems with it becoming operational," he said. "I think it would be very much a last resort if they've decided not to go ahead." The Latrobe City Council approved construction of the incinerator and has a waste offtake agreement with the consortium. "The proposal has an active planning permit and council understands they are continuing with planning for the project," a spokesperson said. events.title: Bougainville landowners 'overwhelmed' at Rio Tinto's $370m pledge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rio Tinto commits $370m to fix toxic legacy of Panguna mine in Bougainville Rio Tinto's Panguna mine project was once responsible for most of Bougainville's exports. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) Rio Tinto will contribute $370 million to address environmental and social impacts caused by the Panguna mining project in Bougainville. An impact assessment has determined mine waste and decaying infrastructure continue to affect thousands of people decades after its closure. Locals say clean water and transport infrastructure are immediate priorities. Nearly 40 years after mining giant Rio Tinto was forced to abandon its Panguna mine in Bougainville, the company says it will provide $370 million to address the site's toxic legacy. Local opposition to the gold and copper mine forced its closure in 1989, sparking a decade-long civil war known locally as the Bougainville Crisis. An estimated 10,000 to 15,000 people were killed in the war that ensued until a peace agreement was reached in 2001. Rio Tinto said it would voluntarily contribute the money over the "coming years" to a new fund set up to address the mine's environmental and social impacts. The company's chief safety and technical officer, Mark Davies, described it as an important milestone. "Rio Tinto's contribution towards addressing findings of the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment (PMLIA) is intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation," he said. Rio Tinto abandoned operations at the Panguna mine in 1989. ( ABC ) The PMLIA was initiated following a human rights complaint brought by Australian non-profit The Human Rights Law Centre on behalf of about 150 Bougainvilleans in 2020. The assessment found that mine waste and decaying infrastructure continued to affect thousands of people in the area, violating their human rights. Landmark report uncovers human rights abuses A large-scale study of social and environmental impacts from Rio Tinto's abandoned Panguna mine in Bougainville finds a plethora of actual and potential human rights violations, including risks to life. It also revealed violations of Indigenous people's rights to water, education and culture. Lead complainant Theonila Roka Matbob, a traditional landowner from Makosi just downstream from the mine, said she was overwhelmed by Rio Tinto's announcement. "Obviously no amount of money will restore our environment to where it was but at least we can be able to invest into education for our children to find their own solutions later on." Theonila Roka Matbob says it has been a long fight for justice. ( Supplied ) Human Rights Law Centre legal director Keren Adams said Rio Tinto's commitment was a significant and historic moment. "This is an environmental disaster that has been unremedied for decades," she said. "The Bougainville government and communities have both spent many years campaigning for justice and for Rio Tinto to return and take responsibility for dealing with the huge problems that have been left by the disaster." Despite the mine ceasing operations in 1989, some families continue to live in the area. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) Rio Tinto was the majority owner of Panguna until 2016, when it gave its stake to the Bougainville and PNG governments. At its peak, it was one of the largest and most profitable gold and copper mines in the world, responsible for almost half of Papua New Guinea's exports. It was forced to close abruptly in 1989 when conflict broke out. However, the Bougainville government has recently indicated plans to reopen it after inking a deal with Indian mining company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (LMEL). To this day, locals are making use of old machinery at Panguna mine in Bougainville. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) Clean water, transport and education Following Rio Tinto's announcement, work will now begin on developing the new fund's structure, governance and activities, with input from affected communities and the Bougainville government. The company said the fund and its activities would remain separate from the Bougainville government's current effort to redevelop and reopen the mine with Indian firm LMEL. Ms Matbob said clean water and transport infrastructure were immediate priorities. BCL discharged mine waste into local river systems when it was in operation, the Human Rights Law Centre alleges. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) "What we are looking at is getting the basics right in accessibility to clean drinking water for our communities and also to ensure that bridges are built to give proper access to our communities, our families and our children," she said.

events.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
events.summary: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things. The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.” “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.” TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response. Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit. Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers. The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
events.summary: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry. Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day. 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says. More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run. events.title: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
events.summary: On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything. That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI , as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs. Four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July . Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets. Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks . Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them. Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment. There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute , which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock. Zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity. You spent a decade at Google , including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did? When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with. How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it? I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator. How far behind are open models right now? A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three. If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch? Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source. In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice , once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect? We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token. Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction. On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet.

events.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
events.summary: Published 20 November 2026, 00:08 GMT There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's. Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish. From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive. "We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah. She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left". Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed". He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk. Casey and Manny often eat at their desk and their favourite pretzel snack is causing some problems given how sticky and crumbly it is But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc". "The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk". Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them. "In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg." She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten." Ashlea Fisher says it's important all of her employees are mindful about the food they are eating at their desk Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick". "I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues. "Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette." While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place. In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other. A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so. However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk. "While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR. "Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health." Finance worker Laura takes a lunch and dinner break when she's working long hours Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity". "I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says. But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time". His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it". "Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says. Do you have comments or questions about this story? events.title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
events.summary: Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature Published 20 November 2026, 00:02 GMT A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned. Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage. France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies . It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix. In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK. Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies. The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability. Tech Life: The everyday tech at risk of hacks As Europe sees a wave of cyber-attacks on commercial fridges, we investigate how everyday devices are vulnerable to basic attacks using easily-available tools. The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes. They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk. Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually. BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week. "It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named. "From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added. There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year: In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM). RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands. As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks. These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites. Each RDM controller can be used to remotely control the temperature of dozens of fridges and freezers "These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners. "There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added. RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware. The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay. "This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

events.title: Anthropic’s US$1.5 trillion debut rewrites venture capital’s playbook
events.summary: Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares. Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut at a US$1.5 trillion valuation gave venture investors huge gains and showed that AI funding now needs much larger checks. Menlo Ventures, Spark Capital and Sequoia made major returns, while many firms used special-purpose vehicles to raise extra money for bigger AI bets. Anthropic’s revenue and valuation rose fast, and strategic backers Amazon and Google now hold about 28.4%, showing how AI needs cash and computing power. For decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies. Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter cheques to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations. The AI lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Nov 19 at a US$1.5 trillion (S$1.94 trillion) valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture investors at a moment when the industry needs fresh liquidity to fund more bets on AI companies. The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price of $83 . To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles. Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital emerged with some of the biggest returns by multiple. Spark Capital was the first venture capital firm to lead an Anthropic investment, in a US$450 million Series C round in 2023 at a valuation of US$4.5 billion. Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi, who spearheaded the investment, remains the only investor who sits on Anthropic’s board. Writing the largest cheque in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5%, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion. To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies. Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets , joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars. Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first cheque at the start of 2026, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February. It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab. Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested more than US$3 billion in Anthropic, now holds over 2% of the company, making it the largest financial investor in the company, according to two people familiar with the matter. The returns are possible because of the rapid rise in Anthropic’s valuation and revenue. Its annualised revenue grew from about US$1 billion at the start of 2025 to about US$81 billion in October, as its valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in the latest private round this May. Strategic backers, too, supply much of the unprecedented capital and computing power needed by AI labs. The combined stake of Amazon and Alphabet’s Google in Anthropic is about 28.4%. “We’re living through a very unique time of profound change happening at a higher velocity than ever before,” said Will Griffith, a partner at Iconiq, which has invested US$6.1 billion, making the fund the second-largest financial investor by ownership in Anthropic. “The scale of the impact of these businesses and the breadth of market opportunities is larger than anything we’ve seen before. “And that is going to afford investment opportunities that are larger than what we’ve seen in the past.” REUTERS

events.title: Next GOP battle: Who defends Trump on House Oversight
events.summary: House Republicans chose fighter Jim Jordan over the more experienced Steve Scalise to lead them after taking a midterms beatdown. Now they're facing a similar choice over who should lead them on House Oversight. Why it matters: Whoever gets the top Republican spot on the Oversight Committee will be the first line of defense on some of the most deeply personal issues for President Trump and his inner circle. A pair of Texas House Republicans, freshman Rep. Brandon Gill, 32, and three-term Rep. Pat Fallon, 58, want the job that could make them a national star, or leave them taking the heat if Democrats land damaging revelations. Driving the news: Democrats are preparing a barrage of investigations that target Trump's family, finances and closest advisers. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is running to chair House Oversight next year, sent a dozen letters Wednesday targeting figures including Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance. Democratic allies want a plan "to compel disclosure and testimony," according to a letter sent to all Democratic members of Congress— led by Public Citizen and Indivisible — that was signed by 103 groups and obtained by Axios. The White House is pushing back on Hill Democrats, with its top lawyer warning that some Democratic investigative tactics could cross into criminality. Zoom in: Gill has made a name for himself with fiery committee confrontations and viral moments. He's also proven to be a prolific fundraiser. "Gill is the next Jim Jordan," a source close to Jordan told Axios. "He practices, he's smart." Fallon has served on Oversight since arriving in Congress in 2021. He previously chaired Oversight's subcommittee on economic growth, energy policy and regulatory affairs. "I've built great relationships and a clear resume of rigorous, result-oriented oversight that reflects what the committee has achieved on behalf of the American people," Fallon told the Texas Tribune in September. Between the lines: Gill's lack of seniority doesn't appear to be a major obstacle among Republicans eager to elevate one of their top fighters. "It will be a tight race with he and Fallon. Brandon is quite capable and will do a great job if elected. Not worried about his experience," a member of the House Republican Steering Committee told Axios. The Steering Committee recommends who should lead committees, subject to a vote of the full House GOP conference. The intrigue : Fallon backed Steve Scalise in the GOP party leader race, and lobbied against Jordan's preferred makeup of the Steering Committee. Gill publicly supported Jordan, calling him the "original congressional brawler." State of play: Gill has close ties to Jordan and the public backing of House GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.). Multiple people Axios spoke with believe Gill has effectively locked up the support needed to win. But others cautioned that the race will be competitive, with one House Republican telling Axios that "anyone that says there's a favorite at this point is bad at whipping." "This is a purely messaging game for the next two years. And if I'm looking at who the better messenger is, I mean it's a clear choice," a senior GOP leadership aide said of Gill. What they're saying: "He's smart. He's good looking. He's the future of the party. We need to push him out front every minute instead of these old guys that we keep dusting off," Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), who sits on the Oversight Committee, told Axios of Gill. "Paying their dues has gotten us killed at the ballot box every dadgum time," Burchett added of elevating more senior colleagues. Yes, but: "He's kind of skipping a few steps here, and he doesn't necessarily have the credentials to do it," one House Republican told Axios of Gill's bid in October. Axios previously reported that some members of the Freedom Caucus want Gill out, with colleagues accusing him of burning bridges and treating fellow Republicans as stepping stones to greater power and influence. The bottom line: Asked about the criticism from Gill's colleagues, Emmer flatly told Axios in an interview last month that Gill "needs to be out front. I don't care where it is." "Brandon is the future of our party, and his communication skills are phenomenal," Emmer added.

events.title: House Democrats recoil at forcing December shutdown to cut Iran war funding
events.summary: House Democrats are largely steering clear of threats to shut the government down in December if Republicans put forward legislation that maintains funding for the war in Iran. Why it matters: Much of the party's left flank — including some members of Congress — think it's a fight they need to pick after their midterm landslide. "The American people were loud and clear on November 3rd: they want an immediate end to Donald Trump's reckless war in Iran," Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said in a joint statement on Wednesday. The pair said they will "oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran" because it would "defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end—now." State of play: The Democrats' majority doesn't officially begin until Jan. 3, while federal funding is set to run out on Dec. 11. Republican leaders are struggling to pass party-line procedural votes and will probably bring up their funding patch under a fast-track process that requires bills to pass with a two-thirds majority. In other words: The GOP will almost certainly need a large number of Democratic votes to pass any funding bill, especially if some of their own members defect. What they're saying: "Whatever they have to do to get it through they should do it, but I hope there's not a shutdown," said Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), the outgoing chair of the center-left New Democrat Coalition. "I don't think we should shut down the government, we take that way too casually as it is, so I'd be leaning into not doing it," said Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.). Said Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio): "Everyone should do whatever they can to avoid a shutdown. The impact it has on the economy, but workers in particular, it's just not fair." Between the lines: Even some progressives acknowledged their imminent House majority takes a lot of the pressure off the December fiscal deadline. "If I can defund [the war] in December, I'd vote to defund it. But if I can't, then I'll vote to defund it in January," said Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.). "We still have a month left of these guys." Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "One would argue that we can move a CR, maybe keep it at base [funding levels] ... but then we negotiate the kind of budget we know we expect." Yes, but: "I think we should do everything in our power to keep it in there, and we should also figure out how to claw back some of this ICE funding," Ramirez added. Said Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.): "The American people have waited too long, they want to see us try now. ... When we fight we win, and we certainly don't win unless we try. I think we should try." Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of left-wing group OurRevolution, said in a statement: "Voters gave Democrats more power because they wanted a change in direction." "This is a chance to show them, before January, that their votes changed what Congress is willing to do," he said. The bottom line: Ansari told Axios in an interview on Thursday that she is "personally drawing a hard line on any funding for the war" but agrees "with the sentiment that, especially during the holidays, we are concerned about our federal workers." "Nobody wants a government shutdown. There's no question of that. I don't want there to be a government shutdown," she said. "I just think we should be able to both: Not have a government shutdown and ... deliver on what I think was the resounding message from voters, which is that the war in Iran needs to end."

events.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX has a plan to eliminate cell phone dead zones
events.summary: CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching. These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week. “We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.” The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion. Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he said. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.” Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.” The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations. Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals. SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI. “I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he said, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
events.summary: Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold? Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion). The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology. Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI. Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it? In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17. Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%. The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies. The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. "Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect." Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever. The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly. It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude. As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot. The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year. That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion. Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since. Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time. But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world. With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market. "There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said. Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting? Published 1 day ago Daniela Amodei: Anthropic and the price of AI So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available. "We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows." A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term. One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached. Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly.

events.title: Thune: Trump and Democrats will have to negotiate on debt
events.summary: The News Senate Majority Leader John Thune is racing to spend the final days of unified Republican power in Washington on confirming lifetime judicial picks, finishing bipartisan deals on permitting and college sports, and avoiding another shutdown. But the debt ceiling will become Democrats’ problem. The South Dakota Republican told Semafor on Thursday afternoon that his party likely lacks the votes to raise the debt ceiling along party lines in either the House or Senate. Any party-line reconciliation bill is a long shot at this point in the year, but if they do one it will focus on defense funding – not avoiding a default. The debt ceiling “probably ends up getting punted” into next year, Thune said — and with extra steps by the Treasury Department, he forecasted a deadline in the second half of 2027. That means President Donald Trump will have to make a deal on it with a Democratic House and Senate for the first time since he took office. “Obviously there’s a theory out there that if we did a [reconciliation] bill, that we could use that to do the debt ceiling like we did last summer, but we’ve got vote issues both here and in the House,” Thune said. “When the Dems have the gavels, they’ll probably have to enter into negotiations with the White House about how they’re going to address it.” Given all that uncertainty, Thune is spending his remaining days as majority leader plotting out how to rack up a few more Republican victories before he leads the opposition. That starts with preserving the Senate’s carefully negotiated work. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., said in a statement on Thursday that the House wants to “pass strong antitrust protections” and alter the Senate’s bipartisan sports bill while keeping together the fragile coalitions in both chambers. Thune said it would be a “big mistake” to change that bill. “People will filibuster” an amended college sports bill in the Senate, Thune said. If the bill sees major changes he described himself as “worried it doesn’t get done. I don’t know how we can process it over here with all the other stuff we have to do, and it’s just a function of the calendar.” To some degree, that bill is out of Thune’s control now that it’s passed the Senate. Funding the government past Dec. 11 is more in his power, and it will need at least seven Democratic votes in the Senate. Yet Democrats are currently busy with a leadership challenge to their leader, Chuck Schumer, from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. Thune said he’s “trying not to weigh in” on the race but it’s nonetheless affecting his job. Van Hollen’s bid has chilled negotiations to fund the government as the Marylander pushes the caucus to insist on including language that would prohibit funding for the Iran war. “That is not happening at all because of the leadership race. I think they’re waiting till they have that resolved. We’ve basically been told: ‘We’re not talking until after that’s over with,’” Thune said. “They don’t want to do anything that rocks the boat, jeopardizes, tips the field at all in that leadership race based on something they might do on funding the government.” That race will conclude on Dec. 1, which will likely supercharge government funding talks. All that in mind, Thune is making sure he’s following through on what he can control: judicial confirmations at a simple majority threshold. He’s teed up four judges for the Senate to confirm before the Thanksgiving recess and said he will soon move to set up votes on three more which just cleared the committee. Those could receive votes as soon as this weekend if Thune decides to keep the Senate in session. Ultimately, Thune foresees confirming 23 additional judges throughout the lame duck, though some need to get through the Judiciary Committee first. “We’re trying to make the most use of the time we have left on the clock and get as much done as we can. So a lot of that’s confirming the judges that are left, the executive branch nominees. We’ll do a stack of those,” Thune said. And, “we’ve got to fund the government.” Backup plans Thune said he views a Pentagon-funding reconciliation bill as an “option” if bipartisan talks with Democrats fall through, even though a targeted defense-only spending bill right now lacks the requisite 50 votes from Senate Republicans. Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., agreed that Republicans aren’t precluding a budget reconciliation bill if talks with Democrats falter. But he said moving forward with a party-line defense spending bill could prompt a shutdown. “It’s no idle threat. If we do that, then they shut down the government,” Johnson said. “We don’t want to shut down the government because we always get blamed, even though it’s the other side’s fault twice this year. We get blamed. So we’re a little gun-shy about that.” Room for Disagreement Trump and Thune are largely on the same page after the election on lame-duck priorities. But Trump is still pushing Thune to pass a bill making Daylight Savings Time permanent and has called Thune “I don’t know how many times on it.” Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton “will filibuster it,” Thune said. “Sunrise in Pierre would be like 9:25 in the morning. It’s a Northern Plains type issue, and that’s a lot of Republican senators. It’s Montana, Idaho, Nebraska, Iowa, South and North Dakota.” Burgess’s view Thune’s last month and a half as leader is no cakewalk. He’ll probably need Trump’s help to get the House to finesse the sports bill and clinch deals on funding the government. But it pales in comparison to the months before the midterms, when he was telling Trump the GOP’s voter ID bill couldn’t pass and that there weren’t the votes to gut the filibuster. Thune would much prefer being the majority leader, of course, but his life may be easier in the minority — which involves a lot of fighting with Democrats and less internecine combat. “When you’re kind of deeper in the minority, there’s more of a sense of, we got to function as a team,” Thune said. “When you’ve got majorities and you got the White House, there tends to be more infighting and more Republican on Republican, which is not helpful.”

events.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
events.summary: Despite recent AI jitters, Anthropic shattered records with its public debut on Nov 19. Anthropic made the biggest IPO ever on Nov 19, raising US$81 billion and becoming the first major AI lab to list publicly. Its shares were priced at US$83, but opened at US$111.50 and closed at US$97.17, giving it a first-day value of about US$1.75 trillion. The debut shows the power of the AI boom, but investors still worry about market volatility, a possible AI bubble, and wider risks from the technology. Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company. The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion ( S$1.29 trillion ) . That kind of number was once unheard of for a company’s first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth – and most recently the AI boom – has changed that. Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars, following SpaceX just months ago, and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits. Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology’s risks overall. Here are some numbers to help understand the IPO on Nov 19 . The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of trading on Nov 19 , it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June. The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix US$26.5 billion in July and oil giant Saudi Aramco US$25.6 billion in 2019. Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion The initial price per share was set at US$83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at US$111.50 a share – pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon Eastern time ( 1am Singapore time on Nov 20 ). By market close on Nov 19 , Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That is still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly US$1.75 trillion. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion. Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11 Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they are not in the S&P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018. How far a trillion US dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 156 million kilometres That would surpass the roughly 150 million kilometres between Earth and the sun. The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million. There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122. AP

events.title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
events.summary: California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public. The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China. Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November. Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf. Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates. events.title: Alibaba tops revenue estimates on AI cloud growth; profit up on investment gains
events.summary: Alibaba, China’s biggest e-commerce company by market share, said revenue from AI cloud and computing services jumped 53%. Alibaba beat revenue estimates as AI cloud and computing services jumped 53% to 60.97 billion yuan, showing strong demand for its AI push. Reported profit more than tripled, helped by investment gains, while non-GAAP net income rose 92% to 19.9 billion yuan. Alibaba is spending more on AI and cloud, with capital expenditure up 60% to 50.48 billion yuan, but free cash flow stayed negative and shares are down about 40% this year. Alibaba beat estimates for September-quarter revenue on Nov 19 as demand for its AI cloud services surged, while investment gains helped more than triple reported profit. China’s biggest e-commerce company by market share said revenue from AI cloud and computing services jumped 53%, highlighting the growing payoff from heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and products. “This quarter, our business delivered strong growth in both revenue and earnings because of our strategic focus on AI + Cloud growth and profit sustainability in Alibaba E-commerce Group,” Chief Financial Officer Toby Xu said. Excluding investment gains and other items, non-GAAP net income leapt 92% to 19.9 billion yuan (S$3.85 billion), helped by stronger profitability and narrowing losses in its quick-commerce business. Alibaba’s shares are down about 40% this year, as investors worry about weak consumer demand in China and rising spending on AI and cloud infrastructure. Free cash flow was an outflow of 34.47 billion yuan in the quarter, compared with an outflow of 21.84 billion yuan a year earlier. Alibaba said the increase reflected higher spending on cloud infrastructure, partly offset by lower losses at Taobao Instant Commerce and higher customer pre-payments for cloud services. Capital expenditure rose 60% to 50.48 billion yuan. Alibaba reported quarterly revenue of 271.52 billion yuan, ahead of analysts’ average estimate of 269.81 billion yuan, according to LSEG data. AI cloud and computing services revenue totalled 60.97 billion yuan. Alibaba has sharply increased spending on AI infrastructure, proprietary models and applications, betting on the technology as a key growth driver. Adjusted earnings per American Depositary Share were 8.10 yuan, below analysts’ expectations of 11.16 yuan. In September, Alibaba unveiled plans to expand global data-centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 and said its next-generation Qwen 4 model was in training. Its chip-design unit T-Head, which confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing earlier in November, also unveiled a new AI processor scheduled for commercial release in early 2027. Alibaba launched a US$10 billion (S$12.92 billion) share placement in August, saying the proceeds would fund computing infrastructure and AI data centres. The company recently reorganised its businesses into four main units: e-commerce, AI cloud and computing services, AI model applications and other businesses. REUTERS
