events.title: ‘It’s been a rough go’: Lumentum’s CEO on his $115 billion Marvell deal
events.summary: The Scene Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston knows shareholders hate his deal. “It’s been a rough go,” he told Semafor in a Thursday interview. He has a message for them: Bear with us. Lumentum was looking to buy a chip company for months. “We felt like we needed semiconductor properties, so we were actually in the market,” Hurlston said. “Marvell got word we were on a shopping spree and they said, ‘Hey, you know, rather than do that, why not combine with us?’” Lumentum and Marvell agreed to a $115 billion all-stock deal earlier this month that tacks Hurlston’s optical tech business — a key part of the data center buildout that allows high-powered GPUs to actually get their data onto users’ screens — to Marvell’s chips businesses. On paper, the deal made all the sense in the world, Hurlston said. “If you accept the premise that we needed to have a semiconductor asset, Marvell is the best semiconductor [maker] in this area,” Hurlston said. Investors howled. Shares in both Marvell and Lumentum are down roughly 40% since the deal was announced on worries over how much runway the AI trade has left. Some Lumentum shareholders also say the company sold too soon. “The deal hasn’t worked as we expected, right?” Hurlston said. “The view from investors is, you took some of your upside off the table, and you’ve now hitched your wagon to a company whose upside is a little bit less known.” Market Jitters Hurlston says he expects shares to rebound once the companies can share more information with analysts, portfolio managers, and other shareholders through regulatory filings and other meetings. And while there’s still a chance the deal falls apart — there is a material adverse change clause baked into the deal terms — “we’re going to have to see this thing through, unless shareholders vote no, or if we don’t get regulatory approval,” Hurlston said. “The set of circumstances under which we can exercise a MAC are very limited.” There is a bit of portfolio-manager-on-portfolio-manager violence going on, Hurlston noted. Despite overlap in the two company’s shareholder bases — 80%, by Hurlston’s math — portfolio managers may hold Marvell but not Lumentum, or vice versa, triggering some forced selling. “The name of the game in hyperscaling, from a supplier, is continuity of supply and time to market,” Hurlston said. “What this system-sell enables is for us to deliver to our customers massive time to market,” he continued, because Marvell and Lumentum products can be shipped out to data centers as one finished product. The companies will also face regulatory review in both the US and in China, which is likely to draw more scrutiny following the Nvidia chip scandal. Nvidia is both a shareholder and major customer of Lumentum’s. Hurlston noted that both he and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have gotten deals through China’s State Authority on Market Regulation, or SAMR, before, and that they already have a good sense of what to expect. “They really want their supply to be there, and we’re a critical supplier” of transistors into the Chinese market. Semafor has also reported that Marvell’s Murphy could be tapped to take the CEO position at Nvidia following Jensen Huang’s resignation. Hurlston said he didn’t know whether Murphy was considering the role or whether he would take it, but said, “I think he can do the job.” “The board is not going to want somebody who has any sort of besmirchment, and I think you want to have somebody who’s been a sitting CEO,” he said. “There’s no argument that this guy’s done a terrific job [at Marvell].”

events.title: Want to see your live AI usage on your Mac’s icons? This clever new app lets you
events.summary: There’s a new way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really! Designer Michael Flarup has just launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper , which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage. Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app. Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!) Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget . But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.) Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools. There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own. Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio , and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers. He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data. Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time. “The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said. That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, new things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking. “That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added. The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: EP slowly being reconnected after power towers tumble — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Independent examination into ElectraNet over tower fall, premier says Topic: Electricity Production and Distribution A crumpled transmission tower in a paddock. ( Supplied: Sam Telfer ) Swathes of South Australia's Eyre Peninsula were left without power after a storm knocked down major electricity transmission towers. Look back at how the situation unfolded. That's where we're leaving our live coverage of the Eyre Peninsula power outage. The situation is continuing to develop and evolve, with the state emergency centre set to host another meeting at 3pm. To stay across further developments, you can continue to follow our coverage online, and on TV and radio . For the moment, it looks like the number of properties without power is continuing to drop. At 2:45pm, the SA Power Networks website showed the number had dipped under 5,000 across SA. Potential fire risk is predicted for central and western parts of South Australia. Temperatures are set to rise to the 30s tomorrow in the state's north, the Bureau of Meteorology's Christie Johnson says. "That combination of the heat and the strong winds is going to give us elevated fire danger," she says. "There is also the risk of thunderstorms too later in the day … along the West Coast, maybe the southern and western parts of Eyre Peninsula, maybe down Kangaroo Island as well. Tomorrow's fire danger ratings will be released by Country Fire Service at 4:30-5:00pm ACST. For Karen Baines, the impacts have been manifold. Ms Baines lives about 20 kilometres from Ungarra , a small township towards the southern end of Eyre Peninsula. When power was cut to the region, her first thoughts were for her parents in Tumby Bay . "I drove up the road to be able to get some mobile signal, just so I could give them a call and just let them know everything was OK and just check on them," she said. "At the moment we're running on a generator. Without the generator running we have no mobile, no power, no landline." She said she also had a block on which she had lost canola. "A lot of farmers through the strip have lost crops through hail and wind," she said. 'Devastating' loss for crop farmers Grain Producers SA's Brad Perry says he's hearing reports of crop wipeout and significant hail damage in Arno Bay and Port Neill. "We certainly feel for those growers," he tell SA Country Hour. "It's looking like a record crop and suddenly having it on the ground is devastating." He says farmers are still assessing damage and it's too earlier to know if it will impact harvest figures this year. Janice Regan, from a Port Lincoln hearing clinic, questioned how a $300 million transmission line could fail within years of its construction. "It shouldn't be happening and it shouldn't continually be happening ," she said, in reference to the three-day outage that accompanied the statewide blackout 10 years ago. She said when the power went out, she went outside and the "street was actually deserted". "The work impact was quite severe because we lost all computer access, we lost all phones," she said. "We couldn't do any repairs to hearing aids, we couldn't make appointments, we virtually were in shutdown mode." Further accounts are emerging of the impact of the blackout on local businesses. Port Lincoln jeweller Shane Pedemonte says he was "busily working away in the workshop for Christmas trade" when the day turned dim. "Unfortunately, being a jewellery shop, security is pretty paramount. Having dark areas is not ideal so yeah, closed up," he said. "We had a couple of appointments in the late afternoon with clients that we had to cancel." Mr Pedemonte said while his power was restored pretty quickly, "whether it stays on or not is another thing". Home flooded after heavy rain yesterday Jeremy Callis also shares these photos of his mother's house at Arno Bay where water has seeped inside. Speaking to 891 ABC Adelaide, Arno Bay farmer Jeremy Callis says he was in a harvester when yesterday's storm hit. He says the rain was so intense that water found its way into sealed tractor cabs. "It was pretty eerie like those black clouds that come through and … you don't see that very often around here it was sort of more like a tropical storm that come through," he says. ElectraNet has completed its visual inspection of the old lines and is preparing to re-energise areas one by one. Earlier we heard from Sarah Prime about how crops were damaged on her family's Eyre Peninsula property when severe weather swept through yesterday. Wind gusts also ripped off metal shed doors.

events.title: AMD shares fall after report flags China exposure
events.summary: AMD shares plunged Thursday after a short seller flagged the chipmaker’s reliance on Chinese markets and supply chains, which the firm rejected as a misrepresentation of its “business practices and relationships.” The report comes less than two weeks after former Nvidia boss Jensen Huang admitted to an illicit relationship with a woman suspected of spying for Chinese intelligence, intensifying scrutiny of US chip sales to China (and momentarily boosting rival AMD’s stock). The Hunterbrook report also cited AMD’s financing arrangements with its own customers, which other analysts have warned could create an artificial impression that risks a large correction. “If the smoke surrounding Nvidia becomes an inferno for the AI buildout, AMD will be engulfed by the flames ,” the report stated. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' sales set to top more than $3 billion in first week
events.summary: Rockstar’s is set to top more than $3 billion in sales in its first week, eclipsing the lifetime grosses of some of the biggest films and concert tours and prompting commentators to salute an era-defining entertainment product. Despite the video game’s expected windfall, “ developers face shrinking incentives to make anything like it again ,” The Economist argued, as the industry experiences mass layoffs. Skyrocketing hardware costs and the rise of generative AI, meanwhile, have incentivized lower-spec titles and devices, developed by smaller teams. In one notable review, The New York Times Magazine hailed Rockstar for creating a satisfying simulacrum of American life, especially now “that the United States resembles a Grand Theft Auto game .” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Trump, Xi, and Putin pledge to boost oil production
events.summary: The leaders of the US, China, and Russia vowed to increase supplies of refined petroleum for the “benefit of all nations,” following a rare trilateral summit that yielded little in the way of meaningful breakthroughs. The pledge, which barely moved oil prices, could prove difficult to bring to fruition amid ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine that have choked off crude oil supplies. Moscow’s refining capacity, in particular, has been damaged by Kyiv’s aerial bombardment, while the growing risk of US escalatory action against Iran threatens to further disrupt oil flows. The International Energy Agency warned this week that the Iran war’s disruptions had “ permanently altered the appetite in many countries for imported oil,” The New York Times wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Exclusive: Rep. Gregory Meeks vows to reclaim Congress' powers from Trump
events.summary: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said Thursday Congress is going to reclaim powers long ceded to the executive branch at the Axios Future of Defense summit. Why it matters: As the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Meeks is putting the Trump administration on notice that it's foreign policy decisions are going to be challenged through legislation and oversight hearings. What they're saying: "Whether it's a Democratic president or Republican president, we've ceded too much and we've got to stand up and take it back," Meeks told Axios' Colin Demarest. "We do, at times, have to make some difficult decisions, and not just punt them away to the executive branch, because when you do that, it's hard to get them back." Meeks also suggested that incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) may be willing to take the Trump administration to court if needed to enforce congressional oversight. "If it takes some litigation to do that, we will do that," Meeks said. "Speaker Johnson wouldn't do it. I think Speaker Jeffries will do it." Catch up quick: Meeks will likely become Foreign Affairs committee chair in January, riding the blue wave that gave Democrats the ability to control Congress' legislative agenda. Zoom in: Meeks didn't rule out calling Secretary of State Marco Rubio to testify before the committee. "The jurisdiction of the House Foreign Affairs Committee is the State Department," Meeks said. Later, he added more broadly, "[y]ou can run, but you can't hide... We're going to use the power that the committee and the Constitution gives us to make sure that we're calling in members of that administration, so they have to answer to the American people, why what has taken place has taken place." Zoom out: Meeks has already sent document-preservation letters to seven agencies, including the State Department, USAID and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, warning them to avoid destroying records that could be relevant to oversight efforts. He threatened the possibility of criminal referrals if someone is found to have done otherwise. What we're watching: Meeks said Democrats plan to address affordability concerns and introduce another War Powers Resolution aimed at the Iran war. He also floated litigation and using Congress' power of the purse, including withholding funds, as ways to force the Trump administration to comply. "The people have spoken loudly and clearly that they are against the war in Iran," Meeks said. "They see how foreign policy directly now connects to domestic policy." He added that Democrats need to investigate what's happening in the Middle East, and explain to Americans what's at stake in the war. "That is the job, a part of the job, of the Foreign Affairs Committee, and that's exactly what we're going to do on day one." Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

events.summary: Customer data from Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan was leaked Thursday after hackers breached a third-party service provider , intensifying the public’s cyber paranoia following a string of technological failures. CEO Dario Amodei “seems to hold two convictions very strongly,” The New York Times wrote: “First, that powerful AI might destroy humanity. events.title: The future of medicine: Could AI help predict and prevent disease?
events.summary: Can AI help build a healthier future? By Doug Burger , Technical Fellow and Corporate Vice President, Microsoft Research Ava Amini , Principal Research Manager Eric Horvitz , Chief Scientific Officer Dr. Eric Topol , Executive Vice President, Scripps Research Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first? Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential. This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come. DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse. Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come. In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI. Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend. Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab) , the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab) . So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician. Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo , a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer. So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here. It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable. And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI. I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava. I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare. Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists. In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcare. And after a couple of years of intensive work, I and just fabulous colleagues at Microsoft worked intensively on taking healthcare challenges when it comes to applications of AI and benchmarking—medical diagnostic challenges, for example—and moved it into what I would call the realm of medical cognition, where instead of looking at a whole case that’s given to an AI system and looking at the accuracies that are reported on its ability to diagnose, for example, a form of differential diagnosis, we instead put the AI system in the, in the shoes of a clinician. You get an initial set of symptoms, you get chief complaint, some history, a little window on what’s going on when a patient comes in in an ambulatory setting, and then it’s up to the clinician to ask the right questions and to then think about tests, balancing the information value with the cost of the tests. This is the sequential diagnosis challenge.

events.title: Scoop: Trump names Kirsten Davies as new national cyber director
events.summary: The White House named Kirsten A. Davies to be its new national cyber director Thursday as President Trump overhauls his AI team, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Davies, who currently serves as the Pentagon's chief information officer , has more experience in the field than the outgoing director , Sean Cairncross . Cairncross' departure was described as amicable by two sources. But two White House officials said President Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, sought the change and pushed out Cairncross because, one said, he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." The search for Cairncross's replacement was begun two weeks ago, a third source said. Zoom out: The Office of the National Cyber Director coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. The position requires Senate confirmation. Davies previously was cleared by the Senate as the Defense Department's chief information officer. "Kirsten has the credentials to excel in this position and has already been Senate-confirmed," an administration official said. At the Pentagon, Davies has been the top adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance," according to her bio. Before serving in the Trump administration, Davies worked for Unilever and "led global cyber resilience for one of the world's largest consumer goods enterprises," her bio says. Davies' career also has included technology and cyber roles at Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard and Siemens. She founded the Institute for Cyber, a nonprofit organization dedicated to citizen safety and security in the digital universe. State of play: The administration's AI team has taken shape on the fly , but Cairncross was involved in key decisions. He held technical meetings with Anthropic leaders over the summer after Commerce Department export controls effectively scrubbed the company's models from the internet. Cairncross brought experience in Republican politics and national security, having worked with the intelligence community and dealt with cyber threats at the Republican National Committee. During Trump's first term, Cairncross represented the White House chief of staff on National Security Council committees before leading the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. Cairncross' head of policy and senior adviser Thomas Lind left in June and joined OpenAI in October, further depleting the Trump administration of technical expertise. The big picture: The latest turnover in cyber personnel comes as the country grapples with critical infrastructure outages and increasingly powerful AI poised to empower cyber defenders and hackers alike. Democrats have criticized the administration's response to outages and warned that U.S. cyber defenses are falling behind AI-fueled threats. What we're watching: Trump is also filling other key cyber positions. His pick for the top job at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps defend federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, Palantir executive Michael LoSapio, faced a combative confirmation hearing Thursday. What they're saying: In a written statement, Cairncross said, "it has been the honor of a lifetime to serve President Donald J. Trump. I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence." This story has been updated with details on Davies' appointment and background.

events.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
events.summary: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported . When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality. Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands. It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience. Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm. events.title: Firmus talks down 'modest' data centre in bid to avoid major project status
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus argues proposed AI data centre not major project amid only 'modest' economic benefits Works at Firmus Technologies' Wesley Vale site. ( Supplied: Erin Woodcock ) Firmus Technologies says one of its AI data centres should not be assessed as a major project. The company argues that unlike previously declared major projects, the data centre has only "modest" economic benefits and about 20 ongoing jobs. The State Planning Office is assessing the major project proposal made by the Latrobe Council. Firmus Technologies is fighting a local council push for one of its proposed AI data centres to be declared a major project. Latrobe Council in Tasmania's north-west has sought to defer a decision on Firmus's proposed Wesley Vale AI data centre to the state government. It has said the council's 1993 planning scheme is dated and councillors would not be able to consider all the relevant issues, such as energy, water and environmental impacts of a large AI data centre. A letter from Firmus's lawyers to Planning Minister Kerry Vincent, who is assessing the request for a major project declaration, has now been made public. "We respectfully ask that the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure not be declared a major project," the letter reads. It states that the project would have only "modest" economic benefits and ongoing job opportunities: Although the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is expected to generate some economic activity, these benefits are relatively modest and largely confined to employment opportunities, with approximately 70 jobs anticipated during the construction phase and around 20 permanent full-time positions once operational. Beyond these direct employment outcomes, the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is not expected to materially alter the economic structure of the region, establish a significant new industry cluster, or drive broader regional economic transformation. The submission states the development cost of its facility would be $31.25 million. It compared this to major projects such as Chambroad's Kangaroo Bay Hotel proposal near Hobart , which it said would support 443 ongoing jobs and generate $42.7 million in additional annual visitor expenditure. Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) "The economic benefits of the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure are considerably more limited in scale and are largely confined to construction activity and a relatively modest number of ongoing jobs," the letter reads. The process of declaring and assessing a major project in Tasmania can take years, while the council approval process is usually much quicker. A sign near Firmus' proposed AI data centre site at Wesley Vale. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Firmus told inquiry of $46b economic benefit from three projects Last week, at a Tasmanian parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres, Firmus co-CEO Tim Rosenfield was asked about the benefits to Tasmania of its three projects. Tim Rosenfield appeared at a Tasmanian inquiry into data centres in Hobart. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) "This is a large-scale investment we're making," he told the inquiry. "We have actually, at the request of the government some months ago, commissioned a third-party study which is close to being finalised. "It puts total state gross product contributions of up to $46 billion to the Tasmanian state economy through 2035. "We're operating these supercomputers, and that requires skills, it requires on-site presence, it requires learning pathways. "The preliminary modelled outcome shows about 8,900 ongoing FTEs [full-time equivalent jobs] through 2035 created." Firmus is building an AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards and has approval for another at Long Reach in northern Tasmania. The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston, showing its research and development lab. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Firmus 'deeply disappointed' by council's referral In addition to saying the economic impact of the project would not be "significant" to the region, the letter from Firmus's lawyers also said the impact on the area's environment and social fabric would be limited. It also said the project would not deliver advanced regional development objectives or significant public infrastructure to the region. events.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
events.summary: It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life. Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days. The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues. Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more. While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly. Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related. The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch. The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said. This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said. Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X . AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with. In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up. When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.” Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said. Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.” Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues. And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said. “There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.

events.title: Wall Street ends sharply lower as Anthropic’s debut fails to revive AI fervour
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Nov 18. Wall Street fell sharply as Anthropic’s record IPO failed to lift AI stocks, and the S&P 500 dropped for a fifth straight session. Chipmakers slid, led by Nvidia and AMD, while some firms rose on strong news, such as Palo Alto Networks, and Walmart fell on weak sales guidance. Investors now expect tighter Fed policy, with markets pricing a 94% chance of a December rate hike, as inflation data and the PCE report loom. NEW YORK - US stocks slumped on Nov 19, after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalise faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early spike in its share price ebbed. All three major US stock indexes ended the session sharply lower, with the benchmark S&P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses. The S&P 500 was on course to post its steepest weekly loss since April 2025. Anthropic’s debut, the largest IPO on record, was priced late on Nov 18 at US$83 per share and was widely viewed as the next high bar to clear for the AI trade. The stock opened at US$111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion), its momentum began to lose steam. “The Anthropic IPO is attracting gobs of attention,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital in St Louis, Missouri. “That money is coming from somewhere; investors are making changes in their portfolio to incorporate Anthropic, so I wouldn’t extrapolate a whole lot of meaning from today’s trading behaviour, whether it’s up or down.” Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for the AI trade has waned. “My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added. “Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact.” “Data centres are going to be more expensive to build, and they’re going to be built more slowly.” Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company. Most chipmakers were lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others. Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed lower. Neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius sustained steep losses. In other stocks, Palo Alto Networks shares jumped after the cybersecurity firm raised its 2027 revenue guidance. Walmart dipped after the retail giant’s annual sales forecast disappointed investors. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46. Following the Nov 18 release of minutes from the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting, investors are recalibrating their expectations pertaining to upcoming rate decisions. The minutes revealed a desire to rein in inflation even prior to the recent release of consumer and producer price indexes, which showed price pressures heating up. Financial markets are currently pricing in about a 94% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the central bank’s December meeting, with a small but growing chance of a super-sized 50-basis-point increase, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. Next week, the Commerce Department is expected to release its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, which includes the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. Analysts expect the report to show year-on-year core inflation of 3.2%, well above the central bank’s 2% annual target. REUTERS

events.title: Uber tests rides for kids as young as 10, with extra pay for drivers
events.summary: Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids , launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin. The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids. The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off. Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber. Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early. Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids web page. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete. The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum. Uber opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens , although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. events.title: China bars Bloomberg reporter from trilateral meeting after she shouted question at earlier event
events.summary: Chinese officials have blocked a Bloomberg TV journalist from a key event for shouting out a question to President Donald Trump NEW YORK -- It's a scenario seen every day: A reporter shouts a question out to a leader at an event. The leader either answers or ignores it. In China, though, Bloomberg TV journalist Annmarie Hordern was blocked from a key event by Chinese officials Thursday, apparently as retribution for having shouted a question in a way that the government considered rude. Hordern was barred from Thursday's trilateral meeting among President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, after having called out a question during an Trump meeting with Xi. She had asked Trump if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. A White House official said the Chinese insisted the reporter not be allowed in despite the White House having pushed for admission. The official insisted on speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity around the issue. The White House did not immediately respond to a query about what steps it took to advocate for the reporter. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents' Association, said on X that it was “commendable that the WH is advocating for press access.” A pool report from the incident said the Chinese “have passed along a message that yelling questions is considered extremely rude and we will be pulled from the room if we do so.” China’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press, and an email to Bloomberg seeking comment was not immediately returned. The incident, which reflected the way China typically seeks to tightly control news events, recalled a previous one in 2022, in which a White House pool reporter said she was knocked off balance after being yanked by her backpack when she tried to shout a question to President Joe Biden. The question was about human rights ahead of a meeting between Biden and Xi in Bali, Indonesia. Two White House staff members intervened and said the producer should be left alone. China's approach to journalists, particularly foreign media, has long been chilly and uneven. In recent decades, international reporters have been expelled both for their coverage and for perceived misbehavior during news events. Resident correspondents are occasionally detained and questioned — and in some cases in past years, compelled to sign “self-criticism” reports — for showing up where the government doesn't want them to be. events.title: Trump administration auctions deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa in first sale of its kind
events.summary: The Trump administration has auctioned deep-sea mining leases for millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa The Trump administration on Thursday auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa , giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters. The two 20-year leases are the first of their kind in the U.S., following President Donald Trump’s directive last year to leverage deep-ocean minerals to counter growing competition for resources from China. The leases are already the source of several legal challenges. The two lease areas each sold for the minimum bid amount of $3 million to deep-sea mining startup Wetstone U.S. Ventures, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. While there were two bidders at the auction, only Wetstone placed bids. Wetstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. The leases grant the company the ability to begin initial surveys of the seafloor to explore for minerals and prepare their testing or mining plans. It has the exclusive right to mine those areas commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. The auction moved forward despite passionate opposition from locals in the territory and three lawsuits seeking to halt the sales. The auction was held at the Ventura County Fire Department Headquarters in Southern California, where a few dozen protesters gathered outside. “We had hoped it would never come to this,” Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, an American Samoa resident who has fought the auction for more than a year, said in a statement Thursday. Globally, deep-sea mining is still at an experimental stage. A handful of other countries have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals, but no company has started commercial operations. The U.S. has never issued a lease for deep-sea minerals beyond a short-lived mining effort in California waters more than 60 years ago. The federal interest in seafloor minerals stems from an April 2025 executive order, when the president directed his administration to search for and responsibly develop critical minerals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. The Marine Minerals Administration is considering further auctions of the seabed near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters. It’s unclear if the leases will withstand legal challenge. On Monday, a court ordered the National Marine Fisheries Service to more thoroughly assess the impacts the mining activities could have on endangered species, saying the agency's “cramped, expedited, informal” review violated the Endangered Species Act. The Marine Minerals Administration said in a statement that it had addressed the court's opinion by starting to consult with the fisheries service on another environmental assessment. But it did not cancel or delay the auction. David Henkin, deputy managing attorney at the environmental law group Earthjustice, said the ruling made Thursday's auction unlawful. In order to issue the notice of sale, the government needed to comply with the Endangered Species Act, he said. Earthjustice is representing Fa’asao Amerika Samoa, a group dedicated to safeguarding the territory’s culture, and the Conservation Council of Hawaii in the suit. Another lawsuit filed Wednesday by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Finafinau, an environmental group founded by Suluai-Mahuka, similarly argues the environmental review process was rushed and is asking the court to strike down the leases. A third lawsuit, brought by a council of local chiefs in American Samoa, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, is challenging the federal government’s authority to auction the waters near their islands. Tony Romeo, head of the deep-sea mining startup Eco Minerals, which did not participate in the auction, said any company going into deep-sea mining needs to be prepared for pushback from environmental groups. “If they can halt it through legal action, they will,” he said. “We’ll see how it ultimately plays out.” Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Association, said in a statement that he expects industry interest and investment to grow in the coming years. “Decades of environmental research and extensive assessments have helped lay the groundwork for responsible ocean mineral development," he said. events.title: Christie’s halts Frida Kahlo painting from auction at Mexico’s request
events.summary: Christie’s has withdrawn a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York after Mexican authorities requested more information about its provenance MEXICO CITY -- Christie’s withdrew a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York this week after Mexican authorities requested additional information about its provenance, the auction house confirmed Thursday. The painting, “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz,” or “Congress of the Peoples for Peace,” had been scheduled for auction on Tuesday. It depicts a white dove on a tree bearing fruit alongside a smiling sun, the moon, and two slices of watermelon. Mexican authorities asked Christie’s to hold the sale until the painting's provenance could be clarified, citing a declaration that recognizes Frida Kahlo’s work as an artistic monument of Mexico . “In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research,” a Christie’s spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. “We look forward to selling this work at a later date." The same painting was auctioned in 2020 by Sotheby’s without any objections. Kahlo’s works in Mexico are considered artistic monuments and are protected under the country's federal law on monuments and archaeological, artistic, and historical sites. Mexican authorities said they were working with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museums Trust, administered by the Bank of Mexico. The painting left Mexico more than three decades before the 1984 decree declaring Kahlo’s work an artistic monument. The decree prohibits the permanent export of her works that were in Mexico when it was published. Kahlo, whose health was seriously deteriorating, sent the painting to the congress through her husband, the painter Diego Rivera. She died in Mexico City two years after creating it. The trip to Vienna was recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s last wife, and has also been mentioned by historians such as Raquel Tibol. Last year, Kahlo’s 1940 self-portrait “El sueño (La cama)," or The Dream (The Bed), sold for $54.7 million , setting an auction record for a work by a female artist. events.title: Anthropic IPO heightens Washington’s tech scrutiny
events.summary: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO is heightening Washington’s scrutiny of the tech sector as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress armed with a long list of AI leaders to investigate. Already, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have raised concerns over the risks, including the potential for advanced AI models to be abused and the additional volatility such IPOs could introduce into the financial system. A bipartisan Senate quartet introduced legislation on Thursday that would require publicly traded companies to disclose more information about AI. “Wall Street shouldn’t be cashing in on a company that could turn out to be a ticking time bomb,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said. “Going public cements a broken business model and rewards its reckless pace.” The Senate Banking Committee’s top Democrat, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, called for quick congressional action on “safeguards on advanced AI development.” Outside groups are using the IPO as an opportunity to push for more stringent controls, too. “Workers’ livelihoods, our children’s safety, and the public’s ability to control this technology cannot depend on whether doing the right thing helps the stock price,” said Shauna Thomas, executive director of the AI accountability group Guardrails Action. — Eleanor Mueller and Ashley Gold

events.title: Suspects charged in brazen train heist ring that netted $22 million in cargo from major retailers
events.summary: Authorities have charged more than a dozen people for allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation LOS ANGELES -- More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers. A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country. Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world's largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon. The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit. “The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech In group chats, the men shared numerous photos and videos of themselves busting into the hulking train cars, and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise. They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars while police helicopters descended overhead. The 13 men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. Two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers. If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison. events.title: Exclusive: Sen. Ernst rebukes lack of "transparency" from Pentagon on Iran
events.summary: Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) said "a lot of people would be able to guess" if she regrets voting to confirm the embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, during Axios' Future of Defense Summit Thursday. Why it matters: The retiring Iowa senator, who served in the military for more than two decades, has been notably skeptical of Hegseth, and hasn't always been in lockstep with the Trump administration. Catch up quick: Despite her hesitancy over his nomination, Ernst ultimately voted to confirm Hegseth . However, she's continued to question him throughout his tenure. She recently questioned whether the embattled Pentagon leader has been "truthful" about the status of the Iran war, which she said Iowans rejected in the midterms. "If there is deception coming from our Pentagon and being transmitted to the president, I would want to know that," Ernst told reporters earlier this month. Driving the news: "There is very little transparency right now with what is being discussed between the White House and the Department of War," Ernst said of Pentagon communication over the war in Iran in a conversation with Axios' defense and space reporter Thomas Novelly. "As Congress, we would expect that we would be read into some of those conversations, and unfortunately, we have not been read into those conversations," she added. State of play: Ernst sits on the Senate Committee on Armed Services, where she chairs the Emerging Threats and Capabilities subcommittee. She predicted in her interview with Novelly that given the "not even hidden animosity" between Democrats and Hegseth, "it will be very difficult" for new Senate Armed Services Committee leadership to receive information. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: The Jensen Huang Blast Radius Has Hit His Favorite Restaurants
events.summary: Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang . In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went. But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero. Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World , a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China. “It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.” At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?” Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023. Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island. “When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.” At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up. “I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.” Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth. Owner Tu Chang-chun said he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop. In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars. The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments. But not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business. The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors. Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.” Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.

events.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
events.summary: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor. Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday . He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.” Evasive and irregular turns “FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.” Read full article Comments

events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 17, 2026: Nvidia posts strong quarterly earnings, says it does not plan to reinstate Huang Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. November 17, 2026: Huang says he sees ‘outpouring’ of calls for him to return, says he ‘would be honored’ to return as CEO Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026 November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’ More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.

events.title: Call for ACCC to take up 'strong case' for burn victim hurt by Temu product
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Calls for consumer watchdog to help family harmed by recalled Temu product Daniella Jacobs-Herd sustained burns to 13 per cent of her body when a spark ignited a hoodie purchased via Temu. ( Supplied: Hannah Jacobs-Herd ) Daniella Jacobs-Herd was injured in 2024 when a hoodie purchased via Temu caught fire. Her family had tried to pursue legal action against the seller, but has run out of options. Consumer experts say the ACCC should take up the case. More than two years after she was badly burnt while wearing a hoodie purchased via Temu, Daniella Jacobs-Herd is still traumatised by flame and smoke. Burnt toast and birthday candles send the 10-year-old Hervey Bay girl into fits of rage. "Half the day is spent trying to calm her down and explain that it's okay and safe," Daniella's mother, Hannah, said. Hannah Jacobs-Herd says her daughter Daniella is triggered by burnt toast and birthday candles. ( ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor ) On a winter's night in 2024, Daniella had been standing near a backyard fire pit at her mother's birthday party when sparks ignited her jumper. She suffered severe burns to 13 per cent of her body. Temu recalled the unicorn-themed hoodie for failing to meet mandatory safety standards, and Ms Jacobs-Herd sought compensation through a local Queensland legal firm. But the online shopping platform said it was merely an intermediary and liability for product safety rested with its suppliers. The Chinese supplier, Sunshine Towels, has not responded to the lawyer's repeated attempts to contact it since the July 2024 incident. Temu recalled the hoodie for failing to meet mandatory safety standards more than four months after the incident. ( Supplied: ACCC ) Last month, law firm Shine Lawyers told Ms Jacobs-Herd it was closing the case and advised her to engage an international lawyer. Ms Jacobs-Herd lives on a disability support pension and said the legal fees were out of her reach. "$15,000 for a 20-minute consult — I don't have that sort of money lying around," she said. 'Nothing more important than safety' In 2010, when Australian consumer law was last updated, online shopping made up 6 per cent of total Australian retail sales. That surged to 24 per cent by 2025, led by online marketplaces selling products made by overseas suppliers. Australian consumer law requires suppliers of goods to comply with mandatory safety standards. Temu has become Australia's most-used retail marketplace app. ( Supplied: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission ) In a complaint to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) in June, consumer advocate Choice said that left a regulatory gap for online marketplaces claiming to be intermediaries between the supplier and consumer. The ACCC acknowledged the need for reform in its response to Choice, noting that a July meeting of consumer affairs ministers had prioritised introducing a general safety provision — laws making the entire supply chain liable for selling unsafe products in Australia. However, those ministers recently decided a general safety provision would not be part of a consultation process currently underway for Australian consumer law reform. Allan Fels says a general safety provision should be introduced as soon as possible. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) Allan Fels was the ACCC chair when a general safety provision was last considered in a 2019 review of Australian consumer law. He said the Jacobs-Herd family's experience showed the provision should have been introduced at that time. "Given the dangers of products like this, it was probably best if they had enacted the law in 2019," he said. "But certainly now, in the light of experience, the law should be enacted as soon as possible." The assistant minister responsible for Australian consumer law, Andrew Leigh, said the government's current focus was on improving processes for recalling unsafe products, and a general safety provision would be a reform option for 2027. Tim Tszyu hunting 'legacy-defining' win on Gold Coast An ex-Queensland premier's cherished link to legendary Wallabies family Lions disrupt high school graduation ceremony with consecutive picks Qld jockey loses bid to reduce jail time after strangling woman Luke Nottage is an expert in consumer product safety law at the University of Sydney. He said there were protections already enshrined in law that meant the Jacobs-Herd family should not be forced to pay for their own international lawyer. Australian consumer law empowers the ACCC to make compensation claims on behalf of consumers harmed by unsafe products.
