events.title: Retailers shake up Thanksgiving meal deals amid rising food costs
events.summary: Major grocery retailers are switching up their Thanksgiving dinner deals this year, with a few lowering prices, others swapping out items and some shifting toward more flexible meal options. The big picture: Lower advertised prices from some retailers could offer relief to Americans already stretching their holiday budgets , but shifting menus mean shoppers may not be getting the same bang for their buck. State of play: Higher fuel costs, poor growing conditions and other inflationary pressures have pushed up food prices ahead of the holiday. The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for ten has increased 6% since 2025, totaling an estimated $58.63. The increase is largely driven by price hikes for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries, the federation said. Driving the news: Walmart is advertising a lower price for its Thanksgiving meal than in 2025, while offering 18% more individual items. The retailer said this year's meal , which serves ten people for $35, is its "lowest priced one-click basket" ever, down from $39.93 last year. The complete meal comes with a turkey, multiple sides and pumpkin pie to finish. It adds ingredients for sweet potato casserole and corn muffins, but drops macaroni and cheese and baby carrots from last year's spread. Fried onions were the only item to switch from name-brand to store-brand in 2026. The other side: Aldi is also promoting a Thanksgiving meal $1 cheaper than in 2025, though several dishes have changed . Instead of a 14-pound turkey, the 2026 dinner will have a 16-pound bird. It includes several sides, but not fan favorites such as mashed potatoes and gravy, macaroni and cheese or green bean casserole. Zoom out: Costco's gourmet Thanksgiving dinner is more elaborate than its cook-at-home grocery counterparts, with a similar menu and the same advertised promotional price as last year. Both 2025 and 2026 dinners cost $199.99, serve eight people and include a five-pound turkey breast. The prepared meal includes the same traditional sides and desserts, with the addition of candied yams. This year's dinner is marketed as 30 pounds, compared with 28 pounds in some descriptions of last year's offerings. The intrigue: Kroger is shifting away from the fixed-price "Freshgiving" Thanksgiving meal bundle it offered in previous years. Instead, it is promoting individual holiday discounts and prepared foods in various portion sizes. Kroger's chief marketing officer said the approach is intended to make holiday meals more convenient and accommodate gatherings of different sizes. In 2025, Kroger advertised a Thanksgiving meal for 10 for under $4.75 a person, providing a 14- to 16-pound frozen turkey and traditional sides. The bottom line: Your food preferences, guest count and budget will help determine if a Thanksgiving meal deal is the right choice for you. Go deeper: Wholesale food prices are on the rise

events.title: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
events.summary: The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations. The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price. Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price. At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn. Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market , though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised. Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes that it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI. Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist. In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”. Anthropic’s San Francisco-born chief executive was educated at Stanford and Princeton universities. He worked at the Chinese tech firm Baidu and then at Google before joining OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT and now Anthropic’s arch-rival, where he had a key position as vice-president of research. In 2020, Amodei left OpenAI, and it has been widely reported that his departure was due to conflicting views over safety. “It is incredibly unproductive to try and argue with someone else’s vision,” he said years later. AI safety remains a major concern for Amodei. He called for a slowdown in AI development in September after the resignation of an employee who cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity and triggered a wave of concern about the existential threat posed by the technology. Amodei is also blunt about the potential impact of AI on jobs, claiming that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs by the end of the decade. Amodei, Dario’s sister, began her career in politics, working in Congress and on a congressional campaign, before switching to tech and taking a job at Stripe, the payment processor. She moved to OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic with her brother. She leads teams on AI model safety and alignment , making sure AI systems adhere to human aims and values. Like other Anthropic employees and co-founders, Amodei is tied to the EA movement. She is married to one of its major donors, Holden Karnofsky, who co-founded GiveWell and the major grant-giving organisation Open Philanthropy. This Brighton-born former journalist has been catapulted into the list of richest Britons with the Anthropic flotation. His paper wealth of approximately $26.6bn (£20.3bn) compares with £38bn for the London-based Hinduja brothers and puts him above the £18.2bn fortune of the Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne and Manchester United’s co-owner Jim Ratcliffe, who is worth £15.2bn. Clark leads the Anthropic Institute, a thinktank devoted to researching the social implications of advanced AI. In a lecture at Oxford University this year, Clark predicted that an AI system will work with humans to make a Nobel prize-winning discovery within 12 months, and that tradespeople will be helped by bipedal robots within two years. He added that it would be better if humans could slow the development of the technology “to give ourselves more time as a species” to deal with the implications of its powers.

events.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
events.summary: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work. An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model , developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation. Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services. Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA.

events.title: UAE highlights $1tn in US investments during Abu Dhabi Investment Forum
events.summary: The UAE on Thursday promoted its more than $1 trillion of investments in the US and its broader framework, as businesses and investors gathered in New York for the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum to expand business ties between the two countries. The Abu Dhabi Investment Forum, organised by the Abu Dhabi Investment Office , was part of broader engagements in New York this week to advance partnerships with US investors and explore commercial opportunities. “What brings us together is more than just investments. It is the strength of the relationship between the United States and the United Arab Emirates, a connection that has been built over many decades through institutions, shared objectives and, more importantly, people,” said Badr Al Olama, the director of Adio. Mr Al Olama said more than half of the 26 financial institutions that have announced plans to establish a presence in the Abu Dhabi Global Market are US companies. Health care and AI were seen as the two major sectors at Thursday's forum, which also touched on advanced manufacturing, travel and food innovation. Abu Dhabi investment firm MGX in July linked up with BlackRock on a $40 billion digital infrastructure investment. MGX also plans to invest up to 80 per cent of its total portfolio in US projects. The company said at the time that it had raised $49 billion from investors across North America, Asia, Europe and the Gulf for its AI Fund. And this month, Adnoc and AI firm G42 signed a multiyear partnership with OpenAI that would increase the company's presence in the Emirates. “We see the next chapter of Abu Dhabi-US investment extending beyond the companies we already know,” Mr Al Olama said. Among the delegates at the forum in Manhattan were representatives from a Brooklyn-based biotech venture company looking to find co-investors to launch in Abu Dhabi. Another delegate from the Colorado-Abu Dhabi Trade and Investment Council was also hoping to deepen ties between the US state and the emirate. Bilateral trade between the US and UAE totalled an estimated $55.4 billion in 2025, a 16 per cent increase from 2024, according to data from the Office of the US Trade Representative. US goods exported to the UAE totalled $31.4 billion, while it imported $7.7 billion in goods. US services trade with the UAE totalled about $16.3 billion last year. The UAE's Ministry of Investment reported in July that the Emirates had attracted $48.3 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, in a 6 per cent annual increase. Total FDI stock rose to $318.9 billion at the end of last year. The UAE aims to attract $65 billion in annual FDI and raise total FDI stock to $600 billion by 2031. No planned FDI into the UAE have been cancelled this year despite the uncertain outlook caused by the Iran war, The National previously reported. The Emirates also continues to back its $1.4 trillion investment and economic framework with the US. In a March letter to the US-UAE Business Council, Yousef Al Otaiba, UAE ambassador to the US and Minister of State, said the Emirates remains “open for business”. “The past year has reminded us that what defines us is not the challenges we face, but how we respond to them with confidence, clarity of purpose and a continued commitment to progress,” said Amna Almheiri, consul general of the UAE in New York. Despite the regional conflict, Abu Dhabi has continued to attract global capital. The Abu Dhabi Global Market said assets under management grew 54 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026 as Bain Capital, Blue Owl Capital and other major US funds have expanded into the financial centre. More than 1,500 US companies are operating in the Emirates, it said. The inaugural Abu Dhabi Investment Form in New York was held last year, when agreements were signed across digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, financial services and new energy.

events.title: For these Australians, the recession has already arrived
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians describe life in a recession-like squeeze Many households feel as though they are in a recession, even though Australia is not technically in one. ( ABC News: Kylie Silvester ) The ripple effects from years of rising living costs continue to make life challenging for Australians. Hundreds of you have shared your experiences with the ABC. Small businesses fear losing customers and staff. Home owners worry about paying bills and putting food on the table. While Australia has so far avoided a technical recession, many of the warning signs associated with one are becoming harder to ignore. The unemployment rate has climbed to 4.9 per cent , its highest level of the post-pandemic period, and a Roy Morgan poll shows consumer confidence is at its lowest in seven months. Artificial Intelligence, offshoring, restructuring and slowing economic activity are why Bunnings, Canva, NAB, Bendigo Bank, ING and Qantas are just some of the major businesses that have cut thousands of jobs in recent months. At the same time, living costs continue to rise faster than many household budgets can absorb. But whether that amounts to a recession depends on how you define one. Technical recession versus lived reality A recession is usually described as a period when the economy stops growing and starts going backwards. The most commonly used measure, known as a "technical recession", is two consecutive quarters of negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP), which is the value of all goods and services produced across the country. When recessions happen, businesses tend to earn less, consumers cut back their spending and unemployment often rises as companies reduce staff or delay hiring them. By that definition, Australia is not in a recession. In fact, the economy is still growing, albeit slowly. GDP rose 0.4 per cent in the June quarter and was up 2.1 per cent over the year. Oxford Economics director of global macro research, Ben May, said some of the conditions that had historically preceded recessions were visible today in economies around the world. "These features are visible in elevated energy prices, rising bond yields, and the AI boom," Mr May said. "Still, compared with the 1970s and 1980s, economies are better positioned to weather shocks. "It would take a further escalation in these or a sharp reversal of the AI boom to push the world economy into recession; a possible but not inevitable outcome." So, Australia is not in an official recession, but there are other measures in the economists' tool box. For instance, years of rising prices, higher mortgage repayments and wages that have struggled to keep pace with household costs have created what economists often describe as a "per capita recession" or a decline in living standards despite continued economic growth. But even here, there's a disparity between how Australians feel about the economy and what the numbers say. Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics, said Australia had not yet entered a per capita recession, with official data showing real GDP per person fell slightly in the March quarter before edging higher in the June quarter. "However, that's far from a stellar outcome," Mr Surya said. "With the economy set to slow markedly, we wouldn't rule out the possibility that Australia enters a per capita recession over the next few quarters." That disconnect has become a growing part of the national conversation. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock recently acknowledged that conditions were "going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer" following the central bank's decision to raise the cash rate to 4.85 per cent. So while the economy may still be growing "on paper", around kitchen tables and business counters, many Australians tell a different story. Albury resident Nicole Thurgate is feeling the economic pain at home. "I feel like I'm in a recession and it definitely feels like we're going backwards," Ms Thurgate said. The 57-year-old said it was around the time of the third interest rate rise of 2026 that the combined pressure of rising mortgage repayments and living costs became impossible to ignore. Since then, she has cut back on almost every discretionary expense she can think of. Her car is off the road because she cannot afford repairs, she has sold personal belongings including her mother's jewellery and a perfume collection, and has stopped buying takeaway food and red meat altogether. "It's not just giving up luxuries here," she said. "[It's] basic things, right down to the kind of tea bag I'm buying. It's become every cent.

events.title: Xi Jinping declares 'complete turnaround' in China's relations with Australia
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chinese President Xi Jinping has met with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in China. ( AAP: Lukas Coch ) Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has met with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Mr Xi said there had been a "full turnaround" in relations between Australia and China since Anthony Albanese became prime minister. Mr Albanese will travel to Beijing for further meetings with senior officials. Chinese President Xi Jinping has declared Australia and China have had a "full turnaround" in relations "despite differences" in the past four years under the Albanese government. Mr Xi made the remarks at the opening of a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen today. "We have jointly promoted the full turnaround of China-Australia relations, and exchanges and cooperation in various fields between our two countries have continued to deepen," Mr Xi said. "I will work with you in the spirit of equality, seeking common ground despite differences, and mutually beneficial cooperation to take forward the China-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership." Chinese President Xi Jinping says there has been a "full turnaround" in relations. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Mr Albanese said the Australia-China relationship "delivers prosperity for both of our countries" but promised "frank" conversations. "And the relationship that we are building is positive, is calm, is not defined by our differences, but one where we can have clear and frank exchanges for our mutual interest," he said. It's the fifth meeting between the pair since Mr Albanese came to office in 2022. At that time relations had plunged to their lowest point in decades, with Beijing imposing trade restrictions on Australian exports and high-level talks between the two countries effectively frozen. Mr Albanese is due to travel to Beijing tonight for formal talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang and the Australia-China CEO roundtable where businesses are expected to push for greater trade certainty. Chinese President Xi Jinping has met with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in China. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Albanese says government 'worked hard' to stabilise relationship Speaking after his meeting with Mr Xi, Mr Albanese said his government had "worked hard to stabilise the relationship" with China "for the interests of our relationship with our major trading partner". Mr Albanese said he discussed a full range of issues with Mr Xi. "It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," he said. Mr Albanese says the Australia-China relationship "delivers prosperity" for both countries. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Asked whether China's longer term ambitions meant differences between the countries would endure, Mr Albanese said the two countries were able to discuss those issues "constructively and very directly". "That's something that we do in meetings," he said. "We have different political systems, different histories, but that doesn't mean that you can't have constructive dialogue, and that's what Australia seeks." Mr Albanese said it was "positive" that Mr Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump had met yesterday. "It is always better to have dialogue than to have conflict," he said. On confronting Mr Putin over Ukraine during his APEC speech, Mr Albanese said he had made it "very clear" Russia needed to stop the war. "Well, he certainly heard it, as did others in the room," Mr Albanese said. "I have a responsibility to put Australia's position clearly and directly, and that is what I did." China talks follow Australia's deals on defence, AI The high-level talks come after Australia signed a series of agreements that Beijing is unlikely to welcome. Just days before arriving in China, Mr Albanese oversaw the signing of a new defence cooperation agreement with the Philippines aimed at strengthening military ties, maritime surveillance and information sharing. He reiterated Australia's support for Manila, which has repeatedly clashed with Beijing over disputed territorial claims in the South China Sea. Mr Albanese also joined Mr Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for a Quad summit in the Philippines, where the four leaders announced plans for a new joint exercise in the region next year. Anthony Albanese was placed near host Xi Jinping for the Economic Leaders Meeting.

events.title: One year on from workplace death, grieving mum urges BlueScope inquest
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jack McGrath was fatally injured while working at BlueScope in November 2025. ( Supplied: Tamara Carlson ) The mother of Jack McGrath, who was fatally struck by a beam at BlueScope's Port Kembla steelworks, says the pain of his death has become harder to process 12 months on. The CFMEU has called for a coronial inquest into his death, arguing it should investigate whether industrial manslaughter occurred. The SafeWork investigation into the incident continues. On the anniversary of her son's death while working at BlueScope, Tamara Carlson is devastated and angered by his final moments. Just days before his 25th birthday, Jack McGrath was fatally struck by a falling beam at the Port Kembla steelworks on November 17 last year. The rigger was contracted by Ventia to work on Australia's largest steelmaking project, relining BlueScope's number six blast furnace , which is costing the company $1.15 billion. Jack McGrath (right) with his family. ( Supplied ) When she saw police officers approaching her home, she had no idea they were about to deliver the tragic news. "It's actually harder to process now than when it first happened," Ms Carlson said. "I think because those first few months you're running on adrenaline and it doesn't sink in. "Now it's 12 months on, babies are being born and birthdays are happening, and the kids are saying things how Jack would've said it." She is backing a union's call for a coronial inquest into his death, as a SafeWork NSW investigation continues. Ms Carlson was incensed by comments made by BlueScope's chief executive Tania Archibald at the annual general meeting earlier this week that safety was the organisation's top priority. "I'm just angry because they announced that last year too, and clearly they're just empty promises," Ms Carlson said. A worker looks out over BlueScope from the top of the blast furnace. ( ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez ) There have been at least six dangerous incidents involving falling tools and building supplies, and the hospitalisation of an injured worker reported to SafeWork NSW, since Mr McGrath's death. The CFMEU NSW wrote to the Coroner's Court on the anniversary of Mr McGrath's death on Tuesday, demanding an inquest to investigate whether he died by industrial manslaughter. The union argued an inquest was mandatory because Mr McGrath might have died as a result of homicide. "By naming this offence industrial manslaughter, we are of the view that parliament has treated a workplace death caused by the grossly negligent breach of a WHS duty as a form of homicide," the union wrote. BlueScope is upgrading one of its blast furnaces, the most expensive project in the company's history. ( Supplied: BlueScope ) Ms Carlson joined the call for an inquest. "We're all for it. Someone needs to be held accountable," she said. The union's letter pointed to legislation that introduced the offence of industrial manslaughter the year before Mr McGrath's death. It allows a body corporate to be held responsible for a workplace death due to "gross negligence", which can be assessed by looking at the organisation's conduct as a whole. The maximum penalty is 25 years' jail for individuals and $20 million for a body corporate. CFMEU work health and safety officer Marko Petrovic said the union's call comes after facing repeated roadblocks in finding out what happened. He said recommendations could also be handed down to help prevent further tragedies and provide closure to Mr McGrath's family and colleagues. "It's only just the anniversary of Jack's death and really all we've got to see is safety notices, safety alerts and dangerous incidents still happening," he said. That 23-year-old scaffolder was working on the same furnace reline project when he fell into a pipe and was taken to hospital with a hip injury on October 30. In a separate incident two weeks prior, another worker was taken to hospital after his back seized while working in a confined space. events.title: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156B to charity
events.summary: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees. As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy. First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold. The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans. Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF. Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30. Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered. All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year. Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact. Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy , GiveWell , Coefficient Giving , Foresight Institute , and Giving What We Can . And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Anthropic tops SpaceX with record $3 trillion market debut Topic: Information Technology Industry Anthropic's market value has blown past $US2.1 trillion ($3.1 trillion) in its Nasdaq debut, higher than SpaceX's June listing. CEO Dario Amodei and six co-founders, who together own about 10 per cent of the frontier AI firm, have stakes now valued at around $US225 billion combined. Investors are watching whether the AI company's enormous valuation can be sustained amid growing concerns about the AI sector. The maker of the Claude AI chatbot opened at $US111.50 ($167) on the Nasdaq, a 34 per cent jump from its initial public offering price of $US83, as investors rushed to buy into the first major frontier AI company to list on a stock exchange. The debut marked a major milestone for the AI industry, but the initial excitement faded as investors took profits and its shares gave up some of the early gains. The main US indexes also retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook. The stock, trading under the ticker ANT, was last quoted at $US96.30, as at 7am AEDT. Claude is a series of large language models developed by Anthropic and used worldwide. ( Supplied: Anthropic ) Anthropic raised $US81.3 billion through its IPO, alongside a further $US26 billion in a concurrent private placement involving major technology companies. The listing comes at a turbulent time for the technology sector, which has been rattled by concerns of an AI bubble, worries over mounting debt among data centre operators and a widening scandal that forced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang to step down as CEO. Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap, said she had expected Anthropic's debut to help revive enthusiasm for AI stocks, but that had failed to materialise. "I think tomorrow you will probably see the stock dropping in the red, there certainly seems like there's enough demand, but the price is still too high." Australians offered access to record IPO Australian investors were among a select group outside the United States given the opportunity to buy shares in Anthropic before its stock market debut. CommSec and Sharesies declined to comment when asked about demand among Australian retail investors. Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said his firm's grey market indicators had pointed to a strong debut for Anthropic. The indicator allows traders to speculate on a company's share price before it officially hits the stock exchange, providing an early indication of investor expectations. The investment boom behind AI is looking increasingly shaky just as it is about to revolutionise our lives. "If you sort of use that as a rough guide, demand's been really strong," he said. Mr Rodda compared the excitement to the launch of a new iPhone. "People lining up around the streets to be some of the first people to get their hands on it," he said. "It's very, very much a similar sort of psychology dynamic amongst investors." Ms Liu from Ten Cap said strong demand for Anthropic shares was partly due to their limited availability, with relatively few shares being offered to investors. Ms Liu believes Anthropic is a "great company" but has decided against buying shares at the current valuation. "It's just too expensive," she said. events.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
events.summary: Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job. Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension , CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there. Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan County Title Extension regional specialist Member grade Senior member Alma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products. Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business. She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside. “We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in. Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and the U.N.’s International Telecommunication Union , and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC) , and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP). She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture . An early love of design and problem-solving Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors. As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs. That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings. “I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says. She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career. She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University , in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education. She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016. That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry , in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020. From outreach to extension work After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College , in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator. She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water. She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain , helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park. In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County ’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns. She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds. Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System , a nationwide network run by land-grant universities , schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states. The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture , managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties. The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program , which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship. Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person. She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says. “We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says. events.title: Eyre Peninsula 'not out of the woods' after 'extremely ferocious' storm
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Power outage continues across Eyre Peninsula after storm downs transmission towers Some SA farmers are now counting their losses from storm damage. ( Supplied: Aisha Finlay ) A potential supercell ripped down several electricity transmission towers, cutting supply to thousands of Eyre Peninsula residents on Thursday. Power has been restored to Port Lincoln but the damaged transmission line may take several days to be repaired. Some schools on the peninsula will be closed on Friday. Power is being restored to Eyre Peninsula after an "extremely ferocious and extremely isolated" weather event toppled three electricity transmission towers yesterday. SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said power had been restored for a "significant cohort" of customers on the lower Eyre Peninsula but outages continued across the upper Eyre Peninsula and into the West Coast. The government hoped those regions would have power again by the afternoon, pending the successful energising of a bypass line. "There are currently, as we speak, helicopters in the sky inspecting the line that would be restored and that would allow for the rest of the Eyre Peninsula to be energised," he said. A storm cell knocked over a transmission tower and powerlines at Wharminda yesterday. ( Supplied: Chris Prime ) While diesel generators had restored power to some parts of the Eyre Peninsula, the aging nature of the equipment meant the region was "not out of woods yet", with more storms forecast for the weekend. "There are still storm events coming our way [and] extreme fire conditions over the course of the weekend," he said. "We should be alive to the prospect that [the generator] may fail, and that's why we continue to monitor it." Electranet executive network manager Alex Trento said the transmission towers that fell were designed to withstand wind speeds of up to 170 kilometres an hour. While it was not known how strong the wind speeds were yesterday, Mr Trento said what happened to the towers was a "very, very rare" occurrence. "We have people at Yadnarie right now and we do think that will be energised later this afternoon, which will power up Wudinna and will get the rest of the communities energised and with electricity," he said. "That is an interim step. The second step is more of a medium- to long-term facilitation of the electricity supply. "Once they're up — and we're thinking that's a two- to three-week undertaking — then we will focus on the permanent fix, which is replacing those structures." Mr Malinauskas reiterated the urgent need for people with solar panels in the Port Lincoln region to switch them off to enable the generator to keep operating. Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis previously said the ElectraNet's $300 million upgrades to the transmission line as had "failed". When asked about that assessment today, Mr Trento said dulicatiing the line as a backup would have doubled the cost of the upgrade and that would have been passed onto customers. "I understand the frustration. However, this does go through a rigorous regulatory test to ensure it is a value-of-money expenditure," he said. Aisha Finlay was in the middle of harvesting for the first time in nearly a decade when the storm hit. ( Supplied: Aisha Finlay ) Asked whether the cost of repairs would also end up with "the mums and dads of South Australia", and about the price tag, Mr Trento replied: "I don't have that figure with me at this point in time but, yes it will, at some level — but that's nowhere near the cost of adding a secondary line of this nature next to that current line." Mr Trento earlier said the towers were built to withstand a "one-in-2,000-year weather event". "What we think has occurred is that the weather in this localised region has been even stronger than the winds that they were designed for." Yesterday's localised and "extraordinary" storm cell hit Port Neill at around 3pm on Thursday. About 24,000 properties on the peninsula lost power before local generators restored power to about 10,000 customers in Port Lincoln and surrounding towns about 9:45pm. Another 1,700 customers in and around Port Pirie did not have electricity due to storm activity. Strong winds hit transmission towers at Wharminda on Thursday afternoon. ( Supplied: Caleb Prime ) Bureau of Meteorology senior forecaster Daniel Hayes said the area experienced severe thunderstorms "with potentially supercells" and very strong wind gusts. "The biggest gust we actually saw was … just under 100km/h up at Roxby Downs," he told 891 Radio Adelaide this morning.

( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Tasmania's four major public hospitals are paying much less for their fixed sewerage charges under TasWater's new pricing model. Customers with large water connections such as sports grounds were initially set to receive price increases of up to 500 per cent. A union wants TasWater to reinvestigate the new pricing structure, calling it "an absolute shambles". Tasmania's financially stretched water utility has slashed public hospital fixed sewerage charges by around 70 per cent, under a new pricing model that saw other customers cop sharp hikes and has been described by one union as an "absolute shambles". Earlier this year, TasWater changed the way some non-residential customers were billed for the fixed component of their sewerage — basing it on water connection size, rather than estimated demand on the sewerage network. A separate variable charge was also introduced, based on how much water a customer uses and how much of that water is likely to go into the sewer. But some customers with large water connections — like sports grounds and businesses with firefighting or operational requirements — were initially set to be charged as much as 500 per cent extra for the fixed component of their sewerage bills. The ABC has now obtained documents from Tasmania's health department through Right-to-Information laws that show fixed sewerage charges at four major public hospitals fell sharply since the change came in. The Launceston General Hospital paid $12,531 for fixed sewerage charges between July 1 and September 30 this year — down from $67,361 over the same period the year before. The Royal Hobart Hospital went from paying $102,108 for the charge in 2024 and $105,683 in 2025 to $38,847 over the same three-month period in 2026. Callan Paske says TasWater always anticipated some customers would be billed "slightly more" and others would be billed "slightly less" under the new model. ( ABC News: Greg Szabo ) The North West Regional Hospital saw a fixed sewerage charge decrease of 73 per cent, although these were over slightly different three-month periods, while the Mersey Community Hospital saw a drop of 65 per cent between 2025 and 2026. TasWater's general manager of customer and community Callan Paske explained facilities with a lot of toilets or bedrooms, which could also include aged care homes, were likely to have lower fixed sewerage charges under the new structure. He said he could not say whether their total bills would be lower, once all fees and charges were taken into account. But he defended the current model, saying it is used around the country, adopted on the advice of a 2024 inquiry and was the subject of broad consultation. "It was always foreseen it would have an impact that way," he said. He said overall, the utility believed it would collect its anticipated revenue. Union labels situation 'simply outrageous' But Amanda Coleman, the Tasmanian state organiser for the Communications, Electrical and Plumbing Union of Australia, said the new model was "an absolute shambles" and symptomatic of an organisation "in dire straits". "All TasWater has done is create an unlevel playing field across their customer base, with significant winners and significant losers," she said. "How can, on one hand, they expect smaller commercial customers to pick up the bill, yet some larger government-owned properties seem to be getting a significant reduction in their bills? "It's simply outrageous that this has occurred." Businesses, clubs left reeling after change in TasWater pricing Businesses have been hit with hefty bill increases by Tasmania's water provider, leaving some wondering if they can remain open. TasWater has repeatedly highlighted its need for more funding to upgrade ageing infrastructure, with around 90 per cent of its sewerage treatment plants falling short of environmental requirements. "[Our members] are already being asked to do more with less," Ms Coleman said. "Now that you overlay this significant mess on top of that, this simply could mean that there is a risk that there is no TasWater." She believes the utility should apologise to the community, reinvestigate the new pricing structure and possibly revert to the old model while that work is done. The Tasmanian Economic Regulator says TasWater is able to charge less than the maximum price it sets.

events.title: Aboriginal family designs award-winning home to tackle heat, overcrowding
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Warumungu-designed Tennant Creek home wins national award as more housing proposed The award-winning Explain Home was designed to better suit Warumungu culture and Central Australia's harsh climate. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) A Tennant Creek home designed by a Warumungu family to address overcrowding, extreme heat and preventable illness has won a national architecture and engineering award. Warumungu-led organisation Wilya Janta is now in discussions with government about a proposed 20-house development. Wilya Janta is progressing plans for a second home while seeking support for the larger housing project in Tennant Creek. After growing up in an overcrowded tin shed and moving between government houses, Warumungu man Norman Frank Jupurrurla wanted something different for his family . Serina Morton and Norman Frank say their new home is a dream come true. ( ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis ) Warumungu-led organisation Wilya Janta received the 2026 Holdmark Innovation Award, presented by Powerhouse in Sydney on Saturday, for its Explain Home, developed with OFFICE and Troppo Architects. Jimmy Jupurrurla Frank holds the 2026 Powerhouse Holdmark award. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) Wilya Janta chief cultural officer Jimmy Jupurrurla Frank travelled from Tennant Creek to Sydney to receive the award, alongside business manager Gabriel Waterford. Mr Waterford said the recognition was an opportunity to showcase Aboriginal-led housing on a national stage. "The team's been working really hard over the last few years to build momentum around the importance of engaging with people the right way and making sure that communities got a say in the way that housing is built," he said. A home built around culture and climate The family's maroon-coloured home, which cost about $1 million to construct, sits on a hill on Mr Frank's grandmother's country, north of Tennant Creek. Waramungu families gather for a house-warming. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) The family moved in earlier this year, into a house designed to accommodate visiting relatives and respond to extreme heat. Large verandahs, indoor and outdoor kitchens, breezeways and a solar-battery system are among its features. Wilya Janta emerging CEO Kat Williams said the house's orientation allowed easterly breezes to travel through its living spaces. Kat Williams says the organisation is working towards delivering more culturally appropriate homes in Central Australia. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) "It's catching that eastern breeze and that breeze is able to channel right through to all the living spaces and through the verandahs," she said. The home also includes doors from internal rooms onto external verandahs, helping relatives observe cultural avoidance practices. Verandahs provide outdoor living spaces and allow breezes to flow through the Explain Home. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) Wilya Janta chief operating officer Simon Quilty, a medical doctor, said conventional government houses often failed to reflect how Aboriginal families lived. "They don't do well in the hot weather. They cost a lot to keep cool," Dr Quilty said. Simon Quilty says overcrowded housing in remote communities contributes to preventable diseases. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) The house is being independently evaluated against four recently built government homes, with researchers monitoring temperatures, room occupancy and other conditions. Dr Quilty said early observations were promising, but acknowledged the health benefits were difficult to prove without further research. Twenty-house proposal not yet funded Wilya Janta hopes to bring its housing designs to a larger scale, with ambitions for a 20-home social housing project in Tennant Creek. The organisation is in discussions with government and community stakeholders about the proposal, but funding, construction arrangements and a location are yet to be confirmed. "We're in conversations with government," Mr Waterford said. Gabriel Waterford says Wilya Janta hopes to expand its housing projects in Tennant Creek. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) If the project proceeds, the homes would be built on urban blocks within Tennant Creek, rather than on a rural property, like the original Explain Home. Locally made mud-brick walls help regulate temperatures inside the Explain Home. ( Supplied: Wilya Janta ) Mr Waterford said Wilya Janta could help guide the development alongside government or a third-party developer, rather than construct the houses itself. Only one Explain Home has been completed so far. Funding has been raised for a second, with a third also proposed; both are separate from the 20-house project.

events.title: Trump to Axios: I'm "not rushing into a decision" on Iran
events.summary: President Trump said in a brief phone interview Thursday that he won't make a determination on his next step in the Iran war until the new year. "I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," Trump told Axios from Air Force One, on his way back to the U.S. from China. Why it matters: The president's comments come as he faces heavy pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to unleash a decisive bombing campaign soon. Yes, but: Trump could change his mind at any moment. And he wouldn't telegraph plans for an imminent attack even if that's what he was intending to do. A day before the war began in February, Trump said he hadn't made a decision, when in fact he had already ordered strikes. Between the lines: Trump's stated timing could mean he's giving more time for the naval blockade and the economic pressure campaign to play out, as many of his advisers and leaders of Gulf countries are urging. But it could also indicate that if Iran doesn't make concessions by the end of the year, Trump wants to leave himself enough time for military action before the new Democratic-controlled Congress settles in. Driving the news: While stating last week that a major new round of strikes on Iran was " quite unlikely ," Trump is still considering a joint attack with Israel, Axios reported on Wednesday. The president's deliberations are likely to pick up when he returns from Asia. Any U.S. operation would involve Israel and could include strikes on suspected Iranian nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain. Bridges and power plants could also be targeted, as well as Iranian military and civilian leaders. Behind the scenes: The White House has asked the Pentagon and intelligence experts for their assessments of how Iran would respond to each of the strike scenarios the U.S. military has prepared, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. The White House has asked whether any of the options would avoid triggering a devastating Iranian retaliation against Gulf countries' oil and gas facilities. The intrigue: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad, Roman Gofman, visited Washington and Miami last week for talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe and White House envoy Steve Witkoff. Gofman, one of Netanyahu's closest confidants, was sent by the Israeli prime minister to press for resuming the war against Iran, an Israeli source said. The Mossad director relayed Israel's concerns about Iranian activities related to chemical weapons development, U.S. and Israeli sources said. Israel claims it has intelligence showing that Iran has stepped up its research and development of chemical weapons as well as conducted tests. Trump was briefed about this new intelligence, a U.S. official said.

events.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask R oll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company . From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees . And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia . More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go. Anthropic, though, has set records by raising $107bn. It is an extraordinary sum, especially for a business founded five years ago. At the listing price, Anthropic was valued at $1.5tn. When shares began trading at £111.50, its market capitalisation was up to $2tn. Only 14 months ago, it raised money at a valuation of a “mere” $183bn . The feat, though, is not wholly inexplicable. Some $26bn of the listing proceeds were virtually in the bag, thanks to the cornerstone placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. That assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names fed worries about the industry’s circular financing. But, on the other hand, every fund manager knew he or she would be betting against the crowd by saying no. Momentum can carry a stock a long way, even before the index funds and index-hugging funds are obliged to buy (Nasdaq entry will be quick; the S&P 500 will take at least a year). Take a step back, though, and ask whether Anthropic – loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish – can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus. The short, and unhelpful, answer is that virtually any valuation could be made to sound plausible if you believe, first, that AI is a generational technology that will be adopted at never-seen-before speed and, second, that “frontier” pioneering firms, of which Anthropic is the leader, will capture an outsized slice of the commercial value for years and years. Consider the assumptions behind that thesis, however. Can Anthropic really improve from $50bn-ish of revenue this year to $600bn in 2030, which is roughly what tech analysts have pencilled in? Given the current rate of growth, perhaps it can. But sustaining the pace, or something like it, for another 16 quarters simply won’t be straightforward or mechanical. What is the real level of demand from corporate users for frontier models? Nobody doubts that AI adoption is still in the early stage, but does everybody need the finest product from Anthropic’s Claude suite? Already executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper “open weight” models from rivals, do the job for basic work. Lasting pricing power in AI is simply unclear. “Commoditisation risk”, in the jargon, could be the next year’s valuation debate. Then there is the investment bill to make it all happen – $900bn of spending commitments were detailed in the prospectus for computing power and infrastructure. The listing proceeds help, as does the visibility and credibility that comes with being on a public market. But debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Obviously, at some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade,” said co-founder Dario Amodei as trading in the shares started. You bet: the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally. Away from the party atmosphere, the European Central Bank has its eye on financial stability in the eurozone. This week, it issued one of those fuddy-duddy reminders about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution , and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers to the boom. “Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026,” its report said, warning of “historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles”. It is not the only one to see warning signs. Anthropic is an astonishingly successful company already and is plainly at the forefront of a significant technological shift.

( Reuters: Lucas Jackson ) Under the Labor government, Victoria has been transitioning to renewable power as coal plants in the Latrobe Valley close. Experts have warned the state could face blackouts by 2028 as the Coalition ditches plans to build new transmission lines through rural Victoria. Victoria's gas reserves are depleting, which is why the Coalition is promising to "throw the doors open" to new gas exploration. Experts warn Victoria could face blackouts in just two years, with Jess Wilson's plan to use more gas deemed unachievable for at least five years — three years after a key coal plant closes. Senior government officials have also warned that the state faces blackouts due to demand outstripping supply in 2028 when Yallourn, in Gippsland, ceases operations. The coal plant has been operating since 1974 and last year accounted for 15 per cent of the state's energy generation. Yallourn coal-fired power station is slated to close in 2028. ( ABC News: William Howard ) "It is an omnishambles because there are too many very important decisions that have been kicked down the road for too long, and they're all coming to a head at the moment,'' the Grattan Institute's Alison Reeve told the ABC. Delays to major projects are also pushing up construction costs, which will be worn by bill payers. Under Labor, the state has been transitioning to renewable power and batteries as old coal plants in the Latrobe Valley gradually close. The plan relies on two new transmission lines through rural Victoria to bring new generation to the grid; VNI West will also connect with NSW and the new Snowy 2.0 Snowy Hydro scheme. The opposition will not build VNI West and have also committed to reviewing the more advanced Western Renewables Link, with Premier Ben Carroll already beginning a cost review of the project. Many regional Victorian residents are concerned about the Western Renewables Link and VNI West. ( ABC Ballarat: Lexie Jeuniewic ) "Without those, there isn't really a lot of space to put in significant amounts of new solar and new wind, which means that it's very difficult for Yallourn to close and for the lights still to stay on in Victoria," Ms Reeve said. Shadow Energy Minister David Davis said the VNI West project had lost its social licence, and the cost had blown out by billions of dollars. Even confronting potential blackouts, Mr Davis says the Coalition will not build it. "We're coming in with a terrible situation, confronting supply shortages, confronting potential blackouts, confronting real challenges,'' he said. There has been vocal community backlash from farming communities to the project, which would see transmission lines cross farms. Jaclyn Symes says offshore wind will provide energy security as the state's coal plants close. ( ABC News ) Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes concedes the government could have worked more closely with communities, but it is unwavering in the party's commitment to the project — which she says will create jobs. She argues not building it will drive away investment and threaten power security. "You can't be flippant and change your position and send different signals to the industry because investment will flee the state if they're not going to have certainty from leadership of government about the projects that we need,'' she said. The Coalition want to focus on more gas electricity. It can also be used in any conditions, especially at night, or when there is not enough wind. But Victoria's gas reserves are depleting, which is why the Coalition is promising to "throw the doors open" to new gas exploration and extraction. The industry estimates there is between 20 to 25 years' worth of untapped supplies in Victoria. Even if that gas is found and extracted, it will take up to five years to turn into energy generation. events.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack
events.summary: Hackers accessed “certain marketing data” held by third-party vendors, which may have included some customer names and email addresses, said JPMorgan Chase on Nov 19. JPMorgan said third-party vendors were hit in a cyberattack, and attackers may have accessed marketing data, including some customer names and email addresses. The bank said this was separate from earlier service problems, while US regulators checked the impact and customer communications after the incident. A group called “n0n” also claimed data linked to Visa and Mastercard. Both firms said their payment systems were not affected, and only limited email data was exposed. NEW YORK - JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Nov 19 that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson said, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly. “There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” the spokesperson added. Earlier this week, the bank experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug which also affected other banks and caused some disruptions. These incidents at JPMorgan followed several other recent problems including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft’s global email outage, while in October crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack. After the outage, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), according to an industry executive, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers. The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a second person said, adding that the OCC routinely checks after any such incidents. “Customers don’t distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here,” said Carissa Robb, of SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm. “There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinising the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared,” Robb said. A cyber extortion group called “n0n” claimed on Nov 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included “hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses,” according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch. The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data. JPMorgan declined to comment on the data. The same hacking group on Nov 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data. A Visa spokesperson said the company is aware of the claims and that they are “associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected.” A Mastercard spokesperson said the company was recently informed of an incident “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit programme. There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards.” The Visa data posted by the group appears to be primarily focused on Asian-Pacific markets, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Macau and others, according to a Reuters review. Across several spreadsheets, the data includes thousands of purported customer email addresses, phone numbers, and Visa marketing campaign data. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the data. The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses. The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. REUTERS
