events.title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
events.summary: After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since . For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures , shifting priorities , and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks. Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring , while operating losses are declining . Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures. Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money. The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.) Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries . Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives. Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes.

events.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
events.summary: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering. The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.  In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.    Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.  Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.  Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.   Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.   While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.” Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology. Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days. What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.   Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods. For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs. “It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”   He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks. Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says. Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs , a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body. Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “ organ medicine” : research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”   “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

events.title: Expats leave Riyadh as Houthi strikes persist
events.summary: ‘No end in sight’ Increasing numbers of foreign executives are leaving Riyadh as the city continues to suffer Houthi attacks that have forced the closure of the city’s main business district and schools. Offices in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) have already been closed for several weeks and some businesses are not expecting it to reopen until next year, according to people familiar with the matter. That was before the Public Investment Fund’s head office in the district was hit on Thursday morning, which is likely to further delay any reopening of the area. As a result, staff are increasingly deciding to work from other countries, Semafor was told. The destinations vary. Some have headed back to homes in Europe, others have joined families that are based in the UAE and normally only visited on weekends, while another group has upped sticks temporarily to third countries. “The office is closed and schools are online. There’s no end in sight, so there’s no point in us staying,” said one executive of a Saudi company, who decamped with his family to Thailand because he was at risk of crossing a UK tax threshold if he spent any more time in his home country. To be sure, the numbers leaving the city are limited and in many ways life carries on as normal. Other parts of the city remain active and business continues as usual in areas so far unaffected by the Houthi attacks. If the security situation improves those that have left are expected to return. Yet the sense of insecurity is a blow to ambitions to make the Saudi capital a regional business and finance hub. The kingdom had aimed to grow Riyadh’s population to 10 million by 2030, up from 7 million in the 2022 census. A significant portion of that growth was based on a rising number of expatriates moving to the city. Some staff at Saudi companies had already made the decision to leave several weeks ago after KAFD offices shut and schools shifted to online learning in the wake of the deadly attack on Riyadh airport in early October. Many businesses based in Riyadh’s other tower blocks have also advised staff to work from home until further notice. That has added to the numbers of people who are no longer required to be in the country to continue working. People have been driving to airports in Bahrain or Qatar to fly out. A recent uptick in attacks on the city, combined with the upcoming Christmas holiday season, is leading more people to decide to move if their jobs do not require them to be in the country. “We were already planning to leave for the holidays in a few weeks, so now we have just bought that forward,” said one executive in Riyadh who planned to drive to Doha. “I really don’t know when we will come back.” KAFD is now almost deserted. Baristas in the area’s coffee shops, many of which have remained open, say they have had few customers for weeks. The attack on the PIF tower comes just over a week after Aramco’s building in the area was also damaged in a Houthi attack. The decision by the city’s expatriates to go is a reversal of the situation in the early months of the Iran war, when Riyadh suffered far fewer direct attacks than other Gulf cities and its airspace mostly remained open. That made the city a key channel for people in Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and the UAE to leave the Arabian peninsula . Notable Saudi Arabian officials foresee the war against Yemen’s Houthis to stretch well into next year , despite setbacks on the battlefield in Yemen and attacks disrupting life at home, according to two Western officials briefed by Saudis on the plans.

events.title: Anthropic IPO: Here's how UAE retail investors can buy shares on listing
events.summary: UAE retail investors who are keen to buy shares of artificial intelligence major Anthropic once it lists can go through brokerage platforms offering access to US-listed equities. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the blockbuster initial public offering, eclipsing the previous record-setting debut of Elon Musk's SpaceX in June. It offered 980 million shares as part of the deal, valuing the Claude chatbot maker ⁠at $1.5 trillion, with prices set at $83 per share. It will make its trading debut on Nasdaq later on Thursday. The company is also raising $26 billion through a private placement, taking the total value of the deal to $107.3 billion. Strong debut Anthropic shares are expected to trade at a premium to the IPO price of $83 per share on its debut on Nasdaq, analysts say. “The opening price will be set by orders in Nasdaq’s auction … so day-one buyers pay the premium the excitement has built,” said Louis Detata, founder of online broker Uexo. However, he warned that share prices can fall fast, erasing price gains on debut. “SpaceX shows how quickly that premium can move: its shares closed well above their offer price on debut and rose much further, then slipped below the IPO price later on.” SpaceX’s share price has remained volatile since it made its trading debut on June 12. It is currently trading at $143.50, down from the opening price of $150 per share when it listed but higher than the IPO price of $135 per share. It fell as low as $123.60 on November 5 over concerns related to an AI slowdown, as US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. Long-term questions While the hype around the IPO has been extensive, investors should pay attention to the company's revenue growth, operating profitability, AI infrastructure spending and competition in the market before investing, experts say. Anthropic's share price could decline if revenue growth is disappointing or operating costs remain elevated. “Developing advanced AI models requires substantial investment in computing infrastructure, which can place pressure on cash flow even as revenue increases,” said Noureldeen Al Hammoury, head of market insights and community engagement at Equiti, another online broker . Investors should keep an eye on growing competition in the AI market from companies such as OpenAI. Calls to regulate the AI sector have grown, meanwhile, over fears of proliferation of the technology that could lead to wide-scale job losses and a slowdown in AI growth. The cost of financing the AI buildout is also expected to rise amid higher interest rates that could put pressure on company earnings. “The critical question is whether the company's revenue growth, profitability and future cash generation can justify the valuation investors are prepared to pay,” Mr Al Hammoury said. For the third quarter of this year, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.95 billion, while its net loss climbed to $23.29 billion compared to a net loss of $12.13 billion from the same quarter last year. Scam tactics Analysts, meanwhile, also warned investors to be wary of scam tactics driven by the hype around the listing. Fraudsters are feared to be claiming to offer Anthropic IPO shares at the offering price in exchange for upfront fees or personal information, and offering “tokenised” or blockchain-based representations of pre-IPO or IPO shares. “Legitimate tokenised securities require full regulatory approval and are not sold through informal channels,” Mr Al Hammoury said. Fraudsters may also impersonate brokers and underwriters on social media, messaging apps and fake websites offering to sell Anthropic shares to cheat people amid higher demand for the company's shares. Worth the attention? Anthropic is attracting attention because investors increasingly see AI as a major technological transformation rather than simply another software trend. The company has established itself as a significant competitor in advanced AI models, particularly through Claude and its enterprise and coding applications. However, the excitement also reflects expectations of extraordinary future growth, which creates a risk as “even strong financial results may disappoint investors if expectations have already become excessive”, Mr Al Hammoury said. Outlook on performance The trajectory of Anthropic's shares depends on whether revenue keeps outrunning the cost of computing power. Monetary policy is the main headwind, with the Federal Reserve expected to raise rates on December 9, which could “weigh hardest on companies whose value lies in earnings years away”, Mr Detata said. Anthropic's first quarterly results as a listed company, due in early 2027, are the next fundamental test.

events.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
events.summary: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack. events.title: Japan's PM Takaichi says Russia and Japan will keep talking as ties remain chilled
events.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says that she met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 30 minutes in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years SHENZHEN, China -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Thursday that she and Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks and agreed to keep communicating in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years. Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, she said she raised the issue of Moscow’s treatment of Japanese businesses in Russia and urged Putin to release a Japanese journalist detained for alleged spying during their meeting late Wednesday in Shenzhen, China. “We reached an agreement to maintain communication at various levels, including direct contact between the president and myself,” Takaichi said. Japan's ties with Russia have long been strained by a territorial dispute dating back decades. Japan lodged a protest with Russia in October over the arrest of a Japanese journalist working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper on suspicion of spying, demanding that Moscow provide an explanation, consular access and humane treatment. Moscow recently seized control of some local subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco , the largest cigarette maker in Russia, and the company reported it expects a 724 billion yen ($4.5 billion) loss for this year due to the takeover. Earlier, Japan Tobacco had forecast a 662 billion yen profit for the financial year ending Dec. 31. The company said it has not given up legal ownership of the Russia-based subsidiaries or withdrawn from operating in Russia. Tensions rose in August after Putin visited Iturup , one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims. Earlier this month, Tokyo protested after two Russian aircraft briefly violated Japanese airspace off southwestern Japan. The last bilateral in-person talks between Japanese and Russian leaders were held between then-Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Putin in September 2019, during the Eastern Economic Forum in the Russian city of Vladivostok. Putin is attending the annual APEC summit for the first time in nine years. He, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump held a summit meeting Thursday after the APEC gathering, an event that seems to underscore Japan's diminished role as a global power. Takaichi herself was given a very minimal reception on her arrival in Shenzhen, provoking speculation over a deliberate snub by her hosts. South Korea’s top court overturns charges against ex-PM for his role in martial law Mongolia's lawmakers accept president's resignation following corruption accusations Crimean bridge attacked for 3rd time in a week, officials say When asked, Takaichi said she did not believe the summit between Xi, Trump and Putin would undermine Japan’s interests. “We have been maintaining close communication with the United States and other allies while carefully monitoring the impact on the international situation and we will continue to respond appropriately,” Takaichi said. "We do not believe that Japan’s interests will be compromised.” She did not elaborate on efforts to repair damage to Japan’s ties with China following remarks she made nearly a year ago about Taiwan. “China is an important neighbor. Given the various issues and challenges that exist between Japan and China, I believe it is essential to engage in dialogue and maintain communication," she said. Yamaguchi reported from Tokyo. events.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
events.summary: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time. This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics. Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry. We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021. Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain. The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO. Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.   This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year. The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics. China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it. Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.) I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority. “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

events.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
events.summary: Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers. Julián Posada is an assistant professor at Yale University and the author of “Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.” Arguments, opinions and essays from a global perspective. The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania. Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers , and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions. They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on. I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day. For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold. This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on . Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out. The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else. One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else. AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books , artists’ works , all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S. Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021. Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers , scientists , and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.

events.title: The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro
events.summary: President Donald Trump and his son Eric Trump at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Florida Joe Raedle/Getty Images Top Trump administration officials intervened to help a longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley secure a half-million-dollar payout from the IRS. A company connected to Trump’s media business also got a half-million. The deal grew out of a little-noticed federal class-action lawsuit filed in 2025 by five individuals and companies. The group got $2.5 million after accusing the IRS of failing to protect their tax information. The law permits a $1,000 payment to victims for each instance of an unauthorized inspection or disclosure of tax data. In this case, however, the government’s monetary settlement is 250 times higher than what the law calls for given the allegations. Victims can receive more money if they show actual damages, but multiple officials say such cases almost never result in payments approaching this size. These generous settlements have raised concerns because IRS Office of Chief Counsel attorneys were not consulted about the settlement terms, as is standard practice, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica. What’s more, those payouts didn’t resolve the lawsuit. After the settlement was made, two more people came forward seeking to continue the litigation — and both are connected to Trump businesses. One is a retired accountant who worked at the same Trump property as the golf pro. The second appears to be a former lifeguard at a different Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York. Gil Rothenberg, a law professor at American University who ran the appellate section at the Justice Department tax division for 15 years before leaving in 2019, said the deal “is not passing the smell test.” “It’s not just the amount that I find odd and unusual,” he told ProPublica. “It’s the fact that this settlement amount occurred before any final decision by the district court, and basically the DOJ is giving up any right to appeal.” The case in question is Safe Harbor International LLC v. Booz Allen Hamilton, Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Department of the Treasury, brought in Maryland federal court. Plaintiffs claim that the IRS and the government contractor Booz Allen failed to implement proper safeguards and were negligent in allowing Booz Allen employee Charles Littlejohn to steal tax records and give them to news organizations, including ProPublica.  President Donald Trump sued over similar claims earlier this year, seeking $10 billion in damages. In response, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization fund” to resolve the case. That settlement was structured to grant the president’s inner circle the authority to green-light payouts of government money to whomever they wanted. The public erupted in outrage. Democratic and even a small number of Republican lawmakers objected to the proposed fund, and the department dropped the idea as Blanche sought Senate confirmation for his position. Critics fear that the DOJ’s unusual payment in the Safe Harbor case could be a backdoor way to revive something similar to the controversial slush fund. In all, plaintiffs claim the size of the class is “in the tens or hundreds of thousands.” If a significant number of those plaintiffs secured the same payment, the total liability for the federal government could reach into the billions of dollars. A judge has yet to rule on whether to allow the case to proceed.  That group could include other Trump allies and friends. It even “opens the door to Trump himself benefiting from this settlement,” said John Koskinen, who served as IRS commissioner from 2013 to 2017. Spokespeople for the Justice Department and IRS said they would not comment on a pending case. A White House spokesperson said that the Justice Department is “promoting efficient resolution of cases to avoid extraordinary liability.” Between 2018 and 2020, Littlejohn, the Booz Allen contractor, leaked confidential IRS data to ProPublica and The New York Times, he has said. The data included years of Trump’s taxes and information on thousands of the wealthiest people in the country. Do You Have a Justice Department Tip for ProPublica? If you know about this case and the government’s handling of it, please contact our reporting team. I’m grateful for any documents that sources can share. Protecting sources is something I take very seriously. Avi Asher-Schapiro If you have tips about Big Tech and the Trump administration, please get in touch. Contact Me ProPublica published stories on the tax-avoidance strategies of the ultrawealthy. The New York Times reported in 2020 on how Trump declared large annual losses to avoid paying taxes. Together, the two news organizations reported that Trump was fighting with the IRS over a long-running audit that could have cost him $100 million . Littlejohn pleaded guilty in October 2023 to unauthorized disclosure of tax information. A judge sentenced him to five years in prison . The IRS sent letters to more than 400,000 individuals and businesses to alert them that their taxpayer information had been “inappropriately disclosed” by Littlejohn. As ProPublica has previously stated, we obtained the tax return information of the top 0.001% of individuals by income, a figure in the thousands. Limited information about other entities appears in the records only to the extent that it is related to the group of top earners. A number of taxpayers who received the notice filed civil lawsuits demanding compensation from the IRS and Booz Allen.  The Safe Harbor class-action initially brought together five such plaintiffs who, at first glance, had nothing in common apart from having received an IRS notice about the leak. Safe Harbor International is an obscure LLC incorporated in Delaware. It has no website or public presence and was most recently registered to a residential home in Washington, D.C. When ProPublica knocked on the door, the person living there said they’d never heard of the company. Safe Harbor’s investors include Donald Wilson , who leads a Chicago-based financial trading firm. Last March, the Securities and Exchange Commission dropped a case brought during the Biden administration against a crypto company that Wilson controlled. A few months later, Wilson’s firm said it had invested $100 million in the president’s publicly traded media company, Trump Media and Technology Group, the owner of Truth Social. A spokesperson for Wilson said he is a passive shareholder in Safe Harbor and “was unaware of this lawsuit until last week and has had no involvement in the litigation or any settlement discussions.” The spokesperson added that there was no connection between Wilson’s Trump Media investment and the SEC’s dismissal. “There was no quid pro quo, and the investment was not made in exchange for any regulatory action,” the spokesperson said. events.title: We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to Disclose
events.summary: Illustration by ProPublica. Source illustrations: Brandon Celi for ProPublica. After President Donald Trump’s “emergency” tariffs were overturned by the Supreme Court in February 2026, the government began processing billions in refunds to importers, including many recognizable public companies. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for. ProPublica requested the information, but U.S. Customs and Border Protection denied our requests. (We’re appealing.)  So our reporters found another way: analyzing the financial disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies. Today, ProPublica published “Cash Back,” a database of figures on refunds for tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The database includes 343 public companies for which we found mentions of refunds, amounting to more than $28 billion recovered or expected. See How Much Companies Are Getting in Tariff Refunds At least nine companies have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses , according to a ProPublica analysis published earlier this week. Recognizable businesses include the tool company Stanley Black & Decker and the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls, and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Many other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money. ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information.  Explore the Cash Back database here. What’s included in the database? The Supreme Court ruled on Feb. 20, 2026, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act doesn’t authorize the president to impose tariffs. The U.S. Court of International Trade ordered U.S. Customs and Border Protection to refund the duties it had collected.  This tracker covers refunds on those tariffs disclosed by publicly traded companies. Public companies must disclose events that affect their finances, such as tariff payments and refunds, on earnings calls and in regular reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We collected information from these public sources through Oct. 7, 2026.  Before publishing, we contacted all companies shown here to check the accuracy of the numbers we had found. We grouped companies by industry using a combination of designations from Morningstar . How did we determine refund amounts?  ProPublica searched through securities filings and earnings calls using key phrases to isolate companies that mentioned tariff refunds. For each company, we created a document that included the extracted text around each phrase. For SEC filings, that included parsed Extensible Business Reporting Language when available. We then used an open-weight artificial intelligence model for a first pass at identifying refund amounts. ProPublica reporters reviewed each company by hand to make sure our database is accurate and contacted all companies to confirm the amounts. Companies normally record tariff refunds in their financial statements under two accounting models: Gain contingency: when the refund has been received or recovery is essentially certain. Loss recovery: when the refund is probable and can be reasonably estimated. To determine a company’s recovered refund, we added up the amounts it recorded that were essentially certain or probable (sometimes known as “receivable”), plus the amounts it disclosed as having been received.  The government is required to pay interest on tariff amounts it is returning, at rates determined by the IRS on a quarterly basis. Companies disclosed that interest in different ways. Some reported the refund and the interest separately, while others reported a single amount that included both. When a company reported them separately, we added the interest to the refund to capture the full amount of money that a company was receiving from the government.  Some companies reported only their net refund instead of the full amount received. For example, a company might report only what was left of the tariff refund after reinvesting into its business or after passing part of the refund onto customers. In these cases, we reported the net amount. When companies reported a range, we used the lower end. In both cases, we noted that information on the company page.  The specific security filings reviewed were: 8-K, 10-Q, 10-K, 8-K/A, 10-Q/A, 10-K/A, 6-K, 6-K/A, 20-F, 20-F/A, 40-F, 40-F/A and any associated exhibits.  Can I get a refund? Only importers or the authorized custom brokers who filed the entries can submit a request for a refund. That means that even if companies passed tariff costs on to customers through higher prices, the refund goes to the company, and it is up to the company to determine how the money is used.  UPS and FedEx are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them. The companies have set up online portals for customers to track their refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals who paid them to ship products. Other companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers, though these companies’ customers are generally other businesses. Trade experts say these business-to-business vendors likely have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs. Some companies have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases.   How do I report incorrect information?  If you see information that may be incorrect, please email tariffs@propublica.org .  We will periodically update our database by pulling information from newer filings, as well as correcting or adding new information when companies reach out to us. Can I download the data? Yes, you can download the data here . We ask that you credit “ProPublica analysis of financial disclosures” and link to this tracker . Do you have information you can share about how a company is using tariff refunds? ProPublica’s investigative journalists are reporting on tariff refunds and how, or if, companies are giving money back to consumers. You can reach our tip line or contact us on Signal at 917-512-0201. Please be as specific, detailed and clear as you can. The post We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Ha

events.title: New alarm over China controlling drug supply chains
events.summary: China is intensifying efforts to control the entire drug supply chain, putting the U.S. at risk of being cut off from future lifesaving treatments, the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warns in a new analysis out Thursday. Why it matters: Western drug giants have invested huge sums in Chinese biotechs to boost their product pipelines. But sharing capital and expertise could give Beijing more control over critical pharmaceutical technologies. Concerns about the U.S. getting boxed out have intensified after the Chinese government proposed new restrictions last month on the export of certain technologies, including cell and gene therapy platforms. Driving the news: Western drug giants are increasingly entering into licensing agreements with Chinese firms that redirect U.S. capital away from U.S. innovation and toward the Chinese pharmaceutical industry, the commission found in its analysis of 57 deals from the beginning of 2023 through last month. The deals are being made earlier in the drug discovery process, allowing the Chinese partners to gain not just capital but know-how in developing and commercializing treatments. This kind of knowledge transfer in automobiles, semiconductors and industrial chemicals gave Chinese industry a competitive edge and leverage to control global markets for the products, according to the commission, which was established by Congress to examine how emerging biotech intersects with national security. "The end game is the same for the [Chinese Communist Party] in the pharmaceutical industry," the commission warns, saying the goal is increased U.S. dependence on Chinese innovation and enrichment of the Chinese pharmaceutical industry. Between the lines: Drugmakers including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Pfizer have been drawn by China's surge of investment in the life sciences and the promise of faster clinical trials and product approvals. Typically a Chinese biotechnology company sells the license to develop or commercialize a treatment it developed to a multinational pharmaceutical company. The Western companies see the arrangements as a way to outsource the burden of drug discovery and verify early results. But the commission found that the deals are increasingly based on preclinical data and that upfront payments are coming earlier in the R&D cycle. The commission says this can result in a "flywheel effect" that sees royalties and equity in joint ventures flow back to China, fueling new research and infrastructure and attracting global talent. What they're saying: "The CCP seeks dominance in biotechnology as a source of economic power and geopolitical advantage, and Beijing has spent decades pursuing a deliberate strategy to achieve that at all levels of the value chain," said commission executive director Caitlin Frazer. "U.S.-China pharma deals are starting to favor the Chinese startups, which risks eroding biotech R&D in the U.S. This trend should be alarming for policymakers." Threat level: The concern is what happens if China scales up and corners a market, establishing a stranglehold on supplies of key products and ingredients. That's especially critical in pharma. While a chip shortage may result in delays replacing a car or phone, a drug shortage delays treatments for controlling seizures, treating infections or managing severe pain, Brookings Institution senior fellow Marta Wosińska has noted . In a report last year to Congress, the commission posed a hypothetical scenario in which Beijing withheld a breakthrough treatment from American patients in the event of a conflict in Taiwan. State of play: Last month, the Trump administration proposed subjecting certain deals with Chinese life sciences companies to new screening requirements or prohibiting them altogether. The administration cited the risk of "outbound investments" being used to create biological weapons or brain-computer interfaces for surveillance, or to make U.S. supply chains overly dependent on a country. Cash-based deals that bring royalties and milestone payments are still permitted, but equity investments in Chinese firms would be prohibited and certain joint ventures could also be targeted, per a Sidley analysis . The commission, in its new analysis, calls the proposal "a prudent step to curtail China's biotechnology ambitions" but adds policymakers "must act now to empower the United States to out-innovate strategic competitors before it's too late." Pharma and biotech interests have been pressing Congress and the administration to take steps to update and streamline U.S. drug development, improve patient access to clinical trials and pass stronger patent protections. What we're watching: Whether this week's meetings between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping yield new agreements on strategic technologies like biotech or lead to tighter export controls.

events.title: Poll: Republicans in early 2028 primary states back Israel, not its critics
events.summary: Republican voters in four early 2028 primary states have favorable views of Israel by wide margins and have negative opinions of three leading right-wing critics of the Jewish state, according to a new poll by a national GOP consulting firm. Why it matters: The poll challenges the notion that Republican opinion toward Israel is fracturing significantly, and points to a potential disconnect between GOP voters' attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online. The survey, conducted by OnMessage Inc . for the Combat Antisemitism Movement 's political arm, essentially provides a roadmap for pro-Israel Republicans' messaging ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign. It seeks to cast the right's leading critics of Israel — Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens and Nick Fuentes — as liabilities in the GOP primary. Zoom in: After the midterms, Vice President Vance called on the U.S. and the GOP to "change our relationship to Israel," elevating the nations' longtime partnership as a 2028 campaign issue at a time when Vance is eyeing a presidential bid. Israel is supported by 68% of Republican voters in Iowa, New Hampshire, Nevada and South Carolina, according to the survey, a result similar to findings by Gallup and Pew . 17% disfavored Israel. 78% said the GOP's "relationship with Israel" makes them more likely to vote Republican. Large majorities also agreed with pro-Israel messages. In contrast , 53% of those surveyed said they disapprove of Carlson, and 30% approve. But among voters under 45 years old, Carlson's approval/disproval ratings were tied at 46%. 49% of the Republicans surveyed disapproved of Owens, while 23% approved. Fuentes, the least-known of the three media figures, was viewed unfavorably by 25% and favored by 13%. Among self-described MAGA Republicans, 22% approved and 23% disapproved of him, however. "The fringe messengers are underwater," says a slide deck for the poll, which was conducted ahead of the Combat Antisemitism Movement's national conference Thursday in Charleston, S.C. Stunning stat: Vance is more popular in the GOP than President Trump. 75% view Trump favorably and 23% disfavor him, a net of +52 points. Vance: 80% favorable and 19% unfavorable, a net of +61. Another bright spot for Vance —59% agreed with this statement, which generally reflects the vice president's position: "Israel has a right to exist, and America should remain its ally, however criticism of its government is legitimate, but when it turns into antisemitism that is unacceptable." The intrigue: Vance is friends with Carlson, whose son used to work in the vice president's office. The two have resisted speaking ill of each other even as Carlson has grown more critical of the president and the war in Iran. 46% of the GOP voters surveyed said a Carlson endorsement of a presidential candidate would make them less likely to support that person; 16% said it would make them more likely and 39% said it wouldn't matter. Between the lines: While GOP support for Israel is still strong, it has declined among Republicans, and other polls show that overall U.S. backing for Israel has dropped in recent years. Yes, but : The poll is conducted for an advocacy group and seeks to provide messaging guidance for candidates and surrogates. So some of its questions are leading. By 83%-5%, Republicans said they viewed Carlson less favorably when told "he endorsed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a radical Muslim socialist recently elected to the U.S. Senate in Michigan whose political associates include someone that said, 'America deserved 9/11.' " The survey tested ways to attack Owens and Fuentes on the campaign trail by describing extreme comments from both and found that outsized majorities of Republican voters would call on a candidate to denounce them. By 86%-7%, respondents agreed with the statement, "There is no place for antisemitism in the Republican Party." And 66% said there's no place in the party for antisemites, while 15% said they should be welcomed under a "big tent." What they're saying: Fuentes declined to comment, Owens couldn't be reached and Carlson questioned the financiers of the poll. "The poll was commissioned by the 'Combat Antisemitism Movement'? Seriously? Pretty funny. Where does their funding come from?" Carlson asked via text. (The donors are primarily Jewish and Zionist contributors, according to Influence Watch ). "If the point is to convince Republican candidates that American voters love [Israeli leader Benjamin] Netanyahu and want more wars for Israel, good luck in the next election," he said. "It's so absurd. But I'm sure you'll have Republican senators waving around the poll results like they mean something." Former Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares, a U.S. Advisory Board Member of the Combat Antisemitism Movement, dismissed the criticism: "For a Republican presidential candidate, standing up against antisemitism is not a political risk — it is the price of admission and good politics. Most importantly, it is simply the right thing to do." The poll of 1,000 respondents (250 from each of the four early states) was conducted Nov. 7-10. The margin of error: +/- 3.1%.

events.title: Putting cyber risk in perspective, from the experts (our own CTO)
events.summary: Axios chief technology officer Dan Cox, who's spent 25 years at some of the world's biggest tech companies, puts the recent spate of high-profile failures in perspective: My parents, my siblings and plenty of other people are asking the same question: How worried should we be? The big picture: I've been in technology a long time. I take these threats seriously , but I'm not in panic mode. When something breaks, we need to understand what happened, how far it reaches and what we can do about it. A frightening headline doesn't answer those questions. Zoom out: The way I think about it, we've put powerful tools in more hands, and people are taking potshots to see what they can hit. Those shots can do real damage, and we need to protect ourselves. But hearing gunfire doesn't, by itself, mean an army is coming over the hill. We need to understand who's firing, what they can actually do and whether the threat is changing. Zoom in: Over the past few weeks, we've identified bad actors snooping around our own website, too. Our talented engineers have investigated threats and put mitigations in place. There may still be attempts on our site, but each incident gives us an opportunity to strengthen our systems. Between the lines: There are thousands of smart, resourceful and dedicated engineers working to protect the systems we all rely on. I see that commitment in our own team. I believe that if the threat grows, more people with those skills will step up. That's part of why I have confidence in our ability to respond, even as the threats evolve. The bottom line: Fred Rogers shared his mother's advice for frightening news: "Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping." I think about that here. There are a lot of capable people working on these problems. I have confidence in them, even while we have real work to do. I want people to feel informed enough to act, rather than frightened enough to assume the worst.

events.title: Doomsday prepping goes mainstream
events.summary: The internet has caught the emergency preparation bug , fueled by fears of AI-led cyberattacks , power grid vulnerabilities, transportation standstills and international threats . The big picture: The "prepper" mindset is resonating with larger slices of society — who are packing emergency bags, stocking up on water and taking inventory of non-perishables. Michael Mills, a University of Greenwich senior lecturer who studies doomsday preparation, says some people are turning to "lightweight versions" of traditional prepping amid doubts about global stability. By the numbers: Sales at Survival Frog, a survival retailer that sells gear like emergency food and radios, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16, compared to prior weeks, CEO and founder Byron Walker tells Axios. Competitors saw similar trends, he says. And most recent buyers at Survival Frog were new customers. Food, including canned meats, leads demand, Walker says, followed by products like radios, solar generators, battery packs and water filters. State of play: Systems the world relies on for travel , communications , business , food, health care and more have been disrupted in recent weeks — whether because of tech shortfalls or malicious acts. While officials assure the incidents aren't broadly connected, fears of critical infrastructure failing are growing, and more people considering how to prepare for crises. "It does seem much more mainstream now," Walker says of preppers. "You can't turn on the news without hearing about a new cyber attack or a tech meltdown." Many of the emergency preparation skills people are using have long been observed in disaster-prone areas. And as many Americans learned during COVID, supply chain disruptions mean having extra water, radios and shelf-stable foods around the house isn't a bad thing. Krystal, known online as the "Queen of Doomsday," spends about five hours daily coaching new preppers and told Axios that recent online engagement with her content, which she says has more than doubled across platforms, has been "mind-blowing." "Families are generally concerned —...people who would have normally turned their nose away from it and thought, 'No, nothing could ever happen.' We've seen lockdowns. We've seen supply chains be crippled. We've seen oil crises, inflation," she says. Between the lines: Overlapping tech oddities boosted "a sense of anxiety about social stability around us, knowing that planes can be grounded, or fridges can all of a sudden become heaters," Mills says. Costco has become an apparent cornucopia for concerned consumers, with sales on goods like rice, canned goods and water reportedly surging. Walker attributes the Survival Frog sales boom to the U.K. government and EU urging households to prepare three days of supplies, as well as the Pentagon readiness plan for military bases to operate at least 90 days, per Fox reporting , if civilian systems fail. That plan fueled rumors about a 90-day "blackout" across the U.S. Worth noting: Asked about the outages and Pentagon preparations, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News' Laura Ingraham that friends have asked whether they should be "preparing to build a bunker" or stock up on food and water. "And my answer to that is no," he continued. "We do not see some crisis coming down." The bottom line: But Krystal said in a video response to Vance, "Yes, we should be preparing." She's not here to fear-monger, but she tells Axios, "one more person prepared is one less person to worry about if there's a crisis." Go deeper: The internet's latest obsession: The end of the world

events.title: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
events.summary: Anthropic will make its Wall Street debut Thursday at a moment of profound contradiction in the history of AI: The humans are embattled — bogged down by scandal, financial turmoil and political revolt. But the machines are ascendant — accelerating toward an "intelligence explosion" they expect will transform civilization. Why it matters: The industry's recent chaos has obscured a breathtaking surge in technological progress, forcing some of the world's leading researchers to reconsider just how soon AI could surpass human intelligence. Zoom in: Inside Anthropic, soon to be valued north of $1 trillion, independent researchers at METR found that AI models are advancing at nearly twice their historical pace — largely fueled, they believe, by AI itself. Anthropic's own data shows Claude went from leading fewer than 1% of the company's AI research tasks in February to more than a quarter by August, with humans still supervising. METR found no clear obstacles to sustaining this pace over the next year, and reviewed confidential evidence suggesting the acceleration itself may be gathering speed. Zoom out: Across the frontier, leading companies are racing up what Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls "the exponential." OpenAI disclosed Tuesday that Astra 6.2 is its first publicly released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement — equivalent, the company says, to giving every researcher another highly capable engineer. The advances span both software and silicon: OpenAI says its models helped AMD compress a year of chip-design progress into less than five months, while Google's Gemini is reducing weeks of chip-layout work to hours. The big picture: These breakthroughs are pushing some of AI's top forecasters to shorten their timelines for the fabled "intelligence explosion" — a runaway cascade of self-improving AI that could propel machine intelligence far beyond human comprehension. The influential AI Futures Project now expects machines to surpass the world's best human AI researchers next year, a dramatic revision driven largely by METR's findings at Anthropic. Paul Christiano, an AI safety pioneer who recently joined OpenAI's board, puts the odds of superintelligence emerging within a year at one in three if development continues at its current pace. Between the lines: For all their extraordinary capabilities, the machines remain at the mercy of a fallible human race. Take Nvidia: Jensen Huang's sex scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis at the very height of its technological and financial power, endangering virtually the entire AI ecosystem. AI leaders' disastrous messaging , veering between promises of utopia and warnings of mass unemployment, has poisoned public trust and helped fuel a revolt against data centers. Meanwhile, the industry's enormous capital requirements, increasingly tangled financial arrangements and intensifying U.S.–China chip war threaten to impose limits that the technology itself has yet to encounter. Then there's the question of control: Months after OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face, the company acknowledged Wednesday that it still cannot fully rely on AI behaving as intended to prevent harm. One of the industry's biggest gambles is that AI itself will help solve the problem of controlling future superintelligence. "You're building the plane as you fly it," Christiano told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel this week. The bottom line: Anthropic's historic IPO captures the central contradiction: Investors are betting on nearly limitless technological progress, while the industry's future remains hostage to distinctly human failures.

events.title: Exclusive: Bots amplified conspiracy theories and panic about recent tech outages
events.summary: Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the outages and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups. While it's unclear who's behind these accounts, the pattern shows that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, bot networks will fill the void to manufacture panic. Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week. Then came the conspiracy theories: When the FAA grounded flights for four hours Friday, people were quick to assume it was tied to the rollout of an AI tool at the agency. Some also tried linking the widespread Microsoft outage to recent company layoffs. Yes, but: There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online. Several companies have attributed their disruptions to technical problems, rather than malicious activity, including efforts to patch vulnerabilities to make software more resilient. Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday saw the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, longer-term patterns are far from unprecedented, as Axios previously reported . By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics. During Microsoft's outage, bots accounted for 26% of conspiratorial posts. Bots accounted for 34% of conspiracy-related posts during Friday's Workday outage, compared with 27% of other posts. Likely bot accounts also made up 31% of conspiracy-related posts about Bank of America's outage and 28% of posts linking Chase's outage to other disruptions. PeakMetrics analyzed social media discussions surrounding six recent outages and classified accounts that were likely to be bots and conspiracy-related posts. Threat level: Jessica Pratt, a spokesperson for PeakMetrics, told Axios that most of the bot activity is aimed at "gaming the platforms' algorithms" and that it sees some foreign influence within that — although the company could not detail precisely how many of the bots are tied to foreign state media and governments. PeakMetrics also observed a "small number of foreign state media and state-aligned accounts in the conversation," Pratt added. Zoom in: The most popular theory being pushed was that each of these incidents must be connected. More than half of posts about Chase's outage linked it to other recent disruptions, including the FAA ground stop and Microsoft's outage. A fabricated statement attributed to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon fueled speculation that North Korean and Russian hackers were behind the banking outages. During Microsoft's outage, suspected bots circulated identical posts linking the disruption to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure and banking outages in Japan and Paraguay. The big picture: Foreign influence operations have historically used bots to amplify political grievances and spread false narratives, but it's unclear who's operating the accounts pushing theories about the latest outages. Between the lines: The longer outages dragged on without clear explanations, the more room conspiracy theories had to spread. During Microsoft's outage, speculative posts nearly tripled on the second day, when the disruption had stretched beyond 12 hours. By then, nearly 1 in 5 posts offered an alternative explanation for the outage, according to PeakMetrics. The intrigue: Questions about whether the outages are connected have also reached Washington, where senior officials and lawmakers are raising concerns about what might be causing the disruptions. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that "it's unclear if [the outages are] all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity." Jeffries said he wants briefings for lawmakers in both chambers. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters that it would be "the greatest coincidence in the history of the world" if these outages aren't connected, according to NBC News. What we're watching: Outages are about to become the new normal as organizations race to patch critical vulnerabilities discovered by AI before hackers can use AI to weaponize them. events.title: Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly
events.summary: Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center. This investigation was produced in partnership with Proof News , a nonprofit newsroom covering AI. Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures. “It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story. Gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than 10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts. An investigation by Proof News and WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the company, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations. In January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake with a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces. Inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store. According to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company. “We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.” One ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment. ShiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.” “Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek said in a statement to Proof News and WIRED. Though ShiftKey advertises open shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions —a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes. The app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof New and WIRED reviewed called for licensed practical nurses or certified nursing assistants , careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic issues within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities. “Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek said.
