events.title: These Teachers Were Charged With Sexual Abuse. California Could Have Revoked Their Licenses Earlier but Didn’t.
events.summary: Anna Vignet for ProPublica and KQED Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap, rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas. But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019. And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them, prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had touched him, too.   The state Commission on Teacher Credentialing also delayed revoking the credentials of two other teachers who were later convicted of sexually abusing students. As with Braff, schools had reported those educators to the agency that determines who can work in California’s public schools. And as with Braff, the commission allowed those teachers to keep teaching — and draw new complaints — until after they were criminally charged, an investigation by KQED and ProPublica found. That includes a middle school math teacher who sent his student a video showing a boy’s genitals and an elementary teacher who touched students’ butts and vaginal areas and placed their hands on his crotch, according to court records. In each of the cases, state investigators did not interview some of the students who had alleged abuse, according to the students, parents and attorneys who spoke to KQED and ProPublica. Several former agency staffers, including investigators, told the news outlets that, at times, the volunteer panel tasked with assessing teacher accusations overlooked evidence of wrongdoing. That perspective from staff members was backed up by two former members of the panel and two people who served on the state commission that ultimately decides teacher discipline.  After police arrested Braff in 2024, a parent emailed Jeffrey Weinstein, superintendent at Santa Paula Unified School District, where Braff was first accused of sexually abusing students. “Who dropped the ball and allowed this monster to still be around kids?” the parent wrote, according to public records obtained by the news outlets. (Weinstein was not working at Santa Paula at the time students accused Braff.)  In his emailed response, Weinstein blamed the state’s teacher licensing agency. He told the parent that the district had conducted its own investigation and reported the guidance counselor to the state as well as to police. He also said he had reviewed the district’s investigative file and “vehemently disagreed” with the agency’s decision not to revoke Braff’s credentials.  “We sent all the evidence we had gathered,” Weinstein said. “The district did everything in its legal capacity it could.” Braff is soon to stand trial for sexually abusing 15 students, including 13 from Santa Paula. He has been in jail since November 2024. He has pleaded not guilty and did not respond to a request for comment sent through the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office’s electronic messaging system. His attorney declined to comment.  Braff had previously told Santa Paula Unified administrators that he did not touch students near their private parts or have them sit on his lap — and that he only gave students side hugs, high-fives, fist bumps and taps on the knee, according to the district’s 2019 report to the state.  “Mr. Braff described keeping an office environment where kids can move around; and he would not be closer than arm’s length,” the report said, summarizing the district’s interview with Braff. “It was not his intent to make them afraid but rather feel that there was someone in their corner; someone to talk to.”  The Santa Paula Unified School District recognized guidance counselor David Braff as employee of the month in 2017. The district reported him to the state for misconduct two years later. Santa Paula Unified School District via Facebook Anita Fitzhugh, a spokesperson for the Commission on Teacher Credentialing, said the state automatically revokes teachers’ credentials when they are convicted of sexual criminal offenses. But she wrote in a statement that “unless the applicant or educator is convicted of a mandatory criminal offense, there are no written criteria that set the level of adverse action for educator discipline matters.” She did not answer questions about specific cases or details of the investigative process.  Fitzhugh said the state does not provide any guidelines for those reviewing teacher misconduct cases about when discipline is warranted or the type of punishment that should be meted out. And she said it was the commission’s role to balance “protecting students as well as the legal rights of educators who have been accused but not convicted.”  California’s system of disciplining educators dates to the 1970s, Fitzhugh said, and “a deep and comprehensive review of the educator discipline system, prioritizing student safety in the schools, is in order.”   “We expect the Commission to take this up in the near future,” she said. Students Not Interviewed In the summer of 2019, California’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing received a detailed report from the Santa Paula school district about Braff’s alleged misconduct at McKevett Elementary School. The state requires districts to report educators when they resign or are fired after allegations of misconduct. Braff, who had been a guidance counselor at the school for four years, had resigned in the midst of the district’s investigation into complaints by at least seven students that he had touched them inappropriately.  The district told the state agency that it had contemplated but did not initiate any discipline against Braff before accepting his resignation. The district said it appeared, based on student interviews, that Braff “had engaged in at least inappropriate conduct.” Its report to the state, submitted two months after he resigned, included a 20-page summary of the principal’s interviews with at least seven accusers and two witnesses. It also included Braff’s defense and noted multiple inconsistencies in his account of what had occurred.  One fifth grade girl said that during a visit to his office, Braff had locked the door, grabbed her by her hips and forced her to sit on his lap, according to the district’s report to the state of its investigation. She said she did not like being touched and cried every time she had to see him for counseling. The girl requested to transfer to another school, district investigators said, because she wanted to “be away from” Braff. events.title: Tech antitrust would be high on Van Hollen’s agenda
events.summary: Big Tech would face some policy threats from the past if Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., somehow pulls off his longshot bid for Senate Majority Leader over current Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, according to an audio recording of Van Hollen’s remarks at a Hewlett Foundation event in California this week that was shared with Semafor. Van Hollen signaled support for bipartisan antitrust legislation that stalled out in 2022, called the American Innovation and Competition Online Act, when asked about two proposals aimed at anticompetitive behavior from Big Tech firms. “That’s exactly the kind of bill, No. 1, that would be expedited under one of [Sen. Jeff] Merkley’s proposals,” he said, referring to the Oregon Democrat’s proposal with Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to overhaul Senate rules in order to pass bills more quickly. “It is definitely the kind of bill that needs to come up for a vote,” Van Hollen said. Those who are hoping the Senate will crack down on Big Tech firms for both anticompetitive behavior and unchecked AI development believe Van Hollen is a better pick due to Schumer’s history of slow-walking tech legislation ( in 2022 , he said he wasn’t sure the competition bills could get 60 votes and didn’t put them on the floor). Critics also note that one of Schumer’s daughters has worked at Meta and another recently started at OpenAI. Van Hollen said at the same conference that AI companies should be liable for any harm they cause, according to Politico. Schumer, for his part, said this week that “we need to ensure the safe development and deployment of AI or we’re going to see more outages and, God forbid, even catastrophic events going forward.”

events.title: Republicans turn to Democrats for Pentagon money
events.summary: The News Senate Republicans are at least temporarily giving up their quest for a party-line defense funding bill, choosing instead to pursue negotiations with Democrats. The main culprit: Republicans don’t have 50 votes for a party-line bill. And some GOP senators think if they don’t begin work on a budget reconciliation bill before breaking for Thanksgiving, the effort is dead altogether. Senate Majority Leader John Thune wouldn’t go that far, saying a party-line bill remains an “option” but that Republicans “want to explore all the possibilities for funding the military.” Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “if we had 50 votes” for a budget resolution, then “I believe we would have done it.” Now the calendar, combined with the dismal vibes after the midterms, are working against Republicans. In December, “I just don’t know how there could be time, otherwise, to literally work the process,” Cramer said. Time Crunch A budget resolution includes up to 50 hours of debate time and an unlimited vote-a-rama. And once both chambers of Congress pass a budget, they need to pass the actual spending bill — which means another vote-a-rama. That would require Republicans in both chambers to have near-unity to pass anything, a steep ask after the midterms. Getting a deal with Democrats won’t be easy either: Democrats will have their own domestic spending demand, and the longshot leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., to Democratic leader Chuck Schumer will make it hard for Democrats to focus on the upcoming Dec. 11 spending deadline and the GOP’s Pentagon priorities. “I don’t know if we’re going to do anything. I think we’re going to continue to confirm judges. I’m pretty sure of that. But everything else, I have no idea what we’re going to do,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., after Republicans held a strategy meeting late Wednesday.

events.title: Democrats seem to back away from shutdown over Iran war
events.summary: House Democrats are backing away from using a December government funding deadline to force an end to the Iran war, arguing they’ll have more control over the process next year. “Until we get that additional leverage, I don’t see how everything moves forward until we’re in control,” said incoming House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y. Progressives are signaling they might be OK with punting the fight, too. “Is it December? Is it January? I don’t know,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. “We’re still working that through to figure out which one gives us the most strength.” Still in the minority for the next month and a half, Democrats have a limited number of options to influence the Republican majority’s funding plans, and there’s little appetite in the caucus to risk a shutdown now. Senate Democrats are grappling with the same question. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: Insurance firms called on to improve claims handling
events.summary: The FCA and Financial Ombudsman Service have published a report setting out what insurers need to focus on to ensure claims are dealt with promptly, clearly and fairly. We are helping firms learn from Financial Ombudsman complaints and strengthen their claims handling in line with our existing rules to improve service quality for insurance customers.The report highlights where claims handling can improve and explains the key rules firms need to meet.Building on findings in our 2025 review of home and travel insurance, it calls on insurers to:Keep claims moving.Give customers clear and timely updates.Take responsibility when problems arise with third parties working on their behalf.While 79% of people who make a claim are satisfied with claims handling (PDF), improvements are needed in consumer understanding and service quality.Chris Knight, director for insurance at the FCA, said: 'Most insurance customers receive a good service, but we know there is room for improvement – and when standards fall short, firms must put things right. These insights will help firms understand our requirements so that claims are handled promptly, clearly and fairly.'The report comes ahead of proposed legislative changes which would require regular joint thematic reports from the Financial Ombudsman and the FCA to help firms learn lessons from complaints handling. It forms part of wider reforms to modernise the redress system to provide greater predictability, certainty and transparency for firms and consumers.Raising insurance standards We have been working to improve standards across insurance markets, expanding this work further following the Which? super-complaint in September 2025.Key actions include:Using our enforcement powers to open 6 insurance Consumer Duty investigations, including 3 involving potential poor claims handling and fair value failures in home and travel insurance.An ongoing premium finance fair value review that has reduced monthly insurance costs. In February, we estimated this was saving consumers around £157m a year.Securing more than £200m in compensation for motor customers with written-off or stolen vehicles.Delivering annual savings of £70m through our GAP insurance intervention following concerns over fair value.More information:Read the joint press release and thematic report on insurance claims handling.We will publish an update by the end of this year on progress against the commitments in our December 2025 response to Which?’s super-complaint.

events.title: IEA says $40bn spent on pipelines will not end Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz dependence
events.summary: Gulf oil exports would remain vulnerable to disruption even if producers built an estimated $40 billion in pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the International Energy Agency said as the Iran war drags on. About 7 million barrels a day of new pipeline capacity is under construction or being considered across the region, which could add about $2 to every barrel of oil exported from the Middle East, the agency said in its annual World Energy Outlook on Thursday. Even if all the projects are completed, producers outside the Gulf pump more and importers cut demand, about 2 million bpd would still pass through Hormuz by 2035, under the IEA’s most extreme case for reducing reliance on the waterway. “As already seen in 2026, if the Middle East is unstable, then alternative routes for Gulf exports are likely to be vulnerable too,” the Paris-based agency said. The fighting that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran at the end of February has caused what the IEA called the largest energy supply shock in history, with cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas. Oil flows through Hormuz fell from about 20 million bpd before the conflict to an average of about 3 million bpd between March and May. The Middle East would remain the largest oil exporter to international markets even under the agency’s most extreme diversification case. Importers can reduce their reliance on the strait over time, but “the same does not apply to the Middle East as a whole”, the IEA said. Partial protection Among the new alternative routes, only the second Habshan-Fujairah pipeline in the UAE is under construction, the IEA said. It would add 1.8 million bpd of capacity to the Gulf of Oman. An expansion of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and two Iraqi routes have yet to be started. Saudi Arabia and the UAE kept exports above 60 per cent of prewar levels by redirecting crude to the Red Sea and Fujairah, respectively. But virtually all of Opec's about 2.6 million bpd of spare capacity outside the UAE was held by countries that ship through the Strait of Hormuz, leaving it unable to reach markets. LNG has no escape route Liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the UAE has no feasible way around the strait. Eliminating LNG shipments through Hormuz would strand both countries’ export capacity, among the cheapest in the world, the IEA said. About 110 bcm of gas passed through the strait last year, mostly from Qatar. Iranian attacks on the Ras Laffan complex knocked out more than 17 bcm of annual capacity, which will take about three years to restore. Qatar is still expected to double its LNG export capacity by 2035 under the IEA’s stated policies scenario, with 87 bcm a year of new capacity online by the early 2030s despite a one-year delay. The scenario reflects measures governments have announced as well as those already in force. The UAE’s 13 bcm Ruwais LNG project is due to start by 2030. The two countries account for about 30 per cent of the 350 bcm of new LNG supply coming to market between 2025 and 2035. UAE emerges stronger The UAE, which left Opec in May , is projected to pump 5.8 million bpd by 2035, up from 4.4 million bpd in 2025 and 1.4 million bpd more than the agency forecast a year ago. Saudi output stays near 12 million bpd, with natural gas liquids reaching about 30 per cent of production as the large unconventional Jafurah gas field is developed. The IEA said both countries benefit from low-cost resources and committed investment, leaving them better placed than producers such as Iraq, which relies more on Gulf shipping routes and has made less progress diversifying its economy. Middle East spending on gas supply is expected to rise 80 per cent to an average of $50 billion a year over the next decade under current policies, driven by restoring Qatari output and growth in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Buyers’ market? An end to the crisis could usher in “a buyers’ market for oil and natural gas, with significant downward pressures on prices”, the IEA said. New supply from the UAE and the Americas and a wave of US-led LNG projects will meet demand reshaped by the crisis. Under current policies, the Middle East’s net oil and gas income will increase from $620 billion in 2025 to $860 billion by 2035. But if importers move faster to cut their dependence on Gulf energy, the region’s oil exports would be about 20 per cent lower by 2035 and LNG exports 60 per cent lower, leaving a harder backdrop for governments reliant on fuel revenue. However, Middle East oil and gas would be difficult to replace entirely given its low costs, scale and long-standing ties with buyers, the agency said.

events.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
events.summary: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington. As Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support. For Iran , relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow. Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran . But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington. That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate? Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit China is now Iran's economic lifeline China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil. In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports , much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions. As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs. Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own. "If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW. But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter. "The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said. Sanctions enforcement raises pressure on Iran That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports. In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny. As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets. "A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said. This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero. That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks. Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating. Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost. But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies. A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping . China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability. Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation. Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.

events.title: FCA launches world-first platform giving firms new insight into AI innovation
events.summary: New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities. The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services.Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector.The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions about adopting AI responsibly.Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'AI is creating significant opportunities across financial services, and we’re committed to helping firms understand how the technology is being used.'The AI Spotlight Observatory provides an open and accessible resource that brings together real-world examples of AI adoption, helping firms, innovators and researchers learn from developments across the sector and identify new opportunities for innovation and growth.'Notes to editorsThe FCA’s AI Spotlight Observatory is the first resource of its kind for a regulator globally. It builds on the FCA’s AI Spotlight Digital Showcase, a repository of practical AI solutions across specific themes, by adding new features and capabilities, such as a common taxonomy for comparison, a distinction between use cases and implementations, and the ability to identify emerging patterns across the market.The platform is open and accessible to all users. Registration is required to access more detailed insights, such as target client information, and to request demonstrations directly from innovators featured on the platform.The Observatory will continue to evolve through the addition of new use cases. Firms can apply to be showcased on the platform.CFTE has supported the development of the Observatory across three main areas: creating the taxonomy, building the repository, and socialising the Observatory with the market.The Observatory forms part of CFTE’s wider collaboration with the FCA on AI capability, industry engagement and market intelligence. Alongside initiatives such as the Agentic Academy, CFTE supports the FCA in helping the financial-services sector better understand, structure and respond to the opportunities and challenges created by AI.NayaOne has been responsible for the design and development of the Observatory platform, including the user interface, navigation, search and filtering capabilities.The platform builds on the FCA’s wider work on AI, including itsAI Discussion Paper, AI Sprint, and AI Lab, which includes AI Live Testing and its groundbreaking Supercharged Sandbox supported by NVIDIA, NayaOne and Anthropic.Last month, the FCA published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services.

events.title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
events.summary: The global rollout of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is underway, taking players back to Vice City LOS ANGELES -- After a 13-year wait, “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun its global rollout, sending players back to Vice City and kicking off one of the most anticipated entertainment launches in years. Players in New Zealand were among the first to enter Rockstar Games’ sprawling Florida-inspired world as midnight Thursday arrived, hours before the game becomes available across the United States. Internet providers there had prepared for a massive surge in downloads. Chorus New Zealand expected about 35 petabytes — 35 million gigabytes — of additional traffic across its network as players downloaded the massive game. “The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, the company’s network strategy manager. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.” In Wellington, Adam Simmons launched the game from his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low so he wouldn’t wake his wife and daughters. “The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep,” he said after about half an hour of play. In the Dallas area, Bryan Banuelos, a mobile auto detailer, told customers he wouldn't be taking calls Thursday so he could focus on “GTA VI.” His social media post actually drove some business beforehand, with customers trying to get their cars detailed before he disappeared into Vice City. “Tomorrow will be the beginning of a new era for the gamers that like GTA,” Banuelos said. The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida. Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture. Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release. The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity. Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight. In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack. Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation. The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day. The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it. “GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

events.title: Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin With PVTW
events.summary: Production test is necessarily built around decisions. PASS. FAIL. Bin 1. Bin 2. Ship. Do not ship. Characterization has a different objective. It asks not only whether the device meets specification, but how far it is from the boundary. That distinction becomes increasingly important as processors integrate compute, memory, high speed interfaces, multiple power domains and advanced packaging into increasingly complex systems. Suppose five devices all pass the product specification, but under the same controlled workload their minimum stable operating voltages are: 0.70 V | 0.71 V | 0.73 V | 0.76 V | 0.79 V Production test sees five passing devices. Characterization sees five different levels of margin. That changes the engineering question from “Why did this device fail?” to something potentially much more useful: What is consuming product margin? PVTW (process, voltage, temperature, workload) gives us a framework for exploring that question. Take the same device and establish its voltage and frequency boundary using conventional ATE content. Then establish another boundary while running a deterministic compute workload. Repeat with SRAM, memory, PCIe and combined workloads. We may discover that the boundaries are different. That difference can tell us which workload is exposing the limiting condition and where deeper characterization should begin. Characterize the boundary Rather than testing at one nominal operating point, deliberately approach the boundary. Sweep voltage at fixed frequency, temperature and workload. Sweep frequency while the other conditions remain fixed. Repeat across temperature. Then manipulate individual power domains. A compute workload may be characterized while the core rail is swept and memory and I/O rails remain fixed. A memory-intensive workload can be characterized while a memory-related rail is swept. PCIe traffic can be maintained while relevant electrical and thermal conditions are changed. Now we are not simply determining whether a subsystem functions. We are measuring how much margin it has under a defined workload. Known good versus marginal populations Population analysis makes this more powerful. Take known good devices and devices showing reduced SLT margin. Characterize both populations under identical PVTW conditions. Instead of asking only which devices fail, compare the shapes of their operating envelopes. Does the marginal population show a consistent voltage shift? Does the difference emerge only at high temperature? Does it appear only under simultaneous compute and memory activity? Is there a particular rail or frequency transition where the two populations separate? The shape of the margin distribution can provide clues to the physical mechanism. A long SLT failure can become a short test Suppose a particular system workload requires 45 minutes before marginal devices begin generating errors. That is useful for learning, but expensive as a production screen. PVTW characterization can help determine why that workload exposes the problem. Once the mechanism is better understood, the ATE capability can search for a shorter electrical, structural or functional signature correlated with the same marginality. Perhaps a voltage and frequency corner exposes it in seconds. Perhaps a targeted functional pattern reproduces the condition. Perhaps a particular power rail response or interface measurement predicts it. If the correlation is strong enough, the shorter test can potentially move into Final Test or even Wafer Sort. The learning flow becomes: SLT discovers → PVTW characterizes → ATE correlates → Production test screens The goal of deeper SLT characterization is therefore not necessarily more SLT. In some cases, its greatest value may be teaching us how to screen the risk earlier and faster. Margin is a continuous engineering variable This is why I believe we should preserve margin data rather than reducing everything immediately to PASS and FAIL. Minimum operating voltage, maximum stable frequency, thermal margin, interface margin, power margin and workload margin can all become continuous characterization parameters. Those measurements can be compared across device populations, process corners, assembly conditions and eventually manufacturing history. A device with 100 mV of margin and a device with 10 mV of margin may both satisfy the production specification today. But they may tell us very different things about process variation, product robustness and future design decisions. Characterizing those differences can help answer a more fundamental question: Where is the product operating boundary, and what moves it? That question does not end at the silicon. The package surrounding the silicon has its own manufacturing history, materials and process variation. In Part 3, I will explore how 2D ID and unit level traceability could connect PVTW margin all the way back to wafer X,Y and substrate panel X,Y. Part 1: PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload The post Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin With PVTW appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: AI Accelerators Drive Changes In Power Delivery Networks
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI accelerators and GPUs consume thousands of amperes at increasingly low voltages, causing a shift to vertical power delivery that brings regulation closer to loads. Advances in integrated voltage regulators and passive components are enabling new power architectures. Power delivery is becoming a system-level co-design challenge, expanding simulation needs and the role of OSATs. Power delivery is now a significant performance limiter in data center chips. The demands of AI and high-performance computing chips running near 0.7 V for a 600W GPU are forcing current to rise to 1,000 amps and beyond, compounding resistive losses and voltage droop across the PDN. Multi-chiplet constructions only compound these issues by further increasing current density and signal congestion. To solve these challenges, designers are turning to vertical power delivery networks, where the voltage regulator modules are relocated much closer to the processors from their position on the device periphery — to the PCB landside (under the PCB), inside the accelerator package, or inside the silicon interposer. Together with the growing customization of AI accelerator modules, there are many approaches on offer with varying design and manufacturing complexity. The vertical PDN trend began nearly a decade ago with the integration of backside power delivery networks (BPDNs) on the wafer backside, enabling fine-tuned power delivery more directly to the transistors while slashing IR drop across the tens of interconnect levels on-chip. That approach is being extended with increasingly sophisticated on-die decoupling capacitors (DCaps) formed in deep trenches as part of the BPDN. While this addresses high-frequency decoupling at the chip level, recent changes inside packages, interposers, substrates, and across data center racks are becoming just as important. Add to that recent developments in the design of compact passive devices, like high-performance inductors, and new architectural solutions become possible, moving the VRMs and DC-DC converters into the interposer or package. But these architectural changes are neither straightforward nor simple because they involve system co-design of the PDN, interposer, power management ICs (PMICs), integrated voltage regulators (IVRs), DC-DC converters, capacitors, and other passive devices, alongside custom HPC, memory devices, and interconnects that perform today’s elaborate AI tasks. “In the most advanced semiconductors, people are moving from discrete PMICs to distributed IVRs. Those IVRs are great because they are placed much closer to the chip, which reduces the IR drop to the chip’s own power delivery network, so it is way more efficient. In addition, closed and fast control loops between the chip power management unit to the IVR reduce the reaction time to voltage droop events from milliseconds to microseconds. Because this reaction is so fast you can tune voltage very accurately, with a high degree of granularity even on different areas of a chip,” said Nir Sever, senior director of business development at proteanTecs . Reconfiguring the PDN is part of a much larger drive to improve energy use. “Energy efficiency becomes the most important performance index for AI-infused platforms moving forward,” said Lipen Yuan, senior director of TSMC’s Advanced Technology Business Development, during a 2024 IEDM short course. Power delivery challenges are most important at points of load. “AI systems are placing unprecedented demands on board-to-chip power delivery, making the final stage of voltage regulation increasingly important,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE . Fig. 1: By regulating voltage at the point of load, OSATs enable fine-tuned voltage control. Source: ASE “The move to multi-die architectures is bringing power integrity to the forefront, alongside thermal, stress, and warpage challenges. But the underlying power-delivery problem already existed in advanced single-die designs,” said Sojan Philips, principal product manager of Redhawk-SC at Synopsys . “AI accelerators are now operating at currents approaching the kiloampere range, where even milliohm-level resistance in the power-delivery network can result in significant IR drop. That loss of voltage margin can directly affect performance and power targets, particularly maximum operating frequency and V min .” Several developments illustrate these trends: Backside PDN : Intel Foundry’s 18A was the first to move backside wafer processing into leading-edge high-volume manufacturing. Samsung and TSMC plan to implement backside PDNs at future advanced nodes, starting next year. Integrated voltage regulators : ASE, Marvell, Empower, and others are moving voltage regulation closer to the processor. Embedded capacitors and inductors : Integration of compact passive components is becoming a key differentiator in high-density power delivery. Co-optimization of package and on-chip power : Power integrity can no longer be optimized independently at the PCB, substrate, interposer, and transistor levels. As a result, OSATs are playing an increasing role in system co-design, electrical validation, and power integrity (PI) simulation. “The OSAT sits where die, substrate or interposer, passives, and board meet, so we are brought in earlier to model the package-level PDN and co-simulate it with the customer’s die power data,” said Alex Kizeev, technical director of signal and power integrity at Amkor’s design optimization team. Kizeev breaks down the supply chain and responsibilities among different companies. “The best results come from a PDN budget partitioned across the die, package, and board. The foundry and fabless teams own the on-die PDN, including the die power map and the bump-map allocation. The substrate supplier defines what stackup and via/plane technology is possible. The OSAT optimizes the package-level pieces, including stackup choice, via and ball assignment, DCap selection and placement, warpage and reliability, and validation.” “Backside power delivery can significantly improve power delivery by reducing IR drop and freeing up frontside routing resources for signals, but it doesn’t eliminate power-integrity challenges,” said Philips. “It also changes the thermal landscape. As power delivery and other structures move to the backside, the paths available for heat removal become more complex. This makes co-optimization of power integrity and thermal management increasingly important. The overall trend is moving toward closer integration in advanced packages and dies, including the integration of inductors, capacitors, and power-conversion components into substrates and interposers. events.title: How Virtual Twins And Machine Learning Optimize DRAM Yield
events.summary: As memory technologies continue to scale, manufacturing processes are becoming increasingly complex. Additional process steps, tighter process windows, and new sources of variation are making it progressively more challenging to reach acceptable yield. Systemic failures are emerging as a source of yield loss during yield ramp. Unlike random defects, these failures are often driven by complex interactions between multiple process modules. Rapid root-cause identification of these systemic defects is critical to quickly improving yield and accelerating time-to-market. 1 But conventional failure analysis relies heavily on wafer experimentation and statistical analysis, which can be slow and costly as manufacturing complexity increases. That’s where calibrated virtual twins and machine-learning optimization can help. Fig. 1: Systemic failures are a key bottleneck during yield ramp. Faster identification and reduction of these failures can accelerate the yield ramp and shorten the time required to reach a targeted manufacturing yield. Process engineers use virtual manufacturing models ( SEMulator3D ) with machine learning (ML) optimization ( Fabtex Yield Optimizer ) to predict process failures. A virtual twin can improve DRAM yield analysis by reproducing process variation in a calibrated digital environment. ML can then evaluate multiple failure mechanisms and process changes simultaneously. Using this technique, engineers can evaluate potential yield improvements, all with limited need for wafer-based experimentation. Detecting multiple DRAM failure modes with virtual metrology As an example of this technique, we built a SEMulator3D model (virtual twin) of a DRAM manufacturing process sequence. During this model-building, we established virtual metrology measurements throughout the process sequence (Figure 2). Fig. 2: Building and calibrating a DRAM virtual twin using process integration, virtual metrology, and silicon data. ML was then used to calibrate the model against silicon data, enabling the virtual environment to better reproduce observed manufacturing behavior and serve as the foundation for downstream failure analysis and optimization. Building and calibrating a DRAM virtual twin For our specific case study, we built a calibrated virtual twin for our DRAM memory device that contained eight known systemic failure mechanisms. Figure 3 displays examples of these failure mechanisms, including shorts, opens, and overlap-related defects between critical DRAM structures. Fig. 3: Reproducing systemic DRAM failure modes and detecting them using virtual metrology. We also specified (in the virtual twin) the virtual metrology needed to detect these failures. By translating each failure into a measurable geometric condition and monitoring it through virtual metrology, we were able to automatically detect and simultaneously analyze multiple failure mechanisms within a single study. Using machine learning to optimize process targets Using the calibrated virtual twin, ML was then applied to help us understand the impact of process and structural variations on the eight predefined failure modes. We then searched for an optimized manufacturing solution (specific process changes) that provided the lowest failure rate across our eight predefined failure modes. Instead of addressing each failure mode independently, the optimization routine evaluated the impact of multiple process changes simultaneously and searched for process targets that improved the overall pass ratio. Case study results: Predicted yield increased to 78.5% As shown in Figure 4, the optimized process settings significantly reduced all eight systemic failure modes. Fig. 4: Simultaneous reduction of multiple systemic failures through ML-based optimization and retargeting analysis. A sample retargeting plot for SNLP (storage node landing pad) open/short failures is highlighted. Under the nominal process conditions used in the study, the predicted total yield was 0.1%. Following optimization, the predicted yield increased to 78.5%, with lower failure rates across all eight failure mechanisms. This analysis also translated the optimized solution into actionable inline fab targets that can be directly applied in the real process, helping engineers identify which process and structural parameters should be adjusted to further reduce systemic failures. Accelerating semiconductor yield improvement This work demonstrates how the combination of process models and ML can be used to accelerate yield improvement during DRAM device development. By reproducing process variability in a calibrated virtual environment, and performing simultaneous optimization and retargeting, engineers can detect multiple device failures and investigate a broad solution space without the time and cost of extensive silicon experimentation. Reference 1 I. Tirkel, “Yield Learning Curve Models in Semiconductor Manufacturing,” IEEE Transactions on Semiconductor Manufacturing, vol. 26, no. 4, pp. 564-571, Nov. 2013. events.title: From Metrology To Autonomy: Scaling Yield, Quality, And Innovation
events.summary: With the growth of increasingly complex devices, improving yield, quality, and manufacturing speed requires a new approach. Across 14 presentations and posters presented at SEMICON West 2026, Intel Foundry leaders and engineers shared research and emerging solutions for the AI-ready foundry of the future. By combining end-to-end metrology, intelligent analytics, and industry-wide standards, we can unlock scalable innovation for our customers. Semiconductor manufacturing is shifting from isolated optimization to connected intelligence, according to Intel Foundry’s Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor research and development, advanced packaging technology and manufacturing (APTM), in her keynote at the conference. Factory autonomy will not emerge from AI alone. It requires a system-first mindset based on a common foundation of trusted measurements, interoperable platforms, and advanced test infrastructure.¹ End-to-end metrology for proactive yield management For decades, metrology has served as a critical manufacturing checkpoint. Today, it is evolving into a control layer for proactive yield management. Modern semiconductor manufacturing demands more advanced metrology and defect control to address rising contamination risks, process sensitivities, and defectivity challenges. Hidden interactions among materials, equipment, chemicals, packaging polymers, and fab environments can undermine yield and often go undetected until late-stage manufacturing, increasing costs and slowing production. Rather than reacting to failures after they occur, semiconductor manufacturers like Intel Foundry are using predictive process control supported by continuous measurement and monitoring.² The requirement for end-to-end visibility does not stop at wafer fabrication. The industry’s transition toward heterogeneous integration has introduced increasingly complex architectures built on chiplets, hybrid bonding, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced 2.5D and 3D packaging technologies. These innovations are blurring the traditional boundaries between front-end manufacturing and back-end assembly. Today’s advanced packaging environments require the same level of process intelligence found in leading-edge wafer fabs, such as nanometer-scale precision, process control discipline, and quality assurance capabilities.³ Test operations increasingly represent the final extension of this measurement strategy. Intel Foundry’s Advanced Chiplet Test services provide wafer-to-system test coverage designed to identify issues early, enable known-good die selection, and optimize back-end yield before expensive assembly operations begin. Through predictive die classification, intelligent die pairing, integrated optical testing, and closed-loop yield analytics, test data becomes a critical input for manufacturing intelligence. AI-powered insights for yield improvement Our work on automatic defect classification (ADC) illustrates how AI can help accelerate yield learning and turn complexity into productivity. Managing thousands of classification recipes across multiple technology nodes and manufacturing sites is increasingly difficult, so engineers developed a human-in-the-loop agentic workflow to assist with log analysis, knowledge retrieval, root cause investigation, and recipe reviews. AI-generated recommendations, combined with human approval checkpoints, speed investigations while maintaining auditability and engineering oversight.⁴ We’re also exploring new approaches to thermal intelligence. Our research combines AI with heat-transfer physics to predict how heat moves through semiconductor devices more accurately and with less training data.⁵ This research complements Intel Foundry’s broader investments in advanced test and reliability methodologies, including system-level testing, burn-in, and precision thermal control for increasingly power-dense AI and heterogeneous computing devices. Together, these capabilities help engineers identify yield limiters earlier, reduce manufacturing variability, and make faster, more reliable decisions across the production flow. Building an AI-ready manufacturing infrastructure and ecosystem Precision measurements and intelligent analytics are key components, but scaling in high volume manufacturing requires a modern digital infrastructure. Traditional vendor-locked automation systems often create data silos that limit operational visibility and slow decision-making. By adopting hardware-independent automation architectures, connected data systems, and AI-enabled edge computing, manufacturers can reduce engineering cycles, lower operating costs, and enable predictive maintenance and AI-driven quality inspection.⁶ Finally, autonomy cannot be achieved by technology innovation alone. Industry standards will play a pivotal role. The Semiconductor Assembly Test Automation and Standardization Research Association (SATAS) consortium brings together more than 40 organizations to develop open standards, interoperable architectures, and automation frameworks that can be adopted across the global semiconductor industry, helping to move semiconductor manufacturing from highly automated operations toward true factory autonomy. SATAS is a multi-year industry initiative sponsored by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) and the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI). Intel Foundry is helping advance interoperable architectures, automation frameworks, material-handling standards, and collaborative pilot environments that can accelerate back-end manufacturing transformation. By enabling a more connected and interoperable semiconductor ecosystem, Intel Foundry is making it easier for customers and partners to integrate processes, automate workflows, and adopt next-generation manufacturing capabilities.⁷ A roadmap for the next generation of manufacturing Operationalizing intelligence across the manufacturing stack is getting closer to reality. It begins with end-to-end metrology and trusted data. It extends through explainable, physics-informed AI and advanced failure analysis methodologies. It relies on resilient automation, edge computing, and advanced packaging platforms. And it scales through ecosystem-wide standards and interoperability. Together, these capabilities help customers lead in the next era of manufacturing. events.title: UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise
events.summary: UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: ‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said:‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.’Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said:‘We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.‘The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.’Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risksSeparately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area.Notes to editorsThe FCA, PRA and the Bank have jointly published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management.The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements. The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.The proposed guidance key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas include:Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future.A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.

events.title: What Is Driving Silicon Wafer Demand Recovery?
events.summary: Global silicon wafer shipments are forecast to grow 11.8% in 2026, according to the Q3 2026 SEMI Silicon Wafer Market Monitor . This increase is primarily due to strong demand for AI, which is projected to drive shipments through 2029. Alongside AI, rising process material sales are also supporting recovery. The positive correlation between material sales and silicon wafer demand not only reflects growth in manufacturing complexity, but it also points to greater material consumption per wafer. Finally, increases in memory demand, precautionary inventory building, and global fab capacity expansions are boosting silicon wafer shipments as well. To better understand today’s landscape, it’s helpful to revisit past silicon wafer demand curves. From 2018 to 2019 and from 2022 to 2023, silicon wafer shipments rose ahead of major increases in memory work-in-process (WIP) inventories, or unfinished memory chips undergoing fabrication. However, shipments lagged at the same time WIP inventory peaked. Because fabrication lines were already producing at full capacity, their need for silicon wafers slowed. While this pattern provides historical context for today’s demand recovery, the high number of new and upcoming production lines is a unique factor influencing this particular cycle. Silicon Wafer Shipments and Memory WIP: Historical Lead–Lag Pattern. Both series use four-quarter moving averages. Sources: SEMI SMG and financial disclosures from Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron. Data for 3Q26–2Q27 are forecasts. Fab investments support wafer demand SEMI’s fab investment outlook predicts continued growth in planned equipment spending beyond 2026. So long as investment plans remain broadly on track, ongoing equipment installation and capacity ramps are likely to support silicon wafer demand. The report also demonstrated a widening gap between YoY growth rates for semiconductor fab equipment spending and silicon wafer manufacturing equipment spending, suggesting that investment support for wafer demand may persist longer than initially expected. This also helps explain why the historical relationship between wafer shipments and WIP does not necessarily imply an imminent slowdown. Wafer procurement momentum can moderate before WIP inventories peak, although investment support may slow if moderation becomes visible in wafer shipments. Investment Spread: A Signal of a Later Wafer-Cycle Slowdown. Spread between the YoY growth rates of semiconductor fab equipment spending and silicon wafer manufacturers’ equipment spending, compared with silicon wafer shipment trends. Sources: SEMI Silicon Wafer Shipment Statistics and SEMI WWSEMS. Shipment data are updated through 2Q26, while equipment spending data are updated through August 2026. The next test is inventory absorption SEMI projects continued wafer shipment growth in 2027, although growth will likely be more moderate than it was in 2026. As inventory stockpiles subside, ongoing production will be important for sustaining demand. If planned capacity expansions continue and customers buy the resulting chips, semiconductor companies can gradually reduce their wafer inventories while also maintaining their purchase rate. However, investment delays or weaker demand for semiconductors would slow this absorption and increase the risk of declining silicon wafer orders. While AI-related investment is a critical source of support, broader semiconductor recovery is still uneven. Because of this, the key to maintaining demand growth will be how quickly fabs can use wafers purchased in advance. Doing so will help shape the duration of this recovery period and the depth of any subsequent wafer inventory adjustments. The post What Is Driving Silicon Wafer Demand Recovery? appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Linking plasma chamber simulation with feature-scale process modeling to predict etch profiles, evaluate wafer uniformity, and optimize plasma etching processes. Plasma etching and deposition processes increasingly determine the manufacturability of advanced semiconductor devices, where smaller features, more complex geometries, stricter wafer-uniformity requirements, and new chemistries demand predictive control of ion fluxes at the wafer surface. Kinetic plasma simulation provides a physics-based route to this control by resolving sheath dynamics, ion-neutral transport, and ion angular and energy distributions that cannot be captured reliably with bulk fluid approximations alone. VSim Plasma applies Particle-in-Cell modeling with Monte Carlo collisions to compute self-consistent electromagnetic fields, charged-particle motion, collisions, and current deposition. Validation against inductively coupled plasma measurements shows strong agreement for electron temperature and plasma potential, reasonable density agreement, and consistent electron energy probability function behavior. Coupling plasma-derived ion angular and energy distributions into Victory Process enables feature-scale etch simulation, linking chamber conditions and waveform design to process variability and profile evolution. events.title: Detachable Fiber Connectors Pose New Challenges For Photonics
events.summary: Key T ake a ways: CPO and NPO require new approaches for connecting optical fibers to chip packages. Detachable connectors can simplify assembly, test, and replacement of optical components. Numerous bespoke designs exist today, but standardization hasn’t begun yet. As photonics shifts from pluggable optical transceivers toward near- and co-packaged optics (NPO, CPO), engineers are devising new ways to attach fibers to the photonics chips on a board. Several different designs exist today, but so far there is no common interface. With pluggable photonics, lasers and connections are attached at the server faceplate, with the board itself housing only electronic components. Yet long electrical connections to the faceplate mean higher power and longer latency. Fibers would need to move onto the interior of the board to solve that. That eliminates the need for pluggables, but it requires new solutions. “With the rapid growth of generative AI, AI data centers are required to process enormous volumes of data faster and more efficiently than ever before,” said Yoshimasa Bando, principal scientist at Mitsubishi Chemical . “To meet this demand, further improvements in communication speed and energy efficiency have become critical challenges.” The goal of CPO and NPO is to reduce reliance on long electrical connections. Long lines One reason for maintaining faceplate pluggables is that lasers are not always reliable. Using a pluggable module makes it easy to replace the laser. “What we are focused on has the laser on the faceplate, because the laser is the highest reliability risk,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs . All connections, whether they have a laser or not, happen in pluggable modules today. That means the signals those fibers carry must travel electrically from their origin to the edge of the board. Bandwidth necessitates serial lines driven by serializer/deserializer (SerDes) circuits. Driving those signals over that distance requires high power. CPO aims to reduce system power by eliminating those long electrical lines and bringing fiber into the processor or switch packages. “CPO unlocks the token economics that everyone cares about,” said Chandrasekar. “The major bottlenecks are compute, memory, and moving data back and forth. If you’re trying to make step changes in hardware every one or two years, the way you make 5× or 10× kinds of improvements is by having new hardware. How do you use that hardware intelligently? How do I ensure that whatever hardware I have, I’m using it for the most important problem so my utilization is good?” Fig. 1: With co-packaged optics, an optical engine is placed inside a package along with other chiplets. The laser remains outside the package for thermal reasons, and in the near term it will remain pluggable. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering Photonics plays a key role in this effort. “You’re trying to reduce copper, so you’re trying to bring the PIC [photonic integrated circuit] closer to the processor or the switch,” said David Harame, COO at AIM Photonics, which operates with NY Creates (New York Center for Research, Economic Advancement, Technology, Engineering, and Science). “The industry is still very much using pluggables; you plug in the front panel. So there’s a lot of copper going between this [and the processor]. The next step is to move the optical transceiver closer to the switch by putting it on the PCB and reducing the copper line length to the switch. This is called near-packaged optics. Essentially, it moves the optical pluggable connector further inside the box on the PC board, so the optical-to-electrical connection takes place closer to the switch. CPO is yet another variant of advanced packaging. “And all the challenges in advanced packaging are the same for co-packaged optics, except for fiber coupling and getting the PIC closer to the target chip,” noted Harame. CPO receives the bulk of the near-term optical development efforts. Fig. 2: In near-packaged optics, the optical components lie on the board near where their signals originate. Lasers will remain pluggable for now. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering Unknown fiber length Both CPO and NPO share the need to connect fiber directly to components on the board. One straightforward way is to attach a nominal length of fiber to the chip package and ship it that way, with the system integrator connecting the other end of the fiber directly to the destination. The challenge there is that chip producers have no way of knowing how long that fiber will need to be. If it’s long enough for designs that require long runs, it will be too long for the many designs that don’t. That said, there are ways of dealing with extra fiber. “The fiber goes into a fiber management tray, and there are spool points on the board,” said Nick Harris, CEO of Lightmatter . “They’re neatly managed for airflow.” Others agree. “Usually, you’ll have some kind of excess fiber management,” explained Obie Roy, vice president, strategic commercial development at Senko . “But depending on the system that you’re building, you could cut it to length and terminate it once you know the exact application.” Some engineers see this as a non-issue, which may be true if one is fusing the fibers or having the integrator attach a connector. “The fiber length is irrelevant,” said Professor Amr Helmy at the University of Toronto. “You connect a strand of fiber to the chip. With the other end, you can connectorize it, cut it, or fuse it with another fiber to make it longer. Fusing is one approach, but each one of these fibers can come with a connector depending on the amount of loss appetite you have.” For ease of assembly, some means of attaching and detaching a fiber would also be helpful, such as a fixture or clip on the end to which another fiber can attach. But several considerations make this decision about more than simply adding wire connections as shown in the figures above. Moving beyond the die edge Today, fibers typically are placed using well-established V-groove technology, where the fibers exit out the side of a photonic chip. This attachment method works at low volumes and low total fiber counts, but it lacks the modularity and convenience needed for high-volume automation. “The V-groove is a great concept, but the fibers are attached,” explained Gerard John, senior director, chiplets/FCBGA business unit at Amkor . “When being assembled onto a board, if one of them breaks, there’s no rework. People are generally thinking in terms of detachables and moving away from V-grooves.” In addition, attachment space is bound by shoreline, which is essentially the real estate on the edge of the die. events.summary: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors? Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his conviction. Continue reading...
