events.title: Can AI Make Its Own Manufacturing Decisions?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI can identify promising process conditions and recognize manufacturing problems, but those results still require physical validation before they can be trusted in production. Incomplete manufacturing data and uncertainty about downstream effects make it difficult to give AI systems authority over process adjustments. Greater manufacturing autonomy will require clear decision boundaries, failure containment, and ways to qualify models that change as they learn. Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on engineers making decisions involving complex interactions among process parameters. An etch recipe, for example, may involve combinations of RF power, pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and timing, each affecting multiple process characteristics. Changing one parameter might improve critical dimension control while creating problems elsewhere. But as devices and manufacturing processes become more complicated, the growing number of variables involved makes those decisions increasingly difficult. AI-driven manufacturing offers a way to manage some of that complexity, from finding better process conditions to identifying defects and responding to problems on the production line. But how much production responsibility engineers are willing to give those systems remains an open question, and one that drew considerable attention at SEMICON West 2026. “No matter how good we are as engineers, no matter how disciplined and objective we are, we tend to approach these difficult problems with historical biases,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research during a conference panel. “A process engineer might look at a set of data and say, ‘I need to move into a lower-pressure, higher-power regime because that’s how we solved this problem 10 years ago.’ But with this massive parameter space, AI can point us in a different direction, into an operating region we might never have considered because we couldn’t see those relationships in the data before.” Finding a process that keeps working Finding an unfamiliar operating condition is useful, but determining whether it will hold up in production is another matter. Two recipes may produce similar results during development, yet respond quite differently to changes in incoming materials or equipment conditions. AI can help engineers identify those differences before committing to a particular process. “It’s not just a question of delivering to a particular performance point. It’s also a question of how stable that particular performance point is, how robust it is,” said Vikas Sharma, senior principal engineer and senior director of pathfinding for Intel Foundry R&D, in a recent presentation. “Minor perturbations in the incoming material or at the tool can lead to a significant drop in performance.” The scale of the optimization problem helps explain why AI-driven manufacturing is attracting so much interest. Fried described a current Lam Research etcher with a potential recipe space on the order of 10²³ combinations. At Intel, Sharma discussed a process involving 350 parameters and approximately 10⁷⁰⁰ theoretical combinations. According to Sharma, engineers working with equipment suppliers spent about a year developing a minimally acceptable recipe for that particular tool and process layer, followed by an extended effort to improve it with limited success. After introducing AI-assisted optimization, they began finding better results within a few months, eventually identifying multiple solutions that improved on the original baseline. The challenge was determining which solutions were worth pursuing. Sharma noted that AI could identify thousands of candidates, but evaluating them still required expensive silicon experiments. Engineers also had to account for nonlinear relationships among parameters, which could change considerably across different operating regions. “AI is not a magic wand. You can’t use the same AI solution for every problem,” Fried said. “Figuring out whether you’re using full physical simulation, surrogate models, machine learning, deep learning, LLM-based AI, or agentic AI, which of these solutions you’re building in which form to solve which problem and address which workflow, that’s more of what we’re spending our time on than actually building it or implementing it.” The different approaches serve different purposes, from exploring process conditions to coordinating engineering workflows. Combining them may allow engineers to investigate more possibilities, but it also raises questions about how the results should be validated and whether the assumptions used in one model remain appropriate when its recommendations are passed to another. When the factory acts on what it sees Inspection is one of the more established applications of AI in manufacturing, particularly in advanced packaging, where finer pitches and more complicated structures have increased the number of connections that must be examined. Some packages can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnects, each presenting a potential failure point. Automated optical inspection and X-ray systems collect extensive information about those structures. Machine learning can identify variations that might be difficult to distinguish visually, but manufacturers still need to determine which differences indicate actual defects. “When we look at X-rays, everybody just sees all shades of gray, but AI can see a thousand shades of gray,” said Ingu Yin Chang, executive vice president at ASE Group . “But the AI only knows if this shade of gray equates to a problem once we say, ‘Hey, this equates to a problem.’ So, you’ve got to have the physical data that says, ‘Okay, that is a problem.’ Then, in the future, they can scan for that shade of gray and that location.” Once manufacturers determine which image characteristics correspond to actual defects, AI-enabled inspection systems can flag abnormalities during production and trigger predefined equipment responses. At ASE, systems can recognize known abnormalities and trigger equipment responses before additional assemblies are affected. “We have figured out how to do a lot of automation and use AI to help us identify potential issues, based on the issues that we physically learned through traditional manufacturing methods,” Chang said. “We will know when a wire bond is not bonded correctly, and the machine will immediately stop. There’s constant AI oversight to ask, ‘Are we doing everything correctly? Are we seeing it as we planned to see it?’” Stopping equipment when a defect is detected can prevent additional losses, but it doesn’t necessarily mean AI is controlling the process independently. The inspection system may identify an abnormal condition while a conventional controller executes a predefined response. UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. The Bank of England’s (the Bank) latest Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in 5 years, 52% above the previous 18-month peak recorded in May 2025. In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them. The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast evolving threat environment. It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers. Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: 'Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance. 'Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.' Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said: 'Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.' Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said: 'We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents. 'The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.' Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area. The consultation closes on 26 February 2027. Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond.

Time: 5pm – 6.30pm | Location: Bank of England The Governor began the meeting by thanking attendees for joining and reminding participants of the purpose of these meetings. The Governor made clear that the MPC would be in listening mode, and that the meeting would be conducted in accordance with relevant competition and conduct laws, as per the terms of reference . Item 2 – International developments Market participants opened by discussing developments in major advanced economies outside the UK. The resilience of global growth and the strength of corporate sector balance sheets, particularly in the United States, were noted. Energy markets were also discussed, with market participants highlighting the inherent difficulty of forecasting energy prices amid continued geopolitical uncertainty. The material support to global growth from AI-related capital expenditure was noted. Participants also discussed the increasing role of debt financing and the potential implications of a change in expectations around AI for risky asset markets, investment and consumption. The discussion also covered potential financial market vulnerabilities arising from elevated hedge-fund leverage, sovereign debt pressures and cyber risks. Market participants discussed the outlook for the UK economy and the implications for monetary policy. Participants noted the resilience of UK growth this year despite the energy shock. This resilience was broadly seen to have strengthened the case for higher rates, with the November increase having been widely expected. Growth in global AI-related investment was noted as one factor supporting UK activity, although there was some discussion over the extent to which the resilience in domestic growth would persist. Participants also discussed the implications of AI-related growth for domestic inflationary pressure. Market participants noted the correlation between energy prices and market rates, and how this relationship had evolved over recent months. In discussing the implications of the energy shock, views differed on the relative importance of its demand and supply-side effects. The distinction between implied pricing in the market curve and modal expectations for policy was also noted by market participants. events.title: Volatility need not mean AI's promise is fading, but a shift is happening
events.summary: Markets are becoming more discerning about artificial intelligence . After strong rallies, recent weeks have brought sharp volatility in technology shares. Last week, Nvidia fell sharply amid an unexpected leadership crisis, intensifying pressure across AI-related stocks. On Monday, the Nasdaq dropped 2.5 per cent, more than 10 per cent below its October peak. Investors are questioning whether vast spending on AI infrastructure can generate sufficient returns, and how much must be financed through borrowing. The pressure extends beyond one company, although Nvidia sits at the centre of the AI ecosystem , supplying chips on which the industry depends. Its leadership change has unsettled investors, while scrutiny of financing links between chipmakers, cloud providers and data-centre developers has raised concerns about circular funding. Previous technological revolutions offer cautionary lessons. The dot-com boom transformed the internet, but many backed companies failed. The infrastructure endured, while investors lost money. Volatility need not mean AI's promise is fading, but it may mark a shift towards judging which businesses can turn innovation into profits. There is an important difference today. Much AI investment is undertaken by some of the world's largest and most profitable companies. Nevertheless, spending is pressuring balance sheets and cash flows, increasing reliance on debt and external finance . Falls in AI supplier shares show investors are questioning the funding chain. If returns disappoint, this could become a source of financial market vulnerability. Perhaps the most underestimated aspect of the AI revolution is its infrastructure. Behind increasingly sophisticated applications are vast data centres, advanced semiconductors, cooling systems, telecoms networks and, above all, electricity. AI is not simply a digital service that can expand without physical constraints. It is an increasingly energy -intensive industry requiring enormous capital investment and reliable power. The International Energy Agency expects global electricity consumption by data centres to more than double by 2030. Countries with abundant, competitively priced energy, available land and the capacity to develop infrastructure quickly will have a significant advantage. Access to advanced chips, water, skilled labour and reliable electricity grids will also be critical. This is where the Gulf's ambitions become particularly relevant. The region is positioning itself not merely as a consumer of AI but as a major participant in the infrastructure and investment underpinning its development. The UAE's planned five-gigawatt AI campus in Abu Dhabi, Saudi Arabia's $100 billion Project Transcendence and Qatar's investment in AI infrastructure demonstrate the scale of regional ambition. Sovereign wealth funds and international technology companies are helping to support these initiatives. The Gulf has several advantages including substantial pools of long-term capital, competitive energy resources, strategic geographical positioning and governments willing to support large-scale infrastructure development. These provide an opportunity to establish the region as an important players in the global AI economy . But building AI infrastructure is not the same as creating an AI economy. Data centres are important, but the real economic prize lies in applying AI across financial services, logistics, healthcare, manufacturing , energy, education and government to improve productivity, reduce costs and create new sources of value. The employment implications are equally important. Some occupations will undoubtedly be displaced, particularly those involving repetitive administrative, analytical and processing tasks. Others will be transformed as employees use AI to work more efficiently, while entirely new occupations and industries are likely to emerge. But the transition will not be straightforward. The immediate challenge may be less about mass unemployment than the uneven distribution of benefits and the tensions that creates. Younger workers entering professional employment are already finding traditional entry-level roles disappearing or changing, while those able to work alongside AI are becoming increasingly productive and valuable. Education, training and labour market policies will need to adapt accordingly. For the Gulf region, this has particular significance. Economic diversification depends not simply on attracting capital and international companies but on developing a skilled domestic workforce capable of participating in higher-value activities. Without investment in local skills and expertise, the region risks becoming heavily dependent on imported technology and talent. Ultimately, AI presents the Gulf with an opportunity extending well beyond the current investment cycle. Its financial resources and energy advantages provide a strong starting point, but success should not be measured by the amount invested or the number of data centres built. The real test will be whether AI makes Gulf economies more productive, competitive and diversified, while creating opportunities for their populations. The technology may be transformative, but its economic benefits are not automatic. As previous technological revolutions have demonstrated, the winners will be those that look beyond the investment boom and focus on how technology changes the way their economies actually work. Tim Fox is a Partner at Capital Gate Advisors and former Chief Economist of Emirates NBD

events.title: Abu Dhabi-owned London Square mixes members’ club with home ownership
events.summary: London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties , has announced a network of members’ clubs to be offered to homebuyers across the UK capital. Charter membership will be embedded within the company's residential developments and included with each purchase. It will also be open to the wider community. Homeowners will have access to professional-grade, co-working spaces, wellness and treatment centres, restaurants and lounges, cultural events, screening rooms, podcast studios and a programme of calendar events and experiences. London Square said it was responding to a growing desire for “greater connection, community and convenience closer to home”. London's first Charter clubs will be at Wimbledon Bridge House, Ransome’s Wharf in Battersea, County Hall Kingston, and Bermondsey. The network will be headed by Amanda Dyjecinski, formerly of Maslow’s, which has private members' clubs in Fitzrovia, Soho and Kensington, and the Conduit Club. London Square plans to deliver about 9,000 homes over the next five years in the UK capital, with a total development value of £5 billion ($6.6 billion), as demand remains resilient. The homes will be built across about 30 sites, with the company aiming at buyers in the affordable segment as well as international investors. London Square, which played a significant part in the development of Nine Elms in Battersea, reported sales of £251 million for the first half of this year, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf. Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity. Ms Dyjecinski said Charter sets out create “vibrant places which offer opportunities for people to meet, discover and live well in their neighbourhood” . Adam Lawrence, chief executive of London Square, said it was breaking new ground in what a residential developer could offer. “Londoners increasingly want places that support more dimensions of their lives,” he said. “Beyond flexible work this includes easy access to well-being, culture, hospitality and, vitally, community and connection. This isn’t just a post pandemic theme, there’s a longer-term, more enduring shift in how Londoners experience life in the city and in how they want to live and work.” Residential developers have expanded amenities in many upmarket buildings in London beyond gyms and meeting rooms. This trend has become particularly prevalent since the pandemic and the rise of working from home, with people spending more time close to home. It cited research showing that while Londoners feel a strong sense of connection to the city, 35 per cent say they experience loneliness. In the same report, almost half of Londoners said they want more community spaces where they can meet. Charter at Wimbledon Bridge House will be the first to open its doors, offering a members-only area, a lounge and event space, co-working and private offices, a podcast studio, screening rooms, gym, therapeutics and a bookable treatment room.

events.title: How Jensen Huang's exit could reshape the AI power game from the Gulf to China
events.summary: Jensen Huang was considered the world's hottest AI and chip diplomat. His absence from the proverbial negotiating table might result in the technology's expansion cooling off. Mr Huang – forced to step down as Nvidia boss after an extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang – has been instrumental in building personal relationships with governments and corporates that have shaped AI investments and programmes, and data centres. With artificial intelligence's biggest champion no longer at the helm, analysts expect the dynamics to shift. They anticipate an incoming Nvidia chief who may be largely untested, uncertainty over the company’s strategic direction, and a potential opening for China to pounce on the opportunity during this transition. “Jensen Huang spent years … often helping negotiate deals that went far beyond chip sales,” Irina Tsukerman, a geopolitical analyst in New York, tells The National . “Governments that negotiated directly with him will now have to establish relationships with new leadership, potentially delaying projects and reopening agreements that appeared settled.” Gulf's conundrum In regions where Mr Huang was particularly hands-on, the AI engine hummed and chugged along. Billions of dollars worth of chips, the power behind the AI boom, have been involved, especially with the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Ms Tsukerman says that the Emirates and Saudi Arabia face more immediate commercial concerns because the Arab world's two biggest economies are spending heavily to develop AI industries. “Mr Huang's personal involvement helped advance relationships with Gulf investors and technology companies. A leadership change could delay negotiations over new computing facilities and complicate discussions with Washington about access to advanced processors,” she said. “Gulf investors may also reconsider the terms of their commitments if Nvidia's new management changes its international priorities.” For Europe and the Gulf, this could mean a more transactional and compliance-driven relationship, particularly around access to advanced chips, technology partnerships and AI infrastructure, says Mazen Hayek, a Dubai-based media consultant. The Nvidia board named Colette Kress as interim chief executive . Analysts have argued that she could be a logical choice. Ms Kress delivered “what investors needed most: reassurance that the business can continue executing without Huang”, says Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Denmark's Saxo Bank. The “emphasis on her long-standing role in executing Nvidia's strategy was important in challenging the perception that the company's competitive advantage rests entirely on one individual”, she adds. But that doesn't paint a clear picture of how she would steer the world's second-most valuable listed company. A more cautious approach from Ms Kress, or whoever takes over on a permanent basis, might mean more delays for AI build-outs. “Nvidia will survive, but a Jensen-less Nvidia would almost certainly be a different proposition: potentially more institutionalised, more cautious and subject to greater governance, regulatory and geopolitical scrutiny,” Mr Hayek tells The National . In its global investment outlook for 2027 released this week, JPMorgan notes that regulations would be a determining factor for whether capital spending for AI build-outs, which is now running in the trillions, will continue to grow. Linda Sui, founder and principal analyst of California-based Smart Analytics Global, says the Gulf and Europe may experience a slowdown in new AI infrastructure projects due to the uncertainty. But Nvidia's “strong technology leadership”, the company's Cuda computing platform and established customer relationships, “will remain intact”. “I do not expect major disruptions to existing partnerships, but Nvidia may lose some momentum in expanding its global influence,” she tells The National . China momentum? However, for China, the stakes are significantly higher. The rivalry between the US and China, long cemented in economic and political realms, has spilt over into AI. The leadership vacuum at Nvidia might be what Beijing needs to close the gap with America. China is, arguably, the biggest strategic beneficiary of any prolonged uncertainty at Nvidia. While opinions differ on whether China is leading the AI race or remains second to the US, there is little doubt that Beijing has the ambition, talent, industrial capacity and resources to challenge American dominance. Developing the best AI model aside, “it is who controls the underlying infrastructure – advanced semiconductors, computing capacity, data, talent and the ecosystems – that turn innovation into geopolitical and economic power”, Mr Hayek says. Noteworthy, however, is that Mr Huang was a huge advocate for maintaining business ties with China , in particular, favouring selling non-high-end chips to the world's second-biggest economy. Beijing could benefit from Nvidia's leadership uncertainty, particularly, if it leads to tighter US export restrictions or weaker co-operation between the US and other countries, Ms Sui says. “Without Mr Huang, Chinese companies may accelerate their shift toward domestic AI chips, particularly Huawei's solutions. However, China still faces major challenges in advanced chip manufacturing and the AI software ecosystem,” she says. “I expect China to gain some opportunities, but not a fundamental competitive advantage in the near term.” Carlos Uraga, chief executive of Spain-based energy technology firm Nantek, circles back to Mr Huang's diplomat role. He sees the Nvidia dilemma's direct effect on chips as close to zero, since the company holds virtually zero per cent of the Chinese market on US export controls, and Huawei is growing fast. China’s gain, therefore, is diplomatic. “The West loses its main advocate against fully cutting China off, Beijing can frame the ouster as US paranoia and countries caught in between could shift towards Huawei if Washington tightens conditions on them,” he tells The National . “The limit is that China’s bottleneck is manufacturing advanced chips, not who runs Nvidia and if a leak is proven [to China through Ms Huang], export controls will only get tougher.” Back in the Gulf, Ms Tsukerman believes Beijing could encourage governments in the region to expand co-operation with Chinese cloud providers, especially on projects where US export restrictions complicate access to advanced processors. The UAE and Saudi Arabia, she says, are particularly attractive markets because both have substantial investment resources and maintain extensive economic relationships with China, which can offer more favourable financing arrangements or greater local participation in infrastructure development. “China also has an opportunity to influence international technology standards,” she says. “If governments begin purchasing AI infrastructure from competing American and Chinese suppliers,

events.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
events.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing. Anthropic , the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record. The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50. The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion. Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months. 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off. In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings. Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters AI doubts trigger market turbulence The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices. Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically. The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple , Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day. In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy . Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated. Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO While OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — has delayed its public listing until next year, some analysts have been left scratching their heads at Anthropic's decision to proceed, even though the IPO is reportedly about six times oversubscribed. "Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week. Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030. "If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued." Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects. "Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize." Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion. "We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money." AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction' Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction." "We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie." In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates. Signs to watch, not reasons to flee With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

events.title: Binance Abu Dhabi mega-injunction ‘one of largest freezing orders ever made’
events.summary: Cryptocurrency platform Binance has received an order from Abu Dhabi's ADGM Courts to support the recovery of assets following the $6.3 billion breach it reported last month. The ADGM has issued a "worldwide freezing injunction against certain persons unknown, being the perpetrators of the fraud", the company said in a statement on Thursday. Binance has interim injunctions against unidentified people, it said. It has also received "interim proprietary orders against certain named defendants who have frozen certain ... stolen assets but against whom no wrongdoing is alleged". The orders granted also include provisions for service and notification of the orders, Binance said. This includes service through blockchain and notification of a constantly updating list of wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets. “This $6.5 billion mega-injunction is one of, if not the, largest publicly known freezing orders ever made," said Kendall Day from law firm Gibson Dunn, which is representing Binance for the case. "Just as significant is how the orders will work in practice: they can be served via the blockchain, and the market will be notified of a constantly updating ‘living list’ of 26,000 wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets, enabling those assets to be frozen rapidly even as they are laundered at pace," he added. The legal action is part of the company's broader effort to use every lawful mechanism available to recover stolen assets and prevent funds from reaching the attackers or those who facilitate those attacks, the company said. In some cases, issuers, exchanges or other partners request a formal court order before frozen assets will be released, transferred or returned. The court order Binance has obtained "assists in creating that pathway", it said. Binance ADGM entities are regulated by ADGM's Financial Services Regulatory Authority. Binance maintained that it has absorbed the financial impact of the stolen funds and continues to ensure users do not bear the cost. The heist, which took place on October 29, has been described as the single biggest theft of crypto on record, exceeding the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025 . The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology. Last week, Binance said fake job interviews and an internal artificial intelligence tool were used for the breach. The culprit leveraged the compromised computer of one of its engineers and used an AI tool to gain control of the wallets of two other engineers, Binance said. The company also said it has taken measures to protect its systems, including rebuilding the affected wallet system in a new environment and internal AI tools and access controls. It has also replaced affected devices and decommissioned credentials and tokens related to the affected engineers. Following the attack, approximately $2.85 billion in digital assets have been frozen or intercepted, subject to reconciliation and market price volatility, Binance said on October 31. The company on Wednesday said it is continuing to work with law enforcement and relevant authorities, coordinate with issuers, exchanges and blockchain intelligence firms, and trace, monitor and recover the assets connected to the attack. "This process will take time, and we will continue to provide updates as the recovery effort progresses," the company said.

events.title: Global investor Morrison seeks UAE partners for renewables and data centres
events.summary: Global infrastructure investor Morrison is seeking to team up with UAE investors for renewables and data centre projects, as the company expands in the Middle East with an office in Abu Dhabi's financial centre ADGM . “The UAE is such a global centre, particularly for infrastructure investing, and some of the most talented individuals in the world are there and are seeing all of the world's best deals, and so we love the idea of working alongside those investors, both within the UAE but also globally,” Paul Newfield, chief executive at Morrison, told The National in an interview. “The focus is to establish ADGM as a regional hub for our business, and run global funds and global activity from there,” he said. The New Zealand-headquartered firm, which has more than $35 billion in assets under management (AUM), joins a growing list of worldwide financial institutions setting up their base at the ADGM. New York alternative investment company New Mountain Capital, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, and the Paris-listed Eurazeo are among those to have set up in Abu Dhabi in recent months. Morrison plans to work with UAE investors and institutions to tap into new opportunities. “We want to build strong relationships with the most sophisticated investors in the region and also a number of the strategic industrial players in the region,” Mr Newfield said. “We’ve got a global pipeline, global existing assets and a lot of operating capability, but over time we hope the UAE invites us into opportunities at home, as well as investing with us internationally.” However, it will initially focus on building relationships with institutions and investors in the region, in sectors such as renewables and artificial intelligence. “We’ve been investing in renewable energy and energy transition since the 1990s. We've been investing in digital infrastructure and data centres for over 10 years now, and there's clearly a lot of alignment with focus areas for the economies in the GCC,” he said. “But I don't see us rushing into specific deals. We’re very long-term investors and we know when we go to a new region, we're better to spend a lot of time building relationships, understanding the market and really making ourselves part of the ecosystem before you just rush into deals.” On the opening of office in Abu Dhabi even as geopolitical tensions continue in the region triggered by Iran war, he said the company is “a long-term investor and has high conviction in the region”. “We are mindful of all of the difficulties that's caused people in the region, so we don't want to ignore that,” he added. “But ultimately, we're a very long-term investor and we're a multi-generational business, so our decision to come to the region is a very long-term decision.” The Middle East conflict has tipped the region into its worst geopolitical crisis in decades. The war, which began on February 28, with Israel and US bombing Iran, and Tehran lashing out at its Arab neighbours in retaliation, has disrupted business across the region. However, the UAE's economy is showing signs of recovery amid an improvement in oil production and in non-oil sectors such as trade and tourism. The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday upgraded its projection for the country's gross domestic product growth to 0.2 per cent for this year, from a previous assessment of a 3.9 per cent contraction. Morrison investment deals Morrison has made several investments in recent years to expand its global portfolio. In July, the firm announced an agreement with telecoms firm Orange to set up a data centre joint venture in France, with a €3 billion ($3.2 billion) investment. It is also investing in the renewable sector in the US, with Morrison’s unit Chrysalis Renewables buying two solar assets with a combined capacity of 357 megawatts in June. Morrison also reached an agreement with Japan’s Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank to be its preferred global infrastructure manager as part of a $2 billion long-term strategic partnership. The company expects its biggest future growth to be in Asia, especially in markets such as Japan, South Korea and Singapore, Mr Newfield said. He did not reveal how much the company is planning to invest in the next two years. “We try not to set ourselves target [in terms of dollars] that we will invest each year because we always want to be focused on generating high returns rather than just getting money invested. So we're always quite cautious,” he said. “What we've found over many years is the firm tends to grow 15 to 20 per cent per annum in AUM but we never set that as the target.” Some of the challenges facing infrastructure investors globally include rising interest rates, inflation, geopolitics and populism, especially around construction of data centres in countries such as the US, he added. “You have a lot of grass roots opposition to people building AI data centres, and I think that a lot of that opposition is for good reason," Mr Newfield said. “The data centre industry has not done as good a job as a lot of other parts of infrastructure in engaging with the community, being a good neighbour, explaining why you can bring benefits to the community. So I think that is going to be a big challenge for the data centre sector in particular.”

events.title: IMF reaches deal with Egypt to unlock $2.3bn as loan programme nears end
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has reached an agreement with Egypt on the final review of its loan programme. The deal would release about $2.3 billion before the arrangement ends next month. If the fund's executive board approves, Egypt would receive about $1.5 billion under its Extended Fund Facility, and up to $800 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, a separate climate-focused arrangement. That would bring total payouts under the two to about $9.6 billion, the IMF said. No timeline has been announced for board approval, and both arrangements expire on December 15. The agreement follows talks in Cairo from October 25 to November 5, led by IMF mission chief Amine Mati. The mission left without a deal, and talks continued online from November 7 to 15. “The authorities' successful implementation of their economic reform programme and proactive response to the implications of the Middle East war have helped preserve macroeconomic stability,” Mr Mati said. The EFF was first approved in December 2022, and was expanded to $8 billion in March 2024. That came after Egypt let its currency fall sharply, and secured a $35 billion investment deal with Abu Dhabi's ADQ to develop the Ras El Hekma peninsula on its Mediterranean coast. Growth up and risks high Egypt's real economic growth reached 5.1 per cent in the 2025 to 2026 financial year, which ended on June 30. The IMF said this was driven by a recovery in Suez Canal and petroleum-related activity, and continued strength in manufacturing, tourism and communications. Inflation, while still high, has been “more favourable than expected”, the fund said. Annual urban inflation slowed to 12.7 per cent in October from 13.9 per cent in September, according to the Central Bank of Egypt. The central bank raised interest rates by 100 basis points in October, taking its overnight deposit rate to 20 per cent. It was the first increase since March 2024. Mr Mati said the move “underscores its commitment to price stability” amid higher international oil prices. He said exchange-rate flexibility “should remain the first line of defence” against external shocks. Higher imports have widened the current account deficit, the IMF said, and the authorities have allowed the pound to adjust. The currency has lost about 13 per cent against the dollar over the past year, and hit a record low of 56.39 in October. It was trading at about 53.75 to the dollar on Tuesday, according to the Egyptian Customs Authority. The fund warned that downside risks “remain significant”. It said an escalation of regional conflicts could disrupt trade and investment, and, combined with tighter global financial conditions, could trigger capital outflows and raise borrowing costs. Debt and the state's footprint Egypt beat its end-of-September targets for the primary surplus, the budget balance before interest payments, and for tax revenue, the IMF said. The government has committed to a primary surplus of 5 per cent of GDP in the 2026 to 2027 financial year. High debt and financing needs remain “key vulnerabilities”. The fund said Cairo should step up efforts to reduce its reliance on short-term borrowing. It also called for timely fuel price adjustments to cover costs at the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation, alongside “targeted social support” to protect vulnerable households. On the state's role in the economy, Mr Mati welcomed the Banque du Caire share sale and plans to speed up the sale of state assets. He said the authorities were committed to ensuring state-owned entities, “including the Future of Egypt”, operate in line with principles of competitive neutrality, oversight and transparency. The presidency-linked Future of Egypt began in 2017 as a desert land reclamation project under the military. It now handles one of the world's largest wheat import programmes and controls major lakes and fisheries. It has moved into housing, renewable energy, infant formula and is set to take charge of licensing informal gold miners. What comes next? President Abdel Fattah El Sisi has indicated that Egypt will not seek new IMF financing, and has directed officials to prepare a national programme to follow it. Speaking at a World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo on Tuesday, he said a National Transformation Programme for 2027 to 2030 would be announced in December. IMF spokeswoman Julie Kozack said last week that what comes next is “very much for the Egyptian authorities”.

events.title: Republicans lose hope in Reconciliation 3.0
events.summary: The Senate GOP's last-ditch effort to pass a defense-heavy, $350 billion reconciliation package is dead on arrival without accompanying spending cuts, House Republicans tell Axios. Why it matters: House Republicans have just 16 days left in session before Democrats take control in January. Many don't want to spend their final days in power adding to the national debt. "My concern is we squander these very few days we have left on something that won't get out of the House," outgoing House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios of the Senate's emerging plan. Republicans have already passed two party-line reconciliation bills this Congress: The "one big, beautiful bill" in the summer of 2025, and nearly $70 billion for immigration enforcement in the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Finding spending offsets could reopen some of the most contentious fights from the GOP's first reconciliation package. Arrington told Axios that Senate Republicans worry that finding cost savings in health care spending could open the door to amendment votes that undo Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. But Arrington, who didn't run for reelection in 2026, told Axios he doesn't believe the Senate's proposal has the votes to pass the House without offsets. State of play: Arrington said he raised his concerns with Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), and argued Republicans shouldn't let the risks deter them from pursuing additional spending cuts. "Some Republican members of the Senate might go rogue and might decide to, I don't know, repeal some of the reforms that we put in the 'big, beautiful bill.' Maybe they do it out of spite for President Trump," he said. "The midterms have passed us. We lost, but we still have this window to do what we think is right," he said. Between the lines: Senate Republicans haven't committed to moving forward with another reconciliation package. Leaving a Wednesday night meeting on reconciliation, Sen. Johnson told reporters the Senate "probably" won't move forward this week, but a reconciliation bill isn't "off the table." Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters he wants to explore working with Democrats on the funding, but that reconciliation remains an "option" Wednesday night. What they're saying: "It needs to have offsets," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, told Axios. Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), another HFC member, also expressed skepticism about the proposal and its chances of passage. "It's not that I don't want to fund the Department of Defense, but it's always, 'Hey, are we just going to add this to the debt, add this to the deficit,'" he told Axios. The intrigue : Even if the two chambers can strike a deal, House GOP leaders are struggling to get their own members to show up for votes. GOP leaders were forced to pull a procedural rule vote Wednesday after 14 Republicans failed to show up, leaving leadership without the votes needed to move forward. Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios his colleagues need to return to Washington: "I mean, they're getting paid until Jan. 3." What's next: The House departs Thursday for Thanksgiving recess.

events.title: "There'll be no hostage-taking": The anti-Jeffries rebellion that failed to materialize
events.summary: The left's campaign to whip up a groundswell of opposition to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) among his members failed in stunning fashion on Wednesday. Why it matters: Fewer than a dozen members voted against Jeffries' nomination for speaker. That bodes well for Jeffries' ability to manage the House going forward, his allies say. "There'll be no hostage taking," Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) told Axios. Driving the news: Jeffries won a resounding victory Wednesday morning when House Democrats met behind closed doors to vote on their nominee for speaker of the House. Out of 264 Democratic House members and non-voting delegates, 251 voted to nominate him, 11 voted against and two did not vote. It was exactly the victory Jeffries' allies had hoped for after Tuesday's announcement that he planned to request a tallied vote rather than being nominated by acclamation. Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Chris Rabb (D-Pa.) and Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) put out a statement shortly after the vote confirming they voted against Jeffries. Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III (D-Texas) also signed on to that statement, but a spokesperson said in a follow-up statement he "narrowly missed the vote" and that his "intended vote was no." Two other members-elect, Don Leonard (D-Ohio) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.), told Axios they also voted no. Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) missed the vote because he was in his district with family following the death of his father, but would have voted for Jeffries, a spokesperson told Axios. Zoom out: Many of the progressives who ultimately voted for Jeffries did so despite a torrent of phone calls and emails from constituents and grassroots activists urging them not to support him. Numerous high-profile progressives had said before the meeting they would vote for Jeffries, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Greg Casar (D-Texas). Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who was floated as a potential challenger to Jeffries, told the Boston Globe she voted for him. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) also voted for him, a spokesperson told Axios. What they're saying: Jayapal said after the vote that Jeffries had "a very strong meeting" with the Congressional Progressive Caucus on Tuesday. "A lot of the issues that matter to us ... on Medicare for All, on immigration, I felt very, very good both about the public direction he's moved in and his commitments to us," she said. "I voted for him, as I have said I was going to do, and I feel like we've been clear about how we're going to continue to need to push." The intrigue: Three "no" votes were still unaccounted for as of Wednesday night. Several progressives who were seen as potential defectors declined to say how they voted. Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pa.), when asked how she voted, told Axios: "I'll say it to Hakeem, who I will talk to first before I talk to anybody in the press." Spokespeople for Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) did not respond to requests for comment. Between the lines: This isn't the posture of a left flank emboldened to take the fight to party leadership next year, as moderates and Jeffries allies gleefully pointed out. "This has been a manufactured crisis," said Rep. Adam Gray (D-Calif.), a leader of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition. "A handful of folks wanted to amplify their voices and perspectives, and it's always been a handful. It was a handful today." What's next: The vote now goes to the House floor, where Jeffries needs 218 votes to secure the gavel when the 120th House convenes for the first time on Jan. 3. He can lose more than 30 votes from his current total — which is unlikely — and still come out on top. "They're not going to hold ... Hakeem hostage. It's gone. Move on from that," centrist Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told Axios.

events.title: Big Republican donor pitches Trump to save $5 billion deal
events.summary: The Scoop The scion of a prominent Republican donor family met with President Donald Trump in an effort to close a $5 billion deal facing fierce regulatory scrutiny. Cintas, an $88 billion uniform and office supply behemoth, has for months been trying to secure regulatory approval to acquire smaller rival UniFirst. Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson is inclined to block the deal , Semafor earlier reported, and the FTC is preparing a “last-rites” meeting, a precursor to suing to stop the merger. Seeking to stave off a lawsuit, Cintas Executive Chairman Scott Farmer met with Trump in recent days, according to an administration official and other people familiar with the matter. Farmer urged the president to intervene and overrule Ferguson, the people said. Cintas and the family that controls it have donated to the president’s 2016 inauguration and helped him raise hundreds of thousands of dollars. A spokesperson for Cintas declined to comment. Spokespeople for the FTC and the White House did not immediately provide comment. The president has indicated that he would defer to Ferguson’s judgment, according to one person familiar with the matter. Cintas has engaged litigation counsel and expects the FTC to sue, according to other people familiar with the situation. In an effort to appease investors souring on the deal, Cintas has indicated to some that it would seek a divestiture package to stave off a lawsuit, according to some of those people, but internally, the company has little appetite to divest, one of the people said. Rohan’s view Corporate America has gotten used to a light regulatory touch around deals, aided by a thriving scene of lobbyists and fixers in Trump’s orbit. Then came the midterms, which delivered a repudiation of both AI and the perceived corporate capture of the White House and regulatory bodies. Those in and around the administration, aware of these shifting tides, have begun to take small, cautious steps to tamp down that perception. The family that controls Cintas has long supported Trump, but their currency in this administration is significantly less valuable than it was a few weeks ago. Administration officials, chastened by the public rebuke, are no longer willing to play ball.

events.title: Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies
events.summary: Alderperson Pat Dowell, center, chair of the Finance Committee, speaks to reporters following a Chicago City Council meeting on Wednesday. Dowell called for an outside review of the city’s finances. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny. The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances. It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days. The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.  Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on. Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.  But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.) The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.” The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.  “We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.” Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance. Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson presides over a special City Council meeting on Wednesday. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.  “The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.” In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.” Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies. Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined by a series of decisions from previous mayors .  Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit. The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a commentary in the Chicago Tribune over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”). Then, in a brief interview with the Chicago Sun-Times on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit. “If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.” Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation. S&P Global, one of a handful of major ratings agencies, released a statement on Wednesday about its “CreditWatch” for Chicago. It cited the intense battle over the budget and an increased likelihood that “the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget.” That means analysts see at least a 1-in-2 chance of issuing a rating cut in the next three months.  Johnson’s administration has sought to portray Gabrysch as someone who fell short in her duties and mismanaged a major transfer of funds — characterizations she has disputed. events.title: Republicans warily eye Trump’s meeting with Putin, Xi
events.summary: The News Republican senators are casting a wary eye on President Donald Trump’s high-stakes Thursday summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, where Xi greeted him warmly on the tarmac. The three leaders are expected to hold a trilateral summit on Thursday. “I’d rather see a summit with our NATO members talking about how we’re going to beat Russia,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told Semafor when asked about the meeting. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost his primary to Trump-backed challenger Ken Paxton, struck a more measured tone — but added a warning. “It’s important that the president engage with our principal adversaries around the world. I just hope he doesn’t give away too much,” the Texas Republican said. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., similarly expressed support for the diplomatic effort, though he acknowledged it is unlikely to produce results. “I’m glad he’s meeting with them. I know that’s what he does,” Scott said. “But, I don’t expect anything to happen, because these are two thugs that hate our way of life.” Nvidia scandal clouds meeting Others implored Trump to confront Xi over Chinese espionage. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., praised the president for being “the toughest negotiator we’ve ever had,” but said he hoped Trump would raise concerns about Chinese intelligence operations. He pointed to the recent controversy swirling around Nvidia, the chipmaker that saw its CEO Jensen Huang step down last week amid revelations of his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “I hope he pushes President Xi on these Chinese espionage issues. They’re obviously targeted at America,” Banks said. “This is a very serious issue. Why is President Xi allowing for Chinese spies to perform operations against our top American CEOs? Those are big questions.” Tillis also questioned whether the circumstances surrounding the Nvidia scandal made for a productive diplomatic atmosphere. “We’ve sent people on Air Force One to Beijing, only to find out that one of them may have been a Chinese asset spying against us,” Tillis said. “How does that serve as a basis for a good, you know, happy meeting? Let’s be realistic.” Room for Disagreement Still, not all Republicans were skeptical of the summit: Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., praised the “historic meeting,” describing the relationship between the US and China as “too big to fail.” The two countries represent “42% of the world economy” and are “both now nuclear superpowers,” Daines said. “I’m glad he’s doing it.”

events.title: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
events.summary: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era. Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce . And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.” By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it: “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.” “Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.” Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again: Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?) Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment. Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase , adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post. And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot. Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this. Paresh Dave contributed to this article. events.title: Mississippi senator-elect turns historic win into nationwide Nike offer
events.summary: High school students across the U.S. have a new reason to vie for the top spot in their class: a custom pair of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers, thanks to a request from Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom . Zoom in: In January, Colom will become Mississippi's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator in almost 150 years. The senator-elect pulled off a stunning upset of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the ruby-red state, which hadn't elected a Black senator since Reconstruction. His victory was fueled in part by voters in the Mississippi Delta, where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. events.summary: At least 80 high-profile technology researchers, executives and academics have called Anthropic reckless before its much-anticipated initial public offering . They have expressed concerns about AI's increasing ability to build new versions of itself, and have signed what is being called the “misanthropic statement". “ Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first,” the message reads. The signatories claim that the company, which makes its debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, has in recent years undercut its own safety pledges and “lobbied for self-serving regulation". “Anthropic is not a safe AI company and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good,” the statement concludes. Turing Award laureate Judea Pearl, Future of Life Institute co-founder Max Tegmark and Centre for Humane Technology president Tristan Harris are among those who have signed the document. I signed this statement because I believe that Anthropic is in many ways the AI company doing the most harm. In public, their leaders warn of recursive self-improvement (RSI) creating uncontrollable systems that could cause human extinction within a decade. But in private, they… https://t.co/tOCBEcgAut — Max Tegmark (@tegmark) November 18, 2026 Since Anthropic's founding in 2021,it has been regarded by AI sector insiders and elected officials as leaning more towards caution, rules and protection for AI. The company is still in the middle of a legal battle with the White House , which demanded that it eliminate some restrictions placed on its AI models used by the US Department of Defence. Nonetheless, Anthropic has alienated some of those who once regarded it as a responsible player in the technology world. “In public, their leaders warn of recursive self-improvement [RSI] creating uncontrollable systems that could cause human extinction within a decade,” renowned physicist Mr Tegmark said. “But in private, they are pedal to the metal on RSI, driving the race and boasting to prospective investors that it is their 'competitive advantage'.” He urged people thinking of investing in Anthropic's IPO to think twice before they risk “the lives of their loved ones". Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Media reports suggest that Anthropic will make its debut on Thursday $83 a share. The ticker symbol for the company will be ANT.

events.title: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
events.summary: This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China . This is known as remote access. But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place. These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life. As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling. The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”) It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips. It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations. The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead. Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week. The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China. At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter. According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.) Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips. But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them.
