events.title: Alaska Native strongholds push Peltola into Senate history
events.summary: Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead. Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence. The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory. By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count . Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes. In Bristol Bay/Aleutians , for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes. In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound , she led by roughly 2,300 votes. In North Slope/Northwest Arctic , she led by approximately 900 votes. Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead. Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled. Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures. About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census . State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation , where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate. Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages. Organizers saw gains in some rural communities, though definitive statewide turnout comparisons remain pending. Zoom in: In Kwethluk, the Yup'ik village where Peltola grew up, she outpolled Sullivan 136–9. In Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island , she led 157–5. In Tlingit communities Angoon and Kake , she led 109–22 and 140–30, respectively. The Navy apologized in 2024 for destroying Angoon in 1882 and bombarding and burning Kake in 1869 . Flashback: In 1915, Alaska's territorial lawmakers required Native citizenship applicants to abandon tribal ties and customs. In 1925, after Congress extended citizenship to Native Americans, Alaska imposed an English literacy requirement that disenfranchised many Native voters. During World War II, the U.S. removed 881 Unangax̂ people from nine villages to Southeast Alaska camps plagued by disease and poor shelter. The intrigue: In April 1969, Sen. Ted Kennedy traveled 3,600 miles over three days through Native communities, following a poverty tour his slain brother Robert had planned. TIME documented villages with 60% unemployment and homes without plumbing, comparing the trip to Robert's visits to Appalachia and the Mississippi Delta. Partisan accusations over publicity overshadowed the poverty Kennedy sought to expose. Yes, but: Alaska Native voters today don't vote as a bloc. The Alaska Federation of Natives endorsed no one in the Senate race. And district returns can't establish how individual Native voters voted — or prove a statewide turnout surge. Between the lines: In communities covered by the EPA's Alaska Native Villages data, 1,129 homes lacked drinking water, wastewater service or both in 2025, down from 6,892 in 2005, per an EPA report . Native leaders continue pressing Washington on subsistence rights, infrastructure, education and self-determination.

events.title: What to expect from Jeffries’ big day
events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning, setting the stage for a floor vote by the full chamber in January. Despite some criticism from the left, no formal opposition has emerged to Jeffries’ bid to become the first Black speaker in US history, and he’s assuaged key constituencies. Democrats will hold a recorded internal vote — it’s the same procedure used when the House flipped in 2018, but it’s also a way for the leader to force his opponents to go public. The vote will “give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned,” Jeffries said. Democrats will elect a full slate of leaders: the speaker, majority leader, whip, caucus chair, vice chair, and assistant speaker. The only contested race is for vice chair, between Reps. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., and Lauren Underwood, D-Ill.; all other current Democratic leaders are set to jump to their equivalent spots in the majority. The caucus will elect the rest of its leadership circle on Thursday, including the co-chairs of the caucus messaging arm known as the DPCC. That race is between Reps. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., and Sarah McBride, D-Del. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: White House pulls Overton's FDA nomination
events.summary: Capitol Hill is grappling with the prospect of the Food and Drug Administration operating without a Senate-confirmed leader indefinitely, after the White House pulled the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the agency Tuesday night. It’d been unclear whether the embattled White House official could get the necessary votes to be confirmed by the Senate’s health committee from lawmakers skeptical of her positions on vaccines, the abortion pill, and flavored vapes. But Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., asserted after the nomination was dropped that he believed the White House “abandoned a viable confirmation path.” “Pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” Cassidy said. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.” Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, is being weighed as a potential replacement, but there are questions swirling about whether anyone could be confirmed on a compressed timeline before Democrats take power. Chris Meekins, a Raymond James healthcare analyst who worked at HHS during Trump’s first term, predicted the FDA will not have a permanent leader anytime soon, a development that “inevitably creates uncertainty.” “Had the White House heeded warnings by many before and after her nomination, they could have avoided this unfortunate outcome,” Meekins said. — David Lim

events.title: Can AI Agents Really Shift Chip Design Left?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agent orchestration at various stages of design, verification, and validation will require new methodologies and coordination across tools. Engineering expertise remains essential, and proprietary data is still siloed. Cost and complexity could limit adoption, giving larger companies an advantage. Experts at the Table : AI agents are moving into more parts of the chip design flow, but connecting them across different tools and processes remains a challenge. Questions also remain about how to capture decades of engineering expertise, protect proprietary design data, and keep costs manageable. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: If AI agents are modifying code, and you keep updating AI models and agents, how much can you really shift left? Darbari : This is going to be a new methodology direction the industry will be taking, much like UVM, where you combine these different flows together. How do you combine all the agents together? I don’t get a sense that anybody really knows today how this combination is going to work. From what I have seen in different presentations, they’re still looking at how these things unfold. A lot of agentic AI companies lack the field experience of having seen these problems firsthand, so what they’re building is not what the consumer wants. In many cases, the big consumers are building their own stuff because they know what they want. They have the field experience. They have data from many years. So, where will the big EDA vendors go to streamline this, and how will that shape the end use? I don’t know. Laviv : One of the challenges with emulation is that when running in co-simulation mode, the simulation slows down. Maybe, instead of having UVM or other languages that slow it down, AI will get its own language and get SystemVerilog RTL synthesizable code that you can put in the machine. Then you’ll need less of the software, and you can run faster in emulation. I’m not sure yet if the methodology would change quickly, but UVM might not stay forever. Darbari : That’s what Nvidia’s head of GPU said at DVCon U.S., isn’t it? The formal is replacing simulation, or is going to replace simulation. I’m less interested in how each of these individual technologies works with each other, but I’m very interested in whether all of this adoption will lead to a coherent story. Schirrmeister : You have lifecycle, manufacturing, digital implementation, functional verification, and you have specification engineering. Making sense of it is the light bulb — making sure it works, getting it to layout, getting it into the actual physical silicon and 3D, and then observing it during the lifecycle. Each of these flows has many sub-components. Functional verification to emulation is like one of the five. There is virtual prototyping, formal, simulation, emulation, and prototyping. Everybody gets their own agent. So you have an agent doing something localized. Now you start getting an agent that orchestrates these things together as a functional thing, and then you get an agent that connects to the front end. This is an onion of agents, with more and more layers on top. EDA vendors are all saying we have Level 5 stuff, and there’s truth to that within the scope of the operating domain. Berg : This is very much about hierarchy. Darbari : But who’s going to pay for all this? Do the small companies have the budget to tokenize their banks and run all of this? Schirrmeister : Do you mean the guys building the product, or the guys building the tools? Darbari : The ones running the product. These are the consumers. They would need to pay for the tokens. I have a feeling that only the big companies will be able to afford this. They’ve been running it full-on, saying they haven’t written any code. All of this is agents. But it would get very interesting if the cost of doing all of this could be significantly reduced. Schirrmeister : What’s exciting about this is that all the smaller designs that used to be difficult because you had to go through all of this will benefit. If you want to be an Nvidia competitor, you still cannot do this out of your garage. That still has to be a big company. Berg : You’ve got levels of agents at this point, and a Level 5 orchestrating the whole thing. The industry is going to work on building each of these and then iterating and improving them. That’s the only way in which you’re going to get agents to learn and replace large groups of engineers doing the grunt work that’s necessary here. SE: But that hierarchy needs to start with whatever shifts left to include in each one of these different blocks, right? You need to at least define, in general, what you’re going to be doing. Berg : You’re going to have information being fed back to ensure that when they go to the specification of the functional, there are constraints placed here. That way, you can improve the probability of manufacturability. Schirrmeister : Can I have an agent model and predict that path? Berg : Yes, you can. Schirrmeister : But you want to check, right? You need to make sure early on what the multi-physics effects of what you’re doing will be. Berg : Yes, and without that, it will be dead on arrival in manufacturing. Schirrmeister : So now the question becomes, ‘How much can you really abstract?’ Laviv : AI is doing a great job on, say, 80% of the challenges. But then you have experience from individuals who have been in the industry for 30 years with unique skills that AI doesn’t have. We had a discussion where we talked about 250 different skills for power, emulation, format, and verification. AI doesn’t have those skills today. The industry needs to figure out how to gather those skills in order to really get to a flow where an agent can talk to an agent and has all the decades of experience that is hidden in Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel. Berg : It took 50 years, but in 2024, the Nobel Prize in chemistry was given in part to a software called AlphaFold , which predicted with uncanny certainty how proteins fold. Proteins are much more complicated than the crystalline structures that we deal with on a daily basis. But it took 50 years to get there. That said, it’s a proof of concept. Whether or not you believe it can be done in semiconductors, it’s going to happen.

events.title: IMF puts UAE back into growth territory for 2026
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has upgraded its projection for the UAE’s economy to 0.2 per cent growth this year, amid the easing of Iran war disruption and a recovery in oil production. The IMF had previously said it would shrink by 3.9 per cent. The change marks a major turnaround for the Arab world's second-largest economy. Real gross domestic product is expected to grow by 7.3 per cent next year, slightly lower than the fund's previous projection of 7.7 per cent, the IMF said after a visit to the UAE this month. “The UAE economy has demonstrated strong resilience to regional disruptions, supported by the authorities’ swift policy response,” Said Bakhache, IMF mission chief for the UAE, said. “Substantial public-sector and external buffers, a well-capitalised banking system and targeted fiscal and financial-sector measures helped cushion the impact.” Oil recovery The fund said oil production had also recovered, while some non-oil sectors were showing signs of gradual recovery, supporting the growth of the UAE economy. The Iran war, in its ninth month, has disrupted a number of sectors across the region, with tourism and aviation among the most affected as airlines cancel or reschedule flights. The Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for crude supply, was effectively shut as Iran attacked ships transiting the channel. Inflation stays high However, regional countries including the UAE and Saudi Arabia began to supply crude to global markets through pipelines as well as via ships. UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told Adipec this month that the country’s oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” during the conflict. The non-hydrocarbon sector is projected to contract by 0.5 per cent in 2026 and expand by 5.4 per cent in 2027, while hydrocarbon growth is expected at 2.3 per cent in 2026 and 13.3 per cent in 2027, the IMF said. Inflation is projected to average about 5 per cent in 2026 before easing to about 3 per cent in 2027 and converging towards 2 per cent over the medium term as supply pressures and base effects unwind. “The outlook remains subject to significant uncertainty. Escalation of regional tensions and disruptions to trade, tourism and supply chains could delay the recovery and add to inflationary pressures,” Mr Bakhache said. “Global financial volatility and cybersecurity risks also warrant continued attention. On the upside, faster normalisation of regional conflict and stronger investment and productivity gains, including from AI, could support higher growth.” The UAE's financial system remains resilient, underpinned by substantial capital and liquidity buffers, while asset quality has continued to improve. Against the backdrop of elevated inflation and strong credit growth, continued close monitoring of liquidity and funding conditions, asset quality, and sectoral exposures remain important, the IMF said. Developments in real estate and financial innovation also require sustained supervisory vigilance and regulatory co-ordination to further safeguard stability, it added. Real estate activity has moderated from earlier peaks, with conditions varying across emirates and market segments. 'Capacity to adapt' The IMF emphasised greater trade integration and diversification of trade routes to strengthen resilience against future disruptions. It also welcomed comprehensive economic partnership agreements signed by the UAE to expand trade partnerships. “The resilience of the UAE economy and its high capacity to adapt to global developments and sustain growth embody … the effectiveness of the country’s proactive policies, which have reinforced the pillars of financial and monetary stability and solidified the UAE’s standing as a leading global economic and financial centre,” Khaled Balama, Governor of the Central Bank of the UAE and Governor for the UAE at the IMF, said in a separate statement. Total banking assets surpassed Dh5.815 trillion ($1.57 trillion) by the end of the third quarter of 2026, reflecting the “strength, soundness, and high resilience of the banking system in supporting sustainable economic development”, Mr Balama added.

events.title: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska, extending Democratic wave
events.summary: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan , flipping another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, the AP projects. Why it matters: Peltola becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, extending a historic blue wave in a race marred by controversy. Her victory comes in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the extraordinary reach of the Democratic backlash against his second term. It also delivers another blow to Republicans after sweeping Democratic victories in states including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina. What they're saying: "As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola wrote on X Tuesday evening. "Thank you, Alaska. Let's get to work," she added. State of play: The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied involvement, but the reporting prompted Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, to order an investigation into whether state laws were broken. The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation and subpoenaed people connected to the alleged effort. No one involved in the race has been charged with a crime. On the campaign trail, the candidates clashed over the cost of living, the Iran war and Alaska's energy industry, with Peltola challenging Sullivan's record in Washington. Peltola campaigned on her signature "fish, family and freedom" message, emphasizing affordability, protecting Alaska's fisheries and putting the state's interests ahead of party politics. Trump traveled to Alaska in October to rally support for Sullivan, whom he praised as one of Washington's most respected senators. Sullivan embraced the president's support , betting it would energize Republican voters despite their party's political headwinds. The big picture: Alaska has long leaned Republican, but Peltola's ability to win crossover support — including votes from Republicans who ranked her above former Gov. Sarah Palin in 2022 — helped put the state in play for Democrats. Peltola made history in that 2022 special election as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She won a full term later that year before losing her House seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024. Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and Marine Corps veteran, has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2015. The two-term Republican campaigned on his record on energy development and national security. Context: Another candidate named Dan Sullivan — a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — became a factor in the race. The Trump administration sued Alaska on Oct. 22, seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan lost and votes for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, ruling that the administration lacked standing to bring the case and that its proposed remedy was unworkable. The Justice Department appealed the decision. Sen. Sullivan committed to accepting the results even if he didn't win. How it works: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system added another wrinkle. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and votes for that candidate are redistributed according to voters' next available choices. The process repeats until a candidate wins a majority. What's next: Alaska election officials will complete the remaining certification steps, with the Justice Department's appeal potentially affecting the process.

events.title: Highlights from my opening of the Ignite keynote this morning on how we’re building a frontier ecosystem to turn advances in AI into real-world impact.
events.summary: People stopped being impressed by AI demos, they just want their work to get easier. ⠀ Microsoft talking about an ecosystem instead of a single model is how that actually happens. Exciting to see GPT-6.2 and Meta's models coming to Foundry, giving businesses more flexibility to build AI solutions around their specific needs. Well said, Sir. A frontier ecosystem only matters when it works on the ground, not just on stage. In my daily work on data centres, I see this gap clearly. AI can show great promise in a demo, but real-world impact comes when power, cooling, connectivity and resilience all hold together under continuous load. When an AI system has to act, decide and execute, there is no room for downtime or latency. That is why this shift from models to real outcomes is so important. The value will not come from how advanced the model is alone, but from how reliably the infrastructure behind it can support it at scale, across different regions, languages and operating conditions like we have in India. Building that dependable layer is what will turn AI advances into actual productivity, and that is where the real work lies. Satya Nadella Opening by owning last week’s outage was the strongest moment of the keynote for me. Customers forgive a bad day. What they remember is how you talk about it the morning after, and take accountability. As AI takes on more of the real work, that kind of candor will matter as much as any model The one thing that struck while looking on this morning was how Microsoft was making itself a one stop shop to better compete. On a micro level, I created an AI Productivity and Workforce Transformation Programme™ with the intent to improve work processes and bridge the gap for those who can't pay or are not as knowledge using AI tools. As such it is also beginner friendly. I have about twelve tools in my Programme that also includes Microsoft Copilot, Excel AI, Word and Microsoft Forms. Looking at the presentation, I was amazed how Microsoft is competing with the Zapier's, Otter AI, Trello, Notion and others - kind of made me feel like I should rewrite the Programne using only Microsoft tools. However, that won't help many because my Programme tells people how to get things done using free AI tools until they can pay/ upgrade to the paid tools for greater, better results and collaboration. I was impressed by Microsoft's presentation today though👍🏼 As Microsoft moves toward more autonomous AI agents, how do you envision measuring success beyond adoption and productivity? Could business outcomes become the primary measure of AI’s value? Keeping Humans at the centre. Human in the Room. Human in the Loop. Satya, appreciate the company's transparency initiatives. Also appreciate MSFT's efforts to integrate Copilot into its products or your own ecosystem to bring efficiency. However, how about prioritizing the use of AI LLMs to make MS Office (and Windows in general) more efficient, less bloated, and, more importantly, a bit more self-aware? Even today, while active on Teams for a meeting, it will ask me to authenticate myself/my account while i attempt to open an MS office document from the meeting. The desktop version of Outlook struggles to synchronize accounts unless they are outlook/msn accounts. I hope MSFT will surprise us with these improvements soon! CHeers and good luck The most consequential takeaway from the keynote isn’t just Copilot evolving into an OS for work-it’s the architectural emphasis on enterprises owning their context layer (Microsoft IQ), tracking unit economics via Agent 365, and enforcing runtime containment through Microsoft Perception and Execution Containers. Scaling autonomous agents in production only works when context governance, FinOps telemetry, and non-human identity boundaries are built into the stack from day one. The move from single-player AI to people working alongside agents is where most mid-size organizations in Latin America will feel Ignite's impact. What we see on the ground is that the technology arrives before the groundwork: identity, permissions and data classification decide whether agents create value or create risk. I'm curious how much of this ecosystem will make that groundwork easier for companies without large security teams. events.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
events.summary: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC , CNN , Equifax , Ledger and Zoom , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content. The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge. According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s. Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “ DarkSword ” and “ Coruna ,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote . “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.” “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.” Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content. One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing. “So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.” Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “ Content Security Policies ” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons. “With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.” How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload. Image: blog.report-uri.com. The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records. Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West. “Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’

events.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
events.summary: Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week. Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen. Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking or a kind of cyber apocalypse. To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have more to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as institutions try to safeguard their systems from a potential hacking onslaught. Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented. Driving the news: National security officials and Wall Street executives have told lawmakers the outages stem from efforts to fix software bugs found by AI systems, according to The Washington Sun. Global institutions are in an all-out race to avoid a "bugmageddon," a scenario in which AI-assisted hackers are able to find and exploit vulnerabilities across the internet before they can be fixed. Apparently, that process has created its own instabilities. Catch up quick : Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday. United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages. Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones. Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks. United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment. Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking. Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed. That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say. AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible. What they're saying : Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios. "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says. "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology." "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right." By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios. However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five. The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame. "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI." Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked. That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover. The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected. When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns. events.title: Europe’s AI sector not ‘doom and gloom,’ but still lags
events.summary: Europe’s tech scene is still fighting the same battles that have held it back in the global AI race, leaders and CEOs from the continent said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said the US, and to an extent China, are “radically in a different league” when it comes to scale and capital. Employing a soccer (or football) metaphor, he said those are the only two countries that are in AI’s Premier League, while the UK sits atop the Championship, the tier below. He’s “not happy enough” with that. Marco-Alexander Breit, director-general at Germany’s digital ministry, argued that Europe still needs more “innovation-friendly regulation” if it wants to compete. He said he agreed with most of the EU’s AI Act, but argued it “actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world.” Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak echoed some of the criticism, saying that “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, the continent is starting to figure out its niche: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch pointed to a rising need for cheaper, open-source, and sovereign AI — models that companies can run on their own premises, without relying on US models or exposing their data. Germany is leaning on its industrial base, with Breit pointing to the troves of data that manufacturers like Siemens and Bosch sit on. Narayan said the UK is looking to make inroads in inference chips and AI for drug discovery. “It’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” Breit said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Recent AI cyberattacks are part of a ‘short period of transition,’ says Yann LeCun
events.summary: The world is “probably” going to enter an era of “unprecedented safety of software systems,” Advanced Machine Intelligence founder and chair Yann LeCun said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I’m worried about very few things when it comes to AI,” LeCun told Semafor’s Shelly Banjo. LeCun predicted a short period “where AI tools facilitate cyberattacks and favor the attacker over the defender,” but that will be “just a short period of transition.” Future software, he suggested, will be “hardened” by AI. LeCun, a winner of the 2018 Turing Award, has long been skeptical that scaling large language models will usher in superintelligence or artificial general intelligence. He left Meta to found his world-model company AMI in 2025; it raised more than $1 billion in seed funding, the largest ever for a European company. He told Banjo that “I think it’s called a coconut when it’s that big.” He spoke on Tuesday about world models’ practical application in physical AI, but acknowledged there is a long way to go in their development. “We’re going to need a few conceptual breakthroughs in AI to make domestic robots that are useful,” he said. “We can use humanoid robots for very narrow tasks in well-controlled environments at the moment,” but domestic robots are “not for tomorrow.” He said he and his peers working on world models are gravitating toward physical AI because it’s a “complete blind spot” of LLMs. When asked about open source models, he remarked that “it made a lot of people really sad in the US, including people who are in the current government, that the most powerful open-source systems are Chinese.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: House Dems can't stand the speaker vote drama anymore
events.summary: House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over. Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel. There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3. Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran. "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios. State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill. A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition. "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible." Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out . Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public. "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday. She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." What we're hearing: Some of Pressley's fellow Congressional Progressive Caucus members, granted anonymity to speak candidly, expressed frustration that she hasn't more forcefully tamped down the speculation. "She's only playing coy with people online," one CPC member told Axios. "The rest of us know she's not running. But that's generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end." Said another CPC member: "Many of us feel like she's stringing people along online to make them think that she's running and it's just not reality. " A third CPC member complained that it's "a bit selfish," with an incoming CPC member saying "it's not real" and chalking it up to Congress being an "attention economy." Yes, but: A second incoming CPC member said the grassroots would be "blowing us up regardless" of whether Pressley shut down the speculation or not. "It's true that the percentage of emails that mention her has grown, but the number was large to begin with," the member-elect added. What they're saying: "Everyone's trying to use whatever leverage they have and I think she's probably hoping that maybe this could be a way to make sure her voice is heard," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.). Gonzales-Torres said she is "fully behind" the policy agenda Pressley has laid out but, asked if she would vote for her for speaker, said, "Where does she stand? What is she doing? Do you know?" Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), one of Jeffries' most outspoken critics in the freshman class, said in a Breaking Points interview that Pressley "would have my support." Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Pressley "would be a great speaker but she's not running, so it's a hypothetical." What's next: House Democrats will meet behind closed-doors Wednesday to vote on their nominee for speaker and other caucus leadership roles. Jeffries plans to request a tallied vote, rather than being nominated by acclamation. He needs a simple majority among Democrats to secure the nomination but at least 218 votes on the House floor to formally win the gavel on Jan. 3. Democrats are expected to have a majority of at least 260 seats, giving Jeffries a wide margin for error. The bottom line: "The whole thing has been a stupid clusterfuck," one of the CPC members told Axios. "This is such a distraction from reality."

events.title: Basel Committee discusses risks and vulnerabilities faced by global banking system
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) Exchanges views on operational risks and vulnerabilities, with information security and third-party dependency continuing to be leading supervisory priorities. Financial risks and vulnerabilities discussed include interest rate risk, interconnections between banks and non-bank financial institutions and financing related to data centres and artificial intelligence-related exposures. Agrees to consult on targeted updates to Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision met in Basel on 18 November 2026 to discuss a range of analytical, supervisory and regulatory initiatives. “ This week’s meeting of the Basel Committee provided the opportunity for the Committee to discuss its work programme and strategic priorities for 2027–28 and related modernisation initiatives, which will be submitted to the Group of Governors and Heads of Supervision for endorsement in early 2027. The Committee also continued its discussions on ensuring that its governance and delivery mechanisms continue to be results-oriented, relevant and responsive to developments in the global banking system. ” Erik Thedéen, Chair of the Basel Committee and Governor of Sveriges Riksbank The Committee exchanged views on operational resilience, with information security and third-party dependency continuing to be leading supervisory priorities. The expanding use of digital channels, cloud services and AI can improve efficiency and innovation, but can also increase exposure to cyber attacks, operational incidents, digital fraud, technology failures and correlated dependencies. Supervisors are responding through increased focus on incident response, contingency planning and the resilience of critical services. The Committee exchanged views on current financial risks and vulnerabilities facing the global banking system. Members noted that macroeconomic and geopolitical risks remain elevated, including due to energy and commodity prices, trade developments and the prospect of interest rates remaining higher for longer. Particular attention was given to interest rate risk in the banking book, unrealised losses, refinancing risks in commercial real estate and growing links between banks and non-bank financial institutions, including private credit and financing related to data centres and artificial intelligence (AI). Banks’ capital and liquidity positions remain broadly strong, and asset quality has not deteriorated materially overall. The Committee is continuing its review of targeted elements of its prudential standard for banks’ exposures to cryptoassets. Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision The Committee has also completed its assessment of targeted updates to its 2008 Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision . It agreed to consult on targeted revisions to the Principles. The consultation will be published next month. The Committee agreed to consult on technical amendments to the counterparty credit risk and Liquidity Coverage Ratio standards. The consultation will be published later this month. The Committee also discussed its Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP), which is a key aspect of ensuring full and consistent implementation of Basel III. The RCAP includes peer-reviewed assessments by the Committee of the extent to which domestic regulations in each member jurisdiction are aligned with the globally agreed standards. To date, the Committee has completed jurisdictional assessments of all aspects of the initial Basel III standards, the liquidity standards and the large exposures framework . The Committee is now commencing the jurisdictional assessments for the outstanding Basel III standards. The first assessment will cover the implementation of the revised credit risk and operational risk standards in Hong Kong SAR and will be published in the coming months. Separately, the Committee agreed that supervisors may allow banks to apply a 0% risk weight on claims to the Inter-American Investment Corporation (IDB Invest), in line with the criteria set out in paragraph CRE20.14 of the Basel Framework. The Committee also discussed the result of a stocktake of the application of proportionality in Pillar 2 across members jurisdictions. This review included how jurisdictions apply proportionality in the internal capital adequacy assessment process, the Supervisory Review Process and Pillar 2 capital add-ons. The Basel Committee is the primary global standard setter for the prudential regulation of banks and provides a forum for cooperation on banking supervisory matters. Its mandate is to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability. The Committee reports to the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision and seeks its endorsement for major decisions. The Committee has no formal supranational authority, and its decisions have no legal force. Rather, the Committee relies on its members’ commitments to achieve its mandate. The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision is chaired by Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. The Basel Committee is chaired by Erik Thedéen, Governor of Sveriges Riksbank.

events.title: Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton's FDA nomination
events.summary: The White House is dropping Heidi Overton 's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda. "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday. Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August. She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda. Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone. The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying." What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said. The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation. What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday. The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

events.title: AI companies lost voters on narrative and execution, Alphabet's Porat says
events.summary: Alphabet’s longtime investment chief acknowledged that Google — and AI companies generally — have come up short convincing US voters that the trillions of dollars being plowed into data centers across the country are worth the cost. A bipartisan backlash against data center building galvanized voters, who almost uniformly moved to block expansion across the country in local measures earlier this month, and elected lawmakers in the midterms who largely backed a slowdown in the AI buildout. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta have been at the center of that expansion — either directly financing massive projects or signing up as the anchor tenants there. “I’ve been traveling the country quite a bit and the pain you saw reflected in polls, I’m hearing firsthand around affordability,” Ruth Porat told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Like many executives at the heart of the buildout, Porat argued that most Americans are willing and excited by the job opportunities that the AI frenzy presents. “What’s most potent is when I have these conversations across the country,” she told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, “what I hear time and time again is, ‘This is creating opportunity that I hadn’t seen in my town.’” Porat also defended the dilutive — and expensive — capital that Alphabet and other big companies have been using to finance their ambitions. “It’s expensive, but the reason we’re investing is we see the extraordinary opportunity,” Porat said. “None of us have lived at a time like this.” Google is expected to spend up to $205 billion in capex this year, and has forecast even higher numbers for 2027. The company’s free cash flow has turned negative in recent quarters, worrying investors who believe that the company — and Big Tech generally — may be getting ahead of its skis. “We want to make sure we’re showing up with a full-stack approach that delivers value and a balance sheet that’s a fortress balance sheet so that we can continue to deliver in a high-quality way,” Porat said. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Lutnick must answer questions from Congress on Nvidia, Sen. Kelly says
events.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., demanded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before Congress as questions mount over his role in delaying restrictions on AI chip exports to China. “He needs to come to Congress,” Kelly, who serves on the Senate Intelligence Committee, told Ashley Gold at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I would like to hear answers to a lot of questions that we have about why he made the decisions he made.” Kelly also alluded to Lutnick’s family business interests in the AI industry, saying they raised additional questions that the commerce secretary needs to address. The Arizona senator added that he believed Lutnick should have been removed from his position at earlier points during President Donald Trump’s second term, saying there had been “multiple times” when his “expiration date in this job had already expired.” Kelly also said he wants answers from Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week amid revelations about his reported extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. “We haven’t received answers to the questions that I have and my colleagues have,” Kelly said, noting that Huang had volunteered to testify before Congress. “What we need is answers.” Kelly also expressed skepticism about the Justice Department’s ability to conduct an impartial investigation into the matter, citing his own experience with the department. The senator said the department had been “weaponized” against individuals — including himself, noting that Trump called for his prosecution over remarks he made reminding military personnel they must refuse unlawful orders. “I might be a little biased here, but I do not have a lot of faith in the folks that are currently running the Justice Department,” Kelly said. Kelly also voiced support for three bipartisan provisions in the Senate’s version of must-pass defense policy legislation that would strengthen restrictions on exports to countries of concern, including China, saying the US must be careful about transferring its most advanced technologies. He specifically called for more “guardrails” on AI technologies and argued that companies and individuals should face penalties when those standards are violated. Liability, he said, “depends on the outcome,” but in cases involving particularly egregious conduct, “individuals could be held accountable.” — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Exclusive: Donald Trump Jr. signals investors underestimated AI pushback
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. signaled that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem in an interview at Axios' annual BFD summit in New York. The big picture: The 2026 midterms reflected deep distrust of the AI race, with voters approving dozens of moratoriums on data centers — which President Trump rallied around. Driving the news: Trump Jr. asserted that "a lot of" the pushback "is manufactured." But he added "that doesn't mean it's not real" in an interview with Axios Pro Rata author Dan Primack Tuesday. "I think some of the big founders of the biggest [AI] companies out there probably have not done themselves the best service as [a] marketing department," he said, adding that they're "probably not the best messengers when they basically say, 'AI is gonna rule the world, and you should be thrilled about it.'" Asked by Primack if investors, peers or the pair themselves underestimated the populist pushback to AI, Trump Jr. said, "I think we saw that very clearly." He likened AI to other "any great innovation," but said, "This is gonna be one of those things, but it is going to take some time for people to learn how to adapt that into their regular lives." State of play: Trump Jr. spoke with Primack alongside 1789 Capital co-founder Omeed Malik, whose venture Trump Jr. joined in 2024. The investment firm has since exploded from overseeing a few hundred million dollars to billions. Zoom in: Trump Jr. agreed that the rage toward data centers represents a broader concern over growing AI influence. That public anger is becoming key to candidates: Democrats in six early 2028 primary states expect their presidential nominee to prioritize AI regulations, according to new polling data first reported by Axios' Maria Curi. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans took note of the sagging views of the data centers needed to power the AI boom. While Trump has prioritized self-regulation for the industry, the November results raise questions about how Republicans will tackle the tech moving forward. Zoom out: Asked if there was anything Democrats and the White House could agree on after a November shellacking that could be good for business, he said "we've got to focus" on costs and inflation. But he argued that "the second they win ... it's about investigations" — which Trump Jr. could find himself targeted by. Editor's note: This story was updated with additional context throughout.

events.title: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
events.summary: Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward. Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital . What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said at the end of a conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this." She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added. In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds . Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world." CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each jumped in after-hours trading. Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly. Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said. The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make." Catch up quick: Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence. She was also an executive with a major Nvidia customer that allegedly helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country. On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones threw cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang . "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said. The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.

events.title: Trump ‘reaches out a lot’: Jeff Bezos says shutting out business leaders is a mistake
events.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says he doesn’t regret aligning himself with President Donald Trump, calling him unusually “communicative.” “He reaches out a lot,” Bezos told Liz Hoffman at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that it was “quantitatively unusual.” It’s a two-way street, with the billionaire and the president both calling one another, he added. The billionaire said he’s worked closely with every president since Bill Clinton and plans to work with “every president going forward as long as they’ll have me,” sidestepping a question on whether tying himself so closely to the administration might create difficulties in a Democrat-controlled Congress. “I’m on the side of America,” he said. “I have never tried to take advantage for Amazon or myself or any of my companies. So, you know, presidents need advice from business leaders, and shutting out business leaders is a mistake. It’s not smart.” Former President Barack Obama was very communicative too, Bezos said. “I still reach out to Obama for advice,” but none of the other presidents “were half as communicative as Trump is” when it comes to the sheer volume of conversations, Bezos said. Blue Origin taps Prometheus Bezos said he’s spending most of his time these days focusing on Prometheus, his artificial intelligence startup that aims to bring AI to the physical world. He said his space company, Blue Origin, is already utilizing Prometheus tools on two projects, though he declined to provide details of how the space business is putting the startup’s products to work. When asked whether he’d follow rival Elon Musk, who’s trying to merge all of his businesses together, Bezos said he didn’t have plans to stitch Prometheus, Blue Origin, and Amazon together. “That’s such a funny idea,” he said. “I have nothing to announce.” Prometheus was founded in 2025 and has so far raised $14.5 billion and employs around 250 people, Bezos said. Vik Bajaj, co-founder of Prometheus, said that they respect the “proprietary nature” of engineering when working with other companies, but can help to shorten their product development significantly. “We help them perform their work much, much, much faster than is possible without the tools that we’re developing,” Bajaj said. Nvidia Bezos also had some advice for the Nvidia board: Don’t hire from outside the company. He urged the board to look internally for a replacement — if it doesn’t bring former CEO Jensen Huang back on, that is. Bezos did skirt around the question of whether or not Huang should be reinstated, saying he didn’t “know enough of the details.” “There’s probably a bunch of stuff that happened inside those board meetings and so on that we don’t know,” he said. He said that an outside pick would have a “vanishingly small chance of success” given Nvidia’s complex business. An outside candidate for CEO should be treated as a “last resort.” Bond It was immediately clear to everyone in the room, including director Denis Villeneuve, that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond, Bezos said. Although they weren’t always sold on the actor due to his level of fame, the choice became clear through “old-fashioned” screen testing. “He is James Bond,” Bezos said. The search had previously been whittled down to just five names, but ultimately the choice was “undebated.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
events.summary: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

events.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
events.summary: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.
