events.title: NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout
events.summary: News Summary: New agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional substrate capacity and expanded production capabilities at existing factories. NVIDIA’s work with Amkor and SPIL expands advanced packaging capacity for current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in the third quarter, leveraging TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Foxconn is deepening its collaboration with NVIDIA, drawing on its global production network to support next-generation GPU and networking platforms. NVIDIA today announced expanded commitments with supply chain partners to support sustainable long-term growth, aligning supply and manufacturing capacity with demand for its accelerated computing and AI infrastructure platforms. Working with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics , Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and TSMC, NVIDIA is expanding manufacturing capacity across substrates, advanced packaging, wafer and contract manufacturing to scale production of its current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. “Our supply chain is a strategic advantage,” said Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations at NVIDIA. “Our work with these partners builds on our manufacturing foundation for long-term growth, expanding capacity across components, advanced packaging and system production to deliver the accelerated computing platforms our customers need.” Increasing Substrate Capacity and Production Capabilities NVIDIA is expanding its substrate supply commitments with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, adding manufacturing capacity and improving production capabilities at existing factories. Under a new agreement with NVIDIA, Kinsus plans to expand its advanced ABF package substrate manufacturing capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by more than 3.5x over current levels from its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan. Production is expected to begin in the second half of 2027, with the additional capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2028. This multiyear agreement builds on the companies’ existing supplier relationship and supports NVIDIA’s long-term supply planning for its accelerated computing platforms. “We believe AI will be one of the most important technology transitions of our lifetime,” said Scott Chen, CEO and president of Kinsus. “After more than a decade of partnership with NVIDIA, we are excited to continue building the future together.” NVIDIA and Samsung Electro-Mechanics have amended their existing substrate supply agreement to improve operational capabilities at existing factories in support of increased production of NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platforms. The amendment builds on the companies’ previously announced multiyear collaboration supporting substrate manufacturing in Sejong and Busan, South Korea, for NVIDIA’s compute and high-speed networking technologies. “By combining our world-class substrate fine-processing technology and high-reliability MLCC technology, we will perfectly fulfill our role as a total solution provider so that NVIDIA’s AI platform can be supplied to the global market on time, with the highest performance and quality,” said Duck-Hyun Chang, CEO of Samsung Electro-Mechanics.   Scaling Advanced Packaging Through Multiyear Agreements NVIDIA’s advanced packaging plans include a new capacity expansion with SPIL and previously announced agreements supporting Amkor’s manufacturing expansion in the U.S. and South Korea. NVIDIA is supporting Amkor’s expansion of advanced packaging capacity in Arizona and South Korea through multiyear agreements announced in July and October 2026, totaling nearly $3 billion. The agreements include prepayments to help Amkor scale manufacturing capacity for NVIDIA’s long-term production needs. “Our agreements with NVIDIA support investments in Arizona and South Korea that will serve multiple generations of AI platforms,” said Kevin Engel, president and CEO of Amkor. “That long-term planning allows us to advance our packaging technologies and add manufacturing capacity as NVIDIA’s production needs grow.” NVIDIA and SPIL are expanding advanced packaging operations in Taiwan under a multiyear agreement supported by multibillion-dollar funding from NVIDIA. The expansion will increase contracted advanced packaging capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by mid-2029. The project includes new production lines with turnkey support spanning bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly and testing. These capabilities support semiconductor products with demanding requirements for computing performance, bandwidth, power efficiency and system integration. “SPIL is proud to strengthen our collaboration with NVIDIA,” said C.W. Tsai, CEO and chairman of the board of SPIL. “This agreement enhances our ability to support next‑generation packaging technologies and deliver the performance and reliability required for future AI systems.” Next-Generation Technologies for Agentic AI The third quarter marked the first volume shipment of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs for agentic AI. These products take advantage of TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. “TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation,” said Dr. Kevin Zhang, senior vice president and deputy co-COO at TSMC. “This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market.” Leveraging Global Manufacturing Footprint for GPU and Networking Platforms “Foxconn continues to deepen its collaboration with NVIDIA across next-generation GPU and networking platforms,” said Young Liu, chairman of Foxconn. “By leveraging its integrated global production network spanning Asia, North America, and Europe, Foxconn is well-positioned to support the volume ramp-up of next-generation AI infrastructure.” Building on Global Supply Chain Expansion These commitments build on NVIDIA’s decades-long partnerships and recent commitments announced in October for manufacturing expansions with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL and Unimicron. events.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
events.summary: Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation. On the company's earnings call, newly appointed chairman Harvey Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," despite a movement among some employees and investors to bring him back. Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit. Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier. S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion. The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion. The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke. The stock was up as much as 5% in after-hours trading Tuesday following the company's earnings call. It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history. On the earnings call, she struck a steady tone, saying the company's momentum and innovation remain substantial. "We've got this," she said. Kress didn't mention Huang by name on the call but acknowledged the turbulent time and the "diverse" opinions — an apparent reference to the campaign to bring back Huang. What we're watching: WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the executives didn't discuss it on the call — but they said their quarterly 10Q filing with the SEC will be delayed. The earnings call came hours after Huang posted a public letter saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO. Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders. Jones said the company would not take questions on Huang's exit. He said the board would consider external and internal candidates and wants to move "as quickly as possible" but won't make a move until it finds "exactly the right person." The intrigue: Huang reportedly faced pushback from Kress as he pushed financing deals to backstop the AI ecosystem. On Tuesday's call, Kress signaled that the company would continue to provide financing where appropriate but would be "selective" and ensure that guarantees are necessary. events.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. But Democrats are also expressing skepticism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't." The intrigue : Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab. "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters. "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said. "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

events.title: Europe the natural location for Mistral IPO, CEO says
events.summary: French AI champion Mistral will likely go public in Europe, and is in preparations to do so, CEO Arthur Mensch said Tuesday. “The natural place to list is Europe,” Mensch said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “We’re not going to do this this year, but we’re definitely getting ready for it.” Mistral, which mostly makes open-weight AI models, aims to carve out a lane as a sovereign AI provider, pitching it as an alternative to closed US models or open Chinese models. That’s especially salient in Europe: Mensch said most of the investor base and half of its customer base is European. A US IPO, though, could offer the company access to more capital: Other European tech companies including Arm, Spotify, and Klarna have listed in New York, drawn by higher valuations and a bigger pool of investors. Mensch also said that regardless of who wins the French presidential elections next year, “we’re very confident as well that in Europe we will still have a lot of support. Support is needed.” He said he has met with most of the candidates to explain how AI and the industry works. “Many of them are not technical, and so they need to get a little more technical because that’s going to be five years of very technical discussions,” he said. He tied the country’s recent protests to young people’s anxiety around AI: “The youth need answers to what they’re going to do. So I think part of the unrest and part of the anguish that the youth is having is because of AI changing the way their jobs are going to be.” He criticized companies’ decisions not to hire young people because of AI. “You can invest in them, they will use AI much better, and they will create a lot of value,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed. The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections. The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition. The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers. Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause. What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement . "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them." Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so. "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed." They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned. The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23. The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands. "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said. By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter. Just 69 are operational. events.title: Sheehy, Klobuchar look to solve hemp dispute
events.summary: Sens. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., and Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., are introducing a new, far-reaching hemp regulatory bill that could smooth over a major point of contention in the government funding negotiations, according to details shared first with Semafor. The bipartisan proposal would bar sales of consumable hemp products to people under 21, ban “gas station” marijuana products derived from hemp and copycat advertising for those products, and also restrict synthetic cannabis products from China. The bill would also require hemp products be produced in the US, preserve access to CBD products, and empower the FDA to inspect hemp facilities. The timing of the compromise is crucial: A new federal definition of hemp goes into effect on Dec. 11 — the same day as the government funding deadline — and without action could upend the industry in the US. Internal Republican disagreements over the issue complicated the last funding bill. Sheehy has made solving the hemp issue within his party a major priority; he’s holding a hemp roundtable on Tuesday afternoon with veterans to discuss the issue. In a statement, the Montana Republican said the compromise with Klobuchar will put “every bad actor in the hemp space out of business and keep intoxicating [productsout of the hands of children,” while shielding farmers, cancer patients, and veterans from criminal penalties. Klobuchar, who will leave the Senate in January after being elected governor of Minnesota, touted her state’s hemp industry and warned that the “looming federal ban on hemp products is threatening farmers, brewers, small businesses, and consumers across Minnesota and the country.” A coalition of veterans groups is also asking congressional leaders to support the bill, according to a letter shared with Semafor . Republican Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., is a leading opponent of delaying the new hemp definition deadline and is gearing up for another push ahead of the December funding deadline. Sheehy and Klobuchar’s bill would go into effect on Dec. 11 if passed.

events.title: Data center industry should repurpose older infrastructure, SambaNova CEO says
events.summary: Data center builders must adapt to AI pushback, SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach “disrupts the communities less,” he told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport. AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria. Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be “much more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,” Liang said. Still, he said, it’s good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. “To distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem — it’s not a bad way to do it,” he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that “compute constraint” in the near term is a real possibility. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Europe needs ‘innovation-friendly’ regulation to catch up on AI, German official says
events.summary: Europe must enact more innovation-friendly regulation if it wants to compete in the AI race, Germany’s director-general for digital policy and economic affairs at the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization said Tuesday. There are “a lot of things we need to do to catch up in the race,” Marco-Alexander Breit said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “One of these is actually having a more innovation-friendly regulatory framework, especially in Brussels.” Germany also needs to “step up” its capacities and capabilities, he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie, adding that the country hopes to quadruple its data center capacity by 2030. Steve Jurvetson, managing director and founder of Future Ventures, who joined Breit on stage, went further, saying Europe is “trapped in a sort of regulatory doom loop” that smothers innovation. Jurvetson said “regulation is the elephant in the room” that “is stifling European innovation at every step of the way.” While Breit pushed back, saying, “it’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” he acknowledged that red tape and regulation needed to be cut, arguing that change would ensure European AI leaders “don’t need to leave Europe to work on AI and change the world and make a lot of money.” Breit said he agreed with the vast majority of the EU AI Act, for example, but continued on to say that “it actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world,” he said. “So it actually hurts our economy, even more than people maybe think in Silicon Valley that it hurts the US companies.” Speaking earlier at Silicon Valley & The World, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak also criticized the EU AI Act, saying “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, Sunak said he supports some regulation, because despite being bullish on new AI technologies, “they bring new risks with them.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
events.summary: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else. Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone. "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change. A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut. Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News . If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime. The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress. Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared. But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy. "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey. State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities. A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather. Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer. Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year. Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick: An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity. A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood. Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring. And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change . Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed. By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly. Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place. Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems. How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police. This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data. Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments. Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab. Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification. Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts. The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035. Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic. In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises. Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said. Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year. Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead. Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey). Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement. Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then. In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels. The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.
